events.enhanced_description: French troops successfully captured the Italian city of Bologna after a two-day battle, marking a significant military achievement during the Italian Wars.
events.name: Capture of Bologna by French Troops

events.enhanced_description: Queen Joanna of Castile established the Consulate of the Sea for the port of Bilbao, enhancing maritime trade and governance in the region.
events.name: Creation of the Consulate of the Sea in Bilbao

events.enhanced_description: The Ottoman Grand Vizier Hadım Ali Pasha and Prince Şehzade Ahmed suppressed the Şahkulu Rebellion in southeastern Turkey, leading to the execution of its leader, Sakhulu Baba.
events.name: Suppression of the Şahkulu Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: Pope Julius II summoned Catholic clerics to convene at the Fifth Council of the Lateran, directing them to meet on April 19 to address critical issues facing the Church.
events.name: Pope Julius II Summons Clerics to Fifth Council of the Lateran

events.enhanced_description: Afonso de Albuquerque, Governor of Portuguese India, initiated an assault on the strategic city of Malacca, capturing it by August 15. This conquest was pivotal in establishing Portuguese dominance in Southeast Asia.
events.name: Afonso de Albuquerque's Assault on Malacca

events.enhanced_description: The Mary Rose, Henry VIII's flagship, was launched from Portsmouth, becoming a symbol of English naval power during the Tudor period.
events.name: Launch of the Mary Rose

events.enhanced_description: The first half of Michelangelo's magnificent painting of Biblical scenes on the Sistine Chapel ceiling was unveiled in Rome to a select group of patrons and church officials, marking a significant moment in Renaissance art.
events.name: Unveiling of Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel Ceiling

events.enhanced_description: Afonso de Albuquerque conquered Malacca, the capital of the Sultanate of Malacca, establishing Portuguese control over the crucial Strait of Malacca, a vital trade route between China and India.
events.name: Capture of Malacca by Afonso de Albuquerque

events.enhanced_description: In Japan, Tokudaiji Saneatsu retired from his position as Chancellor of the Realm after two years of leadership, marking a transition in the political landscape of the time.
events.name: Retirement of Tokudaiji Saneatsu

events.enhanced_description: During the War of the League of Cambrai, Pope Julius II proclaimed a Holy League against French dominance in Italy, forming an alliance with the Papal States, the Swiss Confederation, Venice, and Aragon.
events.name: Pope Julius II Proclaims Holy League

events.enhanced_description: James IV of Scotland's great ship, the Michael, was launched at Newhaven, Edinburgh, becoming the largest ship afloat at that time, symbolizing Scotland's naval ambitions.
events.name: Launch of the Michael

events.enhanced_description: The vessel Frol de la Mar, carrying Afonso de Albuquerque and the treasure from the conquest of Malacca, tragically sank en route to Goa, resulting in a significant loss for the Portuguese.
events.name: Sinking of the Frol de la Mar

events.enhanced_description: Mahmud Shah Begada, the Sultan of Gujarat, died at the age of 66 after a reign of over 50 years, leaving a legacy of significant cultural and political achievements. He was succeeded by his son, Muzaffar Shah II.
events.name: Death of Mahmud Shah Begada

events.enhanced_description: In a powerful sermon at Santo Domingo, Dominican friar Antonio de Montesinos denounced the cruelty of Spanish conquistadors towards the Taino people, challenging the morality of the Encomienda system and refusing to allow slaveholders to partake in confession.

image.caption: Monument to Antonio de Montesinos on the Malecón in Santo Domingo.
image.credit: Mariordo (Mario Roberto Durán Ortiz) — Own work
image.date_qualification: A 2019 photograph of the monument, not a depiction of the 1511 sermon.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Antonio de Montesinos' Sermon

events.enhanced_description: In 1512, Portuguese explorer António de Abreu discovered Timor Island and reached the Banda Islands, Ambon Island, and Seram. This expedition was significant in expanding European knowledge and influence in the region.
events.name: Discovery of Timor Island

events.enhanced_description: In 1512, explorer Francisco Serrão reached the Moluccas, known for their valuable spices. His journey contributed to the European exploration and eventual colonization of the Spice Islands.
events.name: Francisco Serrão reaches the Moluccas

events.enhanced_description: In 1512, Francisco Serrão and shipwrecked sailors, with permission from the Ternate Sultanate, constructed Fort Tolukko, one of the earliest European-style fortresses in Southeast Asia. This fortification marked a significant step in European military architecture in the region.
events.name: Construction of Fort Tolukko

events.enhanced_description: In 1512, Spanish explorer Juan Ponce de León is credited with the discovery of the Turks and Caicos Islands. This discovery was part of his broader explorations in the Caribbean.
events.name: Juan Ponce de León discovers the Turks and Caicos Islands

events.enhanced_description: In 1512, Portuguese explorer Pedro Mascarenhas discovered Diego Garcia and reached Mauritius in the Mascarene Islands. His voyages contributed to the mapping and exploration of the Indian Ocean.

locations.name: Diego Garcia, British Indian Ocean Territory

events.name: Pedro Mascarenhas discovers Diego Garcia

events.enhanced_description: In 1512, Moldavia became a vassal of the Ottoman Empire under conditions similar to those of Wallachia, with the stipulation that the voivode would be an Eastern Orthodox Christian. This arrangement reflected the Ottoman strategy of indirect rule in Eastern Europe.
events.name: Moldavia becomes a vassal of the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 1512, the Florentine Republic began to be dismantled as the Medici Family regained power, marking a significant shift in the political landscape of Florence. This transition would lead to the establishment of Medici rule over the city.
events.name: Dismantling of the Florentine Republic

events.enhanced_description: In 1512, the term 'masque' was first used to denote a poetic drama, reflecting the evolving nature of theatrical performance during the Renaissance. This development contributed to the rich cultural tapestry of the period.
events.name: First use of the word masque

events.enhanced_description: In 1512, Nicolaus Copernicus began writing Commentariolus, an abstract of his heliocentric theory that would later be expanded into De revolutionibus orbium coelestium. This work laid the foundation for modern astronomy and challenged the geocentric view of the universe.
events.name: Nicolaus Copernicus begins Commentariolus

events.enhanced_description: On January 2, 1512, Svante Nilsson, the regent of Sweden since 1504, passed away at the age of 51. Following his death, Eric Trolle was elected as the new regent, although his tenure would be short-lived.
events.name: Svante Nilsson dies; Eric Trolle elected as new Regent

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1512, Neagoe Basarab was proclaimed the new Prince of Wallachia in Târgoviște after the capture and execution of Prince Vlad V. His reign would be marked by efforts to stabilize and strengthen the principality.
events.name: Neagoe Basarab becomes Prince of Wallachia

events.enhanced_description: On February 18, 1512, during the War of the League of Cambrai, French forces carried out the Sack of Brescia, resulting in widespread destruction and looting. This event exemplified the brutal nature of the conflict between France and the Italian states.
events.name: Sack of Brescia during the War of the League of Cambrai

events.enhanced_description: On March 12, 1512, Pope Julius II issued the papal bull Dilecte fili, declaring King Louis XII of France deposed and directing that the French throne be given to King Henry VIII of England. This bold move was part of the complex political maneuvering of the time.
events.name: Pope Julius II issues papal bull Dilecte fili

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, 1512, Donyo Dorje, the ruler of the Kingdom of Ü-Tsang in Tibet, passed away after a reign of over 30 years. He was succeeded by his brother Ngawang Namgyal, who would continue to influence Tibetan politics.
events.name: Donyo Dorje dies; Ngawang Namgyal succeeds him

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1512, the Battle of Ravenna took place during the War of the League of Cambrai, where French troops under Gaston of Foix defeated Spanish and Papal forces led by Ramón de Cardona. The battle resulted in heavy casualties and marked a significant moment in the conflict.
events.name: Battle of Ravenna during the War of the League of Cambrai

events.enhanced_description: The Fifth Council of the Lateran convened on May 3, 1512, in Vatican City, addressing various issues within the Catholic Church. This council aimed to reform church practices and respond to the challenges posed by the Protestant Reformation.
events.name: The Fifth Council of the Lateran begins

events.enhanced_description: On May 12, 1512, Thomas Howard, 2nd Duke of Norfolk, led an English expedition into France, resulting in the burning of the port city of Brest. This military action was part of the ongoing conflicts between England and France during this period.
events.name: Thomas Howard leads English expedition into France

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1512, Selim I ascended to the throne as Sultan of the Ottoman Empire, succeeding his father Bayezid II. His reign would be marked by significant military conquests and the expansion of the empire.
events.name: Selim I succeeds Bayezid II as Sultan of the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1512, Al-Ashraf Qansuh al-Ghuri, the Mamluk Sultan of Egypt, received an envoy from King George II of Kakheti, leading to the decision to reopen the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem. This event underscored the political and religious dynamics of the region.
events.name: Al-Ashraf Qansuh al-Ghuri receives envoy from King George II of Kakheti

events.enhanced_description: On June 16, 1512, Massimiliano Sforza was installed as the new Duke of Milan by the Holy League, a coalition formed to counter French influence in Italy. His appointment was part of the broader struggle for power in the Italian peninsula.
events.name: Massimiliano Sforza installed as Duke of Milan

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1512, Simão de Miranda de Azevedo was appointed as the new Portuguese Governor of Mozambique, succeeding António de Saldanha. His governance would play a crucial role in the Portuguese colonial administration in Africa.
events.name: Simão de Miranda de Azevedo becomes Governor of Mozambique

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1512, Giano II di Campofregoso was elected as the Doge of the Republic of Genoa following the withdrawal of French occupation troops. His election marked a significant political shift in the city-state's governance.
events.name: Giano II di Campofregoso elected as Doge of Genoa

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1512, King Ferdinand II of Aragon dispatched Don Fadrique de Toledo to complete the Spanish conquest of Iberian Navarre. This military campaign was part of Ferdinand's broader efforts to consolidate Spanish territories.
events.name: Ferdinand II of Aragon sends Don Fadrique de Toledo to Navarre

events.enhanced_description: On July 12, 1512, the Treaty of Blois was signed in France, establishing a guarantee of French intervention to keep the Kingdom of Navarre neutral and prevent attacks from the Holy League. This treaty was a significant diplomatic maneuver in the ongoing conflicts of the time.
events.name: Treaty of Blois signed between Navarre and France

events.enhanced_description: On July 23, 1512, Sten Sture the Younger was elected as the new Regent of Sweden, succeeding Eric Trolle. His election marked a continuation of the Sture family's influence in Swedish politics during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Sten Sture the Younger elected as Regent of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Saint-Mathieu, fought on August 10, 1512, marked a significant naval engagement during the War of the League of Cambrai, where the English navy decisively defeated the French-Breton fleet. Both sides utilized cannon fire from their ships, resulting in the destruction of their flagship vessels, the Regent and Marie-la-Cordelière, the latter suffering a catastrophic explosion.
events.name: Battle of Saint-Mathieu

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1512, General Giovanni di Lorenzo de' Medici, acting under the orders of Pope Julius II, successfully recaptured Florence from Piero Soderini, reinstating Medici influence in the city. This pivotal event not only restored Medici power but also safeguarded Rome from a potential French invasion.

image.caption: Colored woodcut view of Florence by Hartmann Schedel, from the Nuremberg Chronicle.
image.date_qualification: The depicted woodcut is from 1493, before the 1512 event; the supplied image_date is the digital reproduction's 2017-02-14 timestamp, not the date of the depicted scene.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Recapture of Florence

events.enhanced_description: On September 10, 1512, Portuguese Admiral Afonso de Albuquerque set sail from Kochi with a fleet of 14 ships and 1,700 troops to reclaim Goa from Bijapur's General Rasul Khan. This expedition was critical in establishing Portuguese dominance in India, although the planned attack was complicated by the enemy's withdrawal.
events.name: Afonso de Albuquerque departs for Goa

events.enhanced_description: On October 19, 1512, Martin Luther was awarded the title of Doctor in Biblia, marking a significant milestone in his academic and theological career. This achievement laid the groundwork for his later challenges to the Catholic Church and the subsequent Protestant Reformation.
events.name: Martin Luther becomes a doctor of theology

events.enhanced_description: On October 21, 1512, Martin Luther joined the theological faculty at the University of Wittenberg, where he would later become a pivotal figure in the Protestant Reformation. His teachings and writings during this period would challenge the established doctrines of the Catholic Church.
events.name: Martin Luther joins the University of Wittenberg

events.enhanced_description: On November 1, 1512, the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel, painted by Michelangelo Buonarroti, was exhibited to the public for the first time. This monumental work of art would later be recognized as one of the greatest achievements of Renaissance art.
events.name: Exhibition of the Sistine Chapel ceiling

events.enhanced_description: On December 27, 1512, the Spanish Crown issued the Laws of Burgos, which aimed to regulate the conduct of settlers towards the indigenous peoples of the New World. These laws were among the first attempts to address the treatment of native populations in the Americas.
events.name: Laws of Burgos

events.enhanced_description: In May 1513, Portuguese explorer Jorge Álvares and his crew became the first Europeans to reach China, landing on Lintin Island in the Pearl River estuary near Guangzhou. This marked a significant moment in the Age of Exploration, opening up new trade routes between Europe and Asia.

image.caption: Statue of Portuguese explorer Jorge Álvares.
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2022-03-01; this is a later statue image, not a depiction of the 1513 landing.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Jorge Álvares lands on Lintin Island

events.enhanced_description: As part of Juan Ponce de León's expedition, Juan Garrido became the first known African to set foot in North America on January 1, 1513. His presence in the expedition highlights the diverse backgrounds of early explorers.
events.name: Juan Garrido becomes the first African known to visit North America

events.enhanced_description: In September 1513, the dispute between Johann Reuchlin and Johannes Pfefferkorn regarding the Talmud and other Jewish texts was escalated to Pope Leo X. This conflict highlighted the tensions surrounding Jewish scholarship in Renaissance Europe.
events.name: Dispute over the Talmud referred to Pope Leo X

events.enhanced_description: In 1513, during the War of the League of Cambrai, the Battle of the Spurs saw English and allied troops under Henry VIII decisively defeat French cavalry led by Marshal La Palice. This victory solidified England's military reputation in the early 16th century.
events.name: Battle of the Spurs

events.enhanced_description: In 1513, Johann Reuchlin was summoned for an inquisition trial initiated by Jacob van Hoogstraaten regarding his defense of the Talmud. The trial's outcome was never revealed, but it underscored the tensions between Christian and Jewish scholarship during the Reformation.
events.name: Johann Reuchlin summoned for an inquisition trial

events.enhanced_description: In November 1513, Gazapati ascended to the throne of Burma following the abdication of his father, King Raza I, in the capital city of Mrauk U, marking a significant transition in the Arakanese monarchy.
events.name: Gazapati becomes King of Burma

events.enhanced_description: In December 1513, a peace proposal was made by an unnamed ruler who offered his daughter Renée to one of King Ferdinand's grandsons, alongside a renunciation of claims on Naples, although the proposal was ultimately rejected.
events.name: Peace attempt with Spain

events.enhanced_description: In 1513, the Canton of Appenzell officially became a member of the Swiss Confederacy, solidifying its political ties and contributing to the unique federal structure of Switzerland.
events.name: Canton of Appenzell joins Swiss Confederacy

events.enhanced_description: In 1513, Louis XII of France reconciled with the Papal States by disavowing the Council of Pisa and committing to adhere to the Lateran Council, thereby restoring relations with the Catholic Church.
events.name: Louis XII makes peace with the Papal States

events.enhanced_description: In 1513, Niccolò Machiavelli was arrested and tortured under suspicion of plotting against the House of Medici. Following his release, he retreated to his farm in San Casciano, where he began writing 'The Prince', a seminal work in political philosophy.

image.caption: Portrait of Niccolò Machiavelli by Cristofano di Papi dell’Altissimo, Palazzo Doria Pamphilj, Rome.
image.date_qualification: Dated between 1552 and 1568; this is later than the 1513 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

locations.city: San Casciano in Val di Pesa
locations.name: San Casciano in Val di Pesa, Tuscany, Italy

events.name: Machiavelli arrested and tortured

events.enhanced_description: In 1513, Leo Africanus, a notable traveler and scholar, visited Timbuktu, which was then the second city of the Songhai Empire, renowned for its wealth and cultural significance.
events.name: Leo Africanus visits Timbuktu

events.enhanced_description: In 1513, Paracelsus, the Swiss physician and alchemist, commenced his studies at Ferrara University, where he would later develop his revolutionary ideas on medicine and chemistry.
events.name: Paracelsus begins studies at Ferrara University

events.enhanced_description: On January 20, 1513, Spanish conquistador Vasco Núñez de Balboa wrote a letter to King Ferdinand II of Aragon advocating for the genocide of native peoples on the Caribbean islands, initiating a campaign of violence against indigenous communities. This letter exemplified the brutal colonial policies of the time.
events.name: Vasco Núñez de Balboa's letter advocating genocide

events.enhanced_description: On February 18, 1513, Pope Julius II issued a papal bull declaring Queen Catherine of Navarre and King John II of Aragon heretics for their refusal to join the War of the League of Cambrai. This declaration highlighted the tensions within the Catholic Church during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Papal Bull declaring heretics

events.enhanced_description: On February 20, 1513, King Hans of Denmark died from injuries sustained in a horse riding accident, leading to the ascension of his son Christian II as the new ruler of Denmark and Norway. This transition marked a significant moment in the history of the Danish monarchy.
events.name: Death of King Hans of Denmark

events.enhanced_description: On February 21, 1513, Pope Julius II passed away just three days after issuing his final papal bull. His death marked the end of a significant papacy characterized by military and artistic endeavors.
events.name: Death of Pope Julius II

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1513, the conclave of Roman Catholic Cardinals commenced at the Niccoline Chapel in the Apostolic Palace in Rome, with 25 of the 31 Cardinals participating. The conclave was crucial in determining the future leadership of the Catholic Church following the death of Pope Julius II.
events.name: Conclave of the Roman Catholic Cardinals

events.enhanced_description: On March 9, 1513, Cardinal Giovanni di Lorenzo de' Medici was elected as the 217th Pope of the Roman Catholic Church, taking the name Pope Leo X. His election followed a contentious conclave and marked the continuation of Medici influence in the papacy.
events.name: Election of Pope Leo X

events.enhanced_description: On March 15, 1513, during the Taino Rebellion, Spanish conquistador Diego Guilarte de Salazar launched an attack on the Taino towns of Yauco and Coxiguex in Puerto Rico. This conflict exemplified the violent confrontations between Spanish colonizers and indigenous populations.
events.name: Taino Rebellion in Puerto Rico

events.enhanced_description: On March 26, 1513, Afonso de Albuquerque, Governor of Portuguese India, led an unsuccessful attempt to capture the port city of Aden from the Mamluk Sultanate. The assault involved 20 ships and 2,500 soldiers but resulted in significant casualties for the Portuguese forces.

image.caption: Portrait of Afonso de Albuquerque, Viceroy of Portuguese India, by an unknown artist.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Palácio do Correio Velho
image.date_qualification: Retrospective portrait, dated after 1545; it is not a contemporary depiction of the 1513 attack.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Afonso de Albuquerque's attack on Aden

events.enhanced_description: On March 27, 1513, Juan Ponce de León became the first European known to sight Florida, mistaking it for another island. This discovery was significant in the context of European exploration and colonization of the Americas.
events.name: Juan Ponce de León sights Florida

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1513, Juan Ponce de León and his expedition made landfall on the east coast of Florida, marking the first known European visit to the region. This event initiated European interest in the area that would later become a significant part of the United States.
events.name: Juan Ponce de León and his expedition become the first Europeans known to visit Florida

events.enhanced_description: On May 25, 1513, Giano II di Campofregoso resigned as Doge of the Republic of Genoa amid political turmoil and the resurgence of French influence. Following his resignation, he departed to serve the Republic of Venice in its conflict against the Duchy of Milan.
events.name: Giano II di Campofregoso resigns as Doge of the Republic of Genoa

events.enhanced_description: On June 6, 1513, during the Italian Wars, Swiss mercenaries decisively defeated the French forces led by Louis II de la Trémoille at the Battle of Novara. This victory forced the French to abandon their ambitions in Milan and significantly altered the power dynamics in Italy.
events.name: Battle of Novara

events.enhanced_description: On June 20, 1513, Ottaviano Fregoso was elected as the new Doge of the Republic of Genoa, succeeding Giano II di Campofregoso. His leadership came during a tumultuous period marked by external threats and internal strife.
events.name: Ottaviano Fregoso becomes Doge of the Republic of Genoa

events.enhanced_description: On June 28, 1513, Pope Leo X sent a letter to King James IV of Scotland, threatening him with ecclesiastical censure for violating peace treaties with England. This action highlighted the intertwining of political and religious authority during the Renaissance.
events.name: Pope Leo X threatens King James IV of Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1513, Christian II was crowned King of Denmark and Norway, marking the beginning of his controversial reign. His rule would later be characterized by attempts to centralize power and conflicts with the nobility.
events.name: Christian II becomes King of Denmark and Norway

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1513, the Earl of Arran set sail from the Firth of Forth with 22 ships, aiming to join forces with France to disrupt England's communications with the continent. This military maneuver was part of the ongoing conflicts between England and Scotland.
events.name: Earl of Arran departs from the Firth of Forth

events.enhanced_description: On August 5, 1513, a force of 7,000 Scottish border troops, commanded by Lord Home, invaded England, wreaking havoc and pillaging villages in Northumberland. This incursion was part of the ongoing hostilities between Scotland and England.
events.name: Scottish border troops invade England

events.enhanced_description: On August 16, 1513, Croatian troops led by Petar Berislavić defeated an Ottoman army commanded by Sanjak-bey Junuz-aga at the Battle of Dubica. This battle was part of the prolonged conflict known as the Hundred Years' Croatian–Ottoman War.
events.name: Battle of Dubica

events.enhanced_description: On August 23, 1513, following the conclusion of a treaty after the Battle of the Spurs, the town of Thérouanne was ceded to Henry VIII of England. This transfer was part of the broader conflict known as the War of the League of Cambrai.
events.name: Thérouanne is given to Henry VIII of England

events.enhanced_description: On September 9, 1513, the Battle of Flodden took place, resulting in the defeat and death of King James IV of Scotland at the hands of an English army led by Thomas Howard, Earl of Surrey. This battle had significant consequences for Scotland, leading to a power vacuum and the ascension of James V.
events.name: Battle of Flodden

events.enhanced_description: On September 19, 1513, following the death of King James IV at the Battle of Flodden, the 35 Lords of Council of the Realm convened at Stirling Castle. They agreed to govern Scotland in the name of James IV's widow, Margaret Tudor, and their infant son, James V.

image.caption: Statue of James V of Scotland at the Royal Palace, Stirling Castle.
image.date_qualification: Photographed 10 March 2012; the image documents a later statue at the event location, not the event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Lords of Council of the Realm meet at Stirling Castle

events.enhanced_description: On September 25, 1513, Vasco Núñez de Balboa became the first European to see the Pacific Ocean from the Isthmus of Darién. This monumental discovery opened up new avenues for exploration and trade for Spain.
events.name: Vasco Núñez de Balboa first sees the Pacific Ocean

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1513, a significant rock avalanche occurred on the southern side of the Swiss Alps at Monte Crenone, devastating the village of Biasca and flooding Bellinzona. The disaster resulted in the formation of a new lake at an elevation of 390 meters.
events.name: Major rock avalanche at Monte Crenone

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1513, Spanish troops under Ramón de Cardona decisively defeated the Republic of Venice's forces led by Bartolomeo d'Alviano at the Battle of La Motta. This battle was a significant event in the ongoing conflicts of the War of the League of Cambrai.
events.name: Battle of La Motta

events.enhanced_description: On October 21, 1513, the coronation of James V, who was only 17 months old, took place in the Chapel Royal at Stirling Castle. This event marked the beginning of his reign amidst the political turmoil following the death of his father, James IV.
events.name: Coronation of James V of Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1513, Pope Leo X issued the decree Dum suavissimos, which revived the Sapienza University of Rome. This action reflected the Renaissance's emphasis on education and the papacy's role in promoting scholarly pursuits.
events.name: Pope Leo X issues decree reviving Sapienza University of Rome

events.enhanced_description: In 1514, Albrecht Dürer created his famous engraving 'Melencolia I', which is renowned for its intricate detail and complex symbolism, reflecting the artist's deep engagement with themes of melancholy and human thought.

image.caption: Detail of Albrecht Dürer’s engraving Melencolia I, showing its magic square.
image.credit: Albrecht Dürer — Unknown source Unknown source
image.date_qualification: The detail is from the engraving dated 1514, the year the article says Dürer created it; the supplied date refers to the artwork, not a photograph.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Albrecht Dürer creates Melencolia I

events.enhanced_description: In 1514, Paolo Ricci, also known as Camillo Renato, moved to Augsburg, a significant center of trade and culture in southern Germany, where he would influence the local artistic and intellectual scene.
events.name: Paolo Ricci moves to Augsburg

events.enhanced_description: By 1514, Nicolaus Copernicus had written his seminal work 'Commentariolus', which outlined his revolutionary heliocentric theory, challenging the geocentric model that had dominated astronomical thought for centuries.
events.name: Nicolaus Copernicus writes Commentariolus

events.enhanced_description: On January 10, 1514, a devastating fire broke out in the Rialto district of Venice, causing significant damage to this vital commercial and cultural hub of the city.
events.name: Great fire in the Rialto of Venice

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1514, during the War of the League of Cambrai, Giacomo Badoer, administrator of the Republic of Venice, ordered a strategic retreat from Udine, Cividale, and Cormons in the face of advancing Holy Roman Empire forces.
events.name: Retreat in the War of the League of Cambrai

events.enhanced_description: On March 12, 1514, a grand embassy sent by King Manuel I of Portugal arrived in Rome, featuring exotic gifts including Hanno, an Indian elephant, aimed at strengthening ties with Pope Leo X.
events.name: Embassy from Portugal to Pope Leo X

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1514, Louis XII of France concluded a peace agreement with Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor, further stabilizing the political landscape of Europe during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Louis XII makes peace with Maximilian I

events.enhanced_description: On April 29, 1514, after extensive negotiations in Linz, representatives from the Holy Roman Empire and the Kingdom of Denmark signed an alliance agreement, secured by the marriage of Emperor Maximilian's daughter Isabella to King Christian II.
events.name: Alliance between Holy Roman Empire and Denmark

events.enhanced_description: On May 2, 1514, the Poor Conrad peasant revolt began in Beutelsbach, targeting Ulrich, Duke of Württemberg, as peasants sought to address their grievances against the nobility.
events.name: Poor Conrad peasant revolt begins

events.enhanced_description: On May 15, 1514, the earliest printed edition of Saxo Grammaticus' 12th-century work 'Gesta Danorum' was published in Paris, edited by Christiern Pedersen and printed by Jodocus Badius, marking a significant moment in the preservation of Scandinavian history.
events.name: First printed edition of Gesta Danorum published

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1514, the 'Henry Grace à Dieu', the largest warship in the world at the time, was dedicated at Woolwich Dockyard in England, symbolizing the naval power of the Tudor monarchy.
events.name: Henry Grace à Dieu dedicated

events.enhanced_description: On July 14, 1514, Hungarian rebel leader György Dózsa was defeated in battle at Timișoara and subsequently tortured to death under orders from King Stephen VIII Báthory, marking a brutal end to his rebellion.
events.name: György Dózsa defeated and executed

events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1514, Christian II was crowned King of Norway in Oslo, marking the last coronation in Norway for over three centuries until King Karl XIV Johan's coronation in 1818.
events.name: Christian II crowned King of Norway

events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1514, King Henry VIII of England finalized an independent peace treaty with France during the War of the League of Cambrai, negotiated by his chief minister, Thomas Wolsey.
events.name: Henry VIII concludes peace treaty with France

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1514, Mary Tudor, sister of King Henry VIII, was married by proxy to King Louis XII of France, as part of the peace treaty concluded on August 7.
events.name: Mary Tudor married by proxy to Louis XII

events.enhanced_description: On August 23, 1514, the Battle of Chaldiran took place, where Ottoman Sultan Selim I decisively defeated the Persian army led by Shah Ismail I, marking a significant expansion of Ottoman territory.
events.name: Battle of Chaldiran

events.enhanced_description: On September 7, 1514, following their victory at Chaldiran, the Ottoman Army, commanded by Sultan Selim I, arrived at Tabriz, the capital of Safavid Iran, where they accepted the surrender of Shah Ismail.
events.name: Ottoman Army arrives at Tabriz

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1514, forces from the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and the Kingdom of Poland, supported by Belarusians, achieved a significant victory against the larger Russian army of the Grand Duchy of Moscow at the Battle of Orsha.
events.name: Battle of Orsha

events.enhanced_description: On September 15, 1514, Thomas Wolsey was appointed Archbishop of York, a position that would elevate his influence in the English church and politics during the reign of Henry VIII.
events.name: Thomas Wolsey appointed Archbishop of York

events.enhanced_description: On October 9, 1514, King Louis XII of France married Mary Tudor, sister of King Henry VIII of England, in Abbeville, solidifying the alliance between England and France following the peace treaty.
events.name: Mary Tudor marries Louis XII

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1514, Mary Tudor was formally crowned as the Queen consort of France in a ceremony held at the Cathedral of Saint-Denis. This event solidified her political alliance with France following her marriage to King Louis XII.
events.name: Mary Tudor is formally crowned as the Queen consort of France

events.enhanced_description: On November 23, 1514, King Henry VIII summoned the English Parliament to assemble at the Palace of Westminster, marking a significant moment in his reign as he sought to consolidate power and address various political issues.
events.name: King Henry VIII summons the English Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On November 28, 1514, Hersekzade Ahmed Pasha resigned from his position as Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire, a role of significant influence and power within the empire's administration.
events.name: Hersekzade Ahmed Pasha steps down as Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1514, Juan Rodríguez de Fonseca and Pietro Martire d'Anghiera completed the first printed map of Central America, documenting their findings from the Pinzón–Solís voyage of 1508-1509, which contributed significantly to European knowledge of the New World.
events.name: Completion of the first printed map of Central America

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1514, Dukaginzade Ahmed Pasha was appointed as the Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire by Sultan Selim I. His tenure was short-lived, as he faced political challenges that led to his execution less than three months later.
events.name: Dukaginzade Ahmed Pasha appointed Grand Vizier

events.enhanced_description: On December 29, 1514, Giovanni Carlo Tramontano, Count of Matera, was assassinated in Matera after demanding a substantial tax from the local aristocracy and populace to settle his debts, highlighting the tensions between rulers and their subjects.
events.name: Assassination of Giovanni Carlo Tramontano

events.enhanced_description: The Cortes of Burgos in 1515 was an assembly convened to address issues of reform in the Spanish Caribbean territories. This gathering reflected the complexities of governance and colonial administration during the Spanish Empire.
events.name: Cortes of Burgos 1515

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1515, King Louis XII of France died after a reign of 14 years, leading to the ascension of his son-in-law, François I, who would become a pivotal figure in the French Renaissance.
events.name: Death of King Louis XII of France

events.enhanced_description: In 1515, Pope Leo X issued a papal bull at the suggestion of Cardinal Albert of Brandenburg, providing for a special indulgence to fund the construction of St. Peter's Basilica, which would later become a focal point of the Protestant Reformation.
events.name: Papal bull issued by Pope Leo X

events.enhanced_description: In 1515, multiple acts of the English Parliament, including the Deepening River at Canterbury Act, were given royal assent by King Henry VIII, reflecting the legislative priorities of his reign.
events.name: Multiple acts of the English parliament given royal assent

events.enhanced_description: In 1515, Cardinal Wolsey ordered the construction of what would become Hampton Court Palace, a significant royal residence for King Henry VIII. This palace would later symbolize the power and opulence of the Tudor monarchy.
events.name: Construction of Hampton Court Palace

events.enhanced_description: In 1515, Bartolomé de las Casas urged Ferdinand II of Aragon to end the enslavement of Amerindians and proposed the establishment of experimental free towns. His advocacy was pivotal in the early human rights discourse in the Americas.
events.name: Bartolomé de las Casas' advocacy

events.enhanced_description: In 1515, the Portuguese became the first Europeans to land on Timor Island, establishing a foothold in the region. This marked the beginning of European colonial interests in the islands of Southeast Asia.
events.name: Portuguese landing in Timor

events.enhanced_description: In 1515, Albrecht Dürer created his famous woodcut titled 'Rhinoceros', based on descriptions and sketches of a rhinoceros that had been brought to Europe. This artwork became iconic in the representation of exotic animals in European art.
events.name: Dürer's Rhinoceros

events.enhanced_description: In 1515, the Ottomans completed their conquest of the last beyliks in Anatolia, including the Beylik of Dulkadir and the Ramadanid Emirate. This consolidation of power marked the end of independent beyliks in the region and strengthened Ottoman dominance.
events.name: Ottomans conquer last beyliks of Anatolia

events.enhanced_description: In 1515, Henry Cornelius Agrippa returned to Northern Italy, where he would continue his work in philosophy and magic, influencing the Renaissance thought. His writings would later contribute to the development of modern science and occultism.
events.name: Henry Cornelius Agrippa returns to Northern Italy

events.enhanced_description: On January 25, 1515, François I was crowned King of France at the Cathedral of Reims, alongside his wife Claude, marking the beginning of a new era in French history characterized by cultural flourishing and military ambition.
events.name: François I crowned King of France

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1515, King Henry VIII opened the English Parliament at the Palace of Westminster, where his chief advisor, Sir Thomas Nevill, was elected Speaker of the House of Commons, reflecting the political dynamics of the Tudor court.
events.name: King Henry VIII opens the English Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On February 11, 1515, George of Kratovo, a silversmith, was burned to death for refusing to convert to Islam, becoming a martyr for the Christian faith and symbolizing the religious tensions of the period.
events.name: George of Kratovo becomes a martyr

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1515, Mary Tudor, the widow of King Louis XII of France, secretly married Charles Brandon, Duke of Suffolk, in the presence of the new King of France, François I, which caused a stir in both English and French courts.
events.name: Mary Tudor marries Duke of Suffolk

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1515, Dukaginzade Ahmed Pasha was executed by order of Sultan Selim I, just days after his appointment as Grand Vizier, illustrating the volatile nature of Ottoman court politics.
events.name: Dukaginzade Ahmed Pasha executed

events.enhanced_description: On March 12, 1515, Costanzo II Sforza, Lord of Pesaro, was mortally wounded by a gunshot while traveling with Maximilian Sforza, Duke of Milan, marking a significant moment in the power struggles of the Italian city-states.
events.name: Costanzo II Sforza mortally wounded

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1515, the Portuguese Navy, led by Afonso de Albuquerque, conquered Hormuz Island after being invited by King Turan Shah, establishing a strategic foothold in the Persian Gulf.
events.name: Portuguese Navy conquers Hormuz Island

events.enhanced_description: On April 15, 1515, the Emirate of Oman, ruled by Muhammad bin Ismail, became a protectorate of Portugal, marking a significant shift in regional power dynamics in the Arabian Peninsula.
events.name: Emirate of Oman becomes a protectorate of Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1515, Nuno Fernandes de Ataíde, the Governor of Safi, led an unsuccessful attack on Marrakesh, facing fierce resistance from defenders led by Emir Nasr ibn Chentaf al-Hintati, illustrating the challenges of Portuguese expansion in North Africa.
events.name: Nuno Fernandes de Ataíde's attack on Marrakesh

events.enhanced_description: On May 13, 1515, Mary Tudor and Charles Brandon, 1st Duke of Suffolk, were officially married at the Palace of Placentia in Greenwich, solidifying their union and further intertwining the royal families of England and France.
events.name: Mary Tudor and Charles Brandon officially married

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1515, 'Ulysses', the first known rhinoceros in Europe, arrived in Lisbon after being transported from India, captivating the public and contributing to the fascination with exotic animals during the Renaissance.
events.name: Arrival of Ulysses, the first known rhinoceros in Europe

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Turnadag on June 13, 1515, marked a significant victory for the Ottoman Sultan Selim I against the Dulkadir beylik led by Bozkurt. This battle was part of Selim I's campaign to consolidate Ottoman control over Anatolia.
events.name: Battle of Turnadag

events.enhanced_description: On July 2, 1515, Hugh Oldham endowed the Manchester Grammar School, establishing it as the first free grammar school in England. This institution played a crucial role in the education of boys in the region and set a precedent for future educational establishments.

image.caption: The front of The Manchester Grammar School.
image.date_qualification: A later photograph of the school site; the image date is not supplied, and it does not depict the 1515 endowment.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Endowment of Manchester Grammar School

events.enhanced_description: The First Congress of Vienna on July 22, 1515, featured a double wedding that solidified political alliances between Hungary and the Habsburgs. Louis II married Mary of Austria, while Ferdinand wed Anna, further intertwining the royal families of Europe.
events.name: First Congress of Vienna

events.enhanced_description: On August 12, 1515, Isabella of Austria was crowned Queen consort of Denmark and Norway following her marriage to King Christian II. This union was significant in strengthening ties between the Habsburgs and the Scandinavian kingdoms.
events.name: Crowning of Isabella of Austria

events.enhanced_description: On August 25, 1515, conquistador Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar founded Havana, which would become a crucial port city in the Spanish Empire. The establishment of Havana marked the beginning of significant Spanish influence in the Caribbean.
events.name: Founding of Havana

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1515, Lopo Soares de Albergaria was appointed as the new Viceroy of Portuguese India, succeeding Afonso de Albuquerque, who resigned due to health issues. This transition marked a significant moment in the administration of Portuguese colonial affairs in Asia.
events.name: Lopo Soares de Albergaria becomes Viceroy of Portuguese India

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Marignano concluded on September 14, 1515, with a decisive victory for Francis I of France against Swiss mercenaries. This battle allowed Francis to reclaim the Duchy of Milan, solidifying French power in Northern Italy.
events.name: Battle of Marignano

events.enhanced_description: On October 2, 1515, Suja Rathore, the ruler of Marwar, passed away after a 23-year reign. His death led to a power struggle between his grandsons, Biram Singh and Rao Ganga, for control of the kingdom.
events.name: Death of Suja Rathore

events.enhanced_description: On October 4, 1515, Maximilian Sforza, the Duke of Milan, surrendered to the French forces led by Francis I. His capture marked a significant shift in power in Northern Italy, leading to French dominance in the region.
events.name: Surrender of Maximilian Sforza

events.enhanced_description: On October 8, 1515, Portuguese explorer Juan Díaz de Solís embarked on a disastrous expedition from Sanlúcar de Barrameda, Spain, towards South America. His journey ended tragically when he and most of his crew were killed by the Charrúa people shortly after landing.
events.name: Juan Díaz de Solís' expedition

events.enhanced_description: On October 11, 1515, King Francis I of France entered Milan alongside Charles III and William IX, solidifying his claim as Duke of Milan. This event marked a significant moment in the French conquest of Northern Italy.
events.name: Francis I enters Milan

events.enhanced_description: On November 8, 1515, Rao Ganga was declared the new ruler of the Kingdom of Marwar after the Rathore nobility determined he was better suited to lead than his older brother and cousin. This decision marked a pivotal moment in the region's leadership.
events.name: Rao Ganga becomes ruler of Marwar

events.enhanced_description: On November 15, 1515, Thomas Wolsey was invested as a Roman Catholic Cardinal. His elevation marked the beginning of his significant influence in English politics and the church.
events.name: Thomas Wolsey becomes Cardinal

events.enhanced_description: Beginning on December 18, 1515, King Francis I of France held four days of meetings in Bologna with Pope Leo X. These discussions resulted in agreements that reinforced the Pope's authority in France and supported Francis' claims in Italy.
events.name: Meetings between Francis I and Pope Leo X

events.enhanced_description: On December 22, 1515, the 3rd English Parliament of King Henry VIII concluded with the King granting royal assent to several important acts, including the Avowries Act and the Kynges Revenues Act. This session was crucial for the legislative framework of the Tudor period.
events.name: Closing of the 3rd English Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On December 24, 1515, Thomas Wolsey was appointed Lord Chancellor of England. This position allowed him to wield significant power in the English court and influence the policies of King Henry VIII.
events.name: Thomas Wolsey named Lord Chancellor

events.enhanced_description: In 1516, Italian explorer Rafael Perestrello commanded an expedition from Portuguese Malacca to Guangzhou, China, engaging in trade with local merchants during the Ming Dynasty, highlighting early European exploration in Asia.
events.name: Rafael Perestrello's expedition to southern China

events.enhanced_description: In 1516, Portuguese soldier Fernão Lopes became the first known permanent inhabitant of Saint Helena, an island in the South Atlantic, which would later serve as a significant stopover for ships traveling to and from Asia.

locations.country: Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha
locations.name: Saint Helena

events.name: Fernão Lopes becomes the first permanent inhabitant of Saint Helena

events.enhanced_description: In 1516, the renowned artist and inventor Leonardo da Vinci accepted an invitation from King François I to come to France, where he would spend his final years and influence the French Renaissance.
events.name: Leonardo da Vinci accepts invitation to France

events.enhanced_description: In 1516, King Henry VIII established the Master of the Posts, which served as the precursor to the Royal Mail, facilitating communication across England. This initiative marked a significant development in postal services, enhancing the efficiency of governmental and commercial correspondence.
events.name: Establishment of the Master of the Posts

events.enhanced_description: Gillingham School, founded in 1516, is recognized as the oldest school in Dorset, England. It has a long-standing tradition of education and has evolved over the centuries to serve the local community.
events.name: Founding of Gillingham School

events.enhanced_description: Fuggerei, established in 1516 in Augsburg, is the world's oldest social housing complex still in use today. Founded by the Fugger family, it was designed to provide affordable housing for the city's poor, reflecting the family's commitment to social responsibility.
events.name: Establishment of Fuggerei

events.enhanced_description: In 1516, the fall of the Nantan meteorite was possibly observed near Nantan in Guangxi, China. This event contributed to the understanding of meteorites and their origins, marking a significant moment in the study of celestial phenomena.
events.name: Observation of the Nantan meteorite

events.enhanced_description: On January 20, 1516, Juan Díaz de Solís became the first European to sail into the Río de la Plata, arriving at what is now Punta del Este, Uruguay. His expedition ended tragically when he and several crew members were killed by the local Charrúa people.
events.name: Juan Díaz de Solís arrives in Río de la Plata

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1516, Ferdinand II of Aragon died, leading to his grandson Charles of Ghent ascending as King of Spain. His mother, Joanna of Castile, also became Queen of Aragon, although she remained confined at Tordesillas.
events.name: Death of Ferdinand II of Aragon

events.enhanced_description: On February 18, 1516, Pope Leo X concluded two months of negotiations with King Francis I in Bologna, resulting in the abrogation of the French Pragmatic Sanction and the establishment of a new Concordat between the Papacy and France.
events.name: Papal negotiations conclude

events.enhanced_description: In February 1516, Sir Edward Poynings was appointed as England's ambassador to Spain for the second time, where he engaged in negotiations with King Carlos I, aiming to strengthen diplomatic ties between the two nations.
events.name: Sir Edward Poynings becomes England's ambassador to Spain a second time and meets with King Carlos I to negotiate a treaty

events.enhanced_description: On February 25, 1516, Henry VIII, in his role as Lord of Ireland, convened the first of six assemblies of the Parliament of Ireland in Dublin, marking a significant moment in the governance of Ireland under English rule.
events.name: Henry VIII opens the first assembly of the Parliament of Ireland

events.enhanced_description: In March 1516, Desiderius Erasmus published his groundbreaking Greek edition of the New Testament, titled 'Novum Instrumentum omne', in Basel, which played a crucial role in the Reformation and the study of biblical texts.
events.name: Desiderius Erasmus publishes a new Greek edition of the New Testament

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1516, at just nine years old, Louis II of Jagiellon ascended to the throne as King of Hungary, Croatia, and Bohemia following the death of his father, King Vladislaus II, marking the beginning of a tumultuous reign.
events.name: Louis II of Jagiellon becomes King of Hungary, Croatia, and Bohemia

events.enhanced_description: On March 29, 1516, the Venetian Ghetto was established in Venice, marking the first official ghetto for Jews in Europe, which would become a significant aspect of Jewish life and culture in the region.
events.name: The Venetian Ghetto is instituted

events.enhanced_description: On April 19, 1516, a treaty of alliance was concluded between England, represented by Ambassador Poynings, and Spain under King Carlos I, solidifying diplomatic relations and mutual support between the two kingdoms.
events.name: Treaty of Alliance between England and Spain

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1516, the Reinheitsgebot, or Beer Purity Law, was instituted in Ingolstadt, Bavaria, regulating the ingredients permissible for brewing beer, which has had a lasting impact on German brewing traditions.
events.name: Reinheitsgebot is instituted

events.enhanced_description: On May 6, 1516, a devastating Category IX earthquake struck Dubrovnik, causing significant destruction and loss of life in the historic city, which was a major center of trade and culture in the Adriatic region.
events.name: Earthquake strikes Dubrovnik

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1516, Le Tuong Duc, the Emperor of Dai Viet, was assassinated by his bodyguards at his palace in Thang Long (modern-day Hanoi), leading to the installation of his young nephew, Le Chieu Tong, as the new emperor.
events.name: Le Tuong Duc is murdered

events.enhanced_description: On June 14, 1516, King John III of Navarre passed away after a 32-year reign, and his widow, Queen Catherine, succeeded him, marking a significant transition in the leadership of Navarre.
events.name: Death of King John III of Navarre

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1516, King James V of Scotland officially opened the Scottish Parliament in Edinburgh, an important event in the governance of Scotland during his reign.
events.name: King James V of Scotland opens the Scottish Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On July 28, 1516, Selim I of the Ottoman Empire captured the city of Malatya, marking the beginning of his military campaign against the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt, which would lead to further invasions in the region.
events.name: Selim I captures Malatya

events.enhanced_description: On July 30, 1516, John V, Count of Nassau-Siegen, died in Siegen, Germany, leading to the division of his realm between his two sons, facilitated by a prior agreement between their respective families.
events.name: Death of John V, Count of Nassau-Siegen

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1516, the Treaty of Noyon was signed, wherein King François I of France recognized Charles I of Spain's claim to Naples, while Charles acknowledged Francis's claim to Milan, establishing a temporary peace between the two powers.
events.name: Treaty of Noyon is signed

events.enhanced_description: On August 18, 1516, King François I of France and Pope Leo X signed the Concordat of Bologna, which defined the relationship between church and state in France, granting the king significant control over ecclesiastical appointments.
events.name: Concordat of Bologna is signed

events.enhanced_description: On August 24, 1516, during the Ottoman–Mamluk War, Sultan Selim I defeated the Mamluk forces led by Sultan Al-Ashraf Qansuh al-Ghuri at the Battle of Marj Dabiq, leading to the Ottoman control over the Middle East.
events.name: Battle of Marj Dabiq

events.enhanced_description: On September 16, 1516, German theologian Andreas Karlstadt completed his series of 151 theses, which criticized corruption within the Roman Catholic Church, contributing to the growing calls for reform during the Reformation.
events.name: Andreas Karlstadt completes his series of 151 theses

events.enhanced_description: On September 17, 1516, Mamluk Admiral Selman Reis led a fleet of 19 ships from Kamaran in the Red Sea in an unsuccessful attempt to capture Yemen and Aden, reflecting the ongoing conflicts in the region.
events.name: Selman Reis leads fleet in an attempt to take Yemen and Aden

events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1516, Ottoman forces under Grand Vizier Sinan Pasha defeated the Mamluks in the Battle of Yaunis Khan near Gaza, further consolidating Ottoman power in the region during the ongoing conflict.

locations.name: Gaza City, Gaza Strip, State of Palestine

events.name: Battle of Yaunis Khan

events.enhanced_description: On November 29, 1516, the Treaty of Perpetual Peace was signed in Fribourg, Switzerland, between representatives of the Thirteen Cantons of the Old Swiss Confederacy and King François I of France, confirming French victory in the Battle of Marignano.
events.name: Treaty of Perpetual Peace is signed

events.enhanced_description: In December 1516, Thomas More's influential work 'Utopia' was completed and published in Leuven, presenting a critical view of contemporary society and proposing a visionary ideal society.
events.name: Publication of Utopia by Thomas More

events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1516, the Treaty of Brussels was signed, declaring peace between the Kingdom of France and the Holy Roman Empire, marking a significant diplomatic achievement for François I.
events.name: Treaty of Brussels is signed

events.enhanced_description: In 1517, Grand Prince Vasili III of Muscovy successfully conquered Ryazan, further consolidating his power and expanding the territory of the Grand Duchy of Moscow. This conquest was part of a broader campaign to unify Russian lands.
events.name: Conquest of Ryazan by Vasili III

events.enhanced_description: In 1517, a third outbreak of the sweating sickness struck Oxford and Cambridge, resulting in the deaths of over 400 students in Oxford within a week. This mysterious illness caused widespread panic and significantly impacted the academic communities.

image.caption: Title page of Euricius Cordus’s publication about the English sweating sickness.
image.date_qualification: Publication dated 1529 in the image description; no depicted date is supplied.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Sweating sickness outbreak in England

events.enhanced_description: On January 22, 1517, the Ottoman army, led by Sultan Selim I, decisively defeated the Mamluk forces commanded by King Tuman Bay II at the Battle of Ridaniya. This victory paved the way for the Ottoman conquest of Egypt and the subsequent decline of the Mamluk Sultanate.
events.name: Battle of Ridaniya

events.enhanced_description: On January 30, 1517, after a three-day battle, the Ottoman Empire captured Cairo, leading to the fall of the Mamluk Sultanate. This event marked a significant expansion of Ottoman power in the region and the end of the Abbasid Caliphate.
events.name: Capture of Cairo by the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: On February 3, 1517, Sultan Selim I made a triumphant entry into Cairo following the defeat of the Mamluk defenders. This event symbolized the consolidation of Ottoman control over Egypt and the broader region.
events.name: Triumphant Entry of Selim I into Cairo

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1517, chronicler Bernal Díaz del Castillo embarked on the Hernández de Córdoba expedition from Jaruco, Cuba. This expedition was significant in the early exploration of the Yucatán Peninsula and the subsequent Spanish conquest of Mexico.
events.name: Bernal Díaz del Castillo sets out with the Hernández de Córdoba expedition

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1517, at the age of 13, Henry II ascended to the throne as King of Navarre following the death of his mother, Queen Catherine, in Pamplona. His reign marked a significant period in the history of Navarre, which was limited to the northern part of the Iberian Peninsula.
events.name: Henry II becomes King of Navarre

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1517, the Cordoba Expedition made the first intentional landing by Europeans on the coast of Mexico at Cabo Catoche. The expedition faced hostility from the Mayans, resulting in a skirmish that marked the beginning of European encounters with indigenous peoples in the region.
events.name: First intentional European landing in Mexico

events.enhanced_description: The Fifth Council of the Lateran concluded on March 16, 1517, after nearly five years of discussions aimed at reforming the Roman Catholic Church. This council addressed various issues within the Church and set the stage for future reforms.
events.name: End of the Fifth Council of the Lateran

events.enhanced_description: On March 26, 1517, Tuman Bay II, the last Mamluk Sultan, was captured alive in Cairo after fleeing the city. His capture marked a pivotal moment in the Ottoman conquest of Egypt and the decline of Mamluk power.
events.name: Capture of Tuman Bay II

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1517, Lopo Soares de Albergaria initiated the siege of Jeddah, aiming to invade the city. However, the Portuguese fleet faced heavy artillery fire from Ottoman and Mamluk defenders, preventing a successful landing.
events.name: Siege of Jeddah by Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On April 13, 1517, Tuman Bay II, the former King of Egypt, was executed along with his aides, effectively ending the Abbasid dynasty. This event solidified Ottoman control over Egypt and marked a significant shift in power in the region.
events.name: Execution of Tuman Bay II

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1517, Dr. Bell delivered a provocative sermon at St Paul's Cross in London, accusing foreign immigrants of taking jobs from English workers. This sermon incited tensions and highlighted the xenophobic sentiments prevalent in society at the time.
events.name: Dr. Bell's inflammatory sermon at St Paul's Cross

events.enhanced_description: On April 22, 1517, Stephen IV ascended to the throne as the new Prince of Moldavia in Suceava following the death of his father, Bogdan III. His reign was marked by efforts to strengthen the principality amidst regional challenges.
events.name: Stephen IV becomes Prince of Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, 1517, after enduring 13 days of storms and failing to achieve their objectives, the Portuguese fleet abandoned their planned invasion of Jeddah. This retreat underscored the challenges faced by European powers in their attempts to expand into the Arabian Peninsula.
events.name: Portuguese fleet abandons invasion of Jeddah

events.enhanced_description: On April 30, 1517, anticipating civil unrest, the Lord Mayor of London announced a curfew to be enforced at 9:00 PM. This decision was met with resistance, leading to a riot that highlighted the tensions within the city.
events.name: Curfew announcement in London

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1517, xenophobic riots erupted in London, known as Evil May Day, as citizens attacked foreigners, including Flemish shoemakers and French courtiers. The Duke of Norfolk led a private army to quell the violence, reflecting the social tensions of the period.
events.name: Evil May Day riots in London

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1517, Claude of France was crowned Queen Consort at the Basilica of St Denis, with Cardinal Philippe de Luxembourg officiating. This event was significant in the context of French royal history, marking the union of two powerful dynasties.

locations.name: Basilica of Saint-Denis, Saint-Denis, Île-de-France, France

events.name: Coronation of Queen Consort Claude of France

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1517, a fleet of eight Portuguese ships, commanded by Fernão Pires de Andrade, arrived in Guangzhou, China, marking the beginning of formal trade relations between Portugal and China. This diplomatic mission was significant for establishing European presence in Asia.
events.name: Portuguese fleet arrives in China

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1517, Pier Gerlofs Donia led a rebellion of Frisians against Dutch inhabitants in Medemblik, resulting in violence and a subsequent massacre in the village of Asperen. This event highlighted the tensions between local populations and minority groups in the region.
events.name: Pier Gerlofs Donia's attack in Medemblik

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1517, Pope Leo X made a historic decision to increase the number of Roman Catholic cardinals, appointing 31 new cardinals, including Adriaan van Utrecht, who would later become Pope Adrian VI. This move was unprecedented and reflected the Pope's influence within the Church.
events.name: Pope Leo X increases the number of cardinals

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1517, Portuguese merchant Fernão Pires de Andrade met with Ming Dynasty officials at the Pearl River estuary, marking the first official diplomatic mission from a European power to China. This encounter was pivotal for establishing trade relations between Portugal and China.

locations.name: Hong Kong, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region

events.name: Fernão Pires de Andrade meets Ming officials

events.enhanced_description: Yunus Pasha, the Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire and Governor of Egypt, was dismissed and executed by decapitation on the orders of Sultan Selim I. His execution marked a significant moment in the political turmoil of the Ottoman Empire following the conquest of Egypt.
events.name: Execution of Yunus Pasha

events.enhanced_description: On October 31, 1517, Martin Luther published his 95 Theses, challenging the practices of the Catholic Church, particularly the sale of indulgences. This act is widely regarded as the catalyst for the Protestant Reformation, which transformed the religious landscape of Europe.
events.name: Publication of the 95 Theses

events.enhanced_description: Ibrahim Khan Lodi ascended to the throne as the Sultan of Delhi on November 21, 1517, following the death of his father, Sikandar Khan Lodi. His reign lasted until 1526, when the Sultanate was overthrown by the Mughal king Babur.
events.name: Ibrahim Khan Lodi becomes Sultan of Delhi

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1517, Bona Sforza of Italy married King Sigismund I of Poland by proxy in Naples, beginning her journey to Kraków to assume her role as queen consort. This marriage strengthened political ties between Poland and Italy.
events.name: Marriage of Bona Sforza and Sigismund I

events.enhanced_description: In 1518, the Rajput Mewar Kingdom, led by Rana Sanga, achieved a significant victory over Sultan Ibrahim Lodi of Delhi. This victory solidified Rana Sanga's reputation as a formidable leader and marked a pivotal moment in the power struggles of northern India.
events.name: The Rajput Mewar Kingdom achieves a major victory over Sultan Ibrahim Lodi

events.enhanced_description: In 1518, a swarm of stinging ants caused significant devastation to crops on the island of Hispaniola. This event highlighted the challenges faced by early settlers in the New World, as they struggled with both natural disasters and agricultural sustainability.
events.name: A swarm of stinging ants devastates crops on Hispaniola

events.enhanced_description: In 1518, Johann Froben published an unauthorized edition of Erasmus's work 'Colloquies'. This publication was significant in the spread of Renaissance humanism, although an authorized version would not appear until 1519.
events.name: Johann Froben publishes Erasmus's work Colloquies

events.enhanced_description: In 1518, Henricus Grammateus published 'Ayn neu Kunstlich Buech' in Vienna, which contained the earliest printed use of plus and minus signs for arithmetic. This work contributed to the development of mathematical notation in Europe.
events.name: Henricus Grammateus publishes Ayn neu Kunstlich Buech

events.enhanced_description: In 1518, the remnants of the Abbasid Caliphate, stationed in Cairo under the Mamluk Sultanate, formally handed over the title of caliph to the Ottoman Empire. This transfer marked a significant moment in Islamic history, as it consolidated Ottoman power and influence.
events.name: The Abbasid Caliphate hands over the title of caliph to the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: On January 25, 1518, Piri Mehmed Pasha was appointed as the new Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire by Sultan Selim I, following the execution of Yunus Pasha. His appointment marked a continuation of Selim's efforts to consolidate power within the empire.

image.caption: Miniature depicting Piri Mehmed Pasha in Süleymannâme, attributed to Fethullah Arifi Çelebi.
image.date_qualification: The image is dated circa 1558, about four decades after the 1518 appointment.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Appointment of Piri Mehmed Pasha

events.enhanced_description: On January 27, 1518, King Henry VIII appointed Sir John Ernley as the new Chief Justice of the Common Pleas, replacing the late Robert Rede. This appointment was part of Henry's efforts to strengthen his judicial system.
events.name: Appointment of Sir John Ernley

events.enhanced_description: On February 2, 1518, Jean Sauvage, a Frenchman, was appointed by Prince Charles as the Chief Judge of the Cortes of Valladolid. His foreign appointment was met with resentment from local court members, leading to his eventual replacement.
events.name: Jean Sauvage appointed Chief Judge

events.enhanced_description: On March 5, 1518, the Dutch priest Erasmus of Rotterdam sent Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses to England, delivering the Protestant manifesto to Sir Thomas More. This act further spread the ideas of the Reformation across Europe.
events.name: Erasmus sends Luther's Theses to England

events.enhanced_description: On March 22, 1518, King Charles I of Spain approved Ferdinand Magellan's expedition to find a westward route to the Spice Islands. This expedition would ultimately lead to the first circumnavigation of the globe.
events.name: Approval of the Magellan expedition

events.enhanced_description: On April 8, 1518, Spanish conquistador Juan de Grijalva set sail from Matanzas, Cuba, on a mission to explore and conquer Mexico. His expedition would pave the way for further Spanish conquests in the region.
events.name: Juan de Grijalva embarks for Mexico

events.enhanced_description: On April 18, 1518, King Sigismund I of Poland married Bona Sforza in Wawel Cathedral, where she was crowned Queen consort. This marriage strengthened the political alliance between Poland and Italy.
events.name: Marriage of Sigismund I and Bona Sforza

events.enhanced_description: On April 26, 1518, Martin Luther defended his theological views at the Heidelberg Disputation, where he was challenged by Johann Eck. This event was pivotal in the development of the Protestant Reformation.
events.name: Heidelberg Disputation

events.enhanced_description: On May 3, 1518, Juan de Grijalva and his crew became the first Europeans to discover Cozumel, Mexico. This marked an important moment in the European exploration of the Caribbean.
events.name: Discovery of Cozumel

events.enhanced_description: On May 9, 1518, a fleet of four Portuguese ships commanded by João da Silveira arrived in Chittagong, then part of the Sultanate of Bengal. This region was known for its wealth and trade potential.
events.name: Portuguese arrival in Chittagong

events.enhanced_description: On May 19, 1518, the renowned Renaissance artist Titian unveiled his painting 'Assumption of the Virgin' in Venice. This work is celebrated for its vibrant colors and dynamic composition, marking a significant contribution to Renaissance art.
events.name: Titian unveils Assumption of the Virgin

events.enhanced_description: At the request of Pope Leo X, Martin Luther wrote a lengthy summary of his theological views on May 30, 1518. This document was part of the ongoing dialogue and conflict between Luther and the Catholic Church.
events.name: Luther writes summary of his theology

events.enhanced_description: On June 8, 1518, the expedition led by Juan de Grijalva brought the first Europeans to the Yucatan Peninsula, arriving in what is now Tabasco, Mexico. This exploration opened the region to further Spanish incursions.
events.name: Grijalva expedition to Yucatan Peninsula

events.enhanced_description: On July 14, 1518, a bizarre case of dancing mania erupted in Strasbourg, where a woman named Frau Troffea began dancing uncontrollably for six days, leading others to join her. This phenomenon, known as the dancing plague, resulted in several deaths due to exhaustion.
events.name: Dancing plague of 1518

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1518, the Battle of Brännkyrka took place, where the forces of the Kalmar Union, led by King Christian II of Denmark, were defeated by the Swedish regent Sten Sture the Younger. This battle was a significant event in the struggle for Swedish independence.
events.name: Battle of Brännkyrka

events.enhanced_description: On August 10, 1518, the construction of the Manchester Grammar School was completed in England, marking an important development in educational infrastructure. The project cost £218 13s 5d.
events.name: Completion of Manchester Grammar School

events.enhanced_description: On August 28, 1518, King Charles I of Spain issued a charter authorizing the direct transportation of slaves from Africa to the Spanish Americas. This decision significantly impacted the transatlantic slave trade and its scale.
events.name: King Charles issues slave transportation charter

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1518, Diogo Lopes de Sequeira was appointed as the new Governor of Portuguese India, succeeding Lopo Soares de Albergaria. His governance was crucial during a period of expansion for Portuguese influence in Asia.
events.name: Diogo Lopes de Sequeira takes office

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of London, signed on October 3, 1518, was a diplomatic agreement aimed at ensuring peace among the major powers of Western Europe, including Spain, France, and England. This treaty was significant in the context of the ongoing conflicts of the period, particularly the Italian Wars.
events.name: The Treaty of London temporarily ensures peace in Western Europe

events.enhanced_description: On November 13, 1518, Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar, the Spanish Colonial Governor of Cuba, was granted the title of Captain General of Yucatán, which included southern Mexico. Although he received the exclusive rights to conquer the region, he later transferred these rights to Francisco de Montejo in 1526.

image.caption: Portrait of Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — John Carter Brown Library
image.date_qualification: The supplied image date is 1728, later than the 1518 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar is granted the office of Captain General of Yucatán

events.enhanced_description: On December 7, 1518, the Deccan sultanates, including Ahmadnagar, Berar, Bidar, Bijapur, and Golconda, formally declared their independence from the Bahmani Sultanate. This marked a significant shift in power dynamics in southern India during the early 16th century.
events.name: The Deccan sultanates declare independence from the Bahmani Sultanate

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1519, Ulrich Zwingli preached for the first time as the people's priest of the Great Minister in Zurich. His sermons would later play a crucial role in the Protestant Reformation in Switzerland.
events.name: Ulrich Zwingli preaches for the first time in Zurich

events.enhanced_description: In 1519, the first civil revolt in Anatolia occurred, led by the Alevi preacher Celâl. This uprising was significant as it highlighted the growing discontent among various social groups within the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: First civil revolt in Anatolia led by Celâl

events.enhanced_description: In 1519, Spanish forces invaded Barbados, marking the beginning of European interest in the Caribbean islands. This event set the stage for future colonization and exploitation of the region's resources.
events.name: Spanish invasion of Barbados

events.enhanced_description: In 1519, Spanish conquistador Gaspar de Espinosa sailed up the Pacific coast from Panama to Nicaragua, landing at the Gulf of Nicoya. This expedition contributed to the Spanish exploration and eventual colonization of Central America.
events.name: Gaspar de Espinosa sails from Panama to Nicaragua

events.enhanced_description: In 1519, the city of Havana was relocated from its original site in southern Cuba to the northern part of the island. This strategic move was crucial for trade and military defense against potential invasions.
events.name: Havana moves to northern Cuba

events.enhanced_description: In 1519, a large pandemic began spreading from the Greater Antilles into Central America and possibly as far as Peru, resulting in the deaths of a significant portion of the indigenous populations. This epidemic marked one of the first widely documented outbreaks in the New World.
events.name: Pandemic spreads from Greater Antilles

events.enhanced_description: In 1519, the population of Amerindians in Central Mexico reached approximately 25.3 million, showcasing the rich and diverse cultures that existed prior to European contact. This demographic data highlights the significant impact that subsequent colonization would have on these populations.
events.name: Central Mexico Amerindians' population reaches 25.3 million

events.enhanced_description: In 1519, the Mexican Indian Wars began, marking the start of violent conflicts between Spanish conquistadors and various indigenous groups in Mexico. These wars were characterized by resistance from the native populations against foreign domination.
events.name: The Mexican Indian Wars begin
