events.enhanced_description: In 1519, cacao was introduced to Europe, leading to the eventual popularity of chocolate among European elites. This event marked a significant cultural exchange between the New World and Europe, influencing culinary traditions.
events.name: Cacao comes to Europe

events.enhanced_description: In 1519, St. Olaf's Church was completed in Tallinn, Estonia. This Gothic-style church became one of the tallest buildings in the world at the time and remains a significant landmark in the city.
events.name: St. Olaf's Church completed in Tallinn

events.enhanced_description: In 1519, the first recorded fatal accident involving a gun occurred in Welton, East Riding of Yorkshire, England. This incident highlighted the dangers associated with firearms during this period.
events.name: First recorded fatal gun accident in England

events.enhanced_description: On January 12, 1519, Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor, died at the age of 59 after a reign of slightly less than 11 years. His death prompted an imperial election scheduled for June 28, which would determine his successor.
events.name: Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor, dies

events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1519, the Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés and his men departed from Cuba towards the island of Cozumel in Mexico, marking the beginning of his expedition that would lead to the conquest of the Aztec Empire.
events.name: Hernán Cortés departs from Cuba toward Cozumel

events.enhanced_description: On February 18, 1519, King Manuel I of Portugal announced that no further appointments of New Christians (converts from Judaism) would be made to government offices in Goa, although those already in office would not be dismissed. This policy reflected the complexities of religious and ethnic dynamics in the Portuguese colonies.
events.name: King Manuel I of Portugal announces policy on New Christians in Goa

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1519, Hernán Cortés and his men landed on the island of Cozumel, Mexico, marking a critical step in his expedition that would lead to the eventual conquest of the Aztec Empire.
events.name: Hernán Cortés and his men land in Mexico

events.enhanced_description: On April 21, 1519, Hernán Cortés reached San Juan de Ulúa and set foot on the beach of modern-day Veracruz the following day. This landing marked the beginning of his campaign against the Aztec Empire.
events.name: Hernán Cortés reaches San Juan de Ulúa

events.enhanced_description: On May 4, 1519, Giulio de' Medici became the Duke of the Florentine Republic following the death of his father, Lorenzo de' Medici. This transition marked a significant moment in the political landscape of Renaissance Italy.
events.name: Giulio de' Medici becomes Duke of the Florentine Republic

events.enhanced_description: The Leipzig Debate began on June 27, 1519, at the Pleissenburg lecture hall in Leipzig, where Martin Luther defended his ideas on the Protestant Reformation against Johann Eck, a leading figure of the anti-Reformation. The debate lasted until July 15 and significantly increased support for Luther's theological positions.
events.name: The Leipzig Debate begins

events.enhanced_description: On June 28, 1519, King Carlos I of Spain was elected as the new Holy Roman Emperor, taking the regnal name Charles V. His reign would significantly impact European politics and the course of the Reformation.
events.name: King Carlos I of Spain is elected Holy Roman Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1519, Martin Luther joined the ongoing debate in Leipzig regarding papal authority, challenging Johann Eck's positions. This engagement further solidified Luther's role as a key figure in the Protestant Reformation.
events.name: Martin Luther joins the debate regarding papal authority

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1519, the Prince of Ning rebellion began when Zhu Chenhao declared the Zhengde Emperor a usurper and led his army north in an attempt to capture Nanjing. This rebellion was part of the larger power struggles within the Ming dynasty.
events.name: The Prince of Ning rebellion begins

events.enhanced_description: On July 26, 1519, King Charles of Spain issued a royal order prohibiting navigator Rui Faleiro from participating in the Magellan expedition due to concerns about Faleiro's mental health. This decision reflected the challenges faced by explorers during this era.
events.name: King Charles of Spain issues royal order regarding Rui Faleiro

events.enhanced_description: On August 10, 1519, Ferdinand Magellan and his fleet of five ships departed from Seville, Spain, embarking on a historic voyage to find a westward route to the Spice Islands. This expedition would ultimately lead to the first circumnavigation of the Earth.
events.name: The Magellan expedition departs from Seville

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1519, Spanish conquistador Pedro Arias Dávila founded Panama City, which would become a crucial hub for trade and exploration in the Americas. The city played a significant role in the Spanish colonization of the region.
events.name: Panama City is founded

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1519, Ming Dynasty philosopher and general Wang Yangming defeated Zhu Chenhao, effectively ending the Prince of Ning rebellion. This victory was notable for the use of advanced artillery, marking a significant moment in military history in China.
events.name: Wang Yangming defeats Zhu Chenhao, ending the Prince of Ning rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On September 20, 1519, Ferdinand Magellan departed from Seville with a fleet of five ships and a crew of 270 men, embarking on a historic journey to sail westward to the Spice Islands. This expedition would eventually lead to the first circumnavigation of the globe.
events.name: Ferdinand Magellan departs from Spain to the Spice Islands

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1519, Hernán Cortés and his men, accompanied by 3,000 Tlaxcalans, entered Cholula, a significant city in the Aztec Empire. This event was part of Cortés's campaign to conquer the Aztecs and establish Spanish control over Mexico.
events.name: Hernán Cortés enters Cholula

events.enhanced_description: On November 8, 1519, Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés entered Tenochtitlan, the capital of the Aztec Empire, where he was received by the Aztec ruler Moctezuma II. This pivotal moment marked the beginning of the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire, leading to significant cultural and political changes in the region.
events.name: Hernán Cortés enters Tenochtitlan

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1519, the Magellan expedition, led by Portuguese explorer Ferdinand Magellan, reached the South American coast, marking a significant milestone in the first circumnavigation of the Earth. This expedition would ultimately reshape European understanding of global geography.
events.name: The Magellan expedition reaches the South American coast

events.enhanced_description: On December 11, 1519, the Sejm of the Kingdom of Poland convened in Torun and voted to approve a war against the Teutonic Knights, alongside assessing new taxes to recruit mercenary troops. This decision was pivotal in the ongoing conflicts between Poland and the Teutonic Order.
events.name: Sejm of the Kingdom of Poland votes for war against the Teutonic Knights

events.enhanced_description: In 1520, during the Feast of Toxcatl, a massacre occurred at the Great Temple of Tenochtitlan, where Spanish Deputy Governor Pedro de Alvarado ordered the killing of over 600 Aztec nobles and warriors. This brutal act intensified the conflict between the Aztecs and Spanish conquistadors.
events.name: Massacre in the Great Temple of Tenochtitlan

events.enhanced_description: In 1520, the caravel Santiago, part of Ferdinand Magellan's expedition, was wrecked in a storm while navigating the Santa Cruz River in Argentina. This incident marked the first loss of a ship in Magellan's historic voyage to circumnavigate the globe.
events.name: Wreck of the Santiago

events.enhanced_description: In 1520, the Franciscan friar Matteo Bassi was inspired to return to a life of solitude and penance, reminiscent of St. Francis. This inspiration led to the formation of the Order of Friars Minor Capuchin, which emphasized a return to the original ideals of Franciscan spirituality.
events.name: Matteo Bassi inspired to return to solitude

events.enhanced_description: In 1520, Portuguese explorer Duarte Barbosa returned to Cananor, India, after his travels. His accounts contributed to the European understanding of the Indian subcontinent and its trade networks.
events.name: Duarte Barbosa returns to Cananor

events.enhanced_description: In 1520, Aleksandra Lisowska, known as Roxelana, was given as a gift to Suleiman I upon his accession to the throne. She would later become one of the most influential figures in the Ottoman Empire, known for her political acumen and role in the harem.
events.name: Roxelana given as a gift to Suleiman I

events.enhanced_description: In 1520, King Manuel I established the Correio Público, the public mail service of Portugal, which significantly improved communication across the kingdom and facilitated trade and governance.
events.name: Creation of the Correio Público

events.enhanced_description: On January 19, 1520, King Christian II of Denmark and Norway defeated the Swedish forces at Lake Åsunden, resulting in the mortal wounding of Swedish regent Sten Sture the Younger. This battle was a crucial moment in the struggle for control over Sweden.
events.name: Battle of Bogesund

events.enhanced_description: On February 3, 1520, Sten Sture the Younger succumbed to his wounds from the Battle of Bogesund, leaving a power vacuum that enabled King Christian II of Denmark to conquer Sweden within the following months.

events.enhanced_description: On February 6, 1520, the Swabian League sold the Duchy of Württemberg to Holy Roman Emperor Charles V for 220,000 florins, along with the payment of the Duchy's substantial debt. This transaction marked a significant shift in territorial control within the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Sale of the Duchy of Württemberg

events.enhanced_description: On March 10, 1520, Thomas Howard, 3rd Duke of Norfolk, was appointed as England's new Lord Deputy of Ireland. His tenure was marked by efforts to consolidate English control over Ireland amidst ongoing resistance from local chieftains.
events.name: Thomas Howard becomes Lord Deputy of Ireland

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1520, the Magellan expedition, led by Ferdinand Magellan, paused at Puerto San Julián on the lower east coast of what is now Argentina. This stop was crucial for repairs and resupply during their historic circumnavigation of the globe.
events.name: Magellan expedition pauses at Puerto San Julián

events.enhanced_description: On April 2, 1520, Juan de Cartagena, formerly captain of the San Antonio, escaped captivity and initiated a mutiny against Ferdinand Magellan at Puerto San Julián. This rebellion highlighted the tensions within the expedition and led to violent confrontations among the crew.
events.name: Juan de Cartagena's mutiny against Magellan

events.enhanced_description: On April 3, 1520, the crew of the San Antonio surrendered to Magellan after being unable to navigate strong winds and facing cannon fire. This event marked a turning point in the expedition, leading to the execution of several mutineers.
events.name: Surrender of San Antonio and Concepción

events.enhanced_description: On April 16, 1520, citizens of Toledo, Castile, opposed to the rule of the Flemish-born Charles V, rose up during the Revolt of the Comuneros. This uprising was fueled by discontent with the royal government's attempts to unseat radical city councilors.
events.name: Revolt of the Comuneros in Toledo

events.enhanced_description: On May 7, 1520, the semi-independent Duchy of Mecklenburg was partitioned into two duchies, Mecklenburg-Schwerin and Mecklenburg-Strelitz. This division had lasting implications for the governance and territorial organization in northern Germany.
events.name: Partition of the Duchy of Mecklenburg

events.enhanced_description: On June 7, 1520, King Henry VIII of England and King Francis I of France met at the Field of the Cloth of Gold, a lavish diplomatic summit aimed at strengthening ties between the two monarchies. This event was marked by extravagant displays of wealth and power, symbolizing the rivalry and cooperation between England and France.

locations.historical_name: Field of the Cloth of Gold
locations.name: Field of the Cloth of Gold

events.name: Meeting at the Field of the Cloth of Gold

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1520, during the Revolt of the Comuneros, Segovia was blockaded by citizens opposing the rule of Charles V. This blockade was part of a larger uprising against the perceived injustices of the royal government.
events.name: Blockade of Segovia during the Revolt of the Comuneros

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1520, Pope Leo X issued the papal bull Exsurge Domine, which condemned the teachings of Martin Luther and threatened him with excommunication unless he recanted his views on indulgences and other Catholic doctrines. This event marked a significant escalation in the conflict between the Catholic Church and the Protestant Reformation.
events.name: Pope Leo X issues the bull Exsurge Domine

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1520, Moctezuma II, the Aztec ruler of Tenochtitlan, was assassinated by other Aztec leaders while attempting to address his people. His death led to the ascension of his brother Cuitlàhuac, marking a pivotal moment in the Aztec resistance against Spanish conquest.

image.caption: N. Mathew’s engraving titled “The emperor Moctezuma.”
image.credit: N. Mathew — The discovery and conquest of the new world , 1892. Irving, Washington; Robertson, W. M.; Davenport, Benjamin Rush
image.date_qualification: The engraving was published in 1892, centuries after the event; 1892 is the depicted-image publication date, not the date of the assassination.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Assassination of Moctezuma II

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1520, during La Noche Triste, the forces of Cuitlàhuac achieved a significant victory against Hernán Cortés and his men, resulting in the deaths of around 400 conquistadors and 2,000 indigenous allies. This event was a major setback for the Spanish in their conquest of the Aztec Empire.
events.name: La Noche Triste

events.enhanced_description: On July 7, 1520, the Spaniards, led by Hernán Cortés, defeated the Aztecs near Lake Texcoco in the Battle of Otumba. This battle was crucial for the Spanish forces as it allowed them to regroup and continue their campaign against the Aztec Empire.
events.name: Battle of Otumba

events.enhanced_description: In August 1520, Martin Luther published his influential work, To the Christian Nobility of the German Nation, which called for reforms within the Church and challenged the authority of the papacy. This publication played a significant role in the Protestant Reformation.
events.name: Publication of To the Christian Nobility of the German Nation

events.enhanced_description: On August 11, 1520, Ferdinand Magellan marooned two mutineers, Captain Juan de Cartagena and Father Pedro Sánchez de la Reina, on an island off the coast of Argentina. This act of discipline highlighted the challenges faced by Magellan in maintaining control over his crew during the perilous voyage.
events.name: Marooned Mutineers by Magellan

events.enhanced_description: After wintering in Patagonia, the Magellan expedition resumed its historic journey on August 21, 1520, aiming to become the first crew to circumnavigate the globe. This marked a crucial step in their quest to find a westward route to the Spice Islands.
events.name: Resumption of Magellan Expedition

events.enhanced_description: On August 24, 1520, the French warrior René of Savoy departed from Marseille on his flagship, Sainte Marie de Bonaventure, on a mission to protect the Knights Hospitaller from an impending attack by the Ottoman Turks. This expedition was part of the broader conflict between Christian and Muslim powers during this period.
events.name: Departure of René of Savoy

events.enhanced_description: On September 7, 1520, Christian II made a triumphant entry into Stockholm after the city surrendered to him. He granted amnesty to the resistance leaders, including Christina Gyllenstierna, marking a significant moment in the Danish-Swedish conflict.
events.name: Christian II's Entry into Stockholm

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1520, Suleiman I succeeded his father Selim I as Sultan of the Ottoman Empire. His reign would later be marked by significant territorial expansion and cultural achievements.

image.caption: Ottoman miniature depicting Selim II awaiting Suleiman I’s body at Belgrade.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Own work , scanned by Szilas from Török miniatúrák by Géza Fehér, Corvina 1978, Budapest
image.date_qualification: A 16th-century miniature depicting the later funeral of Suleiman I, not his accession as sultan. The original image date is recorded as “16 th century date QS:P571,+1550-00-00T00:00:00Z/7”; no supported display date is provided.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Suleiman I becomes Sultan

events.enhanced_description: On October 21, 1520, Portuguese explorer João Álvares Fagundes discovered the islands of Saint Pierre and Miquelon off the coast of Newfoundland, naming them in honor of Saint Ursula. This discovery was part of the broader European exploration of North America.
events.name: Discovery of Saint Pierre and Miquelon

events.enhanced_description: On October 21, 1520, the remaining ships of the Magellan expedition confirmed the discovery of the passage that would later be named the Strait of Magellan, a crucial maritime route connecting the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans.
events.name: Discovery of the Strait of Magellan

events.enhanced_description: On October 23, 1520, Charles V was crowned King of Germany in Aachen, a significant event that solidified his power in the Holy Roman Empire and marked the beginning of his reign over vast territories in Europe.
events.name: Charles V crowned King of Germany

events.enhanced_description: On November 1, 1520, Christian II was crowned King of Sweden in Nikolai Church, followed by a three-day feast in Stockholm. This event marked a significant consolidation of power for Christian II in Sweden.
events.name: Christian II crowned King of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On November 7, 1520, following the coronation feast of Christian II, several leaders of the Swedish resistance against Danish rule were imprisoned and tried for high treason. This marked a significant moment in the consolidation of Danish control over Sweden.
events.name: Imprisonment of Swedish Resistance Leaders

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1520, the Stockholm Bloodbath concluded with the execution of 82 Swedish noblemen and clergymen, sentenced to death for their resistance against Danish rule. This brutal event solidified Christian II's power but also sowed the seeds of future rebellion.
events.name: Stockholm Bloodbath

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1520, Cuauhtémoc ascended to the throne as the last Aztec Emperor following the death of Cuitlàhuac from smallpox. His reign would be marked by the final resistance against Spanish conquest.
events.name: Cuauhtémoc becomes last Aztec Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On November 28, 1520, after navigating through the strait at the southern end of South America, Ferdinand Magellan and his crew became the first Europeans to reach the Pacific Ocean, which he named 'El Mar Pacifico' due to its calm waters. This milestone was crucial in the quest for a westward route to the Spice Islands.

locations.name: Pacific Ocean, near the Korean Peninsula

events.name: Magellan reaches the Pacific Ocean

events.enhanced_description: On December 10, 1520, Martin Luther publicly burned a copy of the Papal bull Exsurge Domine and The Book of Canon Law as a defiant act against the Catholic Church's authority. This act symbolized his break from the Church and was a pivotal moment in the Protestant Reformation.
events.name: Martin Luther burns papal bull

events.enhanced_description: In early 1521, Martin Luther was summoned to appear before the Diet of Worms, where he was to defend his writings against charges of heresy. This event was a critical moment in the Protestant Reformation, as it set the stage for Luther's eventual excommunication.
events.name: Martin Luther is summoned to appear before the Diet of Worms

events.enhanced_description: In April or May 1521, the Battle of Tunmen took place in Tuen Mun, where the Ming Dynasty navy defeated the Portuguese navy. This battle is considered one of the first Sino-European conflicts in history, highlighting the tensions between European powers and Asian empires.
events.name: Battle of Tunmen

events.enhanced_description: In 1521, Jacopo Berengario da Carpi published 'Commentaria cum amplissimus additionibus super anatomiam Mundini' in Bologna, which included significant observations on human anatomy, notably the vermiform appendix. This work contributed to the advancement of medical knowledge during the Renaissance.
events.name: Publication by Jacopo Berengario da Carpi

events.enhanced_description: The Grand Duchy of Ryazan was annexed by the Grand Duchy of Moscow in 1521, consolidating Moscow's power and influence in the region. This annexation was part of the broader expansion of the Russian state during the early 16th century.
events.name: Annexation of the Grand Duchy of Ryazan

events.enhanced_description: On January 3, 1521, Pope Leo X issued the papal bull 'Decet Romanum Pontificem', formally excommunicating Martin Luther from the Catholic Church. This act was a significant escalation in the conflict between the Catholic Church and the Protestant Reformation, marking a pivotal moment in religious history.
events.name: Pope Leo X excommunicates Martin Luther, in the papal bull Decet Romanum Pontificem

events.enhanced_description: On January 22, 1521, Charles V convened the Diet of Worms, a significant assembly of the Holy Roman Empire, to address the growing Protestant Reformation and the challenge posed by Martin Luther's teachings. This event was crucial in shaping the future of Christianity in Europe.
events.name: Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, opens the Diet of Worms

events.enhanced_description: On January 27, 1521, Suleiman the Magnificent successfully quelled a revolt led by Janbirdi al-Ghazali in Damascus, reinforcing Ottoman control over the region. This event underscored Suleiman's military prowess and his commitment to maintaining the stability of the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Suleiman the Magnificent suppresses a revolt by the ruler of Damascus, Janbirdi al-Ghazali

events.enhanced_description: On February 2, 1521, the Nydala Abbey Bloodbath occurred when Danish forces attacked Nydala Abbey, resulting in the murder of the abbot and many monks. This brutal event highlighted the religious and political tensions in Scandinavia during the Reformation.
events.name: The Nydala Abbey Bloodbath

events.enhanced_description: On March 6, 1521, Ferdinand Magellan made the first European contact with Guam, landing in Tumon. This encounter marked the beginning of European exploration in the Pacific and had lasting implications for the indigenous populations.
events.name: Ferdinand Magellan makes the first European contact with Guam

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1521, Ferdinand Magellan arrived in the Philippines, specifically in Eastern Samar. This event was a significant milestone in the Age of Exploration, leading to further Spanish colonization in the region.
events.name: Ferdinand Magellan reaches the Philippines

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1521, the First Mass in the Philippines was celebrated, marking the introduction of Christianity to the archipelago. This event was pivotal in the spread of Catholicism in the region and shaped the cultural landscape of the Philippines.
events.name: The First Mass in the Philippines is held

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1521, Ferdinand Magellan arrived at Cebu, an important event in the history of Spanish exploration in the Philippines. This visit led to significant interactions with local leaders and the eventual establishment of Spanish influence in the region.
events.name: Ferdinand Magellan arrives at Cebu

events.enhanced_description: On April 16, 1521, Martin Luther was examined before Emperor Charles V at the Diet of Worms, where he famously refused to recant his writings, declaring, 'Here I stand.' This moment solidified his role as a leader of the Protestant Reformation and challenged the authority of the Catholic Church.
events.name: Martin Luther is examined before Emperor Charles V and the Diet of Worms

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1521, the Battle of Villalar took place, where Castilian royalists defeated the Comuneros, a group of rebels seeking to reform the Spanish monarchy. The leaders of the rebellion, including Juan López de Padilla, were executed the following day, marking a decisive victory for the royalists.
events.name: Battle of Villalar

events.enhanced_description: On April 26, 1521, after the Diet of Worms, Martin Luther left the city and went into hiding at Wartburg Castle for about a year. This period was crucial for Luther, as he translated the New Testament into German, making the scriptures more accessible to the public.
events.name: Martin Luther leaves Worms and disappears for around a year

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1521, the Battle of Mactan occurred, where Ferdinand Magellan was killed while confronting Lapulapu, the chief of Mactan Island. This battle was significant as it marked the resistance of indigenous leaders against European colonization.
events.name: Battle of Mactan

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1521, Edward Stafford, the 3rd Duke of Buckingham, was executed for treason at Tower Hill in London. His execution was part of the political machinations of King Henry VIII, reflecting the turbulent nature of Tudor politics.
events.name: Edward Stafford, 3rd Duke of Buckingham, is executed for treason

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1521, the Battle of Pampeluna occurred, where an alliance of French and Navarrese forces defeated the Spanish. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts over the control of Navarre and had significant implications for the region's political landscape.
events.name: Battle of Pampeluna

events.enhanced_description: On May 25, 1521, the Diet of Worms concluded with Charles V issuing the Edict of Worms, which declared Martin Luther an outlaw and banned his writings. This decree marked a turning point in the Reformation, leading to increased tensions between Protestant reformers and the Catholic Church.
events.name: The Diet of Worms ends with the Edict of Worms

events.enhanced_description: On May 27, 1521, Zhu Houcong ascended to the throne as the new Ming dynasty Emperor of China, taking the imperial name Jiajing. His reign would be marked by significant cultural and political developments within the empire.
events.name: Jiajing becomes the new Ming dynasty Emperor of China

events.enhanced_description: On June 25, 1521, Suleiman the Magnificent initiated the siege of Belgrade, a crucial military campaign aimed at expanding Ottoman control in Europe. The siege would prove to be a significant event in the Ottoman-Habsburg wars.
events.name: Suleiman the Magnificent begins the siege of Belgrade

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1521, Neacșu's letter was written by a trader from Câmpulung to the mayor of Brașov, Johannes Benkner. This document is notable for being the oldest surviving dateable document written primarily in the Romanian language, warning of Ottoman troop movements.
events.name: Neacșu's letter

events.enhanced_description: On June 30, 1521, the Battle of Esquiroz took place, where French forces under André de Foix were defeated by the Spanish. This battle was part of the larger conflict over the control of Navarre and demonstrated the ongoing struggles between France and Spain.
events.name: Battle of Esquiroz

events.enhanced_description: On July 15, 1521, San Juan Bautista was founded as the new capital of the archipelago of Puerto Rico. This establishment marked an important step in the Spanish colonization of the Caribbean and the development of the region's cultural identity.
events.name: San Juan Bautista is founded as the new capital of Puerto Rico

events.enhanced_description: The Fall of Tenochtitlan on August 13, 1521, marked the surrender of the last Aztec emperor, Cuauhtémoc, to Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés. This event led to the incorporation of the Aztec Empire into the Spanish Empire, effectively ending the Late Postclassic period in Mesoamerica.

image.caption: Painting from the Conquest of México series depicting the Fall of Tenochtitlan.
image.date_qualification: The image is dated to the second half of the 17th century; it depicts the 1521 event retrospectively.
image.image_date: second half of 17 th century date QS:P571,+1650-00-00T00:00:00Z/7
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Fall of Tenochtitlan

events.enhanced_description: The Italian War of 1521–1526 erupted on August 20, 1521, as Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, clashed with Francis I of France. The conflict was marked by Henry III of Nassau-Breda leading Imperial troops into northeastern France, intensifying the struggle for dominance in Italy.
events.name: Italian War of 1521–1526

events.enhanced_description: On August 29, 1521, the Ottoman army led by Suleiman the Magnificent captured Belgrade, a strategic stronghold in the Balkans. This victory was pivotal in expanding Ottoman influence in southeastern Europe.
events.name: Capture of Belgrade

events.enhanced_description: The Revolt of the Comuneros, an uprising against King Carlos I of Spain, culminated in the surrender of Toledo on October 25, 1521. The rebellion highlighted the tensions between the monarchy and the citizens of Castile, ultimately leading to significant political changes.
events.name: Revolt of the Comuneros

events.enhanced_description: On November 23, 1521, Spanish, German, and Papal forces under Prospero Colonna successfully forced French Marshal Odet de Lautrec to abandon Milan. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts during the Italian Wars, significantly impacting the control of northern Italy.
events.name: Spanish–German–Papal forces in Milan

events.enhanced_description: On December 27, 1521, the Zwickau prophets arrived in Wittenberg, causing unrest by promoting the rejection of infant baptism. Their radical ideas contributed to the growing tensions within the Protestant Reformation.
events.name: Arrival of the Zwickau Prophets

events.enhanced_description: In 1522, the third edition of Erasmus's Greek Textus Receptus of the New Testament, titled 'Novum Testamentum', was published in Basel. This work was significant in the development of biblical scholarship and the Protestant Reformation.
events.name: Publication of Erasmus's Greek Textus Receptus

events.enhanced_description: In 1522, He Ru, a War Ministry official of the Ming dynasty, became the first to acquire the Portuguese breech-loading culverin. This acquisition marked a significant advancement in military technology for China, with local craftsmen Yang San and Dai Ming producing copies in Beijing.
events.name: Acquisition of breech-loading culverin by Ming dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In 1522, a Portuguese expedition led by Cristóvão de Mendonça sighted Australia, mapping the continent and naming it 'Jave la Grande'. This event is considered part of the early European exploration of the region.
events.name: Discovery of Australia by Portuguese

events.enhanced_description: In 1522, the Portuguese allied with the Sultanate of Ternate to begin the construction of Fort Kastela on the island of Ternate in Indonesia. This fortification was part of Portugal's efforts to secure their interests in the Spice Islands.

image.caption: Anonymous Dutch rendering of the Spanish fortress of Kastella on Ternate.
image.credit: Anonymous Unknown author — Chatelain reproduction of original dated 1720 titled "Principal Dutch forts of the Indies"
image.date_qualification: A retrospective rendering depicting the fortress in 1607, not a contemporary image of its 1522 construction; the rendering was later reproduced by Chatelain in 1720.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Construction of Fort Kastela

events.enhanced_description: In 1522, the Portuguese, allied with King Ilato of the Goratalo kingdom, constructed the Otanaha Fortress. This fortification was part of their strategic efforts to control trade routes in the region.
events.name: Construction of Otanaha Fortress

events.enhanced_description: On January 9, 1522, the papal conclave concluded with the election of Adriaan Florensz Boeyens as Pope Adrian VI. His election marked a significant moment as he became the last non-Italian pope for nearly 450 years.
events.name: Papal Conclave for Pope Adrian VI

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1522, Spanish conquistador Gil González Dávila embarked on an expedition from the Gulf of Panama to explore the Pacific coast of Central America. His journey led to the discovery of Nicaragua and the naming of Costa Rica due to the abundance of gold found along the Pacific beaches.
events.name: Gil González Dávila's Exploration

events.enhanced_description: On February 5, 1522, the Revolt of the Comuneros was reignited in Castile when King Carlos V reneged on a promised amnesty to the participants of a previous uprising. The situation was calmed by the intervention of Maria de Mendoza, although many rebels faced punishment.
events.name: Revolt of the Comuneros Re-ignited

events.enhanced_description: On February 7, 1522, the Pact of Brussels was signed between Charles V and his brother Ferdinand of Austria, ensuring Charles's support for Ferdinand's claim to the title of King of the Romans. This agreement solidified the political alliance between the two leaders.
events.name: Pact of Brussels

events.enhanced_description: The Grünwald Conference took place on February 10, 1522, where Duke Wilhelm IV and Duke Ludwig X of Bavaria agreed to retain the traditional Roman Catholic Church while initiating their own reformation within the Duchy. This decision was a precursor to the broader Counter-Reformation.
events.name: Grünwald Conference

events.enhanced_description: On February 27, 1522, Daniil of Volotsk was appointed as the new Metropolitan of Moscow by the Grand Duke of Moscow, becoming the leader of the Russian Orthodox Church. His appointment was significant in the religious landscape of Russia.
events.name: Appointment of Daniil of Volotsk

events.enhanced_description: On February 28, 1522, the Viscount of Lautrec, leader of the French Army, spared the Italian residents of Treviglio from retribution after witnessing a miracle involving a fresco of the Virgin Mary. This event reflected the intertwining of faith and military actions during the period.
events.name: Viscount of Lautrec's Decision

events.enhanced_description: On March 5, 1522, Waliullah Shah was installed as the new ruler of the Bahmani Sultanate by Amir Barid I, the Sultan of Bidar. This appointment was part of the ongoing power struggles within the region during the early 16th century.
events.name: Installation of Waliullah Shah

events.enhanced_description: On March 6, 1522, Protestant reformer Martin Luther returned to Wittenberg after being cleared to return by his protector, Frederick the Wise, Elector of Saxony. His return was significant for the Protestant Reformation, as he continued to spread his reformist ideas.
events.name: Martin Luther's Return to Wittenberg

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1522, the Battle of Bicocca took place, where French and Swiss forces under Odet de Lautrec were defeated by the Spanish. This battle was part of the larger struggle for control over Milan during the Italian Wars.
events.name: Battle of Bicocca

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1522, Pope Adrian VI issued the papal bull Exponi nobis at the request of Spanish Emperor Carlos V. This decree allowed mendicant orders in the New World to exercise significant episcopal authority, addressing the needs of the growing Catholic presence in the Americas.
events.name: Papal Bull Exponi nobis

events.enhanced_description: On May 15, 1522, Hernán Cortés sent his third report to Emperor Carlos V from Coyoacán, detailing the events of the past two years, including the conquest of Tenochtitlan. This report was crucial in informing the Spanish crown about the New World conquests.
events.name: Cortés' Report to Carlos V

events.enhanced_description: On May 28, 1522, the Ottoman Empire successfully besieged Knin in the Kingdom of Croatia, leading to the surrender of Mihajlo Vojković. The siege resulted in significant territorial gains for the Ottomans and a demographic shift in the region.
events.name: Siege of Knin

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1522, England formally declared war on both France and Scotland, marking a significant escalation in the ongoing conflicts of the period. This declaration was part of the broader context of the Italian Wars, where England sought to assert its influence in European affairs.
events.name: England formally declares war on France and Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On June 19, 1522, Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, visited King Henry VIII of England to sign the Treaty of Windsor. This treaty pledged a joint invasion of France, thereby formally involving England in the Italian War of 1521–1526, further entrenching the political alliances of the time.
events.name: Treaty of Windsor

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1522, an English fleet and army commanded by Thomas Howard, Earl of Surrey, launched an attack on the regions of Brittany and Picardy after landing at Le Dourduff-en-Mer. The forces engaged in widespread burning and looting, reflecting the brutal tactics employed during the conflicts of the Italian Wars.
events.name: English attack on Brittany and Picardy

events.enhanced_description: On July 23, 1522, the first Battle of Morlaix saw a counter-attack by local peasants and the French Army against the English forces who had recently pillaged the town. The English, caught off guard and inebriated from celebrations, suffered heavy casualties, with around 700 soldiers killed.
events.name: First Battle of Morlaix

events.enhanced_description: On July 28, 1522, Ottoman Sultan Suleiman I initiated a siege to expel the Knights of St. John from Rhodes. This marked the beginning of a significant military campaign that would ultimately lead to the fall of the island to Ottoman control.

image.caption: Manuscript illustration of Ottoman Janissaries and the defending Knights of St. John during the Siege of Rhodes.
image.credit: Fethullah Çelebi Arifi (historian, poet and painter) and/or Matrakçı Nasuh (painter of landscape) and/or other painters at the court of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent — Süleymanname MS. H. 1517, f. 149a, Topkapi Lib. Istambul; scanned from reproduction in "A story of history" by Arnold Toynbee
image.date_qualification: Illustration dated 1558; it is not a contemporary photograph of the 1522 siege.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Siege of Rhodes

events.enhanced_description: On August 3, 1522, Margaret Tudor, regent of Scotland, appointed Lord Erskine as the keeper of her son, King James V, who was only 10 years old at the time. This appointment was crucial for the political stability of Scotland during a period of turmoil.
events.name: Appointment of Lord Erskine

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1522, Ottoman General Mehmed-Bey of Nikopol entered Târgoviște, taking control of the Principality of Wallachia after Radu of Afumați was forced to flee. This event marked a significant expansion of Ottoman influence in Eastern Europe.
events.name: Ottoman control of Wallachia

events.enhanced_description: On August 27, 1522, the Knights' War erupted within the Holy Roman Empire as Franz von Sickingen led a revolt against the Prince-Bishop of Trier. This conflict aimed to seize church properties and reflected the growing tensions between secular and ecclesiastical authorities.
events.name: Knights' War

events.enhanced_description: On August 31, 1522, Pope Adrian VI was crowned at St. Peter's Basilica in Vatican City. His papacy would be marked by attempts to reform the church amidst the rising tide of the Protestant Reformation.
events.name: Crowning of Pope Adrian VI

events.enhanced_description: On September 6, 1522, a group of 18 men led by Captain Juan Sebastián Elcano returned to Sanlúcar de Barrameda, Spain, completing the first circumnavigation of the globe. This monumental journey began nearly three years earlier as part of the Magellan expedition.
events.name: Return of the Victoria

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1522, Martin Luther's translation of the New Testament into Early New High German, titled 'Das newe Testament Deutzsch', was published in Wittenberg, Germany. This translation played a crucial role in the spread of Protestant ideas and the accessibility of the Bible to the German-speaking populace.
events.name: Publication of Luther Bible

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1522, a devastating 6.8 magnitude earthquake struck Almería, Spain, killing over 2,500 people and causing extensive destruction. This earthquake is recorded as the most destructive in Spanish history, with significant damage reported in surrounding towns.
events.name: Almería earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On October 22, 1522, a catastrophic earthquake struck Vila Franca do Campo in the Azores Islands, resulting in the deaths of over 4,000 people. This event highlighted the seismic vulnerability of the region and its impact on the local population.

image.caption: Sixteenth-century map of the Azores, attributed to Abraham Ortelius and based on Luís Teixeira’s map.
image.date_qualification: Map dated 1584, 62 years after the earthquake.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Azores earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On November 17, 1522, the second Diet of Nuremberg convened to address various issues concerning the Holy Roman Empire, including the growing Protestant Reformation. This assembly was significant in shaping the political and religious landscape of Europe during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Second Diet of Nuremberg

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1522, the Ottomans finally breached the defenses of Rhodes, although the Knights of St. John continued to resist fiercely in the streets. This marked a critical moment in the siege, showcasing the determination of the Knights against overwhelming odds.

image.caption: Ottoman Janissaries and the defending Knights of St. John, depicted in a Süleymanname manuscript illustration.
image.credit: Fethullah Çelebi Arifi (historian, poet and painter) and/or Matrakçı Nasuh (painter of landscape) and/or other painters at the court of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent — Süleymanname MS. H. 1517, f. 149a, Topkapi Lib. Istambul; scanned from reproduction in "A story of history" by Arnold Toynbee
image.date_qualification: Retrospective manuscript illustration associated with the 1522 siege; the saved image date is 1558, not the date of the event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Ottoman capture of Rhodes

events.enhanced_description: On December 20, 1522, Suleiman the Magnificent accepted the surrender of the surviving Knights of St. John in Rhodes. This event marked the end of the siege and led to the Knights' eventual relocation to Malta, where they became known as the Knights of Malta.
events.name: Surrender of the Knights of St. John

events.enhanced_description: In May 1523, the Ningbo incident occurred when two rival trade delegations from Japan feuded in the Chinese city of Ningbo, resulting in significant pillage and plunder. This event highlighted the complexities of international trade and relations during this period.
events.name: Ningbo Incident

events.enhanced_description: In July 1523, Martin Luther's translation of the Pentateuch into German was published by Melchior Lotter Jr. in Wittenberg. This translation played a crucial role in making the scriptures accessible to the German-speaking populace, significantly influencing the Protestant Reformation.
events.name: Translation of the Pentateuch

events.enhanced_description: On January 20, 1523, Christian II was forced to abdicate as King of Denmark and Norway after the nobles at the herredag in Viborg renounced their allegiance in favor of his uncle, Frederick, Duke of Holstein. This marked a significant shift in power within the Danish monarchy.
events.name: Abdication of Christian II

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1523, the construction of Fort Kastela by Portuguese invaders on the island of Ternate was completed. This fortification was crucial for Portugal's claim over the Spice Islands, enhancing their control over the lucrative spice trade.
events.name: Completion of Fort Kastela

events.enhanced_description: On February 25, 1523, the Battle of al-Shihr took place on the Arabian Peninsula, where Portuguese troops engaged the Kathiri Sultanate, ruled by Emir Mutran bin Mansur. The Portuguese successfully sacked the capital, establishing a strategic port on the Indian Ocean.
events.name: Battle of al-Shihr

events.enhanced_description: On February 27, 1523, Captain Antón Mayor formally claimed the territory of present-day Nicaragua for Spain after arriving at El Realejo with Andrés Niño and other Spanish troops. This event marked a significant step in the Spanish colonization of Central America.
events.name: Claim of Nicaragua

events.enhanced_description: On March 8, 1523, the rebellion by the Brotherhoods of Mallorca was suppressed after two years of conflict, culminating in the surrender of their capital, Palma de Mallorca, to Spanish and German troops. This marked the end of a significant uprising in the Kingdom of Valencia.
events.name: Suppression of the Brotherhoods of Mallorca

events.enhanced_description: On March 26, 1523, Frederick I was provisionally declared King of Denmark by Danish nobles in Viborg, although his claim faced opposition from loyalists in Copenhagen. This event was pivotal in the power struggles of the Danish monarchy.
events.name: Provisional Declaration of Frederick I as King of Denmark

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1523, a daring rescue plan orchestrated by Sister Katharina von Bora and Protestant reformer Martin Luther was executed by fish merchant Leonhard Köppe, who smuggled von Bora and other nuns out of Nimbschen Abbey. This act was significant in the context of the Protestant Reformation.
events.name: Rescue of Katharina von Bora

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1523, Gil González Dávila and his men arrived at Lake Nicaragua, claiming it for the Spanish crown and naming it Mar Dulce. This event was part of the broader Spanish conquest of Nicaragua and highlighted the interactions with local indigenous peoples.
events.name: Claim of Lake Nicaragua

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1523, Mirza Shah Hossein, the Grand Vizier of Persia, was assassinated in Qazvin by Shia nobles of the Qizilbash sect. His death led to the appointment of Jalal al-Din Mohammad Tabrizi as his successor, marking a significant shift in the Persian political landscape.
events.name: Assassination of Mirza Shah Hossein

events.enhanced_description: On April 15, 1523, Sir Thomas More was appointed by King Henry VIII as the Speaker of the English House of Commons, marking the first parliamentary session since 1515. More's role was significant in shaping the political discourse of the time.

locations.name: House of Commons, Palace of Westminster, London

events.name: Appointment of Sir Thomas More as Speaker

events.enhanced_description: On April 17, 1523, Diriangén, the ruler of the Chorotega speakers, led an attack against Spanish invaders under Gonzáles Dávila in Nicaragua. Despite initial success, the Spanish managed to rout the attackers, marking a significant moment in the resistance against colonization.

locations.name: Bluefields, Nicaragua
locations.region: Región Autónoma de la Costa Caribe Sur

events.name: Attack by Diriangén on Spanish Invaders

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1523, Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, appointed Frans Van der Hulst as the inquisitor general of the Seventeen Provinces, introducing the Spanish Inquisition to the region. This marked a significant escalation in religious persecution in the Netherlands.
events.name: Spanish Inquisition in the Netherlands

events.enhanced_description: On April 24, 1523, the Diet of Hungary passed a decree ordering the confiscation of property and execution of all followers of Martin Luther within the Kingdom. This decree reflected the growing tensions between Catholic and Protestant factions in Europe.
events.name: Diet of Hungary's Decree Against Lutherans

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1523, an assassination attempt was made against King Sigismund of Poland while he was walking outside Wawel Castle in Kraków. This incident highlighted the political tensions and threats faced by the monarchy during this period.
events.name: Assassination Attempt on King Sigismund

events.enhanced_description: On May 6, 1523, the Knights' War, led by Franz von Sickingen, was decisively ended at Landstuhl when troops of the Holy Roman Empire captured Nanstein Castle. Sickingen was mortally wounded in the battle, marking a significant defeat for the knightly class.
events.name: End of the Knights' War

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1523, Andrea Gritti was elected as the new Doge of the Republic of Venice, following the death of Antonio Grimani. Gritti's leadership would play a crucial role in navigating Venice through a period of political and economic challenges.
events.name: Election of Andrea Gritti as Doge

events.enhanced_description: On May 27, 1523, during the Swedish War of Liberation, the city of Kalmar, occupied by Danish troops, fell to a Swedish Army force led by Arvid Västagöte. This victory was pivotal in the struggle for Swedish independence from Denmark.
events.name: Fall of Kalmar in the Swedish War of Liberation

events.enhanced_description: On May 31, 1523, following the Battle of Sincouwaan at sea between the ships of the Chinese Empire and the Kingdom of Portugal, a Malay ambassador reluctantly departed from Guangzhou to demand the restoration of the deposed Sultan of Malacca. This event underscored the tensions between European powers and local states in Southeast Asia.
events.name: Battle of Sincouwaan

events.enhanced_description: On June 3, 1523, Portuguese explorers established Santhome Church over the tomb of Saint Thomas the Apostle in Madras, now Chennai, India. This church became a significant site for Christian pilgrimage and reflects the spread of Christianity in Asia.

locations.name: Fort St. George, Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India

events.name: Establishment of Santhome Church

events.enhanced_description: On June 6, 1523, Gustav Vasa was elected king of Sweden, marking the end of the Kalmar Union and establishing Sweden's full independence from Denmark. This event is often regarded as the foundation of the modern Swedish nation.
events.name: Election of Gustav Vasa as King of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1523, Frederick I began an 8-day siege of Copenhagen, the capital of Denmark. The siege was a critical moment in the power struggle for the Danish throne.
events.name: Siege of Copenhagen

events.enhanced_description: On June 12, 1523, during the Franconian War, the Swabian League destroyed 23 robber baron castles, significantly weakening the power of the nobility in the region. This action was part of a broader campaign to restore order and authority.
events.name: Destruction of Robber Baron Castles

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1523, during the Swedish War of Liberation, the surrender of Stockholm by Denmark was accepted by Sweden's King Gustav Vasa. This marked a significant victory for Sweden and solidified its independence from Danish rule.
events.name: Surrender of Stockholm

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1523, the Spanish expedition into Nicaragua concluded as the Europeans returned to Panama in canoes after being forced to abandon their ships. This marked a significant setback in the Spanish colonization efforts in Central America.
events.name: End of Spanish Expedition into Nicaragua

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1523, Pargali Ibrahim Pasha was appointed as Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire by Suleiman the Magnificent. His tenure would last nearly 13 years, during which he played a crucial role in the administration of the empire.
events.name: Appointment of Pargali Ibrahim Pasha

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1523, Jan van Essen and Hendrik Vos became the first Lutheran martyrs, burned at the stake in Brussels at the Grote Markt. Their execution sparked outrage and led Martin Luther to compose a hymn in their memory.
events.name: First Lutheran Martyrs Executed

events.enhanced_description: On July 7, 1523, Wijerd Jelckama, a Frisian warlord and military commander, was executed in Leeuwarden, effectively ending the Frisian rebellion fought by the Arumer Black Heap. His death marked a significant defeat for the resistance against the central authority.
events.name: Execution of Wijerd Jelckama

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1523, the Spanish conquistador Gonzalo de Sandoval founded the city of Colima in present-day Mexico. This establishment marked a significant point in the Spanish colonization of the region, which would later become an important cultural and economic center.
events.name: Founding of Colima

events.enhanced_description: On August 22, 1523, Lucien Grimaldi, the Lord of Monaco, was assassinated by his nephew Bartolomeo Doria di Dolceaqua at the Prince's Palace. This shocking act of violence led to a power struggle and the expulsion of the Doria family from Monaco.
events.name: Assassination of Lucien Grimaldi

events.enhanced_description: Pope Adrian VI, the last Dutch pope, died on September 14, 1523, after a brief reign of 21 months. His death marked the end of a significant papacy, leading to a prolonged period of Italian dominance in the papacy that would last for centuries.

image.caption: Portrait of Pope Adrian VI, after Jan van Scorel.
image.credit: After Jan van Scorel — Centraal Museum of Utrecht .
image.date_qualification: Portrait, not an image of his death. The image date states the original may date to May 1523, while this version is circa 1625; supported display date is null.
image.image_date: Original: presumably between 24 May and 25 May 1523 Apparently the Venetian envoy Sanuto Marino writes in his diary that on those dates, a young Dutch painter made two portraits of the Pope. (see link above for source) ; This version: circa 1625 date QS:P571,+1625-00-00T00:00:00Z/9,P1480,Q5727902
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Death of Pope Adrian VI

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1523, an agreement was made for an expedition by Spanish conquistadores into Nicaragua, organized by Pedrarias Dávila. This marked the beginning of Spanish efforts to conquer and colonize the region, which would have lasting impacts on its indigenous populations.

locations.name: Bluefields, Nicaragua
locations.region: Región Autónoma de la Costa Caribe Sur

events.name: Spanish Conquest of Nicaragua Agreement

events.enhanced_description: On September 23, 1523, after receiving reports of Portuguese attacks on local sultanates, Emperor Zhengde of China ordered the execution of 23 Portuguese envoys. This brutal act highlighted the tensions between the Portuguese and Chinese empires during the age of exploration.
events.name: Execution of Portuguese Envoys in China

events.enhanced_description: A conclave of 32 cardinals began on October 1, 1523, in Rome to elect a successor to the late Pope Adrian VI. The lengthy deliberations culminated in the election of Cardinal Giulio de' Medici as Pope Clement VII, marking the start of a significant papacy.
events.name: Conclave to Elect Pope Clement VII

events.enhanced_description: On October 27, 1523, Hürrem Pasha, the Ottoman Empire's Governor-General of the Damascus Eyalet, initiated a punitive expedition against the Druze in Lebanon. This campaign resulted in the destruction of numerous villages and significant loss of life among the Druze population.
events.name: Hürrem Pasha's Expedition Against the Druze

events.enhanced_description: On November 19, 1523, Cardinal Giulio de' Medici was elected as the 219th pope, taking the name Clement VII. His election marked the beginning of a long line of Italian popes, which would dominate the papacy for centuries.
events.name: Election of Pope Clement VII

events.enhanced_description: On November 26, 1523, Cardinal Marco Cornaro officiated the coronation of Pope Clement VII at the church of Santa Maria in Via Lata in Rome. This event marked the formal beginning of Clement's papacy amidst a period of significant political and religious upheaval.
events.name: Coronation of Pope Clement VII

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1523, Pedro de Alvarado y Contreras set off from Tenochtitlan with an army of 550 Spanish soldiers and 120 horses to begin the Spanish conquest of Guatemala. This expedition was part of the broader Spanish efforts to colonize Central America.
events.name: Spanish Conquest of Guatemala Begins

events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1524, Frederick I was crowned King of Denmark in a ceremony held in Copenhagen, marking the beginning of his reign. His coronation symbolized the consolidation of power and the continuation of the monarchy in Denmark during a period of significant political and religious upheaval in Europe.
events.name: The coronation of Frederick I of Denmark

events.enhanced_description: Beginning on August 20, 1524, Marseille was besieged by forces of the Holy Roman Empire under the command of Charles III, Duke of Bourbon. The siege lasted until September 26, 1524, and was part of the broader conflicts of the Italian Wars, showcasing the struggle for control over key territories in France.
events.name: Siege of Marseille

events.enhanced_description: On August 22, 1524, Martin Luther and Andreas Karlstadt engaged in a theological dispute in Jena, reflecting the intense debates of the Protestant Reformation. This confrontation highlighted the differing views on reforming church practices and the interpretation of scripture among early Protestant leaders.
events.name: Dispute at Jena

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1524, the Treaty of Malmö was signed, marking Sweden's formal withdrawal from the Kalmar Union with Denmark. This treaty was significant in the context of the shifting power dynamics in Northern Europe and the assertion of Swedish independence.
events.name: Treaty of Malmö

events.enhanced_description: On September 5, 1524, Vasco da Gama arrived in Goa to assume the position of Viceroy of Portuguese India. His arrival marked a significant moment in the Portuguese colonial empire, although he would die just three months later, leaving a complex legacy in the region.
events.name: Vasco da Gama arrives in Goa

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1524, Spanish conquistadors Francisco Pizarro, Hernando de Luque, and Diego de Almagro embarked on an expedition to conquer Peru. However, their venture was halted in Colombia, illustrating the challenges faced by early explorers in their quest for new territories.
events.name: Pizarro's expedition to Peru

events.enhanced_description: On September 23, 1524, the Bundesbrief was adopted by the members of the Three Leagues of Switzerland, establishing a common constitution. This document played a crucial role in the political organization and governance of the Swiss Confederation during a time of internal strife and external threats.
events.name: Adoption of the Bundesbrief

events.enhanced_description: King Charlemagne laid siege to the city of Pavia, which was poorly supplied with food, during his campaign against the Lombards. The siege culminated in the capture of the city, further establishing Frankish dominance in northern Italy and leading to the eventual downfall of the Lombard Kingdom.
events.name: Siege of Pavia

events.enhanced_description: On November 1, 1524, John Fleming, the 2nd Lord Fleming and Lord Chancellor of Scotland, was assassinated by John Tweedie of Drummelzier and others. This event underscored the political instability and factional conflicts that characterized Scotland during this period.
events.name: Assassination of John Fleming

events.enhanced_description: On November 15, 1524, the Treaty of Tordesillas was signed between Honoré I, Lord of Monaco, and King Charles of Spain, placing Monaco under Spanish protection. This treaty reflected the geopolitical maneuvering of small states in the face of larger powers during the Renaissance.
events.name: Treaty of Tordesillas for Monaco

events.enhanced_description: On December 8, 1524, Francisco Hernández de Córdoba founded the city of Granada, Nicaragua, which became the oldest Hispanic city on the mainland of the Americas. This founding was part of the Spanish colonization efforts in Central America, establishing a foothold for further exploration and settlement.
events.name: Founding of Granada, Nicaragua

events.enhanced_description: In early 1525, after a three-month siege, the Spanish conquistadores led by Pedro de Alvarado captured Mixco Viejo, the capital of the Pocomans Maya State. This event marked a significant moment in the Spanish conquest of the region, leading to further colonization efforts.

locations.name: Mixco Viejo Archaeological Site, Chimaltenango, Guatemala

events.name: Fall of Mixco Viejo

events.enhanced_description: In 1525, European-brought diseases swept through the Andes, leading to the death of thousands, including many members of the Inca civilization. This catastrophic event significantly weakened indigenous populations and altered the course of South American history.
events.name: European Diseases in the Andes

events.enhanced_description: In 1525, the Bubonic plague spread through southern France, causing widespread devastation and loss of life. This outbreak was part of a series of pandemics that affected Europe during this period, highlighting the ongoing public health challenges of the time.
events.name: Bubonic Plague in Southern France

events.enhanced_description: In 1525, the printing of the first edition of William Tyndale's New Testament translation into English began in Cologne. However, the process was interrupted by anti-Lutheran forces, forcing Tyndale to flee to Worms, where he continued his work.
events.name: Tyndale's New Testament Printing

events.enhanced_description: In 1525, the printing of Huldrych Zwingli's New Testament translation, known as the Zürich Bible, began in Zürich. This translation was part of the broader Protestant Reformation movement, which sought to make religious texts more accessible to the laity.
events.name: Zürich Bible Printing

events.enhanced_description: The Navarre witch trials began in 1525, marking a period of intense persecution against alleged witches in the region. This event reflects the broader European witch hunts that characterized the era, fueled by superstition and religious fervor.
events.name: Navarre Witch Trials Begin

events.enhanced_description: In 1525, the Chinese Ministry of War under the Ming dynasty ordered the seizure and destruction of ships with more than one mast sailing along the southeast coast. This action aimed to curb piracy and limit private commercial trade abroad, reflecting the dynasty's tightening control over maritime activities.
events.name: Ming Dynasty Ship Seizures

events.enhanced_description: In 1525, the Kheshgi tribe of Pashtuns established the city of Kasur after migrating from Kabul, Afghanistan. This event marked the beginning of Kasur's development as a significant urban center in the region.
events.name: Establishment of Kasur

events.enhanced_description: According to Johannes Trithemius, the Age of Samael ended and the Age of Gabriel began in 1525. This transition reflects the mystical and esoteric beliefs prevalent during the Renaissance period.

image.caption: Tomb relief of Johannes Trithemius, carved by Tilman Riemenschneider.
image.date_qualification: The relief is dated circa 1516, not 1525; the photograph was taken in July 2009. It is a later memorial image, not a depiction of the reported 1525 transition.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: End of the Age of Samael

events.enhanced_description: On January 21, 1525, the Anabaptist Movement was born in Zürich when Conrad Grebel, Felix Manz, George Blaurock, and others baptized each other, breaking away from traditional church practices. This act of defiance against the established church marked a significant moment in the Protestant Reformation.

image.caption: Retrospective illustration of the 1525 Zürich Anabaptist disputation.
image.credit: Heinrich Thomann (1544-1619) — Kopienband zur zürcherischen Kirchen- und Reformationsgeschichte
image.date_qualification: Depicts an event in 1525; the illustration is dated between 1605 and 1606, not a contemporary event image.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Birth of the Anabaptist Movement

events.enhanced_description: On February 24, 1525, the Battle of Pavia occurred, where German and Spanish forces under Charles de Lannoy and the Marquis of Pescara defeated the French army, capturing King Francis I of France. This decisive battle significantly shifted the balance of power in Italy during the Italian Wars.
events.name: Battle of Pavia

events.enhanced_description: On February 28, 1525, Cuauhtémoc, the last Aztec Emperor, was killed by Hernán Cortés. This event marked a tragic end to the indigenous resistance against Spanish colonization in Mexico and symbolized the fall of the Aztec Empire.

image.caption: Relief of Cuauhtémoc in the entrance hall of the Army Museum in Mexico City.
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2021-12-28; the photograph does not depict the 1525 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Death of Cuauhtémoc

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1525, the pamphlet The Twelve Articles was published in Memmingen, marking it as the first human rights-related document written in Europe. This document articulated the grievances of the peasantry and called for reforms, reflecting the social tensions of the time.
events.name: Publication of The Twelve Articles

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1525, during the German Peasants' War, the Battle of Leipheim resulted in significant losses for the peasant forces, who were attacked by Georg, Truchsess von Waldburg. The defeat led to the execution of four peasant leaders, further suppressing the uprising.
events.name: Battle of Leipheim

events.enhanced_description: On April 10, 1525, Albert, Duke of Prussia, committed the Prussian Homage, recognizing the authority of the King of Poland. This act marked a significant shift in the political landscape of Eastern Europe, as it established a vassal relationship.
events.name: Prussian Homage

events.enhanced_description: On May 14, 1525, during the German Peasants' War, the Battle of Frankenhausen saw insurgent peasants led by radical pastor Thomas Müntzer defeated. Following the battle, Müntzer was executed, marking a significant moment in the suppression of the peasant uprising.
events.name: Battle of Frankenhausen

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1525, Martin Luther married Katharina von Bora, a former nun, in Wittenberg. This marriage was significant not only for Luther's personal life but also symbolized the broader changes in societal norms regarding marriage and clerical celibacy during the Reformation.
events.name: Marriage of Martin Luther

events.enhanced_description: On June 18, 1525, King Henry VIII of England appointed his six-year-old illegitimate son, Henry FitzRoy, as Duke of Richmond and Somerset. This appointment was significant as it reflected Henry's desire to legitimize his son and secure a political future for him.
events.name: Appointment of Henry FitzRoy

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1525, the Battle of Pfeddersheim marked the last significant action of the German Peasants' War, resulting in a decisive defeat for the peasant forces. This battle was pivotal as it led to the deaths of over 75,000 peasants and the collapse of the uprising.
events.name: Battle of Pfeddersheim

events.enhanced_description: The seven-ship Spanish expedition commanded by García Jofre de Loaísa set sail from Corunna on 24 July 1525. Its aims included reaching the Spice Islands and searching for the Trinidad.

image.caption: Map showing García Jofre de Loaísa’s expedition route.
image.credit: Holger Behr Hobe — own work, route from various biografis
image.date_qualification: Route map contextualizing the expedition; it is not evidence of the fleet’s departure itself. The image date is 2007-06-15.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The Loaísa expedition sets sail

events.enhanced_description: On July 29, 1525, Spanish conquistador Rodrigo de Bastidas founded Santa Marta, the first city in Colombia. This founding was part of the Spanish efforts to establish settlements in the New World, paving the way for further exploration and colonization.
events.name: Founding of Santa Marta

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1525, Sophie of Pomerania was crowned as Queen consort of Denmark in Copenhagen, a little over a year after her husband Frederick I's coronation. Her coronation was significant as it reinforced the dynastic ties and the political stability of the Danish monarchy.
events.name: Coronation of Sophie of Pomerania

events.enhanced_description: On August 30, 1525, the Treaty of the More was signed at The More in Hertfordshire between the French ambassador and King Henry VIII of England. This treaty aimed to establish peace between England and France during a tumultuous period marked by ongoing conflicts in Europe.
events.name: Treaty of the More

events.enhanced_description: On September 14, 1525, the burning of a significant portion of the book collection of the Stiftsbibliothek of the Grossmünster Abbey in Zürich began, ordered by Huldrych Zwingli. This act was part of the Swiss Reformation, reflecting the tensions between Protestant reformers and the Catholic Church.
events.name: Burning of books in Zürich

events.enhanced_description: On September 24, 1525, Jeremias I was restored to the position of Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople by the order of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent. This event marked a significant moment in the history of the Eastern Orthodox Church, reflecting the complex relationship between the Ottoman Empire and its Christian subjects.

image.caption: Portrait of Ecumenical Patriarch Ieremias I.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Εθνικό Κέντρο Τεκμηρίωσης , Ημερολόγιο Εθνικών Φιλανθρωπικών Καταστημάτων, Κωνσταντινούπολη 1907, σελ. 177
image.date_qualification: Image date: 1907; this is a later portrait, not a contemporary image of the 1525 restoration.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Restoration of Jeremias I as Ecumenical Patriarch

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1525, the Earl of Angus, Scotland's Lord Warden of the Marches, successfully negotiated a three-year peace treaty with the Kingdom of England. This treaty aimed to stabilize the border region and reduce conflicts between the two nations.
events.name: Peace Treaty at Berwick-upon-Tweed

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1525, Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, issued an edict ordering the expulsion or conversion of the remaining Muslims in the Crown of Aragon, which included the Kingdom of Valencia and the Principality of Catalonia. This decree was part of a broader effort to enforce religious uniformity in Spain.
events.name: Edict of Expulsion for Muslims in Aragon

events.enhanced_description: In December 1525, Jean Frangipani became the first French ambassador to reach the Sublime Porte in Istanbul. His mission marked a significant step in Franco-Ottoman relations, paving the way for future diplomatic and military alliances.
events.name: Jean Frangipani's Mission to the Sublime Porte

events.enhanced_description: On December 8, 1525, a second edict was issued in Spain directing Muslims to show proof of baptism as Christians or face expulsion. This edict enforced the earlier decree and set strict deadlines for compliance, reflecting the growing intolerance towards non-Christian populations.
events.name: Second Edict for Spanish Muslims

events.enhanced_description: On December 31, 1525, the deadline for Spanish Muslims to convert to Christianity in Valencia was reached. Those who failed to comply faced severe penalties, including forced exile, imprisonment, or death, marking a dark chapter in the region's history.
events.name: Deadline for Muslims in Valencia

events.enhanced_description: In March 1526, the first complete printed translation of the New Testament into English by William Tyndale arrived in England from Germany, where it was printed in Worms. This translation played a crucial role in the English Reformation and the spread of Protestant ideas.
events.name: First complete printed translation of the New Testament into English

events.enhanced_description: Following a defeat of Afghan soldiers by the Mughal Empire, Emperor Babur and Crown Prince Humayun ordered the execution of 100 captured Afghan prisoners by the brutal method known as 'blowing from a gun.' This event highlighted the harsh realities of warfare during this period.
events.name: Execution of Afghan prisoners by the Mughal Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 1526, King François I of France was released from captivity in Spain after signing the Treaty of Madrid. This treaty was a significant political maneuver in the ongoing rivalry between France and Spain.
events.name: Release of King François I from captivity

events.enhanced_description: In 1526, gunsmith Bartolomeo Beretta established the Beretta Gun Company, which would become one of the oldest firearm manufacturers still in operation today. This company has played a significant role in the history of firearms.
events.name: Establishment of Beretta Gun Company

events.enhanced_description: In 1526, Spanish conquistadors led by Francisco Pizarro first reached Inca territory in South America. This encounter set the stage for the eventual conquest of the Inca Empire.
events.name: Pizarro reaches Inca territory

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1526, the deadline for Spanish Muslims to convert to Christianity or leave was reached in the Crown of Aragon and the Principality of Catalonia. This enforcement of religious conformity led to significant social upheaval and migration.
events.name: Deadline for Muslims in Aragon and Catalonia

events.enhanced_description: On February 6, 1526, Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent agreed to form a military alliance with France after King François I sent a proposal via his envoy, Jean Frangipani. This alliance was significant in the context of European power dynamics and conflicts of the era.
events.name: Military Alliance between France and the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: On February 9, 1526, a group of 16 deserters from the Spanish colonial army destroyed Iximche, the capital of the Kaqchikel Maya kingdom, and burned the palace of the Ahpo Xahil. This act of violence exemplified the chaos and brutality of the Spanish conquest in Central America.

image.caption: Iximche archaeological site in Guatemala.
image.date_qualification: A site image, not a depiction of the 1526 destruction; the saved image date is 2024-10-25.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Destruction of Iximche

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1526, Spanish author Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo y Valdés published his chronicle 'La Natural Historia De Las Indias' (The Natural History of the Indies). This work is considered one of the first comprehensive accounts of the natural history and indigenous peoples of the Americas.
figures: Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo y Valdés
events.name: Publication of La Natural Historia De Las Indias

events.enhanced_description: On February 21, 1526, Lopo Vaz de Sampaio was appointed as the new Governor of Portuguese India following the death of Governor Henrique de Meneses. His leadership would play a crucial role in the administration of Portuguese colonial interests in the region.
events.name: Lopo Vaz de Sampaio becomes Governor of Portuguese India

events.enhanced_description: On February 25, 1526, the Battle of Hisar Firoza was fought between the Mughal Empire, led by Prince Humayun, and the Delhi Sultanate, commanded by Hamid Khan. Humayun's victory in this battle marked an important step in the consolidation of Mughal power in India.
events.name: Battle of Hisar Firoza

events.enhanced_description: On February 27, 1526, the League of Torgau was formed as an alliance of German princes opposing the 1521 Edict of Worms. This coalition represented a significant resistance movement against the Holy Roman Empire's attempts to suppress the Protestant Reformation.
events.name: Formation of the League of Torgau

events.enhanced_description: On March 7, 1526, the Canton of Zurich enacted a law against the Anabaptist movement, specifically outlawing a second baptism for adults previously baptized as infants. This law was a reflection of the growing tensions between Protestant reformers and traditional religious authorities.
events.name: Zurich Law Against Anabaptists
