events.enhanced_description: On March 10, 1526, Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain, married Princess Isabella of Portugal at the Alcázar of Seville. This union strengthened the ties between the Spanish and Portuguese crowns, influencing European politics for years to come.
events.name: Marriage of Charles V and Isabella of Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1526, King François I of France crossed the Bidasoa River into France, while his sons, the Dauphin François and Prince Henri, entered Spain as hostages to ensure compliance with the Madrid Treaty. This act marked a significant moment in the ongoing conflict between France and Spain.
events.name: François I crosses the Bidasoa River

events.enhanced_description: On April 21, 1526, the Battle of Panipat marked the beginning of the Mughal Empire in India, as Babur defeated the Sultan of Delhi, Ibrahim Lodi. This victory established Mughal rule, which would last for over three centuries.
events.name: Battle of Panipat

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1526, King François I of France repudiated the Treaty of Madrid and formed the League of Cognac, an alliance against Charles V that included Pope Clement VII and several Italian states. This coalition aimed to counterbalance the power of the Holy Roman Emperor.
events.name: Formation of the League of Cognac

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1526, Emperor Go-Nara ascended to the throne of Japan, marking the beginning of his reign during a period of significant political and social change in the country.
events.name: Ascension of Emperor Go-Nara

events.enhanced_description: On July 24, 1526, Milan was captured by Spanish forces, marking a significant event in the Italian Wars. This capture solidified Spanish influence in northern Italy during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Capture of Milan by the Spanish

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1526, the Spanish ship Santiago, part of García Jofre de Loaísa's expedition, became the first ship to sail from Europe to the west coast of North America, anchoring at the Gulf of Tehuantepec. This voyage marked a significant milestone in the Age of Exploration.
events.name: Santiago reaches the Pacific Coast of Mexico

events.enhanced_description: On August 9, 1526, Lucas Vázquez de Ayllón founded the failed colony of San Miguel de Gualdape in present-day Winyah Bay, Georgetown County, South Carolina. This settlement is notable for being the first European settlement in what would later become the continental United States.

image.caption: Detail of Diego Ribero’s map showing land on the southeast coast of North America granted to Lucas Vázquez de Ayllón.
image.credit: Map by Diego Ribero, Seville 1529 — Library of Congress - https://hdl.loc.gov/loc.gmd/g3200.ct002450
image.date_qualification: Map dated 1533 in the supplied image metadata; it postdates the 1526 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Foundation of San Miguel de Gualdape

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1526, the first official translation of the New Testament into Swedish was completed, marking a significant step in the spread of Protestantism in Sweden. The entire Bible would be completed in 1541.
events.name: First official translation of the New Testament into Swedish

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 1526, Spanish explorer Alonso de Salazar became the first European to sight the Marshall Islands in the Pacific Ocean. This discovery contributed to the European understanding of the Pacific region.
events.name: Alonso de Salazar sights the Marshall Islands

events.enhanced_description: On September 19, 1526, a German contingent from the Holy Roman Empire overwhelmed Spanish Muslims led by Selim Almanzo in the Sierra de Espadán mountain range. The aftermath saw the massacre of 5,000 Muslims, highlighting the brutal conflicts of the era.
events.name: Massacre of Spanish Muslims

events.enhanced_description: In October 1526, Cuthbert Tunstall, the Roman Catholic Bishop of London, issued a proclamation directing followers to destroy all copies of Tyndale's New Testament. This act reflected the tensions between Catholic authorities and the Protestant Reformation.
events.name: Proclamation against Tyndale's New Testament

events.enhanced_description: On October 24, 1526, the Bohemian Diet elected Archduke Ferdinand of the House of Habsburg as the King of Bohemia. This election was pivotal in the Habsburgs' consolidation of power in Central Europe.
events.name: Election of Archduke Ferdinand as King of Bohemia

events.enhanced_description: On November 10, 1526, a group of lesser nobles proclaimed John Zápolya as the King of Hungary in Székesfehérvár. This event marked the establishment of the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom amidst the power struggles following the Battle of Mohács.

image.caption: Woodcut portrait of John Zápolya by Erhard Schön.
image.credit: Erhard Schön (1491-1542) — Engraving by Erhard Schön, first uploaded to hu.wikipedia.org
image.date_qualification: The image is identified as a 16th-century woodcut portrait of John Zápolya, not a depiction of his proclamation as king. No supported display date is available.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Proclamation of John Zápolya as King of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: On December 17, 1526, the Diet at Pozsony (modern-day Bratislava) elected Archduke Ferdinand as the King of Hungary. This election was a crucial step in the Habsburgs' efforts to establish control over Hungary following the Battle of Mohács.
events.name: Election of Ferdinand as King of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: Ferdinand of the House of Habsburg was formally crowned as King of Bohemia on January 1, 1527, in Pressburg, now Bratislava. This event was pivotal in establishing Habsburg influence in Central Europe.

image.caption: Portrait painting of Ferdinand I of Habsburg, identified as King of Bohemia.
image.credit: Hans Krell — Lobkowiczské sbírky, Pražský hrad, vlastní foto, fotoreprodukce Filip Leksa
image.date_qualification: The image description identifies Ferdinand as King of Bohemia; it is a portrait, not a depiction of his coronation. The saved image date is “polovina 16. století” (mid-16th century), but supported_display_date is null.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Ferdinand crowned King of Bohemia

events.enhanced_description: In 1527, the seven articles of the Schleitheim Confession were formally adopted by the Mennonite Anabaptist Christians in Schleitheim, Switzerland. This document became a foundational statement of Anabaptist beliefs and practices.
events.name: Adoption of the Schleitheim Confession

events.enhanced_description: In 1527, the Protestant Reformation began in Sweden when the Riksdag of the Estates in Västerås adopted Lutheranism as the state religion. This decision led to significant changes in the religious landscape of Sweden, including the confiscation of church property.
events.name: Protestant Reformation in Sweden

events.enhanced_description: During the Diet of Odense in 1527, King Frederick I of Denmark declared religious tolerance for Lutherans, allowed priests to marry, and prohibited seeking papal approval for royal appointments of church officials. This marked a significant step in the establishment of Lutheranism in Denmark.
events.name: Diet of Odense

events.enhanced_description: In 1527, the second Dalecarlian rebellion broke out in Sweden, reflecting the ongoing tensions between the peasantry and the nobility. The rebellion ultimately failed, and the leader, known as Daljunkern, fled to Rostock, highlighting the struggles for power and rights in the region.
events.name: Second Dalecarlian Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: In 1527, members of the University of Wittenberg fled to Jena due to fears of the bubonic plague. This movement illustrates the impact of disease on academic and social life during the Renaissance period.
figures: Members of the University of Wittenberg
events.name: Fleeing from the Bubonic Plague

events.enhanced_description: In 1527, Bishop Vesey's Grammar School was founded in Sutton Coldfield, West Midlands, by Bishop John Vesey. This institution has played a significant role in the education of young men in the region and reflects the educational reforms of the time.

locations.name: Bishop Vesey's Grammar School, Sutton Coldfield

events.name: Founding of Bishop Vesey's Grammar School

events.enhanced_description: In 1527, the Ming dynasty government of China significantly reduced the quotas for grain collection, which severely impacted the state's ability to manage famine relief through its granary system. This decision had lasting effects on the agricultural and economic stability of the region.
events.name: Ming Dynasty Grain Quota Reduction

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of her husband, Louis II of Hungary, Queen consort Mary of Hungary was appointed regent. On February 14, 1527, she requested to step down in favor of the newly elected Frederick of Habsburg, but her request was denied by the Hungarian Diet, reflecting the political tensions of the time.
events.name: Mary of Hungary's request to step down as regent

events.enhanced_description: The Mughal–Rajput wars commenced on February 21, 1527, with the Mughal Emperor Babur facing off against the Rajput Confederacy. The Rajputs achieved a significant victory at the Battle of Bayana, marking the beginning of a series of conflicts that would shape the region's history.
events.name: Beginning of the Mughal–Rajput wars

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1527, the Battle of Khanwa was fought, where Mughal Emperor Babur defeated the Rajput ruler Rana Sanga. This decisive victory solidified Mughal dominance in northern India, following earlier successes in the region.

image.caption: Persian miniature depicting Babur’s army fighting Rana Sanga’s forces, with bombards and field guns.
image.credit: "Mirza 'Abd al-Rahim, Khan-i khanan (Mirza 'Abd al-Rahim, Khan-i khanan)" — https://warfare.tk/Moghul/Baburnama/1527-Battle_of_Kanvaha.htm
image.date_qualification: Retrospective miniature of the Battle of Khanwa; the artwork dates to 1590, decades after the 1527 battle.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Khanwa

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1527, the Confederation of Shan States launched an attack on Ava, the capital of the Ava Kingdom, resulting in its sacking. This event marked a significant shift in power dynamics in the region.
events.name: Sack of Ava

events.enhanced_description: On May 6, 1527, Spanish and German troops led by the Duke of Bourbon sacked Rome, forcing Pope Clement VII to negotiate peace with Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor. This event marked a significant decline in the power of the Papacy and the end of the High Renaissance.
events.name: Sack of Rome

events.enhanced_description: On May 16, 1527, the Piagnon, a group devoted to the memory of Girolamo Savonarola, successfully drove out the Medici from Florence for a second time, re-establishing the Republic of Florence until 1530. This event reflected the ongoing conflict between republican and princely governance in the city.
events.name: Piagnon drive out the Medici

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1527, the Narváez expedition, led by Spanish conquistador Álvaro de Saavedra Cerón, set sail from Zihuatanejo, Mexico, on a voyage to explore and conquer Florida. This expedition was part of the broader Spanish efforts to expand their territories in the New World.
events.name: Narváez expedition to conquer Florida

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1527, Jakarta, the modern capital of Indonesia, was founded as Jayakarta. This city would later become a significant center of trade and culture in Southeast Asia.
events.name: Foundation of Jakarta

events.enhanced_description: On July 5, 1527, General Div Sultan Rumlu, the regent for the young Safavid Shah Tahmasp I, was assassinated and replaced by Chukha Sultan Tekali. This event marked a significant shift in the power dynamics within the Safavid Empire.
events.name: Assassination of Div Sultan Rumlu

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1527, the Battle of Sződfalva was fought near Szeged, Hungary, where a coalition of Hungarians and Romanian Transylvanians defeated a Serbian army led by Jovan Nenad, the self-proclaimed Emperor of the Serbs. Following the defeat, Nenad was assassinated, marking a significant moment in the regional power struggles.
events.name: Battle of Sződfalva

events.enhanced_description: On August 3, 1527, John Rut sent the first known letter from North America while at St. John's, Newfoundland. This letter marked an important moment in the documentation of European exploration in the New World.

locations.name: St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada

events.name: First known letter from North America

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1527, sixty Anabaptists convened at the Martyrs' Synod in Augsburg. This gathering was significant for the Anabaptist movement, as it addressed issues of faith and community among its members.
events.name: Martyrs' Synod in Augsburg

events.enhanced_description: On September 27, 1527, the Battle of Tarcal took place, where Ferdinand, the future Holy Roman Emperor, defeated John Zápolya, gaining control over most of Hungary. Following the defeat, Zápolya sought assistance from the Ottomans, highlighting the complex political landscape of the region.
events.name: Battle of Tarcal

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1527, French and Venetian troops committed a massacre in the Italian city of Pavia, killing thousands of civilians despite the defenders' agreement to surrender. This event underscored the brutal realities of warfare during this period.
events.name: Massacre in Pavia

events.enhanced_description: On October 31, 1527, Spanish conquistador Álvaro de Saavedra Cerón departed from Zihuatanejo, Mexico, on an expedition to explore the Pacific Ocean. This journey was part of Spain's broader efforts to expand its influence and territories in the New World.
events.name: Saavedra's expedition to the Pacific

events.enhanced_description: On November 3, 1527, Archduke Ferdinand of Austria was formally crowned as the King of Hungary at the Basilica of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary in Székesfehérvár. This event was crucial for the Habsburgs' consolidation of power in Hungary.

locations.historical_name: Basilica of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary
locations.name: Basilica of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Székesfehérvár, Hungary

events.name: Ferdinand crowned King of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1527, Puranmal ascended to the throne as the new Raja of the Kingdom of Amber following the death of his father, Raja Prithviraj Singh I, who succumbed to wounds from the Battle of Khanwa earlier that year. This transition marked a significant moment in the history of the Amber Kingdom.
events.name: Puranmal becomes Raja of Amber

events.enhanced_description: On November 15, 1527, the lands of the Bishopric of Utrecht were ceded to the control of the Habsburgs in exchange for their assistance in suppressing a rebellion by the citizens of Utrecht. This event marked a significant shift in power dynamics in the region, as the Habsburgs consolidated their influence over the Netherlands.
events.name: Cession of the Bishopric of Utrecht

events.enhanced_description: On November 22, 1527, Spain completed its conquest of Guatemala's highlands, moving the capital of the colonial government from Santiago de los Caballeros de Guatemala to the newly established Ciudad Vieja. This transition symbolized the consolidation of Spanish power in the region and the establishment of colonial governance.

locations.historical_name: Santiago de los Caballeros de Guatemala
locations.name: Ciudad Vieja, Sacatepéquez, Guatemala

events.name: Conquest of Guatemala's Highlands

events.enhanced_description: On November 23, 1527, the Érdy Codex, the largest collection of Hungarian legends and literature in the Hungarian language, was completed by an unidentified Carthusian monk at the seminary in Nagyszombat, now Trnava, Slovakia. This codex is a vital source for understanding Hungarian folklore and literary history.
events.name: Completion of the Érdy Codex

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1527, Pope Clement VII was released from captivity at Castel Sant'Angelo after being held for seven months following the sack of Rome. His release marked a significant moment in the political and religious turmoil of the time, as the Pope sought to re-establish his authority.
events.name: Release of Pope Clement VII

events.enhanced_description: On December 15, 1527, during a storm, two of the three ships of Álvaro de Saavedra were separated from his vessel, La Florida. The Espiritu Santo and Santiago, which sailed ahead, were never heard from again, marking a tragic moment in early Spanish exploration of the Americas.

locations.name: La Florida, Buenos Aires Province, Argentina

events.name: Separation of Álvaro de Saavedra's Ships

events.enhanced_description: In February 1528, a peasant uprising occurred in Dalarna, Sweden, but the campaign ultimately failed. The rebel leader, later known as Daljunkern, fled to Rostock, illustrating the ongoing struggles between the peasantry and the ruling class.
events.name: Peasant Uprising in Dalarna

events.enhanced_description: In February 1528, Diego García de Moguer explored the Sierra de la Plata along the Río de la Plata and began his journey up the Paraná River. This exploration contributed to the European understanding of the South American interior.
events.name: Exploration by Diego García de Moguer

events.enhanced_description: Montenegro gains autonomy under the influence of the Ottoman Empire, marking a significant shift in its political status. This event reflects the broader dynamics of power and control in the Balkans during the early 16th century.
events.name: Montenegro gains autonomy

events.enhanced_description: Spanish conquistador Francisco de Montejo attempts to invade the Yucatán Peninsula but is repelled by the resilient Maya peoples. This event underscores the fierce resistance faced by European colonizers in the Americas.
events.name: Francisco de Montejo's invasion attempt

events.enhanced_description: Spain asserts direct control over Acapulco, a strategic port on the Pacific coast. This move is part of Spain's broader efforts to consolidate its colonial territories in the New World.
events.name: Spain takes control of Acapulco

events.enhanced_description: A significant outbreak of bubonic plague occurs in England, contributing to the ongoing public health crises of the period. This event highlights the persistent threat of infectious diseases in early modern Europe.
events.name: Bubonic plague outbreak in England

events.enhanced_description: St George's Chapel in Windsor Castle is completed, serving as a significant site for royal ceremonies and burials. This architectural achievement reflects the grandeur of Tudor England.
events.name: Completion of St George's Chapel

events.enhanced_description: Construction begins on the Château de Fontainebleau, a royal residence that will become one of the most important palaces in France. This project reflects the artistic and architectural ambitions of the French monarchy.
events.name: Construction of Château de Fontainebleau

events.enhanced_description: Michelangelo Buonarroti begins work on the fortifications of Florence, showcasing his versatility as an artist and architect. This project is part of the broader efforts to protect the city during a time of political instability.
events.name: Michelangelo's work on Florence fortifications

events.enhanced_description: Baldassare Castiglione publishes The Book of the Courtier, a seminal work that outlines the ideals of courtly behavior and the role of the gentleman in Renaissance society. This book becomes influential in shaping European social norms.
events.name: Publication of The Book of the Courtier

events.enhanced_description: A devastating drought strikes Henan province during the mid Ming dynasty, leading to widespread famine and significant loss of life. This environmental disaster highlights the vulnerabilities of agrarian societies to climatic changes.
events.name: Drought in Henan province, China

events.enhanced_description: The Perak Sultanate and Johor Sultanate are established, both ruled by the sons of Mahmud Shah of Malacca. This development marks a significant moment in the political landscape of the Malay Peninsula.
events.name: Establishment of Perak and Johor Sultanates

events.enhanced_description: On January 12, 1528, Gustav I of Sweden was crowned king, having already reigned since his election in June 1523. His coronation solidified his authority and marked the beginning of a new era in Swedish history.
events.name: Crowning of Gustav I of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1528, the Canton of Bern became the second canton in Switzerland to officially adopt Protestantism after a 21-day debate known as the Bern Disputation. This decision was pivotal in the spread of the Reformation throughout Switzerland.
events.name: Adoption of Protestantism in Bern

events.enhanced_description: On February 16, 1528, King Stanisław II Augustus of Poland established the zloty as the official currency of the Kingdom as part of extensive monetary reforms. This reform aimed to stabilize the economy and facilitate trade.
events.name: Establishment of the Zloty in Poland

events.enhanced_description: On February 29, 1528, John Zápolya, ruler of Eastern Hungary, formed an alliance with Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent of the Ottoman Empire. This alliance provided Zápolya with protection and autonomy in exchange for allowing Turkish occupation of his territory.
events.name: Alliance of John Zápolya with Suleiman the Magnificent

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1528, the Battle of Szina was fought between John Zápolya of Eastern Hungary and Archduke Ferdinand of Austria, the Habsburg King of Western Hungary. Zápolya's forces were defeated by Habsburg mercenaries, further complicating the political landscape of Hungary.
events.name: Battle of Szina

events.enhanced_description: On March 22, 1528, the French Army, commanded by Marshal Odet of Foix, initiated the siege of Melfi, a southern Italian city. The siege resulted in the massacre of over 3,000 inhabitants and the plundering of the city, showcasing the brutality of warfare during this period.
events.name: Siege of Melfi

events.enhanced_description: On May 9, 1528, King James V of Scotland, who had been held captive for over two years by the Earl of Angus, successfully escaped from Edinburgh to Stirling. This escape marked a pivotal moment in his reign and the ongoing power struggles within Scotland.
events.name: Escape of King James V of Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1528, the fourth major outbreak of the sweating sickness was recorded, noted in a letter to Bishop Tunstall from an individual who fled his home due to the infection of a servant. This outbreak highlighted the ongoing public health crises of the time.
events.name: Outbreak of Sweating Sickness

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1528, the Italian city of Rimini and its surrounding area, ruled by the House of Malatesta, were conquered by troops of the Papal States and subsequently annexed. This event marked a significant expansion of Papal authority in Italy.
events.name: Conquest of Rimini

events.enhanced_description: On July 3, 1528, Pope Clement VII issued the bull Religionis zelus, officially recognizing the Order of Friars Minor Capuchin as a reformist branch of the Franciscans. This recognition was significant for the Catholic Church's response to the Reformation.
events.name: Recognition of the Capuchin Order

events.enhanced_description: On July 8, 1528, after surviving a mutiny and the death of 18 men in an ambush in what is now Argentina, explorer Sebastian Cabot sent his flagship, Trinidad, back to Spain with reports against the mutineers and a request for military aid. This incident highlighted the dangers faced by early explorers.
events.name: Mutiny of Sebastian Cabot's Crew

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1528, the 'Peace of St. Ambrose' was signed in Milan at the Basilica of Sant'Ambrogio, effectively ending the civil strife between the Milanese nobility and local merchants. This agreement was crucial for restoring stability in the region.
events.name: Peace of St. Ambrose

events.enhanced_description: In a significant power shift within the Songhai Empire, Askia Muhammad I is forced to abdicate by his son Askia Musa, who subsequently declares himself the new emperor. This event marks a pivotal moment in the political landscape of West Africa during the 16th century.
events.name: Abdication of Askia Muhammad I

events.enhanced_description: The Kyōroku era begins in Japan, marking a new period in the traditional Japanese calendar. This transition follows the conclusion of the Daiei era, reflecting the ongoing historical and cultural developments of the time.
events.name: Beginning of the Kyōroku Era

events.enhanced_description: Admiral Andrea Doria leads a decisive victory against former allies, the French, solidifying Genoa's independence. This battle is a crucial moment in the struggle for control over the Italian city-states during the early 16th century.
events.name: Andrea Doria defeats the French

events.enhanced_description: Spanish explorer Álvaro de Saavedra Cerón arrives in the Maluku Islands, a region known for its valuable spices. His arrival marks a significant moment in the European exploration of Southeast Asia during the Age of Discovery.
events.name: Álvaro de Saavedra Cerón arrives in the Maluku Islands

events.enhanced_description: Cardinal Thomas Wolsey establishes a college in his birthplace of Ipswich, which evolves into the modern-day Ipswich School. This institution incorporates educational traditions dating back to 1299, reflecting the importance of education during the Renaissance.

image.caption: Photograph of the Ipswich School buildings.
image.date_qualification: A modern photograph of the school site, not a depiction of its 1528 founding. Image date: 2018-09-15 13:59:25.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Founding of Ipswich School

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Gorinchem is signed between Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, and Charles, Duke of Guelders, marking a significant diplomatic agreement in the context of European power dynamics during the 16th century.
events.name: Treaty of Gorinchem

events.enhanced_description: Spanish conquistador Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca and his companions become the first known Europeans to set foot on present-day Texas after being shipwrecked on Galveston Island. Their survival story highlights the challenges faced by early explorers in the New World.
events.name: Cabeza de Vaca's arrival in Texas

events.enhanced_description: A new three-member executive junta is appointed by the King of Spain to govern New Spain and the West Indies, marking the establishment of the first Audiencia Real. This governance structure reflects the complexities of colonial administration during the Spanish Empire.
events.name: Formation of the first Audiencia Real

events.enhanced_description: In 1529, Aylesbury was granted the status of county town of Buckinghamshire by King Henry VIII. This designation marked an important administrative change, reflecting the town's growing significance within the region.
events.name: Aylesbury granted county town status

events.enhanced_description: In 1529, Stephen Báthory was appointed as the governor of Transylvania, a position that allowed him to exert significant influence over the region during a period of political instability and conflict. His leadership would play a crucial role in the governance of Transylvania in the years to come.
events.name: Stephen Báthory becomes governor of Transylvania

events.enhanced_description: In 1529, Borommarachathirat IV ascended to the throne of the Kingdom of Ayutthaya, succeeding Ramathibodi II. His reign marked a continuation of the Ayutthaya period, characterized by significant cultural and political developments in Thailand.

locations.name: Ayutthaya, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya, Thailand

events.name: Borommarachathirat IV succeeds Ramathibodi II as king of Ayutthaya

events.enhanced_description: In 1529, Georg Agricola, a notable German polymath, provided the first detailed description of fluorite, a mineral that would later be recognized for its diverse applications in industry and science. His work laid the groundwork for future mineralogical studies.
events.name: Fluorite is first described, by Georg Agricola

events.enhanced_description: In 1529, the Italian painter and architect Giorgio Vasari visited Rome, where he would later draw inspiration from the city's rich artistic heritage. His experiences in Rome significantly influenced his later works and writings on Renaissance art.
events.name: Giorgio Vasari visits Rome

events.enhanced_description: In 1529, Pietro Bembo was appointed as the historiographer of Venice, a role that allowed him to document and influence the historical narrative of the Venetian Republic. His contributions to literature and history were significant during the Renaissance.
events.name: Pietro Bembo becomes historiographer of Venice

events.enhanced_description: In 1529, Heinrich Bullinger became the pastor of Bremgarten, Switzerland, where he played a crucial role in the Protestant Reformation. His leadership and writings significantly shaped the theological landscape of the region.
events.name: Heinrich Bullinger becomes pastor of Bremgarten, Switzerland

events.enhanced_description: In 1529, German polymath Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa published 'Declamatio de nobilitate et praecellentia foeminei sexus', a groundbreaking work that argued for the theological and moral superiority of women. This text contributed to early feminist thought during the Renaissance.
events.name: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa publishes Declamatio de nobilitate et praecellentia foeminei sexus

events.enhanced_description: In 1529, a significant engineering achievement was realized with the opening of a summit level canal between the Alster and the Trave rivers in Germany. This canal facilitated navigation and trade, showcasing advancements in hydraulic engineering of the time.
events.name: A summit level canal between Alster and the Trave in Germany opens to navigation

events.enhanced_description: Basarab VI is installed as the new Prince of Wallachia in Târgoviște, shortly after the assassination of Voivode Radu of Afumați. His reign is short-lived, lasting only a month before he is removed from power.
events.name: Installation of Basarab VI as Prince of Wallachia

events.enhanced_description: Zhang Qijie rises to prominence as the primary wife of the Jiajing Emperor, becoming the most powerful woman in the Ming dynasty shortly after the death of Empress Xiaojiesu. Her influence reflects the complexities of gender and power in imperial China.
events.name: Zhang Qijie becomes powerful in Ming dynasty China

events.enhanced_description: Mughal Emperor Babur departs from Agra to confront the Rajputs and rebel Afghans who have captured Ghazipur. This military campaign is part of Babur's efforts to consolidate his power in India.
events.name: Babur departs from Agra

events.enhanced_description: Peter Vannes, envoy for King Henry VIII of England, arrives in Rome to negotiate a papal dispensation allowing the king to divorce and remarry. The mission ultimately fails, reflecting the tensions between the English crown and the Catholic Church.
events.name: Peter Vannes' mission to Pope Julius II

events.enhanced_description: The Örebro Synod convenes, laying the theological groundwork for the Swedish Reformation. This synod follows the economic reforms initiated by Gustav I of Sweden, marking a significant shift in the religious landscape of Sweden.
events.name: Örebro Synod and the Swedish Reformation

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Shimbra Kure, fought on March 9, 1529, was a significant conflict in the Ethiopian-Adal War, where Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi led a force of 12,000 men to defeat the much larger army of Emperor Dawit II, estimated at 200,000. This battle showcased the effectiveness of matchlock firearms in warfare and marked a pivotal moment in the struggle for control over the Horn of Africa.
events.name: The Battle of Shimbra Kure

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1529, a blood libel incident occurred in Bosen (modern-day Pezinok, Slovakia) against the local Jewish community following the mysterious disappearance of a boy. The unfounded accusations led to the execution of three Jews, only for the boy to be later found alive, having been kidnapped, highlighting the dangers of anti-Semitic hysteria during this period.
events.name: Blood libel against the Jewish community of Bosen

events.enhanced_description: The Flensburg Disputation, held on April 8, 1529, was a theological debate between Lutheran leaders and radical Anabaptists, presided over by Johannes Bugenhagen. This event was significant in the Danish Reformation, marking a clear rejection of more radical reformist ideas and solidifying Lutheran doctrine in the region.
events.name: The Flensburg Disputation

events.enhanced_description: The Westrogothian rebellion broke out on April 9, 1529, in Västergötland, Sweden, as local nobles and peasants rose against the central authority. This uprising reflected the growing discontent with the political and economic pressures imposed by the crown and was part of a broader pattern of regional resistance during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Westrogothian Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On April 19, 1529, the Diet of Speyer convened, where a coalition of German princes and free cities protested against the reinstatement of the Edict of Worms, which had condemned Martin Luther's teachings. This event is considered a foundational moment for the Protestant Reformation, as it marked the formal beginning of the Protestant movement in Germany.
events.name: Diet of Speyer

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Zaragoza, signed on April 22, 1529, established a demarcation line between the Spanish and Portuguese empires in the eastern hemisphere, specifically placing it 297.5 leagues east of the Moluccas. This treaty was crucial in defining colonial territories and reducing conflicts over newly discovered lands.
events.name: Treaty of Zaragoza

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1529, the Ottoman army under Suleiman I departed from Istanbul (Constantinople) to launch another invasion of Hungary, marking a significant escalation in the Ottoman-Habsburg conflicts. This campaign would culminate in the famous Siege of Vienna later that year.

image.caption: Profile portrait of Sultan Suleiman, a painting from the circle of Titian.
image.credit: Circle of Titian — Kunsthistorisches Museum Wien
image.date_qualification: The portrait is dated to the 1530s, after the 1529 campaign; it is contextual portraiture, not a depiction of the invasion.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Ottoman invasion of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: In May 1529, Cardinal Thomas Wolsey opened a legatine court at Blackfriars in London to adjudicate the legality of King Henry VIII's marriage to Catherine of Aragon. The court's proceedings, which lasted until July 16, were pivotal in the eventual English Reformation and the king's subsequent break with the Catholic Church.
events.name: Cardinal Wolsey's legatine court

events.enhanced_description: On August 5, 1529, the Treaty of Cambrai, also known as the Ladies' Peace, was signed between Charles V and Francis I, concluding hostilities in the War of the League of Cognac. Francis I renounced his claims in Italy but retained the Duchy of Burgundy, marking a temporary peace in the ongoing conflicts between France and the Habsburgs.
events.name: Treaty of Cambrai

events.enhanced_description: In September 1529, Sancti Spiritu, the first European settlement in Argentina, was destroyed by local indigenous peoples. This event underscored the challenges faced by European colonizers in establishing and maintaining settlements in the New World.
events.name: Destruction of Sancti Spiritu

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1529, the Ottoman forces successfully recaptured Buda, a significant stronghold in Hungary, during their campaign to expand into Central Europe. This event was part of the larger conflict between the Ottoman Empire and the Habsburgs.
events.name: Recapture of Buda

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Vienna commenced on September 27, 1529, when the Ottoman Turks, commanded by Suleiman the Magnificent, laid siege to the city. This pivotal moment in the Ottoman wars in Europe marked a significant attempt to expand Ottoman influence into Central Europe, ultimately culminating in a failed siege.
events.name: Siege of Vienna

events.enhanced_description: On October 15, 1529, with the siege season coming to an end, Suleiman the Magnificent decided to abandon the Siege of Vienna. This retreat marked a turning point in the Ottoman wars in Europe, as it halted the Ottoman advance into Central Europe for the time being.

image.caption: Engraving of the Siege of Vienna by Bartel Beham.
image.date_qualification: The image date is not provided; the siege took place from 27 September to 15 October 1529.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Abandonment of the Siege of Vienna

events.enhanced_description: On October 26, 1529, Cardinal Thomas Wolsey fell from power due to his inability to secure an annulment of King Henry VIII's marriage to Catherine of Aragon and to manage Habsburg expansion in Europe. His downfall paved the way for Thomas More to succeed him as Lord Chancellor, influencing the course of the English Reformation.
events.name: Fall of Cardinal Wolsey

events.enhanced_description: The first session of the English Reformation Parliament was seated on November 4, 1529, marking a significant step in the legislative process that would lead to the English Reformation. This parliament would address issues related to the Church of England and the king's marital status.
events.name: First session of the English Reformation Parliament

events.enhanced_description: The first session of the Reformation Parliament concluded on December 17, 1529, after addressing various issues concerning the Church and the monarchy. This session was crucial in laying the groundwork for the subsequent changes in English religious and political life.
events.name: End of the first session of the Reformation Parliament

events.enhanced_description: The ducal palace of Celle was constructed in 1530 in what is now Lower Saxony, Germany. This Renaissance-style palace became a significant residence for the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg and is noted for its distinctive architecture.
events.name: Construction of the ducal palace of Celle

events.enhanced_description: In 1530, Austrian forces captured Esztergom, a key city in Hungary, and conducted raids as far as Buda. This military action was part of the ongoing conflicts between the Habsburgs and the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Austrian forces capture Esztergom

events.enhanced_description: In 1530, the renowned scholar Erasmus published 'On Civility in Children' (De Civilitate Morum Puerilium Libellus), a work that became widely popular and translated into multiple languages. This publication emphasized the importance of manners and education in childhood.
events.name: Erasmus publishes On Civility in Children

events.enhanced_description: The first complete edition of the Zürich Bible, translated by Huldrych Zwingli, was published in 1530 by Christoph Froschauer. This translation played a significant role in the Protestant Reformation and the spread of Reformed theology.
events.name: First complete edition of the Zürich Bible

events.enhanced_description: On January 5, 1530, Strasbourg joined the Christliches Burgrecht, a Protestant alliance of Swiss cities. This alliance was significant in the context of the Reformation, as it represented a consolidation of Protestant power in the region.
events.name: Strasbourg joins the Christliches Burgrecht

events.enhanced_description: On January 20, 1530, Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés led a mission to conquer the Kingdom of Michoacán, crossing the Lerma River. This expedition marked a significant step in the Spanish colonization of Mexico, as they advanced into indigenous territories.
events.name: Hernán Cortés leads a group of soldiers across the Lerma river

events.enhanced_description: On January 21, 1530, Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, issued letters from his winter residence in Bologna, inviting members of the Imperial Diet to convene in Augsburg. This meeting was crucial for addressing theological disputes arising from the Reformation.
events.name: Charles V issues letters from Bologna

events.enhanced_description: On February 14, 1530, Tangaxuan II, the last cazonci of the Purépecha Empire, was executed by conquistador Nuño de Guzmán, effectively ending the independence of the Purépecha Empire from Spanish rule. This event marked a significant moment in the Spanish conquest of Mexico.
events.name: Tangaxuan II executed by conquistador Nuño de Guzmán

events.enhanced_description: On February 24, 1530, Charles V was crowned Holy Roman Emperor in Bologna by Pope Clement VII. This coronation solidified his authority and influence over the Holy Roman Empire during a tumultuous period marked by religious conflict.
events.name: Charles V crowned emperor in Bologna

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, 1530, the Grand Master of the Order of St. John of Jerusalem reached an agreement with Charles V regarding the Tribute of the Maltese Falcon. This agreement allowed the Knights to rule over Tripoli and the islands of Malta and Gozo.
events.name: The Tribute of the Maltese Falcon agreement reached

events.enhanced_description: On April 8, 1530, the Imperial Diet convened in Augsburg at the invitation of Charles V to discuss theological issues stemming from the Protestant Reformation. This session was pivotal in shaping the future of Protestantism in the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Imperial Diet opens session at Augsburg

events.enhanced_description: On May 9, 1530, the Kaqchikel people, a Maya tribe in what is now Sacatepéquez, Guatemala, surrendered to Spanish conquistadors. This event marked a significant moment in the Spanish conquest of Central America.
events.name: Kaqchikel people surrender to Spanish conquistadors

events.enhanced_description: On June 25, 1530, the Augsburg Confession was presented to Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor. This document became a foundational text for Lutheranism and was crucial in the development of Protestant theology.
events.name: Augsburg Confession presented to Charles V

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1530, King François I of France married Eleanor of Austria, the daughter of King Philip I of Castile. This marriage was politically significant, strengthening ties between France and the Habsburg dynasty.

locations.name: Basilica of Saint-Denis, Saint-Denis, Île-de-France, France

events.name: François I marries Eleanor of Austria

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1530, the Tetrapolitan Confession, a Protestant confession of faith, was submitted to Charles V on behalf of the southern German cities of Konstanz, Lindau, Memmingen, and Strasbourg. This act represented a unified Protestant stance during the Reformation.
events.name: Tetrapolitan Confession submitted to Charles V

events.enhanced_description: On July 19, 1530, Turkish Ottoman troops attempted to capture the Hungarian town of Nagykörű. According to local legend, the soldiers became lost in a marsh, which protected the city from conquest.
events.name: Turkish Ottoman troops attempt to take Nagykörű

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1530, the formal transfer of Tripoli from Spain to the Knights of Malta was accomplished. This transfer was part of a broader strategy to strengthen the Knights' presence in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Transfer of Tripoli from Spain to the Knights of Malta

events.enhanced_description: On July 30, 1530, Nikolaus Federmann became the acting governor of Klein-Venedig (Little Venice) in what is now Coro, Venezuela. His leadership came during a challenging period for the German colony in South America.
events.name: Nikolaus Federmann becomes acting governor of Klein-Venedig

events.enhanced_description: On August 3, 1530, the Battle of Gavinana resulted in the capture of Florence by Spanish troops under Prince Philibert of Chalon, who was killed in the action. This battle marked the end of the Siege of Florence and the restoration of the Medici family to power.
events.name: Battle of Gavinana

events.enhanced_description: On September 15, 1530, a miraculous portrait of Saint Dominic appeared in Soriano Calabro, Calabria. This event was significant for the local community and contributed to the veneration of Saint Dominic in the region.
events.name: Miraculous portrait of Saint Dominic appears in Soriano

events.enhanced_description: On October 8, 1530, a significant flood engulfed Rome, causing widespread damage and disruption. This natural disaster highlighted the vulnerabilities of the city to extreme weather events.
events.name: Flood engulfs Rome

events.enhanced_description: On October 26, 1530, the Knights of Malta were formally established when the Knights Hospitaller were granted the island of Malta by Charles V. This marked the beginning of a significant chapter in the history of the Knights as they transferred their capital from Mdina to Birgu.
events.name: Knights of Malta formed

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1530, St. Felix's flood struck Zeeland, leading to the loss of a significant portion of the Verdronken Land van Reimerswaal, a reclaimed land area. This catastrophic event contributed to the decline of the city of Reimerswaal, which was heavily impacted by the flooding.
events.name: St. Felix's flood

events.enhanced_description: On November 24, 1530, Tabinshwehti ascended to the throne of the Toungoo dynasty following the death of his father, Mingyi Nyo. His reign marked a significant period in Burmese history, characterized by military expansion and consolidation of power.
events.name: Tabinshwehti succeeds Mingyi Nyo

events.enhanced_description: In December 1530, Martim Afonso de Sousa set out from Lisbon on an expedition to Brazil, aiming to establish Portuguese dominance in the region. This expedition was pivotal in the early colonial history of Brazil.
events.name: Martim Afonso de Sousa's expedition

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of Babur on December 26, 1530, his son Humayun began his reign over the Mughal Empire. Humayun's rule was marked by challenges, including conflicts with Afghan and Rajput rulers, which would shape the future of the empire.
events.name: Humayun starts to rule the Mughal Empire

events.enhanced_description: In February or March 1531, the Battle of Antukyah took place, where Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi of the Adal Sultanate defeated the Ethiopian army. This battle was part of the larger conflict between the Adal Sultanate and the Ethiopian Empire.
events.name: Battle of Antukyah

events.enhanced_description: In April 1531, the Battle of Puná occurred, where Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro defeated the native inhabitants of Puná Island, located off the coast of present-day Ecuador. This battle was part of Pizarro's campaign to conquer the Inca Empire.

image.caption: Retrospective illustration titled “Hernando Pizarro herido en Puná,” depicting Hernando Pizarro wounded at Puná.
image.credit: Fondo Antiguo de la Biblioteca de la Universidad de Sevilla from Sevilla, España — "Hernando Pizarro herido en Puná".
image.date_qualification: Illustration published in 1851; the supplied image_date, 2009-10-01 13:28, is an upload/date metadata value, not the depicted event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Puná

events.enhanced_description: In 1531, Andrea Alciato published 'Emblemata', a collection of emblems that combined images and texts, significantly influencing the genre of emblematic literature in Europe.
events.name: Publication of Emblemata

events.enhanced_description: In 1531, Conquistador Francisco de Montejo claimed Chichen Itza as the capital of Spanish-ruled Yucatán. This marked a significant moment in the Spanish colonization of the region.
events.name: Claim of Chichen Itza

events.enhanced_description: In 1531, Gazi Husrev-beg founded the University of Sarajevo, which was based on Sufi philosophy. This institution played a crucial role in the educational landscape of the region.
events.name: Foundation of the University of Sarajevo

events.enhanced_description: In 1531, Kōpu Lighthouse was completed, serving as a crucial navigational aid for maritime traffic in the Baltic Sea. It is one of the oldest lighthouses in Estonia.
events.name: Completion of Kōpu Lighthouse

events.enhanced_description: In 1531, a severe drought in Henan province, China, combined with a locust swarm, led to extreme famine, forcing many in agricultural communities to resort to cannibalism to survive.
events.name: Drought and famine in Henan

events.enhanced_description: In 1531, Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, abolished the worst abuses of the encomienda system due to pressure from Bartolomé de las Casas, marking a significant step towards reforming colonial practices in the Americas.
events.name: Abolition of abuses in the encomienda system

events.enhanced_description: In 1531, a witch-hunt was conducted in the town of Schiltach, Germany, reflecting the broader European trend of witch trials during this period, driven by superstition and social tensions.
events.name: Witch-hunt in Schiltach

events.enhanced_description: In 1531, the Zástřizl family held the lands of Bohdalice and Pavlovice in present-day Czech Republic, a testament to their influence and power in the region since 1413.
events.name: Zástřizl family's landholdings

events.enhanced_description: On January 15, 1531, the third session of the Reformation Parliament was opened under King Henry VIII. This parliament was crucial in the establishment of the Church of England and the legal framework surrounding the English Reformation.
events.name: Opening of the third session of the Reformation Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1531, a devastating earthquake struck Lisbon, Portugal, resulting in the deaths of more than 30,000 people. The earthquake was followed by a tsunami, causing widespread destruction and significant loss of life.
events.name: 1531 Lisbon earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On February 27, 1531, Lutheran princes in the Holy Roman Empire formed an alliance known as the Schmalkaldic League. This coalition was established to defend their rights and religious freedoms against the Catholic Emperor Charles V.
events.name: Formation of the Schmalkaldic League

events.enhanced_description: On March 28, 1531, the fortress of Mandu, the capital of the Malwa Sultanate, fell to Bahadur Shah of Gujarat as Sultan Mahmúd II and his sons surrendered. This event marked a significant shift in power in the region.
events.name: Fall of Mandu

events.enhanced_description: On March 29, 1544, King Henry VIII granted royal assent to several laws passed by the English Parliament, including the Third Succession Act and the amended Treason Act. This legislative action was part of Henry's efforts to consolidate power and address succession issues.
events.name: Royal assent by King Henry VIII

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1531, Emperor Askiya Musa of the Songhai Empire was assassinated by his brothers after a brief reign of less than two years. Following his death, Askia Mohammad Benkan was enthroned, marking a significant power shift within the empire.
events.name: Assassination of Askiya Musa

events.enhanced_description: On April 16, 1531, the city of Puebla was founded in Mexico. This city became a significant cultural and economic center, known for its colonial architecture and rich history.

image.caption: Palacio de Gobierno del Estado de Puebla in Puebla de Zaragoza, Mexico.
image.date_qualification: A photograph of a government building in Puebla, made long after the city’s 1531 founding; it is a site image, not a depiction of the founding event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Founding of Puebla

events.enhanced_description: On May 18, 1531, the third Dalecarlian rebellion in Sweden was settled on St. Eric's Day at Arboga. King Christian II returned church bells that had been confiscated, a gesture aimed at pacifying the rebellious villages.
events.name: Settlement of the third Dalecarlian rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On May 27, 1531, Minkhaung of Mrauk-U, the Burmese King of Arakan, was killed in a coup d'état orchestrated by the rebellious Governor of Thandwe, Min Pa. This event marked a significant power shift in the region.
events.name: Coup d'état of Minkhaung of Mrauk-U

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1531, the city of San Juan del Río was founded in Mexico. This city played an important role in the region's development and became known for its agricultural and commercial activities.

locations.name: San Juan del Río, Querétaro, Mexico

events.name: Founding of San Juan del Río

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1531, the city of Santiago de Querétaro was founded in Mexico. This city became a significant cultural and historical center, known for its colonial architecture and vibrant community.
events.name: Founding of Santiago de Querétaro

events.enhanced_description: On August 22, 1531, the Battle of Obertyn took place, where Polish forces under Jan Tarnowski defeated Moldavian troops. This victory allowed the Poles to recapture Pokucie, enhancing their influence in the region.
events.name: Battle of Obertyn

events.enhanced_description: On August 26, 1531, Comet Halley reached its perihelion, the point in its orbit where it is closest to the Sun. This event is significant in the study of comets and their periodic appearances.
events.name: Comet Halley achieves its perihelion

events.enhanced_description: On September 15, 1531, the first Parliament of Ireland in over nine years was convened at Kilkea Castle, County Kildare. This session was significant for addressing various legislative matters in the kingdom.
events.name: First Parliament of Ireland in nine years

events.enhanced_description: On September 16, 1531, General Min Pa was formally crowned as King Min Bin of Arakan in Mrauk U, Myanmar. This coronation followed the coup that led to the death of the previous king, Minkhaung.
events.name: Coronation of General Min Pa

events.enhanced_description: On September 24, 1531, King Gustav I Vasa of Sweden married Catherine of Saxe-Lauenburg in Uppsala, marking his first marriage at the age of 35. This union was significant in strengthening political alliances in the region.
events.name: Marriage of King Gustav I Vasa

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Kappel occurred on October 11, 1531, where the forces of Zurich were decisively defeated by the Catholic cantons. This battle also resulted in the death of the prominent Swiss reformer Huldrych Zwingli.
events.name: Battle of Kappel

events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1531, the Battle of Amba Sel took place, where Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi defeated the army of Dawit II, Emperor of Ethiopia. This victory allowed Ahmad to gain control over the southern parts of Ethiopia.
events.name: Battle of Amba Sel

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1531, Christian II's invasion force arrived in Oslo, Norway, as part of his efforts to reclaim the throne of Denmark and Norway. This marked a significant moment in the power struggles of the Scandinavian kingdoms.
events.name: Christian II's invasion of Oslo

events.enhanced_description: On December 9, 1531, the Virgin of Guadalupe is said to have first appeared to Juan Diego at Tepeyac, Mexico City. This event is pivotal in Mexican Catholicism and has profound cultural significance.
events.name: First appearance of the Virgin of Guadalupe

events.enhanced_description: On December 12, 1531, Mary, mother of Jesus, appeared imprinted on the tilmàtli of Juan Diego Cuauhtlatoatzin at Tepeyac, near Mexico City. This miraculous event is celebrated as a cornerstone of Mexican identity and faith.
events.name: Imprint of Our Lady of Guadalupe

events.enhanced_description: In April 1532, the Battle of Quipaipan took place in Peru, where Atahualpa emerged victorious in the civil war against his brother Huáscar, solidifying his power in the Inca Empire.
events.name: Battle of Quipaipan

events.enhanced_description: In 1532, five years after the death of its author, Niccolò Machiavelli, his seminal work 'The Prince' was published. This influential treatise on political power and statecraft has since become a cornerstone of political philosophy.
events.name: Publication of The Prince

events.enhanced_description: In 1532, François Rabelais published 'Pantagruel', a satirical novel that explores themes of humanism and the absurdity of life. This work is part of Rabelais' larger series that critiques contemporary society and institutions.

image.caption: Gustave Doré illustration from a Russian-language edition of Pantagruel.
image.date_qualification: 1901 is the date supplied for the illustration, not the 1532 publication date of Pantagruel.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Publication of Pantagruel

events.enhanced_description: In 1532, King Henry VIII granted a Royal Charter to the Thorne brothers to establish Bristol Grammar School, marking a significant development in education during the Tudor period. This institution would go on to play an important role in the educational landscape of England.

image.caption: Interior of Bristol Grammar School’s Great Hall, showing the high table, north window, entrance and organ.
image.credit: Rwendland — Transferred from en.wikipedia to Commons by Mattbuck using CommonsHelper . Photo by User:Rwendland.
image.date_qualification: A photograph of the school hall during an open day, not a depiction of its 1532 foundation; the hall was built in 1879. Image date: 2003-09-13.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Foundation of Bristol Grammar School

events.enhanced_description: In 1532, Stamford School was founded by William Radcliffe, contributing to the educational development in England during the Renaissance. The school has a long-standing tradition of academic excellence.
events.name: Foundation of Stamford School

events.enhanced_description: In 1532, the Paris Parlement ordered the arrest of the city's beggars, forcing them to work in the sewers while chained together. This harsh measure reflected the social attitudes of the time towards poverty and public order.
events.name: Arrest of Paris beggars

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of the Maule, possibly occurring in 1532, was a significant conflict between the Incas and the Mapuches, as noted by historian Osvaldo Silva. This battle exemplified the resistance of indigenous peoples against Inca expansion.
events.name: Battle of the Maule (possible date)

events.enhanced_description: On January 22, 1532, São Vicente was established as the first permanent Portuguese settlement in Brazil, marking a significant step in the Portuguese colonization of South America.
events.name: Establishment of São Vicente

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1532, 'The Deceived Ones' (Gl'ingannati), a stage comedy written by the Accademia degli Intronati, debuted during the annual carnival festivities in Siena, showcasing the vibrant cultural life of the city.
events.name: Debut of The Deceived Ones

events.enhanced_description: On February 24, 1532, William Warham, the Archbishop of Canterbury, publicly disassociated himself from acts of the English Parliament that undermined papal authority, reflecting the tensions between the Church of England and the Catholic Church.
events.name: William Warham's declaration

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1532, the Supplication against the Ordinaries was presented to King Henry VIII by Thomas More, Speaker of the House of Commons. This event highlighted the growing tensions between the monarchy and the church.
events.name: Supplication against the Ordinaries

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1532, Pope Clement VII abolished the democratic government of the Republic of Florence, establishing a hereditary monarchy under Alessandro de' Medici. This marked the end of a significant era in Florentine history.
events.name: Abolition of the Republic of Florence

events.enhanced_description: On May 13, 1532, Francisco Pizarro landed on the northern coast of Peru, marking a significant moment in the Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire.
events.name: Francisco Pizarro lands in Peru

events.enhanced_description: On May 16, 1532, Sir Thomas More resigned as Lord Chancellor of England, a decision influenced by his opposition to King Henry VIII's separation from the Catholic Church.
events.name: Thomas More resigns as Lord Chancellor

events.enhanced_description: On June 25, 1532, Suleiman the Magnificent led another invasion of Hungary, continuing the Ottoman Empire's expansion into Central Europe.
events.name: Suleiman the Magnificent's invasion of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: On July 23, 1532, the Nuremberg Religious Peace was granted to members of the Schmalkaldic League, allowing them religious liberty and marking a significant step towards religious tolerance in the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Nuremberg Religious Peace

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Güns began on August 5, 1532, as the Ottoman army, led by Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent, attempted to capture the fortified town of Güns (modern Kőszeg) with a massive force of 100,000 troops. Despite being vastly outnumbered, the defenders, consisting of fewer than 800 Croatian soldiers under Nikola Jurišić, mounted a fierce resistance, setting the stage for a significant confrontation in the ongoing conflict between the Ottoman Empire and the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Siege of Güns

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1532, the Duchy of Brittany was absorbed into the Kingdom of France, marking the end of its independence and the consolidation of royal power in France.
events.name: Union of Brittany and France

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Güns concluded on August 30, 1532, when heavy rains and the arrival of reinforcements from Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, forced Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent to retreat. This event marked a significant setback for the Ottoman Empire in their campaign against the Holy Roman Empire, showcasing the resilience of the defenders.
events.name: Failure of the Siege of Güns

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1532, Anne Boleyn was created Marquess of Pembroke by her fiancé, King Henry VIII of England. This elevation in title was a significant step in her rise to power and influence, ultimately leading to her marriage to Henry and her role in the English Reformation.
events.name: Creation of Anne Boleyn as Marquess of Pembroke

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1532, King Min Bin of Arrakan led a substantial invasion force of 12,000 troops into Bengal, India, marking a significant military campaign in the region. This invasion involved a coordinated three-pronged attack and showcased the ambitions of the Burmese monarch during this period.
events.name: Invasion of Bengal by Min Bin

events.enhanced_description: On November 16, 1532, Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro captured Inca emperor Atahualpa in a surprise ambush at Cajamarca, resulting in the slaughter of many of Atahualpa's followers. This pivotal event marked the beginning of Spanish dominance in the Inca Empire, with Atahualpa later offering a ransom of gold for his release.
events.name: Capture of Atahualpa

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1532, the Burmese Army under King Min Bin marched into Dhaka, the capital of Bengal, without facing any resistance. This event marked a significant moment in the expansion of Burmese influence in the region.
events.name: Burmese Army enters Dhaka

events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1532, a fire struck the cathedral in Chambéry, which was then part of the Duchy of Savoy. The fire damaged the Shroud of Turin, believed by many to be the burial cloth of Jesus, but it was subsequently repaired by nuns at the cathedral, preserving its significance.
events.name: Fire at the Cathedral in Chambéry

events.enhanced_description: On December 20, 1532, the first payment for the ransom of Atahualpa was made as gold was delivered to Cuzco to fill a room, marking a crucial moment in the Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire. This payment was part of Atahualpa's desperate attempt to secure his freedom from the Spanish captors.
events.name: First payment for Atahualpa's ransom

events.enhanced_description: In 1533, Spanish explorer Pedro de Heredia founded Cartagena de Indias, which would become a key port city in the Spanish Empire. The city played a crucial role in trade and military operations in the Caribbean and South America.
events.name: Cartagena, Colombia, is founded by Pedro de Heredia

events.enhanced_description: On this date, Thomas Cranmer, the Archbishop of Canterbury, crowned Anne Boleyn as queen consort of England in Westminster Abbey. This event marked a significant moment in the English Reformation and the establishment of the Church of England.
events.name: Cranmer crowns Anne Boleyn as queen consort of England, in Westminster Abbey

events.enhanced_description: In 1533, Pechenga Monastery was founded in the far north of the Grand Duchy of Moscow. It became an important center for the Russian Orthodox Church in the region.

locations.name: Pechenga Monastery, Pechenga, Murmansk Oblast, Russia

events.name: Pechenga Monastery is founded

events.enhanced_description: Between 1533 and 1534, Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent elevated his harem girl Roxelana to the status of his legal wife, a move that significantly influenced the politics of the Ottoman Empire and its court.
events.name: Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent makes Roxelana his legal wife

events.enhanced_description: On January 25, 1533, King Henry VIII of England secretly married Anne Boleyn, marking a pivotal moment in English history that would lead to the English Reformation and the establishment of the Church of England.
events.name: Secret marriage of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1533, Thomas Audley was appointed Lord Chancellor of England, a key position in the Tudor government. His tenure would be marked by significant legal and political changes during the reign of Henry VIII.
events.name: Appointment of Thomas Audley as Lord Chancellor

events.enhanced_description: On February 4, 1533, King Henry VIII summoned the Reformation Parliament, which would play a crucial role in the English Reformation by passing legislation that ultimately led to the establishment of the Church of England.
events.name: Summoning of the Reformation Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1533, King Min Bin of Burma began receiving tributes from local lords in Bengal, reflecting the expanding influence and power of the Burmese monarchy in the region during this period.
events.name: Tributes received by King Min Bin

events.enhanced_description: On February 14, 1533, a treaty recognized the German city of Münster as a Lutheran city, marking a significant moment in the Protestant Reformation and the changing religious landscape of Europe.
events.name: Münster recognized as a Lutheran city

events.enhanced_description: On February 18, 1533, Pope Clement VII granted papal approval to the order of the Clerics Regular of Saint Paul, known as the Barnabites. This approval marked an important development in the Catholic Church's response to the Reformation.
events.name: Papal approval of the Barnabites

events.enhanced_description: On March 30, 1533, Thomas Cranmer was appointed Archbishop of Canterbury, a pivotal role in the English Reformation. His leadership would be instrumental in the establishment of the Church of England and the annulment of Henry VIII's marriage to Catherine of Aragon.
events.name: Thomas Cranmer becomes Archbishop of Canterbury

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1533, the Statute in Restraint of Appeals was given royal assent in England, declaring the king to be the supreme sovereign and prohibiting judicial appeals to the papacy. This legislation was a key step in the English Reformation and the assertion of royal authority over religious matters.
events.name: Statute in Restraint of Appeals

events.enhanced_description: On April 10, 1533, King Frederick I of Denmark died at the age of 61, leaving a power vacuum that led to a succession dispute known as the Count's Feud. His death marked a significant turning point in Danish history, as factions emerged to support different claimants to the throne.
events.name: Death of King Frederick I of Denmark

events.enhanced_description: On May 23, 1533, Archbishop Thomas Cranmer declared the marriage of King Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon annulled. This decision was pivotal in the English Reformation, as it allowed Henry to marry Anne Boleyn and led to a break with the Catholic Church.
events.name: Annulment of Henry VIII's marriage

events.enhanced_description: On June 1, 1533, Spanish explorer Pedro de Heredia founded Cartagena, Colombia, establishing a key port city that would become vital for trade and military operations in the Spanish Empire. The city's strategic location played a significant role in the colonization of the region.
events.name: Foundation of Cartagena, Colombia

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1533, Pope Clement VII excommunicated King Henry VIII of England and Archbishop Thomas Cranmer. This act was a pivotal moment in the conflict between the English crown and the papacy, leading to the establishment of the Church of England.
events.name: Henry VIII is excommunicated by Pope Clement VII, as is Archbishop Cranmer

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1533, the Treaty of Constantinople was signed, marking a significant diplomatic agreement between the Ottoman Empire and the Archduchy of Austria. Ferdinand I renounced his claims to Hungary, allowing János Szapolyai to become King of Hungary under Ottoman suzerainty.
events.name: Treaty of Constantinople between the Ottoman Empire and the Archduchy of Austria

events.enhanced_description: On July 26, 1533, Atahualpa, the last Sapa Inca of the Inca Empire, was executed by garotte on the orders of Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro in Cajamarca. This event marked a significant turning point in the Spanish conquest of Peru.
events.name: Sapa Inca Atahualpa is executed by garotte, at the orders of Francisco Pizarro in Cajamarca

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1533, King François I of France sent Colonel Pierre de Piton to Morocco with a letter to Sultan Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn Muhammad, aiming to establish a trade agreement. This marked an important diplomatic initiative in Franco-Moroccan relations.
events.name: King François of France dispatches Colonel Pierre de Piton to Morocco

events.enhanced_description: On September 7, 1533, Anne Boleyn gave birth to a daughter, Elizabeth, at Greenwich. Elizabeth would later become one of England's most renowned monarchs, reigning for over 44 years.
events.name: Anne Boleyn gives birth to a daughter at Greenwich

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1533, Spanish Colonial Governor Antonio Sedeño and his troops faced an attack from the indigenous Kalinago people in Trinidad. Despite suffering losses, Sedeño managed to defeat the Kalinago and secure Spanish control over the island.
events.name: Antonio Sedeño attacked by the Kalinago people in Trinidad

events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1533, Henry, Duke of Orléans, and Catherine de' Medici were married in Marseille. This union would have significant political implications for France, as Catherine would later become queen consort and mother to several future kings.
events.name: Marriage of Henry, Duke of Orléans and Catherine de' Medici

events.enhanced_description: On November 15, 1533, Francisco Pizarro arrived in Cusco, the former capital of the Inca Empire. His arrival marked the consolidation of Spanish power in Peru following the conquest of the Inca.
events.name: Francisco Pizarro arrives in Cusco, Peru

events.enhanced_description: On December 3, 1533, Ivan IV ascended to the throne as Grand Prince of Muscovy at the tender age of three, following the death of his father, Vasili III. His reign would later see the transformation of Muscovy into a powerful Tsardom.
events.name: Ivan IV succeeds his father Vasili III as Grand Prince of Muscovy

events.enhanced_description: On December 21, 1533, Hernando de Grijalva and his crew became the first Europeans to discover the uninhabited Revillagigedo Islands off the Pacific coast of Mexico, naming one of the islands Isla Santo Tomé.
events.name: Hernando de Grijalva discovers the Revillagigedo Islands

events.enhanced_description: On December 28, 1533, Hernando de Grijalva and his crew discovered Isla de los Inocentes, likely present-day San Benedicto Island. This discovery added to the European knowledge of the Pacific islands.
events.name: Grijalva discovers Isla de los Inocentes

events.enhanced_description: Manco Inca Yupanqui was crowned as Sapa Inca in Cusco, Peru, by Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro, on an unspecified date in 1534, following the death of his brother Túpac Huallpa.
events.name: Crowning of Manco Inca Yupanqui

events.enhanced_description: In 1534, François Rabelais published 'Gargantua', a satirical work that would become a cornerstone of French literature and a significant influence on the Renaissance.
events.name: Publication of Gargantua

events.enhanced_description: In 1534, the first book in Yiddish, 'Mirkevet ha-Mishneh', a Tanakh concordance by Rabbi Asher Anchel, was printed in Kraków, marking a significant development in Jewish literature.
events.name: First book in Yiddish printed

events.enhanced_description: On January 15, 1534, the Parliament of England passed the Act Respecting the Oath to the Succession, which recognized the marriage of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn, legitimizing their children as heirs to the throne. This act was a crucial step in the English Reformation.
events.name: Parliament of England passes the Act Respecting the Oath to the Succession

events.enhanced_description: On February 23, 1534, a group of Anabaptists led by Jan Matthys seized the city of Münster, declaring it The New Jerusalem. They began to exile dissenters and forcibly baptize others, leading to a significant religious conflict.

image.caption: Erhard Schön’s illustration of Münster under siege by Prince-Bishop Franz von Waldeck.
image.date_qualification: Retrospective illustration of the 1534 siege; the saved image date is 1535, not the event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Anabaptists seize Münster and declare it The New Jerusalem

events.enhanced_description: On March 10, 1534, the Portuguese crown divided Colonial Brazil into fifteen donatory captaincies, establishing hereditary titles similar to duchies. This division facilitated the administration and colonization of Brazil.

locations.historical_name: Part of the regions inhabited by indigenous populations in southern South America
locations.name: Buenos Aires

events.name: Portuguese crown divides Colonial Brazil into fifteen donatory captaincies

events.enhanced_description: On March 30, 1534, the Submission of the Clergy Act became law in England, requiring clergy to submit to the king. This act was part of Henry VIII's efforts to consolidate power over the Church of England.
events.name: Submission of the Clergy Act 1533 becomes law in England

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1534, Anabaptist leader Jan Matthys was killed by the Landsknechte during the siege of Münster, which he had predicted would coincide with the Second Coming of Christ. His death led to John of Leiden taking control of the city.

image.caption: Erhard Schön’s illustration of Münster under siege by Prince-Bishop Franz von Waldeck.
image.date_qualification: Illustration dated 1535; depicts events of 1534. It does not specifically document Matthys’s death on 5 April 1534.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Jan Matthys is killed during the siege of Münster

events.enhanced_description: On April 13, 1534, Sir Thomas More testified before a royal commission regarding the Act of Succession. He accepted Parliament's authority but denied the spiritual validity of Henry VIII's marriage to Anne Boleyn, leading to his imprisonment in the Tower of London.
events.name: Sir Thomas More testifies before a royal commission

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1534, French explorer Jacques Cartier began his exploration of Newfoundland while searching for the Northwest Passage. His voyages laid the groundwork for future French claims in North America.

locations.name: St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada

events.name: Jacques Cartier explores Newfoundland

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1534, Jacques Cartier and his crew became the first Europeans to discover the Gulf of St. Lawrence. This discovery was crucial for the future exploration and colonization of Canada.
events.name: Jacques Cartier discovers the Gulf of St Lawrence

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1534, Copenhagen opened its gates to Count Christopher of Oldenburg, leading the army of Lübeck and the Hanseatic League. This event marked a significant moment in the Count's War, influencing the political landscape of Denmark.
events.name: Copenhagen opens its gates to Count Christopher of Oldenburg
