events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1534, Jacques Cartier discovered Prince Edward Island during his explorations of North America. This discovery contributed to the European understanding of the geography of the region.
events.name: Jacques Cartier discovers Prince Edward Island

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1534, Christian III was elected King of Denmark in the town of Rye, marking a significant moment in Danish history as he would go on to establish the Lutheran Reformation in Denmark.
events.name: The Election of Christian III as King of Denmark

events.enhanced_description: On July 7, 1534, Jacques Cartier made the first known contact between Europeans and the indigenous peoples of the Gulf of St. Lawrence, paving the way for future exploration and colonization of Canada.
events.name: First known exchange between Europeans and natives of the Gulf of St. Lawrence

events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1534, Henry VIII granted a Royal Charter to Cambridge University Press, establishing it as the first university press in the world and a significant institution in the history of publishing.

locations.name: Clare College, Cambridge, Cambridgeshire, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Royal Charter granted to Cambridge University Press

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1534, Ignatius of Loyola and six companions took vows in Montmartre, leading to the establishment of the Society of Jesus, known as the Jesuits, which would play a crucial role in the Counter-Reformation.
events.name: Establishment of the Jesuits

events.enhanced_description: On August 26, 1534, Piero de Ponte was elected as the 45th Grandmaster of the Knights Hospitaller, an order known for its military and hospitable roles during the Crusades.
events.name: Piero de Ponte becomes Grandmaster of the Knights Hospitaller

events.enhanced_description: On September 24, 1534, the first of Brazil's capitancias, the Capitancy of Pernambuco, was established, marking a significant step in the Portuguese colonization of Brazil.
events.name: Establishment of the Capitancy of Pernambuco

events.enhanced_description: On October 4, 1534, Martin Luther's complete translation of the Bible into German was offered for sale at the Michaelmas fair in Wittenberg, significantly influencing the spread of Protestantism.
events.name: Martin Luther's Bible offered for sale

events.enhanced_description: On October 13, 1534, Cardinal Alessandro Farnese was elected as Pope Paul III after a conclave, becoming a pivotal figure in the Catholic Church during the Reformation.
events.name: Election of Pope Paul III

events.enhanced_description: The Affair of the Placards on October 17, 1534, was an anti-Catholic protest in France that involved the posting of placards denouncing the Catholic Mass. This event escalated tensions between Catholics and Protestants, contributing to the French Wars of Religion.
events.name: Affair of the Placards

events.enhanced_description: On November 3, 1534, the English Reformation Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy, declaring Henry VIII as the supreme head of the Church of England, a pivotal moment in the English Reformation.

image.caption: Coat of arms of King Henry VIII of England.
image.date_qualification: The image was created or dated 2010-08-26; it does not depict the 1534 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True; Restrictions: insignia

events.name: Act of Supremacy passed

events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1534, the Ottoman army under Suleiman the Magnificent captured Baghdad from the Safavids without a struggle, initiating nearly 400 years of Ottoman rule in Iraq.
events.name: Capture of Baghdad by the Ottomans

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1534, Sebastián de Belalcázar led over 200 Spanish settlers to found what would become Quito, Ecuador, a key city in the Spanish colonization of South America.
events.name: Founding of Quito, Ecuador

events.enhanced_description: On May 19, 1535, French explorer Jacques Cartier set sail for his second voyage to North America, accompanied by three ships and 110 men, including the sons of Chief Donnacona, whom he had previously captured. This expedition aimed to further explore the territories of New France and establish French claims in North America.
events.name: Jacques Cartier's Second Voyage to North America

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1535, William Tyndale was arrested in Antwerp for heresy due to his translation of the Bible into English. He was subsequently imprisoned in Vilvoorde, where he would face trial for his beliefs and translations that challenged the Catholic Church's authority.
events.name: William Tyndale's Arrest

events.enhanced_description: Beginning on June 1, 1535, the Conquest of Tunis by Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, commenced with the destruction of Barbarossa's fleet. This military campaign aimed to reclaim the city from the Ottoman Empire, resulting in significant bloodshed and the massacre of around 30,000 inhabitants.
events.name: Conquest of Tunis

events.enhanced_description: On June 8, 1535, the Battle of Bornholm took place, where the combined fleets of Sweden and Denmark achieved a decisive victory over the Hanseatic navy. This battle was part of the larger conflict between the Scandinavian kingdoms and the Hanseatic League.
events.name: Battle of Bornholm

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1535, Cardinal John Fisher, Bishop of Rochester, was executed for refusing to swear an oath of loyalty to King Henry VIII, which would have recognized the king as the head of the Church of England. Fisher's steadfastness made him a martyr for the Catholic faith.
events.name: Execution of Cardinal John Fisher

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1535, the Anabaptist state of Münster was conquered and disbanded after a prolonged siege. This event marked a significant defeat for the radical Anabaptist movement in the Holy Roman Empire, which sought to establish a theocratic society.
events.name: Münster Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On July 6, 1535, Sir Thomas More was executed for treason after refusing to acknowledge King Henry VIII as the head of the Church of England. More's refusal to separate from the Roman Catholic Church and his steadfast adherence to his faith made him a symbol of resistance against the Reformation.
events.name: Execution of Sir Thomas More

events.enhanced_description: On July 15, 1535, Archdeacon Charles Reynolds, an envoy to James V of Scotland, Charles V, and Pope Paul III, was buried in Rome after dying of malaria. He had been lobbying for the excommunication of King Henry VIII for heresy, reflecting the tensions of the Reformation.
events.name: Death of Archdeacon Charles Reynolds

events.enhanced_description: On August 17, 1535, Pope Paul III issued the papal bull Sublimis Deus, appointing a commission of cardinals and bishops to reform the city of Rome and the Roman Curia. This decree aimed to address spiritual and secular abuses within the Church.
events.name: Papal Bull Sublimis Deus

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1535, Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, became the first person to pass through the newly constructed Porta Nuova in Palermo, celebrating the European conquest of Tunis. This event symbolized the power and reach of the Habsburg Empire in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Charles V at Porta Nuova

events.enhanced_description: On October 2, 1535, Jacques Cartier reached the island in the Saint Lawrence River that would eventually become Montreal. This marked a significant moment in the French exploration of North America and the establishment of French influence in the region.
events.name: Jacques Cartier Reaches Montreal

events.enhanced_description: On October 4, 1535, the first complete English-language Bible was printed in Antwerp, featuring translations by William Tyndale and Myles Coverdale. This monumental work played a crucial role in the spread of Protestantism and the English Reformation.
events.name: First Complete English Bible Printed

events.enhanced_description: On November 1, 1535, Charles V claimed the Duchy of Milan as his inheritance following the death of Francesco II Sforza. This claim was contested by King François I of France, leading to renewed hostilities between France and the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Claim to the Duchy of Milan

events.enhanced_description: On November 30, 1535, Jakob Hutter, the leader of the Hutterites, was arrested along with his wife in Klausen, located in the Tyrol region. They were subsequently imprisoned at the fortress in Bronzolo, reflecting the persecution faced by Anabaptists during this period.
events.name: Arrest of Jakob Hutter

events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1535, the governing body of the Republic of Venice, known as the Consejo de i Diexe, voted to replace the wooden treasury with the Zecca, a new structure featuring stone vaults. This decision marked a significant architectural and political development in the Venetian Republic.
events.name: Replacement of Venice's Treasury

events.enhanced_description: On December 28, 1535, James Atkenhead, the envoy of King James V of Scotland, departed for France to evaluate Mary of Bourbon as a prospective queen consort. This diplomatic mission was part of the broader political maneuvering surrounding royal marriages in Europe.
events.name: James Atkenhead's Envoy to France

events.enhanced_description: On a misty morning in 1536, Robert Pakington, a London merchant and member of Parliament, became the first person in Britain to be murdered with a handgun while walking near his home on Soper's Lane.
events.name: Murder of Robert Pakington

events.enhanced_description: In 1536, Robert Aske met with royal delegates at York, including the Duke of Norfolk, to negotiate the return of Catholic properties and secure safe passage for himself and other representatives to meet King Henry VIII.
events.name: Robert Aske meets royal delegates

events.enhanced_description: During the expedition of Diego de Almagro, Spanish conquistadors defeated a group of Mapuches at the Battle of Reynogücelén in 1536, marking a significant encounter in the Spanish conquest of Chile.
events.name: Battle of Reynogücelén

events.enhanced_description: In 1536, the Takeda Family forces achieved victory over Hiraga Genshin at the Battle of Un no Kuchi, contributing to the ongoing conflicts during Japan's Sengoku period.
events.name: Battle of Un no Kuchi

events.enhanced_description: In 1536, Luis Sarmento was appointed as the Imperial ambassador to Portugal, reflecting the political dynamics of the time between the Holy Roman Empire and Portugal.
events.name: Luis Sarmento appointed ambassador

events.enhanced_description: On January 22, 1536, John of Leiden, Bernhard Knipperdolling, and Bernhard Krechting were executed in Münster for their leadership roles in the Münster Rebellion, a radical Anabaptist uprising that sought to establish a theocratic society. Their deaths marked a significant moment in the suppression of Anabaptism in the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Execution of John of Leiden and others

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1536, King Henry VIII of England suffered a severe injury during a jousting tournament in Greenwich when he fell from his horse, which subsequently fell on him. This incident left him unconscious for two hours and exacerbated his existing health issues, marking a turning point in his reign.
events.name: Henry VIII's jousting accident

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1580, Spanish explorer Juan de Garay founded the first permanent Spanish settlement at the site of Buenos Aires, naming it Santísima Trinidad. This settlement would eventually grow into the modern capital of Argentina, playing a crucial role in Spanish colonial expansion in South America.
events.name: Foundation of Buenos Aires

events.enhanced_description: On February 18, 1536, a Franco-Ottoman alliance was established, allowing French merchants to operate freely within the Ottoman Empire and exempting them from local laws. This agreement significantly enhanced trade relations between France and the Ottomans.
events.name: Franco-Ottoman alliance

events.enhanced_description: On February 25, 1536, Jacob Hutter, the leader of the Anabaptist movement and founder of the Hutterites, was burned at the stake in Innsbruck for heresy. His execution exemplified the harsh repression faced by radical Protestant groups during the Reformation.
events.name: Execution of Jacob Hutter

events.enhanced_description: In March 1536, the first edition of John Calvin's 'Institutes of the Christian Religion' was published in Basel, marking a pivotal moment in the Protestant Reformation. This work laid the foundation for Reformed theology and significantly influenced Christian thought.
events.name: Publication of Calvin's Institutes

events.enhanced_description: On March 8, 1536, Pargalı Ibrahim Pasha, the Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire, was executed after falling out of favor with Hürrem Sultan. His death marked a significant shift in the power dynamics within the Ottoman court.
events.name: Execution of Pargalı Ibrahim Pasha

events.enhanced_description: On March 14, 1536, Ayas Mehmed Pasha was appointed as the new Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire by Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent, following the execution of Pargalı Ibrahim Pasha. This appointment was part of the ongoing political maneuvering within the empire.
events.name: Appointment of Ayas Mehmed Pasha

events.enhanced_description: In April 1536, the Act for Laws & Justice to be ministred in Wales was passed, further integrating the legal system of Wales into that of England. This act was part of the broader efforts to unify the governance of the two regions.
events.name: Legal incorporation of Wales into England

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1536, Malmö surrendered to King Christian III of Denmark during the Count's Feud, a civil war in Denmark and Sweden. This event marked a significant victory for Christian III and solidified his power in the region.
events.name: Count's Feud: Malmö surrenders

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1536, the Reformation Parliament in England passed the Act for the Dissolution of the Monasteries, leading to the closure of numerous religious houses. This act was a crucial step in the English Reformation, allowing Henry VIII to consolidate power and wealth.
events.name: Dissolution of the Monasteries

events.enhanced_description: On May 2, 1536, Anne Boleyn, the second wife of Henry VIII, was arrested on charges of incest, adultery, and treason. Her arrest marked the beginning of a dramatic downfall that would lead to her execution just weeks later.
events.name: Arrest of Anne Boleyn

events.enhanced_description: On May 6, 1536, Incan emperor Manco Inca Yupanqui initiated a revolt against Spanish conquistadors by laying siege to Cuzco, which lasted for ten months. This uprising was part of the broader resistance against Spanish colonial rule in Peru.
events.name: Siege of Cuzco begins

events.enhanced_description: On May 14, 1536, Thomas Cranmer, the Archbishop of Canterbury, declared Henry VIII's marriage to Anne Boleyn null and void. This declaration was a pivotal moment in the English Reformation, facilitating Henry's subsequent marriage to Jane Seymour.
events.name: Cranmer declares marriage null

events.enhanced_description: On May 19, 1536, Anne Boleyn was executed at the Tower of London on charges of treason, adultery, and incest. Her death marked a significant moment in the English Reformation and the tumultuous reign of Henry VIII.
events.name: Execution of Anne Boleyn

events.enhanced_description: On May 23, 1536, the Inquisition was officially implemented in Portugal, aiming to maintain Catholic orthodoxy and suppress heresy. This institution would have a profound impact on Portuguese society and its colonies.
events.name: Implementation of the Inquisition in Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1536, Henry VIII married Jane Seymour, just days after the execution of his second wife, Anne Boleyn. This marriage was significant as Jane would later give birth to Henry's only legitimate male heir, Edward VI.
events.name: Henry VIII marries Jane Seymour

events.enhanced_description: On June 2, 1536, Pope Paul III announced plans to send three legates to key European leaders, including Charles V and François I, in an effort to prevent an outbreak of war in Europe. This diplomatic initiative reflected the Pope's desire to maintain peace during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Papal legation to prevent war

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1536, Cristóbal de Oñate founded San Juan Bautista del Teul in New Spain, contributing to the Spanish colonization efforts in the Americas. This settlement played a role in the expansion of Spanish influence in the region.

locations.name: San Juan Bautista del Teul, Zacatecas, Mexico

events.name: Foundation of San Juan Bautista del Teul

events.enhanced_description: On June 26, 1536, Spanish navigator Andrés de Urdaneta and his companions arrived in Lisbon after completing a westward circumnavigation that began with the Loaísa expedition in 1525. This journey was significant for establishing new maritime routes.
events.name: Urdaneta's circumnavigation completion

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1536, Pedro de Alvarado founded San Pedro Sula in Honduras, furthering Spanish colonial expansion in Central America. This settlement became an important center for trade and agriculture.
events.name: Foundation of San Pedro Sula

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1536, a papal legation consisting of Cardinals met with Emperor Charles V in Savigliano, Italy, on orders from Pope Paul III. This meeting aimed to address tensions in Europe and prevent further conflict.
events.name: Papal legation meets Charles V

events.enhanced_description: On July 21, 1536, the papal legation arrived in Lyon, France, to meet with King François I. This diplomatic mission was part of Pope Paul III's efforts to maintain peace and address the political tensions in Europe.
events.name: Papal legation arrives in France

events.enhanced_description: On July 24, 1536, troops of the Holy Roman Empire invaded France, crossing the Var River from Nice and launching a second force into Picardy. This military action occurred shortly after diplomatic efforts to avoid conflict with the Holy Roman Emperor.
events.name: Invasion of France by Holy Roman Empire

events.enhanced_description: The Count's Feud concluded on July 29, 1536, when Copenhagen surrendered to King Christian III of Denmark. Following the surrender, Christian III took decisive actions to consolidate Protestant reforms in Denmark.
events.name: Surrender of Copenhagen

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Heiligerlee, fought on May 23, 1568, marked a significant early victory for the Dutch rebels against Spanish rule, led by Louis of Nassau, brother of William the Silent. This battle effectively initiated the Eighty Years' War, a protracted conflict for Dutch independence from Spanish control.
events.name: Battle of Heiligerlee

events.enhanced_description: Francis III, Duke of Brittany, died on August 10, 1536, after falling ill following a game of tennis. His secretary, Sebastiano de Montecuccoli, was tortured into confessing to poisoning him and was executed shortly thereafter.
events.name: Death of Francis III, Duke of Brittany

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1536, King James V of Scotland became the first Scottish monarch since 1346 to voluntarily leave his kingdom, sailing from Kirkcaldy to France to meet his future bride, Princess Madeleine of Valois, arriving in Dieppe a week later.

image.caption: Portrait painting of James V of Scotland by Corneille de Lyon.
image.credit: Corneille de Lyon — Weiss Gallery Image
image.date_qualification: Portrait, not a depiction of James V’s departure from Scotland; dated circa 1536 in the saved image metadata.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: James V of Scotland leaves his kingdom

events.enhanced_description: The Pilgrimage of Grace, a significant rebellion against King Henry VIII's church reforms, began on October 1, 1536, in Lincolnshire and quickly spread across Yorkshire and parts of northern England.
events.name: Pilgrimage of Grace begins

events.enhanced_description: On October 6, 1536, English Bible translator William Tyndale was executed by burning at the stake in Vilvoorde, Flanders, for heresy, marking a significant moment in the history of the English Reformation.
events.name: William Tyndale's execution

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1536, barrister Robert Aske emerged as the leader of the Pilgrimage of Grace rebels, who had grown to 9,000 strong, and marched towards York to present their grievances against King Henry VIII.
events.name: Robert Aske leads Pilgrimage of Grace

events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1536, the three negotiators representing Pope Paul III departed France after three months of discussions with representatives of King François I, aiming to negotiate peace between the Holy Roman Empire and France.
events.name: Negotiators of Pope Paul III depart France

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1536, Cardinal Agostino Trivulzio, the envoy of Pope Paul III, filed his report regarding his peace mission to negotiate an agreement between the Holy Roman Empire and France.
events.name: Cardinal Agostino Trivulzio files peace report

events.enhanced_description: On November 26, 1536, the marriage contract between King James V of Scotland and King François I of France was signed at the Château de Blois, despite concerns over the health risks for François' daughter, Madeleine.
events.name: Marriage contract between James V and Madeleine

events.enhanced_description: The Pilgrimage of Grace concluded on December 5, 1536, at Pontefract Castle after Thomas Howard, 3rd Duke of Norfolk, promised to present the rebels' demands to King Henry VIII, including a reprieve for abbeys from dissolution.
events.name: End of the Pilgrimage of Grace

events.enhanced_description: In 1537, Princess Madeleine of Valois married King James V of Scotland in a ceremony at Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris. Tragically, Madeleine's health was already failing, and she died just six months later.
events.name: Marriage of James V and Madeleine

events.enhanced_description: In January 1537, at the Battle of Ollantaytambo, Inca Emperor Manco Inca Yupanqui led his forces to victory against the Spanish led by Hernando Pizarro, marking a significant resistance against Spanish colonization.
events.name: Battle of Ollantaytambo

events.enhanced_description: In 1537, the Ottoman Empire, under the command of Suleiman the Magnificent, launched an invasion of southern Italy, targeting the cities of Otranto and Brindisi. This campaign was part of the broader conflicts between the Ottomans and European powers.
events.name: Ottoman Empire invades southern Italy

events.enhanced_description: In 1537, Spanish conquistadors in what are now Peru and Colombia became the first Europeans to discover the potato, a staple food for indigenous residents. This discovery would later lead to the introduction of the potato to Europe, transforming agriculture and cuisine.
events.name: Spanish conquistadors discover the potato

events.enhanced_description: In 1537, Muhammad Shah, the sultan of the Kashmiri Shah Mir Sultanate, passed away, leading to the ascension of Shams al-Din Shah II. This transition marked a significant moment in the political landscape of Kashmir during the 16th century.
events.name: Death of Muhammad Shah and succession of Shams al-Din Shah II

events.enhanced_description: In 1537, Spanish mutineers from Hernando de Grijalva's expedition are believed to have sighted Kiritimati, also known as Christmas Island. This event is significant in the context of European exploration in the Pacific Ocean.
events.name: Sightings of Kiritimati (Christmas Island)

events.enhanced_description: The city of Bengaluru, known as Bangalore until 2006, was first mentioned in print in 1537. This marks an important moment in the historical documentation of the city, which has since grown into a major urban center in India.
events.name: First mention of Bangalore in print

events.enhanced_description: In 1537, King Christian III of Denmark-Norway initiated the dissolution of monasteries in Norway, including notable religious institutions such as Bakke Abbey and Munkeby Abbey. This event was part of the larger Protestant Reformation movement in Scandinavia.
events.name: Dissolution of Monasteries in Norway

events.enhanced_description: In 1537, two complete translations of the Bible into English were published, based on William Tyndale's earlier work. Myles Coverdale's translation was the first to be printed in England, marking a significant moment in the history of English Christianity.
events.name: Publication of English Bible Translations

events.enhanced_description: In 1537, as part of the English Reformation, King Henry VIII dissolved several religious organizations, including Castle Acre Priory. This event significantly altered the religious landscape of England and led to the redistribution of church lands.
events.name: Dissolution of Monasteries in England

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1537, Alessandro de' Medici, Duke of Florence, was assassinated by his cousin Lorenzino de' Medici, who sought to restore republican rule in Florence but fled to Venice after the act.
events.name: Assassination of Alessandro de' Medici

events.enhanced_description: On January 16, 1537, Bigod's Rebellion, led by Francis Bigod, began with an unsuccessful attempt to seize Scarborough Castle in Yorkshire, reflecting the tensions of Roman Catholics against Henry VIII's Protestant Reformation.
events.name: Bigod's Rebellion begins

events.enhanced_description: On January 19, 1537, most of Bigod's forces were captured by the English Army during a dawn raid at Beverley, Yorkshire. Bigod managed to escape to Mulgrave and later to Cumberland.
events.name: Capture of Bigod's forces

events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1537, Francis Bigod, the leader of Bigod's Rebellion, was captured by the English Army in Cumberland and subsequently imprisoned at Carlisle Castle, where he would later be executed.
events.name: Capture of Francis Bigod

events.enhanced_description: On March 8, 1537, the Spanish conquistadors Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada and his brother Hernán Pérez de Quesada founded Chipatá, marking the establishment of the first settlement in what would become the Spanish colony of Nueva Granada.
events.name: Foundation of Chipatá

events.enhanced_description: Recife was founded by the Portuguese on March 12, 1537, as a strategic port city in Brazil. It became a significant center for trade and cultural exchange, particularly during the Dutch occupation in the 17th century.
events.name: Recife is founded by the Portuguese

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1537, Archbishop Olav Engelbrektsson fled from Trondheim to Lier, Belgium, as part of his efforts to escape the Protestant Reformation sweeping through Norway. His flight marked a significant moment in the struggle between Catholicism and Protestantism in Scandinavia.

image.caption: Memorial plaque for Archbishop Olav Engelbrektsson in St. Gummarus church, Lier, Belgium.
image.credit: Orf3us (changes by Rabanus Flavus ) — File:Fra højalteret i Gummaruskirken i Lier.jpg
image.date_qualification: A later photograph of a memorial plaque at the site associated with his exile and death; it does not depict the 1537 flight. The original image date is given as 2018-06.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Archbishop of Norway flees from Trondheim to Lier

events.enhanced_description: On April 18, 1537, Diego de Almagro successfully charged against Manco Inca's siege of Cuzco, thereby saving the Pizarro brothers from being overthrown. This event was pivotal in the ongoing conflict between Spanish conquistadors and the Inca Empire.
events.name: Diego de Almagro charges Manco Inca's siege of Cuzco

events.enhanced_description: On April 20, 1537, Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada conquered Bacatá, the main settlement of the Muisca Confederation, effectively ending the Confederation in the Colombian Eastern Andes. This conquest was a crucial step in the Spanish colonization of the region.

image.caption: Portrait of Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada, founder of Santafé de Bogotá.
image.credit: Ricardo Gómez Campuzano — Catálogo de Pinturas de la Academia Colombiana de Historia
image.date_qualification: Portrait of Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada, not a depiction of the conquest. The saved catalogue evidence does not establish an image creation date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Spanish conquest of the Muisca: Bacatá is conquered

events.enhanced_description: The siege of Steinvikholm Castle, the former residence of the last Roman Catholic Archbishop of Norway, ended in January 1537 when the Catholic defenders surrendered to Danish commander Tord Roed. This event was significant in the context of the Protestant Reformation in Norway.
events.name: Siege of Steinvikholm Castle ends

events.enhanced_description: On June 2, 1537, Pope Paul III published the encyclical Sublimis Deus, which declared that the natives of the New World were rational beings with souls, and thus must not be enslaved or robbed. This document was significant in the context of European colonialism and the treatment of indigenous peoples.
events.name: Pope Paul III publishes Sublimis Deus

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1537, the Siege of Hamar ended with the arrest of Bishop Mogens Lauritssøn, marking the definitive end of the Catholic rebellion in Norway. This event was a key moment in the Protestant Reformation in the region.
events.name: Siege of Hamar ends

events.enhanced_description: On July 12, 1537, Rodrigo Orgóñez occupied and sacked the Inca center of Vitcos during the battle of Abancay. However, Manco Inca Yupanqui managed to escape and later established the independent Neo-Inca State in Vilcabamba.
events.name: Rodrigo Orgóñez occupies Vitcos

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1537, Ratan Singh ascended to the throne as the new ruler of the Kingdom of Amber following the death of his father, Bhim Singh. This transition marked a significant moment in the history of the Rajput states in India.
events.name: Ratan Singh becomes ruler of Amber

events.enhanced_description: On July 23, 1537, the Third Ottoman–Venetian War commenced as Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent led an invasion of the Republic of Venice. This conflict would last until October 2, 1540, significantly impacting the balance of power in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Third Ottoman–Venetian War begins

events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1537, the Battle of Montemurlo occurred as residents of the former Republic of Florence attempted to overthrow Cosimo I de' Medici. The battle ended in failure, leading to severe reprisals against the republic's supporters.
events.name: Battle of Montemurlo ends in failure

events.enhanced_description: On August 12, 1537, Christian III was crowned as King of Denmark and Norway in Copenhagen. His reign marked significant religious and political changes in both kingdoms, particularly the establishment of Lutheranism.
events.name: Christian III crowned King of Denmark and Norway

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1537, Juan de Salazar de Espinosa founded the city of Asunción, which would become the capital of Paraguay. This establishment played a crucial role in the Spanish colonization of the region.
events.name: Asunción is founded

events.enhanced_description: On August 25, 1537, the Honourable Artillery Company was formed, becoming the oldest surviving regiment in the British Army. This organization has played a significant role in the military history of the United Kingdom.
events.name: Honourable Artillery Company formed

events.enhanced_description: On August 26, 1537, the Ottoman Navy, commanded by Suleiman the Magnificent, began the siege of Corfu. The siege would ultimately be abandoned in September due to an outbreak of plague among the Ottoman troops.
events.name: Siege of Corfu begins

events.enhanced_description: On September 2, 1537, King Christian III appointed Gjeble Pederssøn as Norway's first Lutheran bishop for the Church of Norway, marking a significant shift in the religious landscape of the country during the Reformation.
events.name: Gjeble Pederssøn appointed as Lutheran bishop

events.enhanced_description: On September 12, 1537, King Carlos I of Spain issued a royal decree allowing citizens of the Province of Rio de la Plata to elect a replacement for the late Captain-General Pedro de Mendoza. Domingo Martínez de Irala was subsequently elected, marking a significant moment in colonial governance.
events.name: Royal decree for election in Rio de la Plata

events.enhanced_description: On October 15, 1537, following the baptism of her son Edward VI, Jane Seymour began suffering from puerperal fever, which ultimately led to her death nine days later. Her passing had significant implications for the Tudor dynasty.
events.name: Jane Seymour suffers from puerperal fever

events.enhanced_description: On November 1, 1537, Spanish conquistador Alonso de Cáceres arrived at the Peñol de Cerquín, the mountaintop fortress of King Lempira, an indigenous leader resisting European rule. Lempira's refusal to surrender marked the beginning of a significant conflict.
events.name: Alonso de Cáceres arrives at Peñol de Cerquín

events.enhanced_description: On November 27, 1537, Alfonso d'Avalos, the Marquis of Vasto, entered into a three-month truce with the French Duke of Montmorency to negotiate peace regarding territorial control. This truce was part of the ongoing conflicts in Italy during this period.

image.caption: A printed portrait of Alfonso d’Avalos from Guillaume Rouillé’s Promptuarii Iconum Insigniorum.
image.date_qualification: The portrait was published in 1553, after the 1537 truce; it is not a contemporary depiction of the truce.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Alfonso d'Avalos enters truce with French Duke

events.enhanced_description: On December 9, 1537, Petar Keglević took office as the new Ottoman Governor of Croatia and Slavonia, marking a significant moment in the Ottoman administration of the region.
events.name: Petar Keglević takes office as Ottoman Governor

events.enhanced_description: On December 28, 1537, King François I of France signed the Ordonnance de Montpellier into law, establishing the first system in Europe requiring writers to submit copies of their printed work for government review. This law aimed to regulate the publishing industry and preserve literary works.
events.name: Ordonnance de Montpellier signed into law

events.enhanced_description: In 1538, the Truce of Nice was established, declaring peace between Emperor Charles V and King Francis I of France. This agreement temporarily halted hostilities between the two powers in the context of the ongoing Italian Wars.
events.name: Truce of Nice

events.enhanced_description: The formal wedding of Mary of Guise and King James V of Scotland took place at St Andrews Cathedral in 1538. This marriage was significant for the political alliances between Scotland and France.

image.caption: Portrait of Mary of Guise, attributed to Corneille de Lyon.
image.credit: Attributed to Corneille de Lyon — Google Arts & Culture — fwG2lIrXjB0p6g
image.date_qualification: Circa 1537, as stated in the image metadata; it is not an image of the June 1538 wedding.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Formal wedding of Mary of Guise and King James V

events.enhanced_description: The dissolution of Byland Abbey occurred in 1538 as part of the broader Dissolution of the Monasteries initiated by King Henry VIII. This event marked a significant shift in the religious landscape of England, leading to the redistribution of monastic lands and wealth.
events.name: Dissolution of the Monasteries in England: Byland Abbey is dissolved

events.enhanced_description: In 1538, Michelangelo began his work on the Piazza del Campidoglio, a significant architectural project on the Capitoline Hill in Rome. This design would influence the development of public squares in Europe and is considered a masterpiece of Renaissance architecture.
events.name: Michelangelo starts work on the Piazza del Campidoglio on the Capitoline Hill in Rome

events.enhanced_description: Beginning in 1538, central and southeastern China experienced a decade-long series of severe famines and epidemics, exacerbated by previous grain quota reductions. This crisis significantly impacted the population and economy during the Ming dynasty.
events.name: The first in a decade-long series of severe famines and epidemics sweep central and southeastern China during the Ming dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In 1538, a tsunami inundated fields in Haiyan County, Zhejiang province, flooding them with saltwater and ruining crops. This disaster led to food shortages and forced many residents to resort to foraging for survival.
events.name: In China, a tsunami floods over the seawall in Haiyan County of Zhejiang province

events.enhanced_description: On January 14, 1538, Leonard Grey, the Lord Deputy of Ireland, successfully negotiated a truce in the semi-independent County Laois. This agreement involved local leaders Peter O'Moore and Rory Lysaght, reflecting the complex political dynamics of Ireland during this period.
events.name: Truce in County Laois

events.enhanced_description: On January 31, 1538, General Johann Katzianer of the Holy Roman Empire escaped from trial in Vienna, where he faced charges related to a failed campaign against the Ottoman Empire. He fled to Kostajnica Fortress, where he would later be murdered under orders from Nikola IV Zrinski.
events.name: Escape of General Johann Katzianer

events.enhanced_description: On February 24, 1538, the Treaty of Nagyvárad was signed, establishing peace between Ferdinand I of the Holy Roman Empire and the Ottoman Empire. The treaty recognized John Zápolya as King of Hungary while Ferdinand retained control over the northern and western regions.
events.name: Treaty of Nagyvárad

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1538, Garcia de Noronha was appointed as the new Governor-General of Portuguese India by King João III. He sailed to Goa, marking a significant moment in the administration of Portuguese colonial rule in the region.
events.name: Appointment of Garcia de Noronha

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1538, Sher Shah Suri, formerly the Mughal Empire's Governor of Bihar, declared the founding of the Sur Empire and crowned himself Emperor in a ceremony in Delhi. This marked the beginning of a significant dynasty in Indian history.
events.name: Founding of the Sur Empire

events.enhanced_description: On April 26, 1538, the Battle of Las Salinas took place in Peru, where Francisco Pizarro defeated Diego de Almagro. This victory allowed Pizarro to seize control of Cusco, solidifying Spanish dominance in the region.
events.name: Battle of Las Salinas

events.enhanced_description: On May 9, 1538, Mary of Guise was wed by proxy to King James V of Scotland while she was at the Château de Châteaudun in France, and he was in London. This marriage was politically significant, strengthening ties between Scotland and France.

image.caption: A double portrait of James V of Scotland and his second wife, Mary of Guise, at Falkland Palace.
image.date_qualification: Dated to the 16th century; the supplied date metadata specifies circa 1550, not the proxy wedding date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Proxy wedding of Mary of Guise and King James V

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1538, Mahmud Khan, the 11-year-old nephew of the late Sultan Bahadur Shah, was enthroned as Mahmud Shah III, Sultan of Gujarat. This event marked a continuation of the political lineage in the region.
events.name: Enthronement of Mahmud Shah III

events.enhanced_description: On May 27, 1538, a joint delegation of Lutherans from various German cities arrived in London for discussions with King Henry VIII, Archbishop Thomas Cranmer, and Chief Minister Thomas Cromwell. This meeting highlighted the growing influence of Lutheranism in England.
events.name: Lutheran delegation arrives in England

events.enhanced_description: On June 19, 1538, Bisham Abbey was dissolved as part of the larger Dissolution of the Monasteries initiated by King Henry VIII. This event was part of the English Reformation and led to significant changes in the religious landscape of England.
events.name: Dissolution of Bisham Abbey

events.enhanced_description: On July 17, 1538, the betrothal ceremony of 12-year-old Princess Elisabeth, niece of Charles V, to 17-year-old Prince Sigismund II Augustus took place in Innsbruck. This union was significant for the political landscape of Europe.
events.name: Betrothal of Princess Elisabeth and Prince Sigismund II Augustus

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1538, Spanish conqueror Francisco de Orellana founded the city of Guayaquil in present-day Ecuador, naming it Santiago de Guayaquil. This establishment was crucial for Spanish colonial expansion in South America.
events.name: Founding of Guayaquil

events.enhanced_description: On August 6, 1538, Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada founded Bogotá, now the capital of Colombia. This event marked the establishment of a significant urban center in the Andes region.
events.name: Founding of Bogotá

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1538, Ştefan V Lăcustă was appointed as the new Prince of Moldavia by Ottoman Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent, replacing his uncle Petru Rareș. This appointment was part of the Ottoman Empire's strategy to control the region.
events.name: Appointment of Ştefan V Lăcustă as Prince of Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1538, the Battle of Preveza occurred, where the Ottoman fleet commanded by Hayreddin Barbarossa defeated the Holy League led by Andrea Doria. This victory solidified Ottoman naval dominance in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Battle of Preveza

events.enhanced_description: The last significant volcanic eruption in the Phlegraean Fields began on September 29, 1538, resulting in the formation of a new volcanic cone, Monte Nuovo. This eruption was notable for its impact on the local population and landscape, marking a significant geological event in the region.
events.name: The last significant volcanic eruption in the Phlegraean Fields of Italy begins and lasts one week

events.enhanced_description: The eruption of the Phlegraean Fields concluded on October 6, 1538, after seven days of intense volcanic activity. This eruption resulted in the creation of Monte Nuovo, which stands as a testament to the geological forces at work in this region.
events.name: The eruption of the Italian volcano ends after seven days, having created Monte Nuovo

events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1538, the Universidad Santo Tomás de Aquino was established in Santo Domingo, marking it as the first university in the New World. This institution played a crucial role in the education and cultural development of the Spanish colonies in the Americas.
events.name: The first university of the New World, the Universidad Santo Tomás de Aquino, is founded on the island of Hispaniola in Santo Domingo

events.enhanced_description: The siege of Diu concluded on November 5, 1538, when the combined forces of Gujarat and the Ottoman Empire withdrew from the Portuguese-held city. This event marked a significant moment in the struggle for control over trade routes in the Indian Ocean.
events.name: The siege of the Indian city of Diu ends as the Gujarat and Ottoman forces withdraw from the Portuguese held city

events.enhanced_description: On November 30, 1538, Sucre was founded as Ciudad de la Plata de la Nueva Toledo. This city would later become a significant cultural and political center in Bolivia, reflecting the Spanish colonial influence in the region.
events.name: Sucre, Bolivia, is founded under the name Ciudad de la Plata de la Nueva Toledo

events.enhanced_description: On December 17, 1538, Pope Paul III confirmed the excommunication of King Henry VIII of England from the Roman Catholic Church. This act was a pivotal moment in the English Reformation, solidifying the break between England and the papacy.
events.name: Pope Paul III confirms the excommunication of Henry VIII of England from the Roman Catholic church

events.enhanced_description: In January 1539, during the Toungoo–Hanthawaddy War, the Toungoo forces achieved a decisive victory over the Hanthawaddy at the Battle of Naungyo. This battle was significant in the context of the struggle for control over Burma.

image.caption: Map of Toungoo military campaigns, 1534–1547.
image.date_qualification: Map illustrating campaigns from 1534–1547; the recorded image creation date is 2013-11-03, not the date of the depicted events.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Toungoo–Hanthawaddy War – Battle of Naungyo, Burma

events.enhanced_description: Lutheranism was forcibly introduced into Iceland, despite strong opposition from Bishop Jón Arason, marking a significant moment in the Protestant Reformation's expansion into the Nordic countries.
events.name: Lutheranism introduced into Iceland

events.enhanced_description: The establishment of the first printing press in North America took place in Mexico City, marking a pivotal moment in the dissemination of literature and ideas in the New World.
events.name: First printing press in North America

events.enhanced_description: Teseo Ambrogio published 'Introductio in Chaldaicam lingua, Syriaca atq Armenica', introducing several Middle Eastern languages to Western Europe for the first time, significantly contributing to the field of linguistics and cultural exchange.
events.name: Teseo Ambrogio's publication

events.enhanced_description: The first edition of the Calvinist Genevan Psalter was published, playing a crucial role in the spread of Calvinism and the development of Protestant worship practices.

image.caption: Title page of the 1539 Genevan Psalter, also known as the Huguenot Psalter.
image.date_qualification: Dated 1539; the image depicts the title page of the publication, not the act of publication.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Calvinist Genevan Psalter published

events.enhanced_description: On January 4, 1539, Giannandrea Giustiniani Longo was elected as Doge of the Republic of Genoa, succeeding Giovanni Battista Doria. His leadership would influence the political landscape of Genoa during a period of significant maritime activity.
events.name: Giannandrea Giustiniani Longo is elected to a two-year term as Doge of the Republic of Genoa in Italy

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Toledo was signed on January 12, 1539, between Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, and Francis I of France, establishing a mutual agreement to refrain from forming alliances with England. This treaty was a strategic response to the political shifts following Henry VIII's break with Rome.
events.name: Treaty of Toledo: Charles V and Francis I agree to make no further alliances with England

events.enhanced_description: On February 9, 1539, the first recorded horse race took place at Chester Racecourse, which is recognized as the oldest racecourse still in use in England. This event marked the beginning of a long tradition of horse racing in the country.

image.caption: View of Chester Racecourse from the city walls.
image.credit: No machine-readable author provided. Smurrayinchester assumed (based on copyright claims). — No machine-readable source provided. Own work assumed (based on copyright claims).
image.date_qualification: A 2006 view of the venue, not a photograph of the first race in 1539; the saved image date is identified as an original upload date, not a depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The first horse race is held at Chester Racecourse, the oldest in use in England

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1539, King Henry VIII summoned Parliament to convene, with the session set to begin on April 28. This marked a significant moment in the political landscape of England as the king sought to consolidate his power.
events.name: King Henry VIII of England summons Parliament to meet

events.enhanced_description: On March 2, 1539, Askia Isma'il, the ruler of the Songhai Empire, died after a brief reign. He was succeeded by Askia Ishaq I, marking a transition in leadership during a period of significant political change in West Africa.
events.name: Askia Isma'il, ruler of the Songhai Empire, dies

events.enhanced_description: On March 30, 1539, Canterbury Cathedral surrendered and reverted to its previous status as a college of secular canons. This event was part of the larger context of the English Reformation and the dissolution of monastic institutions.
events.name: Canterbury Cathedral surrenders, reverting to a college of secular canons

events.enhanced_description: On April 17, 1539, Heinrich IV of the House of Wettin ascended to the position of Duke of Saxony following the death of his brother, Georg der Bärtige. His rule would be marked by significant political and religious developments within the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Heinrich IV becomes the new Duke of Saxony

events.enhanced_description: On April 19, 1539, the Treaty of Frankfurt was signed in Frankfurt am Main between Charles V and Philip Melanchthon, representing the Protestant states. This treaty established a 15-month truce, marking a significant moment in the religious conflicts of the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: The Treaty of Frankfurt is signed

events.enhanced_description: On April 28, 1539, the English Parliament convened for the first time since 1536, following a summons by King Henry VIII. This session was significant for the legislative agenda of the Tudor monarchy during a period of religious and political upheaval.
events.name: The English Parliament meets for the first time since 1536

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1539, the English House of Lords established a committee to examine and determine religious doctrine, which eventually led to the formation of the 'Six Articles.' This event was pivotal in shaping the religious landscape of England during the Reformation.
events.name: The English House of Lords creates a committee to examine doctrine

events.enhanced_description: On May 25, 1539, the inaugural declaration of the Protestant Reformation occurred in Leipzig, with Martin Luther present. Duke Henry IV pledged to adopt Lutheranism as the official religion of the Duchy of Saxony, marking a significant moment in the Reformation.
events.name: The inaugural declaration of the Protestant Reformation takes place in Leipzig

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1539, Hernando de Soto landed at Tampa Bay, Florida, with a contingent of 600 soldiers in search of gold. His expedition would lead to significant encounters with Native American tribes and the introduction of pigs to North America.
events.name: Hernando de Soto lands at Tampa Bay, Florida

events.enhanced_description: On June 26, 1539, the Battle of Chausa took place near Buxar, where Sher Shah Suri decisively defeated the Mughal emperor Humayun. This victory allowed Sher Shah to establish the Sur Empire and gain control over much of Mughal territory.
events.name: Battle of Chausa in modern-day Buxar, India

events.enhanced_description: The Six Articles, passed by the Parliament of England, reaffirmed certain Catholic doctrines within the Church of England, reflecting the ongoing tensions between Protestant reformers and traditional Catholic practices during Henry VIII's reign.
events.name: The Six Articles

events.enhanced_description: Lütfi Pasha was appointed Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire by Sultan Suleiman the Great, following the death of Ayas Mehmed Pasha, marking a significant moment in the administration of the empire during its peak.

image.caption: Engraved portrait of Lütfi Pasha by Jean-Jacques Boissard.
image.date_qualification: Retrospective portrait published in 1596, after Lütfi Pasha’s appointment; it is not a contemporary depiction of the appointment.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Lütfi Pasha becomes Grand Vizier

events.enhanced_description: The siege of Castelnuovo commenced under the command of General Hayreddin Barbarossa, as the Ottoman forces sought to reclaim the city from Spanish control. The siege was marked by a significant numerical advantage for the Ottomans, leading to a swift conclusion.
events.name: Siege of Castelnuovo begins

events.enhanced_description: After 19 days of intense fighting, the siege of Castelnuovo concluded with the Ottoman victory, resulting in heavy casualties for the attackers and the execution of the surviving Spanish defenders, including their commander.
events.name: Siege of Castelnuovo ends

events.enhanced_description: King Francis I of France issued the Ordinance of Villers-Cotterêts, which established French as the official language of legal proceedings in France, significantly impacting the administration of justice and the cultural landscape of the nation.
events.name: Ordinance of Villers-Cotterêts

events.enhanced_description: The revolt of Ghent erupted as members of the city's guilds demanded the right to elect their own leaders, challenging the authority of the Spanish-sponsored officials. Within days, the guild leaders gained control of the city.
events.name: Revolt of Ghent begins

events.enhanced_description: Guru Angad Dev was appointed as the second Guru of the Sikhs, succeeding Guru Nanak Dev Ji, and played a pivotal role in the development of Sikhism, including the establishment of the Gurmukhi script.
events.name: Guru Angad Dev becomes Guru

events.enhanced_description: King Henry VIII entered into a marriage contract with Anne of Cleves, marking his fourth marriage. This political alliance was short-lived, as the marriage would be annulled just six months later.
events.name: Henry VIII contracts to marry Anne of Cleves

events.enhanced_description: Joachim II Hector, the Margrave of Brandenburg, became the second Prince-Elector to adopt Lutheranism, marking a significant shift in the religious landscape of the Holy Roman Empire and influencing the spread of Protestantism.
events.name: Joachim II Hector introduces Lutheranism

events.enhanced_description: Abbot Marmaduke Bradley and 31 monks signed the deed surrendering Fountains Abbey to the English Crown, a key event in the Dissolution of the Monasteries under Henry VIII, which led to the significant decline of monastic life in England.

image.caption: Photograph of Fountains Abbey.
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2013-08-04; depicts the later site, not the 1539 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Fountains Abbey surrender

events.enhanced_description: Juan Pardo de Tavera, the Archbishop of Toledo, commenced his role as the Grand Inquisitor of Spain, overseeing the Spanish Inquisition during a period marked by religious intolerance and persecution.
events.name: Juan Pardo de Tavera begins as Grand Inquisitor

events.enhanced_description: In the Spanish colony of Nueva Granada, Spanish conquistador Baltasar Maldonado engaged in a decisive battle against the indigenous Muisca Confederation, led by Tundama, marking a significant conflict in the Spanish conquest of the region.
events.name: Battle of Duitama

events.enhanced_description: Anne of Cleves arrived in England as part of her marriage contract with King Henry VIII, which included a substantial dowry. The marriage would ultimately be annulled just days after the wedding.
events.name: Anne of Cleves arrives in England

events.enhanced_description: Europe experienced a severe heat wave and drought lasting approximately seven months, leading to the drying up of major rivers like the Rhine and Seine. The resulting lack of safe drinking water caused widespread illness and death.
events.name: Heat wave and drought in Europe

events.enhanced_description: Georg Joachim Rheticus published 'De libris revolutionum Copernici narratio prima' in Gdańsk, marking the first printed work on Copernican heliocentrism. This publication played a crucial role in the dissemination of revolutionary astronomical ideas.
events.name: Publication of Copernican heliocentrism

events.enhanced_description: Martin Luther expelled theologian Caspar Schwenckfeld from Silesia, reflecting the growing tensions within the Protestant Reformation. This event underscored the fractious nature of religious reform during this period.
events.name: Martin Luther expels Caspar Schwenckfeld

events.enhanced_description: The musket was introduced into Japan from Europe, marking a significant technological advancement in warfare for the Japanese. This introduction would eventually influence the course of conflicts in Japan.
events.name: Introduction of the musket into Japan

events.enhanced_description: King Henry VIII married Anne of Cleves, his fourth queen consort, in a politically motivated union that lasted only six months before being annulled, highlighting the tumultuous nature of his marital history.
events.name: Henry VIII marries Anne of Cleves

events.enhanced_description: Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, entered Ghent without resistance, effectively quelling the Revolt of Ghent and executing numerous rebels, thus reasserting imperial authority in the region.
events.name: Charles V enters Ghent

events.enhanced_description: Waltham Abbey was the last monastery to be closed as part of Henry VIII's dissolution of the monasteries, marking the end of a significant chapter in English religious history.
events.name: Waltham Abbey closure

events.enhanced_description: Estêvão da Gama was appointed as the new Governor of Portuguese India, overseeing the Portuguese colonial administration during a period of expansion and conflict in the region.
events.name: Estêvão da Gama becomes Governor

events.enhanced_description: On Easter Sunday, the cathedral priories of Canterbury and Rochester were transformed into secular cathedral chapters, marking a significant conclusion to the Dissolution of the Monasteries and the reorganization of ecclesiastical governance in England.
events.name: Transformation of cathedral priories

events.enhanced_description: The first translation of the New Testament into the Icelandic language was completed under the patronage of King Christian III of Denmark. Oddur Gottskálksson's text was meticulously compared to the original Latin, marking a significant moment in Icelandic literature and religious history.
events.name: Printing of the first translation of the New Testament into the Icelandic language

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Kannauj, Sher Shah Suri decisively defeated Mughal Emperor Humayun, leading to the establishment of the Sur Empire in India. This battle marked a significant shift in power dynamics in the Indian subcontinent.
events.name: Battle of Kannauj

events.enhanced_description: Thomas Cromwell, the Chief Minister for King Henry VIII, was arrested during a meeting of the Privy Council in Westminster and charged with treason. His arrest marked the beginning of his downfall, leading to his execution later that year.
events.name: Arrest of Thomas Cromwell

events.enhanced_description: Spanish conquistador Francisco Vázquez de Coronado captured the village of Hawikuh in present-day New Mexico, which was believed to be part of the fabled Seven Cities of Gold. Despite the conquest, Coronado failed to find the legendary riches he sought.
events.name: Capture of Hawikuh by Francisco Vázquez de Coronado

events.enhanced_description: King Henry VIII's marriage to Anne of Cleves, his fourth queen consort, was annulled just six months after their wedding. This annulment was part of Henry's ongoing quest for a male heir and his tumultuous marital history.

image.caption: Portrait of Anne of Cleves, painted by Barthel Bruyn the Younger.
image.date_qualification: circa 1570s; postdates the annulment in 1540
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Annulment of Henry VIII's marriage to Anne of Cleves

events.enhanced_description: Thomas Cromwell was executed for treason on the orders of King Henry VIII, marking a dramatic end to his political career. His execution coincided with Henry's marriage to Catherine Howard, further highlighting the king's tumultuous reign.
events.name: Execution of Thomas Cromwell

events.enhanced_description: Spanish captain García Manuel de Carbajal founded Villa Hermosa de Arequipa in Peru, which would later gain city status by royal decree from Charles V. This establishment played a crucial role in the Spanish colonial presence in the region.
events.name: Founding of Villa Hermosa de Arequipa

events.enhanced_description: Gelawdewos succeeded his father, Lebna Dengel, as Emperor of Ethiopia, continuing the legacy of the Solomonic dynasty. His reign would be marked by efforts to consolidate power and defend against external threats.
events.name: Gelawdewos succeeds as Emperor of Ethiopia

events.enhanced_description: Gibraltar was sacked by the fleet of Barbary pirate Ali Hamet, resulting in the capture of many leading citizens. This event prompted the construction of the defensive Charles V Wall, enhancing the fortifications of the city.
events.name: Sack of Gibraltar by Ali Hamet

events.enhanced_description: Pope Paul III approved the Society of Jesus (Jesuits) through his papal bull Regimini militantis Ecclesiae. This marked the formal establishment of the Jesuits, who would play a significant role in the Counter-Reformation and global missionary work.
events.name: Approval of the Society of Jesus

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Alborán, a Habsburg Spanish fleet commanded by Bernardino de Mendoza defeated an Ottoman fleet led by Ali Hamet. This naval engagement was part of the larger conflict between the Spanish Empire and the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Battle of Alborán

events.enhanced_description: Spanish conquistador Hernando de Soto led an expedition that resulted in the destruction of the fortified village of Mabila, killing the paramount chief Tuskaloosa. This event exemplified the violent encounters between European explorers and Native American tribes.
events.name: Destruction of Mabila by Hernando de Soto

events.enhanced_description: William Whorwood was appointed as the new Attorney General for England and Wales, succeeding Sir John Baker. His appointment came during a tumultuous period in English politics marked by the Reformation.
events.name: William Whorwood becomes Attorney General for England and Wales

events.enhanced_description: Honoré I, Lord of Monaco, reached the age of 19, ending a lengthy period of regency. His coming of age marked a significant transition in the governance of the principality.
events.name: Honoré I reaches the age of 19

events.enhanced_description: Stephen V, Prince of Moldavia, was assassinated by nobles Mihul and Trotsanul amid political intrigue involving his replacement by Petru IV Rareș, who had bribed the Ottoman Sultan for the position. This assassination highlighted the volatile nature of Moldavian politics.
events.name: Assassination of Stephen V of Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: Estêvão da Gama, Governor of Portuguese India, embarked on an expedition from Goa with plans to disrupt Ottoman access to the Indian Ocean by attacking Suez. However, the expedition ultimately failed to achieve its objectives.
events.name: Estêvão da Gama's failed expedition

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1541, Queen Catherine Howard was arrested after revelations of her affairs with Thomas Culpeper and Francis Dereham. Her arrest marked a significant turning point in the Tudor court, leading to her eventual execution.
events.name: Arrest of Catherine Howard

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1541, Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, departed from Algiers, abandoning his army after a failed military campaign. This decision had significant implications for the Spanish Empire's military strategy in North Africa.
events.name: Charles V Departs Algiers

events.enhanced_description: In 1541, Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent ordered the sealing of the Golden Gate in Jerusalem, influenced by a prophecy that the Messiah would enter the city through this gate. This act was part of his broader efforts to fortify Jerusalem and assert Ottoman control over the holy city.
events.name: Ottoman Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent seals off The Golden Gate in Jerusalem

events.enhanced_description: In 1541, Iceland officially adopted Lutheranism as its state religion, marking a significant shift from Catholicism. This transition was largely facilitated by Gissur Einarsson, who played a crucial role in promoting Protestant reforms on the island.

image.caption: Map of Iceland showing the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, tectonic plates, Reykjavik, Thingvellir, and active volcanoes.
image.date_qualification: A geological map of Iceland, not a depiction of the adoption of Lutheranism. Original image date: 1999-05-05.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Iceland adopts the Lutheran faith

events.enhanced_description: In 1541, the renowned cartographer Gerardus Mercator created his first globe, which was a significant advancement in the field of cartography. His innovative approach to map-making laid the groundwork for modern geography and navigation.
events.name: Gerardus Mercator makes his first globe

events.enhanced_description: In 1541, the first complete translation of the Bible into Swedish, known as the Gustav Vasa Bible, was published. This translation played a crucial role in the spread of Lutheranism in Sweden and the development of the Swedish language.
events.name: The first official translation of the entire Bible into Swedish is made, called the Gustav Vasa Bible

events.enhanced_description: In 1541, John Calvin completed the French translation of his seminal work, 'Institutio Christianae religionis', which became known as 'L'Institution chrétienne'. This work was pivotal in shaping Reformed theology and the Protestant Reformation in France.
events.name: John Calvin translates his Institutio Christianae religionis into French, as L'Institution chrétienne

events.enhanced_description: In 1541, Elia Levita's 'Bovo-Bukh', a chivalric romance, was first printed in Venice, marking it as the earliest published secular work in Yiddish. This publication played a significant role in the development of Yiddish literature.
events.name: Elia Levita's chivalric romance, the Bovo-Bukh, is first printed

events.enhanced_description: Leonardo Cattaneo della Volta was elected as the new Doge of the Republic of Genoa, succeeding Giannandrea Giustiniani Longo. His election came during a period of political maneuvering and economic challenges for the republic.
events.name: Election of Leonardo Cattaneo della Volta as Doge of Genoa

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Koriyama, initiated by Amago Haruhisa against the Mōri clan, ended in defeat for the attackers. This battle highlighted the ongoing conflicts among feudal lords in Japan during the Sengoku period.
events.name: Siege of Koriyama

events.enhanced_description: Pedro de Valdivia founded Santiago del Nuevo Extremo, which would later become the capital of Chile. This establishment was a key moment in the Spanish colonization of South America.
events.name: Founding of Santiago del Nuevo Extremo

events.enhanced_description: Petru Rareș reclaimed the title of Prince of Moldavia, overthrowing Alexandru Cornea with the backing of the Ottoman Sultan Suleiman. This event marked a significant shift in Moldavian leadership and Ottoman influence in the region.
events.name: Petru Rareș becomes Prince of Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Suakin, fought on March 8, 1541, was a significant conflict where Portuguese General Estêvão da Gama and his brother Cristóvão led an assault on the Ottoman port city of Suakin. This battle was part of the broader Portuguese efforts to expand their influence in the Red Sea region.
events.name: Battle of Suakin

events.enhanced_description: On March 12, 1541, the Portuguese fortress at Agadir fell to Moroccan general Mohammed al-Shaykh after a 24-day siege. This event marked a significant shift in power dynamics in the region, showcasing the resilience of Moroccan forces against Portuguese colonial ambitions.
events.name: Fall of Agadir

events.enhanced_description: On March 28, 1541, San Francisco de Quito was officially declared a city by a decree from King Charles I of Spain, solidifying its status within the Viceroyalty of Peru. This event was pivotal in the colonial administration of Spanish territories in South America.
events.name: Declaration of Quito as a City

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1541, Francis Xavier departed from Lisbon on a mission to the Portuguese East Indies, marking the beginning of his significant role in the spread of Christianity in Asia. His journeys would later contribute to the establishment of Jesuit missions across the continent.
events.name: Francis Xavier's Departure

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Sahart, fought on April 24, 1541, resulted in the defeat of Ethiopian Emperor Gelawdewos by the forces of Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi. This battle was part of the larger conflict between the Ethiopian Empire and the invading forces from the Adal Sultanate.
events.name: Battle of Sahart

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1541, Spanish explorer Hernando de Soto reached the Mississippi River, which he named the Rio de Espiritu Santo. This discovery was significant for Spanish exploration and expansion in North America, as it opened new territories for exploration and conquest.
events.name: Hernando de Soto Reaches the Mississippi River

events.enhanced_description: On May 23, 1541, Jacques Cartier departed from Saint-Malo, France, on his third voyage to the New World. This expedition aimed to establish a French presence in North America and explore the St. Lawrence River.
events.name: Jacques Cartier's Third Voyage

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1541, King Henry VIII opened the Parliament of Ireland for a session that would last for two years. This event was part of his efforts to consolidate control over Ireland and assert English authority in the region.
events.name: Opening of the Parliament of Ireland

events.enhanced_description: On June 16, 1541, Şehzade Mustafa, the son of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent, was appointed as the new Ottoman Governor of the Amasya region. This appointment was part of the Ottoman Empire's administrative structure to maintain control over its provinces.
events.name: Şehzade Mustafa Appointed Governor

events.enhanced_description: On June 26, 1541, Francisco Pizarro, the Spanish conqueror of the Inca Empire, was assassinated in Lima by supporters of Diego de Almagro II. This assassination was a significant event in the power struggles that followed the conquest of Peru.
events.name: Assassination of Francisco Pizarro

events.enhanced_description: On July 7, 1541, Takeda Shingen overthrew his father, Takeda Nobutora, to become the head of the Takeda clan, which ruled the Kai Province. This power shift marked a significant moment in Japanese feudal history, leading to Shingen's rise as a prominent warlord.
events.name: Takeda Shingen Becomes Head of the Takeda Clan

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1541, Estêvão da Gama departed from Massawa, leaving behind troops under his brother Cristóvão to assist the Ethiopian Emperor against Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi's invasion. This event highlights the Portuguese involvement in the Horn of Africa during the 16th century.
events.name: Estêvão da Gama Departs Massawa

events.enhanced_description: Francisco Vázquez de Coronado reached Quivira on July 29, 1541, and spent twenty-five days there searching for richer kingdoms. He found settled villages and agricultural fields, but no wealth of the kind he sought.

image.caption: A U.S. postage stamp commemorating Coronado’s expedition.
image.credit: U.S. Post Office -- U.S. Bureau of Engraving and Printing — Smithsonian National Postal Museum
image.date_qualification: Commemorative stamp issued in 1940, not a contemporary image of the expedition or its arrival at Quivira.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Coronado’s expedition reaches Quivira

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 1541, the Janissaries of Suleiman the Magnificent besieged Buda, wounding Wilhelm von Roggendorf, who later died from his injuries. This siege was part of the Ottoman Empire's campaign to expand its influence in Central Europe.
events.name: Siege of Buda

events.enhanced_description: On September 9, 1541, Beatriz de la Cueva, the Spanish governor of the colony of Guatemala, was killed in a mudslide caused by Volcán de Agua, which devastated Ciudad Vieja. Her death marked a significant loss in the colonial administration of Guatemala.
events.name: Death of Beatriz de la Cueva

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1541, John Calvin returned to Geneva after three years of exile, where he began to reform the church under a doctrine that would later be known as Calvinism. His return was pivotal in shaping Protestant Reformation in Europe.
events.name: John Calvin Returns to Geneva

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1541, King Charles V of Spain began preparations for a disastrous expedition against the Regency of Algiers, assembling a fleet of 500 ships and 24,000 soldiers at Majorca. This campaign would ultimately fail, highlighting the challenges of military operations in North Africa.
events.name: Charles V Assembles Fleet for Algiers Expedition

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1541, Arequipa was granted its coat of arms through royal decree, symbolizing its importance in the colonial administration of Peru. This act was part of the broader efforts to establish identity and governance in Spanish colonies.
events.name: Royal Decree for Arequipa's Coat of Arms

events.enhanced_description: On October 24, 1541, during the Algiers Expedition, heavy storms struck the Spanish, German, and Italian forces that had surrounded Algiers, leading to significant losses and forcing a retreat. This event underscored the difficulties faced by European powers in their military campaigns in North Africa.
events.name: Algiers Expedition Storm

events.enhanced_description: On November 1, 1541, King Henry VIII was informed of the affair between his queen consort, Catherine Howard, and Thomas Culpeper. This revelation would lead to significant political and personal turmoil within the Tudor court.
events.name: Catherine Howard's Affair Revealed

events.enhanced_description: On November 19, 1541, King Tabinshwehti of Burma led an attack on the Kingdom of Prome with a force of 17,000 troops and 1,400 boats. This military campaign was part of his efforts to consolidate power and expand the Burmese kingdom.
events.name: Tabinshwehti's Attack on Prome

events.enhanced_description: On December 3, 1541, Holy Roman Emperor Charles V returned to Spain, arriving at Cartagena. His return marked the end of a challenging military campaign in North Africa and the beginning of renewed focus on European affairs.
events.name: Return of Charles V to Spain

events.enhanced_description: On December 10, 1541, Thomas Culpeper and Francis Dereham were executed at Tyburn after being convicted of treason for their adulterous affairs with Queen Catherine Howard. Their executions served as a grim reminder of the political dangers within the Tudor court.
events.name: Executions of Culpeper and Dereham

events.enhanced_description: The first recorded contact between Japan and the West occurred when a Portuguese ship, blown off course, landed on Tanegashima, introducing Western influence to Japan. This event marked the beginning of significant cultural exchanges between Japan and Europe.
events.name: First contact of Japan with the West

events.enhanced_description: Bartolomé de las Casas completed his influential work, A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies, which would later be published in 1552. This account provided a critical perspective on the Spanish colonization of the Americas and the treatment of Indigenous peoples.

image.caption: Monument to Bartolomé de las Casas in Seville, Spain.
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2015-04-18; this is not the event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Bartolomé de las Casas completes A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1542, Spanish colonists founded the town of Mérida in the Yucatán Peninsula, after several failed attempts due to resistance from local tribes. This establishment marked a significant step in the Spanish colonization of the region.
events.name: Spanish colonists create the new town of Mérida

events.enhanced_description: On January 16, 1542, the 8th Parliament of Henry VIII convened at Westminster, following a summons issued on November 23 of the previous year. This assembly was crucial for the legislative changes during Henry's reign.
events.name: The 8th Parliament of Henry VIII assembles at Westminster

events.enhanced_description: On January 20, 1542, the first legislature for the Voivode of Transylvania convened in Vásárchely, marking a significant development in the political structure of the region. This assembly was instrumental in shaping the governance of Transylvania.
events.name: The first legislature for the Voivode of Transylvania meets

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1542, Tutul-Xiu, the Mayan ruler of the Maní, arrived at the Spanish settlement of Mérida with food supplies and offered assistance to the Spaniards in their conquest of Yucatán. His support was pivotal for the Spanish in establishing control over the region.
