events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1557, during the Italian War of 1551–1559, Gaspard II de Coligny, the French governor of Picardy, executed surprise attacks on the cities of Douai and Lens, successfully capturing both for France. This military action was part of France's broader strategy to expand its influence in the region.
events.name: Gaspard II de Coligny captures Douai and Lens

events.enhanced_description: On January 13, 1557, Sigismund II Augustus, the King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania, issued an edict against Protestants, influenced by Archbishop Mikołaj Dzierzgowski. This edict reflected the growing tensions between Catholic and Protestant factions in Poland during the Reformation.
events.name: Sigismund II Augustus issues an edict against Protestants

events.enhanced_description: On January 28, 1557, Bayinnaung, the King of Burma and head of the Toungoo dynasty, successfully conquered the Shan States of Mongmit and Hsipaw. This expansion was part of his larger campaign to unify the region under Burmese rule, which was later commemorated with an inscription on the Shwezigon Pagoda Bell.
events.name: Bayinnaung conquers Shan States

events.enhanced_description: On February 4, 1557, Pope Paul IV established the metropolitan archdiocese of Portuguese India, based in Old Goa, thereby separating the Goan diocese from the ecclesiastical province of Lisbon. This move was significant in strengthening the Catholic Church's presence in India during the colonial period.
events.name: Pope Paul IV creates the metropolitan archdiocese of Portuguese India

events.enhanced_description: On February 24, 1557, delegates from Sweden, Finland, and Russia convened in Novgorod to negotiate a treaty aimed at ending the ongoing war between the two empires. This meeting was crucial in shaping the future diplomatic relations in the region.
events.name: Delegates negotiate treaty in Novgorod

events.enhanced_description: In March 1557, the Takeda clan besieged Katsurayama Castle in eastern Japan, leading to its eventual destruction. This siege was part of the Takeda clan's efforts to expand their territory in Shinano Province.
events.name: Takeda clan besieges Katsurayama Castle

events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1557, the Toungoo dynasty forces led by King Bayinnaung captured the capital of the Mongkawng state, Mong Kawng, following the earlier surrender of Mong Yang. This conquest was part of Bayinnaung's campaign to expand his kingdom into the Shan States.
events.name: Burmese conquest of Mong Kawng

events.enhanced_description: On April 2, 1557, the Treaty of Novgorod was formally enacted as delegates from Sweden and Russia participated in a ceremonial act of kissing the cross, a demand by Tsar Ivan IV. This treaty marked a significant step towards peace between the two nations.
events.name: Treaty of Novgorod is put into effect

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1557, Spanish settlers founded the city of Cuenca in present-day Ecuador. This settlement became an important cultural and economic center in the region, reflecting the Spanish colonial expansion in South America.
events.name: Spanish settlement of Cuenca is founded

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, 1557, English aristocrat Thomas Stafford attempted a rebellion against Queen Mary by landing at Scarborough with two ships and 32 followers. He captured Scarborough Castle and proclaimed himself 'Protector of the Realm', challenging the authority of the Queen.
events.name: Thomas Stafford attempts rebellion against Queen Mary

events.enhanced_description: On April 28, 1557, Henry Neville, the 5th Earl of Westmorland, arrived in Scarborough and successfully ended the rebellion led by Thomas Stafford, arresting him and his followers. This swift action restored order and reaffirmed the Queen's authority.
events.name: Henry Neville ends Stafford rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On April 30, 1557, during the Arauco War, Spanish forces led by Governor Francisco de Villagra launched a surprise attack against the Mapuche, commanded by their leader Lautaro, at Mataquito. This battle was part of the ongoing conflict between Spanish colonizers and indigenous peoples in Chile.
events.name: Battle of Mataquito during Arauco War

events.enhanced_description: On May 4, 1557, the Stationers' Company, officially known as the Worshipful Company of Stationers and Newspaper Makers, was granted a royal charter, establishing a monopoly on the English publishing industry. This charter allowed the company to regulate and censor the printing industry for the next 150 years.
events.name: The Stationers' Company is granted a royal charter

events.enhanced_description: On May 23, 1557, the Shwezigon Pagoda Bell, weighing 7,560 pounds, was dedicated in Bagan, Myanmar. Commissioned by King Bayinnaung, the bell bears an inscription commemorating the 16th-century Burmese conquest of the Shan States.
events.name: Dedication of the Shwezigon Pagoda Bell

events.enhanced_description: On May 28, 1557, Thomas Stafford and 32 of his followers were executed by beheading at the Tower of London after being convicted of treason. This event underscored the severe penalties imposed on those who challenged the authority of Queen Mary.
events.name: Execution of Thomas Stafford and followers

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1557, King Philip II of Spain signed a treaty in London with Iacopo VI, restoring him to rule over the Principality of Piombino. This agreement was part of a broader political maneuvering involving Cosimo I de' Medici.
events.name: Treaty signed by King Philip II of Spain

events.enhanced_description: By June 1557, an influenza pandemic, likely originating in China, began to spread across Europe, affecting populations and causing widespread illness. This pandemic would have significant social and health implications for the continent.

image.caption: Map of Europe in 1559.
image.credit: Friedrich Wilhelm Putzger (1849-1913). — F.W. Putzgers Historischer Schul-atlas zur alten, mittleren und neuen geschichte: in 234 haupt- und nebenkarten (from: Internet Archive ) .
image.date_qualification: The map is dated 1559; the source gives Leipzig 1902 as the image date, not the date depicted.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The 1557 influenza pandemic spreads to Europe

events.enhanced_description: On June 7, 1557, Mary I of England allied with her husband, Philip II of Spain, joining him in his military campaign against France. This alliance was part of the larger conflict known as the Habsburg-Valois Wars.
events.name: Mary I of England joins Philip II in war against France

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1557, the New Testament of the Geneva Bible, a Protestant translation into English, was published in Geneva under the supervision of William Whittingham. This translation played a significant role in the spread of Protestant ideas in England.
events.name: Publication of the New Testament of the Geneva Bible

events.enhanced_description: On June 16, 1557, Sebastião I was crowned as the new King of Portugal, just five days after the death of his father, King João III. His ascension marked the beginning of a reign that would be characterized by military campaigns and exploration.
events.name: Sebastião I crowned as King of Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On June 18, 1557, mass executions by burning at the stake resumed in England under Queen Mary, targeting Protestants convicted of heresy. Over five days, 24 individuals were executed, reflecting the intense religious persecution of the time.
events.name: Mass executions of Protestants resume in England

events.enhanced_description: On July 3, 1557, the Stato dei Presidi, a small section of Spanish territory on the Tuscan coast, was created by a treaty between Cosimo I de' Medici and King Felipe II of Spain. This agreement reshaped territorial control in Italy during the period.
events.name: Creation of Stato dei Presidi

events.enhanced_description: On July 24, 1557, King Henri II of France issued the Edict of Compiègne, which mandated the death penalty for Protestants committing various offenses. This edict intensified the persecution of Protestants in France during the Wars of Religion.
events.name: Edict of Compiègne issued by King Henri II of France

events.enhanced_description: In a significant event during the Mughal expansion, Sikandar Shah Suri, the Sultan of the Sur Empire, surrendered the fortress at Mau after a protracted six-month siege by the Mughal Empire. Following his surrender, he was allowed to live in exile, while the Raja of Nurpur faced dire consequences for his allegiance.
events.name: Sikandar Shah Suri surrenders the fortress at Mau

events.enhanced_description: The Colloquy of Worms was convened as a dialogue aimed at addressing the religious disputes between the Catholic Church and the Lutheran reformers. This significant event highlighted the growing tensions of the Reformation period, although it ultimately failed to produce a resolution.
events.name: Colloquy of Worms convenes

events.enhanced_description: Pope Paul IV solidified the Spanish occupation of the Papal States by signing the Peace of Cave-Palestrina with the Duke of Alba, who had amassed troops outside Rome. This treaty was a crucial moment in the power dynamics between the Papacy and Spain during the 16th century.
events.name: Pope Paul IV signs the Peace of Cave-Palestrina

events.enhanced_description: The Colloquy of Worms concluded without reaching a consensus on the theological differences between Catholicism and Protestantism, particularly regarding original sin and justification. This failure underscored the deepening divide within Christianity during the Reformation.
events.name: Colloquy of Worms adjourns without resolution

events.enhanced_description: Mohammed al-Shaykh, the Sultan of Morocco, was assassinated by Ottoman soldiers who had infiltrated his army, following his attempts to forge an alliance with Spain against the Ottomans. His death marked a significant shift in Moroccan politics, leading to the ascension of his son, Abdallah al-Ghalib.
events.name: Assassination of Mohammed al-Shaykh

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of his father, Emperor Go-Nara, Prince Michihito ascended to the throne as Emperor Ōgimachi. This transition marked a continuation of the imperial lineage during a period of significant political and social change in Japan.
events.name: Prince Michihito becomes Emperor Ōgimachi

events.enhanced_description: Mircea the Shepherd assumed leadership in Bucharest, marking a significant moment in the political landscape of Wallachia. His rule would influence the region's governance and relations with neighboring powers.
events.name: Mircea the Shepherd becomes ruler in Bucharest

events.enhanced_description: During the Italian War of 1551–1559, King Henri II of France reached out to Suleiman the Magnificent, requesting the dispatch of Ottoman naval forces to protect the French coast. This diplomatic maneuver highlights the complex alliances and conflicts of the period.
events.name: Henri II of France sends letter to Suleiman the Magnificent

events.enhanced_description: John Knox's controversial work, The First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstruous Regiment of Women, was published anonymously in Geneva, critiquing female rulers and reflecting the tumultuous gender politics of the Reformation period.
events.name: Publication of John Knox's The First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstruous Regiment of Women

events.enhanced_description: English explorer Anthony Jenkinson embarked on a significant journey from Moscow to Astrakhan and Bukhara, becoming the first Englishman to document the changing course of the Amu Darya River, contributing to the understanding of Central Asian geography.
events.name: Anthony Jenkinson's exploration

events.enhanced_description: Queen Elizabeth I of England granted rest and refreshment to pilgrims and travelers at the Holy Well Spring in Malvern, reflecting her support for religious practices and the importance of pilgrimage during her reign.
events.name: Queen Elizabeth I grants rest to pilgrims

events.enhanced_description: A pandemic occurred during this year, impacting populations across Europe, though specific details regarding the disease and its effects are less documented.
events.name: Pandemic

events.enhanced_description: French troops, commanded by Francis, Duke of Guise, successfully captured Calais, marking the end of English territorial claims on the continent. This siege was a pivotal moment in the ongoing conflicts between France and England during the 16th century.
events.name: Siege of Calais

events.enhanced_description: The Livonian War commenced, involving a complex conflict among several powers including Russia, Poland, Sweden, and Denmark, all vying for control over the strategically important region of Livonia. This war would have lasting implications for the balance of power in the Baltic region.
events.name: Livonian War begins

events.enhanced_description: The University of Jena was founded in Thuringia, Germany, marking an important development in the landscape of higher education during the Renaissance. This institution would become a significant center for learning and scholarship in the region.
events.name: University of Jena founded

events.enhanced_description: Takeda Shingen was appointed as the shugo (military governor) of Shinano Province following a successful military campaign, solidifying his power in the region. His leadership would play a crucial role in the ongoing conflicts of the Sengoku period in Japan.
events.name: Takeda Shingen becomes shugo of Shinano Province

events.enhanced_description: During the Arauco War, Spanish forces led by Pedro de Avendaño captured Caupolicán, the Mapuche Gran Toqui, who was leading a revolt against Spanish rule. This event underscored the fierce resistance of the indigenous people against colonial forces.
events.name: Arauco War: Capture of Caupolicán

events.enhanced_description: Duke John founded the city of Pori on the shores of the Gulf of Bothnia, establishing a new settlement that would grow in importance over the years. This founding was part of broader efforts to develop the region during the 16th century.
events.name: Founding of Pori

events.enhanced_description: The siege of Thionville marked a significant military engagement during the Italian Wars, where the French Army, led by Francis, Duke of Guise, initiated an assault on the strategically important fortress held by the Spanish Empire.
events.name: The siege of Thionville

events.enhanced_description: The marriage of Mary, Queen of Scots, to Francis, Dauphin of France, was a politically motivated union that aimed to strengthen the ties between Scotland and France, solidifying their alliance against England.
events.name: Marriage of Mary, Queen of Scots, and Francis, Dauphin of France

events.enhanced_description: The Imperial Diet of the Holy Roman Empire formally recognized Ferdinand I as Holy Roman Emperor, following his proclamation as the successor to his brother Charles V, marking a significant transition in imperial leadership.
events.name: Recognition of Ferdinand as Holy Roman Emperor

events.enhanced_description: An armada from the Ottoman Empire, commanded by Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent at the behest of King Henry II of France, launched an assault on the coastal city of Sorrento, showcasing the complex alliances and conflicts of the period.
events.name: Ottoman attack on Sorrento

events.enhanced_description: The successful siege of Thionville by French forces concluded a two-month military operation, resulting in the recovery of the fortress from Spanish control, significantly impacting the balance of power in the region.
events.name: Siege of Thionville successful

events.enhanced_description: The Ottoman Empire besieged the Spanish garrison at Ciutadella de Menorca, leading to the capture of the town and the enslavement of its surviving inhabitants, illustrating the brutal nature of territorial conflicts during this era.

locations.name: Ciutadella de Menorca, Balearic Islands, Spain

events.name: Siege of Ciutadella de Menorca

events.enhanced_description: On August 8, 1588, the Battle of Gravelines took place, where the Spanish Armada was decisively defeated by the English naval forces. This battle was crucial in thwarting Spain's plans to invade England and marked a turning point in the Anglo-Spanish War.
events.name: Battle of Gravelines

events.enhanced_description: The city of Tartu, the capital of the Bishopric of Dorpat, surrendered to Russian forces, marking a significant territorial gain for Russia during the Livonian War.
events.name: Surrender of Tartu

events.enhanced_description: In a significant event during the Spanish Inquisition, Bartolomé Carranza, the Archbishop of Toledo, was arrested on charges of heresy, reflecting the tensions between religious authority and reformist ideas in Spain.
events.name: Arrest of Bartolomé Carranza

events.enhanced_description: King Sigismund II Augustus appointed an Italian merchant to organize a consolidated postal service in Poland, laying the groundwork for what would become the national postal service, Poczta Polska.
events.name: Establishment of postal service in Poland

events.enhanced_description: On her deathbed, Queen Mary I of England designated her half-sister Elizabeth as her successor, a pivotal moment that would lead to the establishment of Protestantism in England under Elizabeth's reign.
events.name: Mary I designates Elizabeth as successor

events.enhanced_description: The execution of the five Canterbury Martyrs marked the culmination of Queen Mary I's persecution of Protestants, as they were burned at the stake, becoming symbols of the religious strife that characterized her reign.
events.name: Execution of the Canterbury Martyrs

events.enhanced_description: Queen Mary I of England died of uterine cancer at the age of 42, marking the end of her reign and the beginning of a new era under her half-sister Elizabeth, who would shift the religious landscape of England.

image.caption: Tomb of Elizabeth I and Mary I in Westminster Abbey.
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2023-01-12; depicts a later memorial, not the 1558 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Death of Queen Mary I

events.enhanced_description: Shortly after ascending to the throne, Queen Elizabeth I summoned Parliament to Westminster, initiating a legislative agenda aimed at restoring Protestant laws and repealing those enacted during Mary I's reign.
events.name: Elizabeth I summons Parliament

events.enhanced_description: In 1559, John Calvin founded the University of Geneva, which became a center for Reformed theology and education. The university played a pivotal role in the spread of Calvinist thought and the training of Protestant ministers.
events.name: Founding of the University of Geneva

events.enhanced_description: In 1559, John Calvin published the final edition of his seminal work, the Institutes of the Christian Religion, which laid the theological foundations for Reformed Christianity. This work significantly influenced Protestant thought and practice.
events.name: Publication of the Final Edition of Institutes of the Christian Religion

events.enhanced_description: In 1559, Oda Nobunaga successfully secured control over his native province of Owari, marking a significant step in his rise to power during the Sengoku period in Japan. His military strategies and alliances would eventually lead to the unification of Japan.
events.name: Oda Nobunaga Wins Control of Owari

events.enhanced_description: In 1559, Margaret of Parma was appointed as the Governor of the Netherlands, taking over the role from her half-brother, King Philip II of Spain. Her governance would be marked by increasing tensions between the Spanish crown and the Dutch populace.
events.name: Margaret of Parma Becomes Governor of the Netherlands

events.enhanced_description: In 1559, Jean Nicot, the French ambassador to Portugal, introduced tobacco to the French court in the form of snuff, highlighting its medicinal properties. This introduction would lead to the widespread popularity of tobacco in Europe, with nicotine later named in his honor.
events.name: Introduction of Tobacco to the French Court

events.enhanced_description: In 1559, Pope Paul IV promulgated the Pauline Index, an early version of the Index Librorum Prohibitorum, which listed prohibited books. This action reflected the Catholic Church's efforts to control the spread of Protestant ideas and maintain doctrinal purity.
events.name: Promulgation of the Pauline Index

events.enhanced_description: The first generation of the Protestant Reformation is considered complete as various reformers, including Martin Luther, John Calvin, and Huldrych Zwingli, established significant theological and ecclesiastical changes across Europe, challenging the authority of the Roman Catholic Church and leading to the formation of various Protestant denominations.
events.name: Completion of the first generation of the Protestant Reformation

events.enhanced_description: Elizabeth I was crowned in Westminster Abbey, marking the beginning of her reign and the Elizabethan era, which would be characterized by significant cultural and political changes in England.
events.name: Coronation of Elizabeth I

events.enhanced_description: Queen Elizabeth I established the Church of England through the Act of Uniformity and the Act of Supremacy, reinstating the Oath of Supremacy and solidifying the Protestant Reformation in England.
events.name: Establishment of the Church of England

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Gelawdewos of Ethiopia was killed in battle while defending his kingdom against the invasion of Nur ibn Mujahid, marking a significant moment in Ethiopian history as his brother Menas succeeded him.
events.name: Death of Emperor Gelawdewos of Ethiopia

events.enhanced_description: The Westminster Conference of 1559 convened with leading Catholic churchmen and Protestant reformers, aiming to address the religious divisions in England, though it ultimately failed to reach a consensus.
events.name: Westminster Conference 1559

events.enhanced_description: The Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis was a treaty that ended the Italian War of 1551-1559, resulting in France making significant territorial concessions while retaining some key bishoprics and the town of Calais.
events.name: Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis

events.enhanced_description: John Knox returned from exile to Scotland, emerging as a leading figure in the Scottish Reformation and advocating for Protestant reforms against the Catholic establishment.
events.name: John Knox returns to Scotland

events.enhanced_description: Queen Elizabeth I granted royal assent to the Acts of Supremacy and Uniformity, which reinforced her authority as the Supreme Governor of the Church of England and mandated attendance at Anglican services.
events.name: Queen Elizabeth I gives royal assent to Acts of Supremacy and Uniformity

events.enhanced_description: On May 13, 1559, the body of David Joris, a prominent Dutch Anabaptist leader, was exhumed and burned in Basel following his posthumous conviction for heresy. This act symbolized the intense religious conflicts of the Reformation period and the harsh measures taken against dissenters.
events.name: Exhumation and Burning of David Joris

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1559, a Protestant mob, incited by the fiery preaching of John Knox, stormed and sacked St Andrews Cathedral, a significant event during the Scottish Reformation. This act of violence marked a turning point in the struggle between Protestant reformers and the Catholic Church in Scotland.
events.name: Sacking of St Andrews Cathedral

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1559, Philip II of Spain married the 14-year-old Elisabeth of Valois in Madrid, following a proxy marriage earlier that year. This union was politically significant, strengthening ties between Spain and France amidst ongoing tensions.
events.name: Marriage of Philip II of Spain and Elisabeth of Valois

events.enhanced_description: On June 30, 1559, King Henry II of France participated in a jousting tournament at the Place des Vosges, where he suffered a fatal injury from a splintered lance during a match against Gabriel de Lorges, Count of Montgomery. Henry's death led to a significant power shift in France.
figures: Gabriel de Lorges, Count of Montgomery
events.name: Jousting Tournament and Death of Henry II of France

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1559, Francis II ascended to the throne of France following the death of his father, Henry II. His reign was marked by political instability, as factions within the court, particularly the House of Guise and his mother Catherine de' Medici, vied for control.
events.name: Francis II Becomes King of France

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1559, the Articles of Leith were signed in Edinburgh, marking a significant agreement between the Protestant Lords of the Congregation and Mary of Guise, the Roman Catholic regent. This agreement allowed for the practice of Protestantism in Scotland, reflecting the shifting religious landscape.
events.name: Signing of the Articles of Leith

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1559, Pope Paul IV authorized the establishment of the University of Douai, which would later evolve into the University of Lille. This institution played a crucial role in the education of clergy and laypeople during the Counter-Reformation.
events.name: Creation of the University of Douai

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1559, a Spanish missionary colony led by Don Tristán de Luna y Arellano arrived at Pensacola Bay, establishing the oldest European settlement in the mainland United States. This settlement marked the beginning of Spanish influence in the region.
figures: Don Tristán de Luna y Arellano

locations.name: Pensacola, Escambia County, Florida, United States

events.name: Founding of Pensacola

events.enhanced_description: On August 18, 1559, Pope Paul IV passed away at the age of 83 after a four-year papacy marked by his staunch opposition to Protestantism. His death left the papal seat vacant for several months, leading to a significant period of uncertainty within the Catholic Church.
events.name: Death of Pope Paul IV

events.enhanced_description: On September 4, 1559, Dravya Shah established the Gorkha state by defeating local Khadka kings, laying the foundation for what would eventually become the modern nation of Nepal. This event marked the rise of the Shah dynasty in the region.
events.name: Establishment of Gorkha State

events.enhanced_description: On September 5, 1559, the papal conclave convened at the Apostolic Palace in Vatican City to elect a new pope following the death of Pope Paul IV. The conclave lasted for 101 days, reflecting the intense political maneuvering within the College of Cardinals.
events.name: Opening of the Papal Conclave

events.enhanced_description: On September 19, 1559, just weeks after its founding, the Spanish missionary colony at Pensacola was devastated by a hurricane that resulted in significant loss of life and property. The survivors faced famine and attacks, ultimately leading to the abandonment of the settlement in 1561.

locations.name: Pensacola, Escambia County, Florida, United States

events.name: Hurricane Devastation of Spanish Colony

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1559, Francis II was crowned King of France in Reims. The ceremony was marked by a notable incident where the crown was too heavy for him, requiring support from the nobles present.
events.name: Coronation of Francis II of France

events.enhanced_description: On September 25, 1559, at just 12 years old, Petru cel Tânăr (Peter the Younger) was named Prince of Wallachia in Târgoviște following the death of his father, Mircea the Shepherd. His ascension was met with opposition from local boyars, leading to a series of conflicts for control of the principality.
events.name: Peter the Younger Named Prince of Wallachia

events.enhanced_description: On October 24, 1559, the army of Wallachia, supported by Ottoman troops, defeated the boyars at the Battle of Boiani. This victory solidified Petru cel Tânăr's position as the rightful ruler of Wallachia within the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Battle of Boiani

events.enhanced_description: On October 27, 1559, Frederick III was removed from his position as Duke of Legnica by orders of Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor. Following his dismissal, Frederick was placed under house arrest, and his son, Henry XI, was restored to the dukedom.
events.name: Dismissal of Frederick III as Duke of Legnica

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1559, Crichton Castle, the stronghold of the powerful Earl of Bothwell, was besieged and captured by forces led by the Earl of Arran. This event underscored the ongoing power struggles and factional conflicts in Scotland during the Reformation.

image.caption: Retrospective illustration of the ruins of Crichton Castle.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — T Pennant, A Tour In Scotland And Voyage To The Hebrides 1772, London 1774
image.date_qualification: The image is associated with an account published in 1774; the supplied 2012-02-25 image date is not the depicted or original publication date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Siege and Capture of Crichton Castle

events.enhanced_description: On November 6, 1559, the Ottoman Empire concluded its unsuccessful siege of Manama Castle in Bahrain, which had begun on July 2. This failure marked a significant setback in the Ottoman efforts to expand their influence in the Persian Gulf region.
events.name: End of Ottoman Siege of Bahrain

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1559, Giovanni Angelo Medici was elected as the 224th pope, taking the name Pope Pius IV after a conclave lasting nearly four months. His papacy would focus on the Counter-Reformation and the Catholic Church's response to Protestantism.
events.name: Election of Pope Pius IV

events.enhanced_description: The complete Geneva Bible was published in 1560, becoming one of the most significant translations of the Bible during the Protestant Reformation, widely used by English Protestants.
events.name: Publication of the Geneva Bible

events.enhanced_description: In 1560, the Academia Secretorum Naturae was founded in Naples by Giambattista della Porta, marking the establishment of one of the first scientific societies dedicated to the study of natural philosophy.
events.name: Foundation of the Academia Secretorum Naturae

events.enhanced_description: In 1560, Solihull School was founded in the West Midlands of England, becoming one of the oldest schools in the region and contributing to the educational landscape of England.

image.caption: The coat of arms of Solihull School, featuring the motto Perseverantia.
image.date_qualification: The image is a school emblem, not a depiction of the 1560 founding. Its supplied image date is 1882-12-31; the date’s relationship to the emblem is not independently established.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Founding of Solihull School

events.enhanced_description: In 1560, the oldest surviving violin, known as the Charles IX, was crafted in Cremona, Italy, marking an important development in the history of string instruments.
events.name: Creation of the oldest surviving violin

events.enhanced_description: In 1560, the Mongols invaded and occupied Qinghai, a region in present-day China, reflecting the ongoing conflicts and territorial expansions of the Mongol Empire during this period.
events.name: Mongol invasion of Qinghai

events.enhanced_description: The great age of piracy in the Caribbean, often marked by notorious pirates such as Blackbeard and Captain Kidd, begins around this time, leading to significant maritime conflict and cultural impact in the region.
events.name: The great age of piracy in the Caribbean starts around this time

events.enhanced_description: On January 7, 1560, French troops commanded by Henri Cleutin and Captain Corbeyran de Cardaillac Sarlabous engaged the Lords of the Congregation at Pettycur Bay, marking a significant confrontation in the context of the Scottish Reformation and the struggle against French influence in Scotland.
events.name: Battle of Pettycur Bay

events.enhanced_description: In March 1560, Bairam Khan, the prime minister (Vakil) of the Mughal Empire, was forced to retire by Emperor Akbar, marking a significant shift in the power dynamics within the Mughal court.
events.name: Bairam Khan's retirement

events.enhanced_description: On March 7, 1560, a Spanish-led expedition under Juan de la Cerda, 4th Duke of Medinaceli, successfully captured the Tunisian island of Djerba, showcasing the ongoing conflicts between European powers and the Ottoman Empire in the Mediterranean.
figures: Juan de la Cerda, 4th Duke of Medinaceli
events.name: Capture of Djerba

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1560, leaders of the Amboise conspiracy, including Godefroy de Barry, attempted to storm the Château d'Amboise, where the young French king and queen were residing. The conspiracy failed, leading to the execution of La Renaudie and many of his followers.
figures: Godefroy de Barry, seigneur de La Renaudie
events.name: Amboise Conspiracy

events.enhanced_description: On April 15, 1560, Denmark-Norway purchased the Estonian island of Ösel from its last prince-bishop, consolidating its influence in the Baltic region during the Northern Wars.
events.name: Purchase of Ösel

events.enhanced_description: On May 11, 1560, the Ottoman fleet, commanded by Piali Pasha, decisively defeated a large joint European fleet, primarily Spanish, in the Battle of Djerba, sinking about half of its ships and demonstrating Ottoman naval superiority.
events.name: Battle of Djerba

events.enhanced_description: On June 12, 1560, Oda Nobunaga achieved a stunning victory against Imagawa Yoshimoto at the Battle of Okehazama, a pivotal moment that significantly advanced Nobunaga's power and influence in Japan during the Sengoku period.
events.name: Battle of Okehazama

events.enhanced_description: On July 6, 1560, the Treaty of Edinburgh was signed, formally ending the Siege of Leith and resulting in the withdrawal of French troops from Scotland, which significantly altered the political landscape and concluded the Auld Alliance.
events.name: Treaty of Edinburgh

events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1560, during the Livonian War, Russian forces defeated the Livonian Brothers of the Sword at the Battle of Ergeme, leading to the dissolution of the order and a shift in power in the region.
events.name: Battle of Ergeme

events.enhanced_description: On August 17, 1560, the Scottish Reformation Parliament adopted a Protestant confession of faith, rejecting papal authority and marking the beginning of the Scottish Reformation, which led to the disestablishment of Roman Catholicism in Scotland.
events.name: Scottish Reformation Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 1560, a total solar eclipse was observable across Europe, which sparked Tycho Brahe's interest in astronomy, leading to significant advancements in the field.
events.name: Total Solar Eclipse of 1560

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1560, the Duke of Châtellerault and the Earl of Arran commenced a siege of Castle Semple, where Robert Sempill, a Scottish Catholic, resisted the Reformation. The siege escalated with artillery fire beginning on September 23.
events.name: Siege of Castle Semple

events.enhanced_description: On September 29, 1560, Eric XIV ascended to the throne of Sweden following the death of his father, Gustav Vasa, marking the beginning of his reign during a tumultuous period in Swedish history.
events.name: Eric XIV becomes King of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On October 4, 1560, Queen Elizabeth I announced the devaluation of existing coins in England, instructing treasurers to replace them with new currency, a significant economic reform aimed at stabilizing the economy.
events.name: Devaluation of English currency

events.enhanced_description: On October 19, 1560, the siege of Castle Semple concluded after 31 days when the defenders surrendered, marking a significant victory for the forces supporting the Scottish Reformation.
events.name: End of the Siege of Castle Semple

events.enhanced_description: On October 29, 1560, Queen Elizabeth I directed the minting of the first machine-produced coins in England, replacing the traditional hammered coinage, which represented a significant advancement in coin production technology.
events.name: Minting of machine-produced coins

events.enhanced_description: On November 8, 1560, Eloy Mestrelle was authorized to commence the production of new English coinage using machines imported from France, marking a pivotal moment in the evolution of currency production in England.
events.name: Production of new English coinage

events.enhanced_description: On December 5, 1560, Charles IX ascended to the French throne following the death of his brother Francis II, with their mother, Catherine de' Medici, serving as regent during his minority.
events.name: Charles IX becomes King of France

events.enhanced_description: In 1561, the nobility of Harrien-Wierland and the town of Reval (modern-day Tallinn) pledge their allegiance to Sweden, marking a significant shift in power dynamics in the region during the Northern Wars.
events.name: The nobility of Harrien-Wierland swear allegiance to Sweden

events.enhanced_description: In July 1561, during the Arauco War, the despised encomendero Pedro de Avendaño and two other Spaniards are killed, igniting the Second Great Rebellion of the Mapuche against Spanish colonial rule.
events.name: Arauco War: Pedro de Avendaño killed

events.enhanced_description: Merchant Taylors' School was founded in 1561 in the City of London by prominent figures including Sir Thomas White and Sir Richard Hilles. This institution has since played a significant role in the education of many notable individuals throughout its history.
events.name: Merchant Taylors' School founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1561, the first Calvinists settled in England after fleeing persecution in Flanders. Their arrival marked a significant moment in the religious landscape of England, contributing to the development of Protestantism in the region.
events.name: First Calvinists settle in England

events.enhanced_description: The Anglo-Genevan metrical psalter was published in 1561, featuring the Old 100th hymn, which is attributed to William Kethe. This publication played a crucial role in the development of English hymnody and the spread of Calvinist worship practices.
events.name: Publication of the Anglo-Genevan metrical psalter

events.enhanced_description: In 1561, Ruy López de Segura, a Spanish priest and chess player, developed modern techniques of chess playing, which significantly influenced the game. His work laid the foundation for future chess strategies and theories.
events.name: Ruy López de Segura develops modern chess techniques

events.enhanced_description: William Baldwin's 'Beware the Cat', published anonymously in 1561, is recognized as one of the earliest examples of horror fiction in English literature. Although written in 1553, this edition was suppressed, and no copies are known to survive.
events.name: Publication of Beware the Cat

events.enhanced_description: Between 1561 and 1670, a total of 3,229 alleged witches were executed in southwestern Germany, with the majority being burned at the stake. This period reflects the intense witch hunts that characterized early modern Europe.
events.name: Witch executions in Germany

events.enhanced_description: Paolo Battista Giudice Calvi is elected as the new Doge of the Republic of Genoa, a position he holds for only eight months before his untimely death in September 1561.
events.name: Paolo Battista Giudice Calvi elected as Doge of the Republic of Genoa

events.enhanced_description: The Ordinance of Orléans is enacted, temporarily suspending the persecution of Protestant Huguenots in France, reflecting the ongoing religious tensions during the French Wars of Religion.
events.name: The Ordinance of Orléans suspends the persecution of the Protestant Huguenots

events.enhanced_description: Queen Elizabeth I of England summons Spanish Ambassador Álvaro de la Quadra for a private audience to discuss the potential political ramifications of her marrying Robert Dudley, 1st Earl of Leicester.
events.name: Queen Elizabeth summons Spanish Ambassador Álvaro de la Quadra

events.enhanced_description: Lope de Aguirre, a Basque Spanish conquistador, initiates a rebellion against the Spanish Crown, seeking to seize control over large parts of Spanish South America, marking a significant moment in colonial resistance.
events.name: Lope de Aguirre begins rebellion against the Spanish Crown

events.enhanced_description: In a decisive battle at Sarangpur, the Mughal Empire's army, led by General Adham Khan, defeats the Sultanate of Malwa, forcing Sultan Baz Bahadur to flee, thus consolidating Mughal power in the region.
events.name: Mughal Empire defeats the Sultanate of Malwa

events.enhanced_description: Ángel de Villafañe is appointed as the new Governor of Spanish Florida, overseeing the provinces of La Florida and Punta de Santa Elena, which is now known as Parris Island in South Carolina.
events.name: Ángel de Villafañe becomes Governor of Spanish Florida

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, the citizens of Nuremberg report witnessing what appears to be an aerial battle, followed by the sighting of a large black triangular object and a crash outside the city, leading to widespread speculation and intrigue.
events.name: Citizens of Nuremberg witness aerial battle

events.enhanced_description: Diego López de Zúñiga, 4th Count of Nieva, is appointed as the fourth Spanish Viceroy of Peru, taking charge of the administration of most of South America following the death of his predecessor.
events.name: Diego López de Zúñiga becomes Viceroy of Peru

events.enhanced_description: The Edict of 19 April is issued by the regency council for King Charles IX of France, aimed at preventing civil war between Roman Catholics and Protestant Huguenots, reflecting the intense religious conflicts of the time.
events.name: The Edict of 19 April is promulgated

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1561, Philip II declares Madrid as the capital of Spain, a decision that would shape the city's political and cultural landscape for centuries to come.
events.name: Madrid declared the capital of Spain

events.enhanced_description: On June 4, 1561, the spire of Old St Paul's Cathedral in London catches fire, crashing through the nave roof, likely due to a lightning strike. The spire is never rebuilt, marking a significant moment in the cathedral's history.
events.name: Fire at Old St Paul's Cathedral

events.enhanced_description: On June 25, 1561, Francis Coxe, an English astrologer, is publicly pilloried at Cheapside in London, where he confesses to his involvement in 'sinistral and divelysh artes', reflecting the era's tensions surrounding astrology and witchcraft.
events.name: Francis Coxe pilloried in London

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1561, Erik XIV is crowned King of Sweden, marking the beginning of his reign during a tumultuous period in Swedish history characterized by conflicts with Denmark and internal strife.
events.name: Erik XIV crowned King of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On July 12, 1561, Saint Basil's Cathedral in Moscow is completed, becoming an iconic symbol of Russian architecture and a testament to the artistic achievements of the time.
events.name: Saint Basil's Cathedral completed

events.enhanced_description: On August 19, 1561, Mary, Queen of Scots, is denied passage through England upon her return from France, arriving instead at Leith, Scotland, which heightens tensions between her and Elizabeth I.
events.name: Mary, Queen of Scots denied passage through England

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1561, English merchant Anthony Jenkinson arrives in Moscow on his second expedition, marking an important moment in Anglo-Russian trade relations.
events.name: Anthony Jenkinson arrives in Moscow

events.enhanced_description: On September 2, 1561, the Entry of Mary, Queen of Scots into Edinburgh is celebrated as a civic event, but it is overshadowed by religious controversy, reflecting the tensions of the Reformation period.
events.name: The Entry of Mary, Queen of Scots into Edinburgh

events.enhanced_description: An inconclusive three-day debate begins on September 28, 1561, in Maybole, Ayrshire, between Protestant reformer John Knox and Quintin Kennedy, highlighting the ongoing religious disputes in Scotland during the Reformation.
events.name: Debate between John Knox and Quintin Kennedy

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1561, the Siege of Moji in Japan concludes with the defenders successfully retaining their position, marking a significant event in the context of Japanese feudal conflicts.
events.name: The Siege of Moji ends

events.enhanced_description: The Fourth Battle of Kawanakajima, fought on October 18, 1561, was a significant conflict between the warlords Takeda Shingen and Uesugi Kenshin, marking the climax of their long-standing rivalry. This battle is notable for its fierce combat and the tactical prowess displayed by both leaders, ultimately resulting in a victory for Takeda Shingen.
events.name: Fourth Battle of Kawanakajima

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1561, Afonso II Mpemba a Nzinga ascended to the throne of the Kingdom of Kongo following the death of his father, Diogo I Nkumbi a Mpudi. His reign was short-lived, as he was overthrown by his brother Bernardo just a month later, highlighting the political instability within the kingdom.
events.name: Afonso II Mpemba a Nzinga becomes King of Kongo

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Vilnius, concluded on November 28, 1561, marked a pivotal moment during the Livonian War, establishing the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth's influence over Livonia. This treaty not only secured protection for the Livonian estates from Russian aggression but also reaffirmed their traditional privileges.
events.name: Treaty of Vilnius

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1561, Bernardo Mpemba a Nzinga successfully overthrew his brother Afonso II, claiming the throne as King Bernardo I of the Kingdom of Kongo. This event underscored the turbulent political landscape of the kingdom during this period.
events.name: Bernardo Mpemba a Nzinga becomes King Bernardo I

events.enhanced_description: The play 'Gorboduc', written by Thomas Norton and Thomas Sackville, was performed for the first time in 1562 before Queen Elizabeth I. This performance is significant as it is recognized as the first known English tragedy and the first English play to use blank verse.
events.name: Gorboduc performed for the first time

events.enhanced_description: Mughal Emperor Akbar successfully conquered the region of Malwa, leading to the flight of its last Sultan, Baz Bahadur. This conquest was part of Akbar's broader campaign to expand the Mughal Empire across India.
events.name: Mughal conquest of Malwa

events.enhanced_description: Dudley Grammar School was established in England, reflecting the growing emphasis on education during the Renaissance period. This institution would contribute to the educational landscape of England in the years to come.
events.name: Establishment of Dudley Grammar School

events.enhanced_description: Gresham's School received a royal charter, marking its official recognition as an educational institution. This development was part of a broader movement towards formalizing education in England during the 16th century.
events.name: Gresham's School granted royal charter

events.enhanced_description: Fausto Sozzini published 'Brevis explicatio in primum Johannis caput', a work that laid the foundations for Socinianism, a theological movement that emphasized rationalism and the use of reason in religious belief. This publication contributed to the development of modern religious thought.
events.name: Publication of Brevis explicatio

events.enhanced_description: Giacomo Barozzi da Vignola published 'Regola delli cinque ordini d'architettura', which would become one of the most influential architectural texts in history. This work established the principles of classical architecture and influenced generations of architects.
events.name: Publication of Regola delli cinque ordini d'architettura

events.enhanced_description: The Pünte at Wiltshausen, a small hand-operated ferry, was first recorded in 1562. This ferry would later become a historic monument, symbolizing the importance of transportation in the region.
events.name: First recording of the Pünte at Wiltshausen

events.enhanced_description: The Portuguese army faced a devastating defeat at the Battle of Mulleriyawa, where they were outmatched by the Sitawaka forces led by Prince Tikiri Bandara. This battle marked one of the worst defeats for the Portuguese in their colonial endeavors in Sri Lanka.
events.name: Battle of Mulleriyawa

events.enhanced_description: An arsenal in Paris exploded, causing widespread destruction and loss of life. Ambroise Paré documented the event, describing the chaos and devastation that ensued, which shook the city and left many injured or dead.
events.name: Explosion of an arsenal in Paris

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1562, Shane O'Neill of Tír Eoghain presented his case to Queen Elizabeth I at the Palace of Whitehall, where she recognized his status. This meeting was pivotal in the context of Irish-English relations during the Tudor period.
events.name: Shane O'Neill pleads before Queen Elizabeth I

events.enhanced_description: On January 17, 1562, the Edict of Saint-Germain was issued, granting recognition and rights to the Huguenots in France. This edict was a significant step towards religious tolerance during a time of intense conflict between Catholics and Protestants.
events.name: Huguenots recognized under the Edict of Saint-Germain

events.enhanced_description: The Council of Trent reconvened on January 18, 1562, after a decade-long hiatus. This council was crucial in the Catholic Counter-Reformation, addressing issues of church reform and clarifying Catholic doctrine.

image.caption: Painting depicting the Council of Trent, displayed in the Museo del Palazzo del Buonconsiglio, Trento.
image.credit: Laurom — Self-photographed Laurom Taken on 11 November 2009
image.date_qualification: The 2009 date is the photograph date, not the date of the Council or necessarily the painting.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Council of Trent reconvenes

events.enhanced_description: On February 6, 1562, Emperor Akbar of the Mughal Empire married Mariam-uz-Zamani, the daughter of Raja Bharmal of Amber. This marriage was significant for political alliances and cultural integration within the empire.
events.name: Akbar marries Mariam-uz-Zamani

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1562, Catherine of Austria resigned as regent for her grandson, King Sebastian of Portugal, transferring authority to Cardinal Henrique de Aviz. This transition marked a significant shift in the governance of Portugal during a critical period.
events.name: Catherine of Austria steps down as regent

events.enhanced_description: The siege of the Portuguese fort of Mazagan began on February 18, 1562, as the Sultanate of Morocco sought to reclaim control from Portuguese occupiers. This conflict was part of the broader struggle for dominance in the region.
events.name: Siege of Mazagan begins

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1562, over 80 Huguenots were massacred by Francis, Duke of Guise, in Wassy-sur-Blaise, an event that ignited the First War of Religion in France. This brutal act escalated tensions between Catholics and Protestants, leading to widespread conflict.
events.name: Massacre of Huguenots in Wassy

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1562, Prince Abu Abdallah Mohammed II Saadi arrived at Mazagan with a formidable force of 100,000 troops, intensifying the siege against the Portuguese fort. This marked a significant escalation in the conflict between Morocco and Portugal.
events.name: Abu Abdallah Mohammed II Saadi arrives at Mazagan

events.enhanced_description: On March 15, 1562, English merchant Anthony Jenkinson had an audience with Ivan the Terrible in Moscow, marking a significant moment in Anglo-Russian relations. Following this meeting, Jenkinson embarked on a journey through the Grand Duchy of Moscow towards Persia.
events.name: Anthony Jenkinson meets Ivan the Terrible

events.enhanced_description: On March 24, 1562, Portuguese Navy Captain Álvaro de Carvalho arrived at Mazagan with a relief force of 600 troops, aiming to bolster the defenses against the ongoing siege by Moroccan forces. This event was critical in the struggle for control of the fort.
events.name: Álvaro de Carvalho reaches Mazagan

events.enhanced_description: On April 2, 1562, civil war erupted in France as Louis I, Prince of Condé, declared war against the Catholic rulers in retaliation for the massacre of Huguenots in Wassy. This conflict led to significant uprisings and battles throughout the country.
events.name: Civil war breaks out in France

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1562, French navigator Jean Ribault landed in Florida and later established a Huguenot colony at Charlesfort on Parris Island, South Carolina. This event marked an important moment in the French colonization efforts in North America.
events.name: Jean Ribault lands in Florida

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1562, Prince Abdullah of Morocco withdrew his troops from the siege of Mazagan after realizing the Portuguese defenses were too strong to overcome. This decision marked a significant moment in the ongoing conflict between Morocco and Portugal.
events.name: Prince Abdullah withdraws troops

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Rouen was a significant military engagement during the French Wars of Religion, where Claude, Duke of Aumale, led a force of 3,000 troops against the Huguenot stronghold. The siege lasted five months, marked by a retreat in June, followed by a return on July 29 with reinforcements and heavier artillery.
events.name: The Siege of Rouen

events.enhanced_description: Thomas Somerset, an English Catholic printer, was imprisoned at Fleet Prison for translating a prayer by the Cardinal of Lorraine without authorization. His imprisonment lasted over 19 years, highlighting the tensions between religious authorities and freedom of expression during the Reformation.
events.name: Imprisonment of Thomas Somerset

events.enhanced_description: During a dinner at Dunfermline Castle, Mary, Queen of Scots, presented a heart-shaped diamond ring to symbolize goodwill towards Queen Elizabeth I of England. This gesture was intended to foster diplomatic relations and possibly set the stage for a future summit.
events.name: Mary, Queen of Scots, sends a gift to Queen Elizabeth

events.enhanced_description: On the full moon of Waso in the Burmese calendar, King Bayinnaung established a military garrison at Dawei as part of his preparations for an impending attack against the Kingdom of Ayutthaya in Siam. This move was indicative of the ongoing conflicts in Southeast Asia during this period.
events.name: Establishment of an army garrison at Dawei

events.enhanced_description: Fray Diego de Landa, the acting Bishop of Yucatán, infamously ordered the burning of sacred Maya texts, believing them to be idolatrous. This act represented a significant cultural loss and marked a turning point in the Spanish colonial approach to indigenous beliefs.
events.name: Fray Diego de Landa burns Maya sacred books

events.enhanced_description: A severe hailstorm struck Wiesensteig, leading to significant property damage and prompting Mayor Ulrich von Helfenstein to accuse several women of witchcraft. This incident initiated a series of witch trials, resulting in the execution of six women and marking the beginning of a broader witch hunt.
events.name: Hailstorm and witchcraft accusations in Wiesensteig

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Mozhaysk was signed between Denmark and Russia to prevent conflict over the contested Kingdom of Livonia, which is now divided into modern Estonia and Latvia. This treaty exemplified the diplomatic efforts to maintain peace in Northern Europe during a time of territorial disputes.
events.name: Treaty of Mozhaysk

events.enhanced_description: In Bar-sur-Seine, a violent massacre occurred where at least 300 Huguenots were killed by Catholic soldiers following the recapture of the citadel. This brutal act was part of the larger conflict between Catholics and Huguenots during the French Wars of Religion.
events.name: Massacre of Huguenots in Bar-sur-Seine

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Hampton Court was a significant agreement between Queen Elizabeth I of England and Huguenot leader Louis, Prince of Condé, aimed at providing military support to the Huguenots in their struggle against the French Crown. This treaty underscored the political alliances formed during the French Wars of Religion.

locations.name: Hampton Court Palace, East Molesey, Surrey, England

events.name: Treaty of Hampton Court

events.enhanced_description: Maximilian II succeeded his father, Ferdinand I, as the ruler of the Kingdom of Bohemia, marking a significant transition in leadership during the Habsburg dynasty. His reign would influence the political landscape of Central Europe during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Maximilian becomes ruler of Bohemia

events.enhanced_description: In October, privateer John Hawkins embarked on his first slave trading voyage, attacking Portuguese ships off the West African coast. He forcibly transported enslaved Africans to Spanish colonies, violating Spanish law and marking a dark chapter in the history of transatlantic slavery.
events.name: John Hawkins' slave trading voyage

events.enhanced_description: Under the command of Ambrose Dudley, 3rd Earl of Warwick, English forces landed at Le Havre to support the Huguenots against the French Crown. This military intervention was part of the broader conflict of the French Wars of Religion, reflecting England's interest in French affairs.
events.name: English forces land at Le Havre

events.enhanced_description: The La Herradura naval disaster occurred when a storm sank twenty-five ships anchored in the bay, resulting in the deaths of at least 3,000 people. This tragic event highlighted the dangers faced by maritime vessels during the period and had significant implications for naval operations.
events.name: La Herradura naval disaster

events.enhanced_description: Royalist forces led by Antoine de Bourbon captured Rouen, a pivotal moment in the French Wars of Religion. Tragically, Bourbon was mortally wounded during the assault, marking a significant loss for the Royalist cause.
events.name: Capture of Rouen by Royalist forces

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Corrichie was a decisive conflict in Scotland where the rebellion led by George Gordon, Earl of Huntly, was crushed by the forces of James Stewart, Earl of Moray. This battle underscored the ongoing power struggles within Scotland during the Reformation.
events.name: Battle of Corrichie

events.enhanced_description: Maximilian II was elected King of the Romans, a title that signified his role as the heir to the Holy Roman Empire. His election was a pivotal moment in the political landscape of Europe, influencing the Habsburg dynasty's future.
events.name: Maximilian elected King of the Romans

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Dreux was a significant engagement during the French Wars of Religion, where Huguenot and Catholic forces clashed in a bloody confrontation. The battle ended with a narrow victory for the Catholics, and both sides suffered heavy casualties, including the capture of their leaders.
events.name: Battle of Dreux

events.enhanced_description: The Instituto Bancario San Paolo di Torino was established as a significant financial institution in Italy, contributing to the development of banking and finance in the region. It later became part of the larger Sanpaolo IMI group, playing a crucial role in the Italian banking sector.
events.name: Instituto Bancario San Paolo di Torino founded

events.enhanced_description: At the young age of 14, Sarsa Dengel ascended to the throne of Ethiopia, following the death of his father, Menas. His reign would be marked by efforts to consolidate power and navigate the complex political landscape of the region.
events.name: Sarsa Dengel becomes Emperor of Ethiopia

events.enhanced_description: Francis, Duke of Guise, a prominent figure in the French Wars of Religion, was assassinated by Jean de Poltrot while besieging Orléans. This event significantly impacted the power dynamics in France during a tumultuous period of religious conflict.

image.caption: Portrait of François I de Lorraine, Duke of Guise, by Marc Duval.
image.date_qualification: The image date supplied is an upload date (12 April 2010), not the date the portrait was created; no depicted date is established.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Assassination of Francis, Duke of Guise

events.enhanced_description: The Edict of Amboise was signed at the Château d'Amboise, granting limited toleration to Huguenots in France and officially ending the first phase of the French Wars of Religion. This agreement was a significant step towards religious coexistence in a divided nation.
events.name: Signing of the Edict of Amboise

events.enhanced_description: The English galleon HMS Grehound tragically sank off the coast of Rye after striking a sandbar, resulting in the loss of all hands, including Admiral John Malyn. This incident highlighted the perils of naval warfare during the period.
events.name: Sinking of HMS Grehound

events.enhanced_description: Queen Elizabeth I granted royal assent to several significant laws, including the Highways Act and the Witchcraft Act, reflecting her administration's efforts to address social issues and consolidate power. These laws had lasting impacts on English society.
events.name: Royal assent by Queen Elizabeth I

events.enhanced_description: The cornerstone for El Escorial, a monumental royal palace and monastery, was laid, marking the beginning of a grand architectural project that would take over two decades to complete. This site became a symbol of Spanish power and religious devotion.

locations.name: San Lorenzo de El Escorial, Community of Madrid, Spain

events.name: Laying of the cornerstone for El Escorial

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Yudokoru was a significant conflict in Japan where Takanobu Takeda achieved a decisive victory over the shogun Toyokazu Yamana. This battle exemplified the ongoing power struggles during Japan's feudal period.
events.name: Battle of Yudokoru

events.enhanced_description: Elizabeth College was founded in Guernsey by order of Queen Elizabeth I, marking a significant development in education on the island. The college has since played a vital role in the educational landscape of the region.

image.caption: Photograph of Elizabeth College’s gatehouse and surrounding buildings in St. Peter Port, Guernsey.
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2021-09-06; not contemporaneous with the 1563 founding.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Founding of Elizabeth College, Guernsey

events.enhanced_description: The Danish fleet engaged the Swedish navy near Bornholm, resulting in a significant defeat for Denmark and escalating tensions that would lead to the Northern Seven Years' War. This conflict marked a critical point in Scandinavian military history.
events.name: Danish fleet fires on Swedish navy at Bornholm

events.enhanced_description: The Parliament of Scotland enacted the Witchcraft Act, imposing severe penalties for witchcraft and consulting with witches, reflecting the intense societal fears of the time. This law would lead to numerous trials and executions in the following years.
events.name: Witchcraft Act passed by the Parliament of Scotland

events.enhanced_description: After a prolonged siege, the English forces surrendered Le Havre to the French, marking a significant turning point in the French Wars of Religion. This event underscored the shifting power dynamics between England and France during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Surrender of Le Havre to the French

events.enhanced_description: Denmark–Norway and the Free City of Lübeck declared war against the Kingdom of Sweden, marking the official commencement of the Northern Seven Years' War. This conflict would reshape the balance of power in Northern Europe.
events.name: Declaration of war in the Northern Seven Years' War

events.enhanced_description: Merchants from the Bungo Province launched an attack that resulted in the destruction of the Portuguese settlement in Yokoseura, reflecting the growing tensions between local Japanese powers and foreign influences during this period.
events.name: Destruction of Portuguese settlement in Yokoseura

events.enhanced_description: During the Northern Seven Years' War, King Frederick II of Denmark successfully captured Old Älvsborg from Swedish forces, marking a significant military achievement that would bolster Denmark's position in the ongoing conflict.
events.name: Capture of Old Älvsborg by Denmark

events.enhanced_description: Giovanni Battista Lercari was elected as the new Doge of the Republic of Genoa, a position of significant political influence in the maritime republic. His leadership would be pivotal in navigating the challenges faced by Genoa during a period of political strife.
events.name: Election of Giovanni Battista Lercari as Doge of Genoa

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Mared, the Swedish Army, led by King Erik XIV, suffered a devastating defeat against the Danish forces commanded by King Frederik II. The battle resulted in significant casualties for Sweden and marked a critical moment in the Northern Seven Years' War.
events.name: Battle of Mared

events.enhanced_description: The Council of Trent made significant amendments to Roman Catholic canon law, particularly regarding marriage, requiring public announcements of the names of the bride and groom. This reform aimed to strengthen the sanctity and recognition of marriages within the Church.
events.name: Amendments to Roman Catholic canon law by the Council of Trent

events.enhanced_description: The Council of Trent officially closed after nearly two decades of deliberation, reaffirming key Roman Catholic doctrines and addressing issues raised by the Protestant Reformation. Its decisions would shape Catholic doctrine and practice for centuries.
events.name: Closure of the Council of Trent

events.enhanced_description: In 1564, the first recorded report of a 'rat king' was made, a phenomenon where multiple rats become intertwined at their tails. This peculiar occurrence has since become a part of folklore and cultural references.

image.caption: Woodcut emblem depicting a rat king, from J. Sambucus’s *Emblemata*.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — the German Wikipedia
image.date_qualification: Image dated broadly to the 16th century; the supplied evidence does not establish that it was made in 1564 or depicts that specific report.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: First Recorded Report of a Rat King

events.enhanced_description: In 1564, Idris Alooma began his rule over the Kanem-Bornu Empire, a significant state in Central Africa. His reign is noted for military conquests and administrative reforms that strengthened the empire.
events.name: Idris Alooma Starts to Rule Kanem-Bornu Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 1564, the first Scottish Psalter was published, marking a significant development in Scottish literature and religious practice. This publication contributed to the spread of Protestantism in Scotland.
events.name: Publication of the First Scottish Psalter

events.enhanced_description: During the Livonian War, the Battle of Ula saw Lithuanian forces launch a surprise attack against the numerically superior Russian army, resulting in a decisive victory for Lithuania. This battle exemplified the shifting alliances and conflicts in the region.
events.name: Battle of Ula

events.enhanced_description: In a significant event of the Burmese–Siamese War, Burmese forces successfully breached the defenses of Ayutthava, capturing vital artillery and ships. This victory marked a turning point in the conflict, showcasing the military prowess of the Burmese invaders.

locations.name: Ayutthaya, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya, Thailand

events.name: Burmese–Siamese War: Capture of Ayutthava

events.enhanced_description: The Burmese–Siamese War concluded with the surrender of King Maha Chakkraphat of Ayutthaya to King Bayinnaung of Burma. This event marked a significant shift in power in Southeast Asia, with Ayutthaya becoming a vassal state under Burmese control.

locations.name: Ayutthaya, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya, Thailand

events.name: End of the Burmese–Siamese War

events.enhanced_description: Francisco Coutinho III, the Count of Redondo and Viceroy of Portuguese India, passed away, leading to the succession of João de Mendonça Furtado. This transition was significant for the administration of Portuguese territories in India during a period of colonial expansion.
events.name: Death of Francisco Coutinho III

events.enhanced_description: Diego López de Zúñiga, the Spanish Viceroy of Peru, was assassinated by a group of conspirators, leading to a temporary succession by Hernando de Saavedra. This assassination highlighted the political instability and power struggles within the Spanish colonial administration.
events.name: Assassination of Diego López de Zúñiga

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Angol, Spanish Conquistador Lorenzo Bernal del Mercado achieved a significant victory against the Mapuche leader Illangulién, marking an important moment in the Spanish conquest of Chile. This battle exemplified the ongoing resistance of indigenous peoples against colonial forces.
events.name: Battle of Angol

events.enhanced_description: On April 20, 1564, French explorer René Goulaine de Laudonnière set sail from Le Havre with a group of 300 Huguenot Protestants aboard three ships: L'Élisabeth, Le Faucon, and Le Breton. Their mission was to establish a French colony in what is now Florida, marking a significant moment in the early European exploration of North America.
events.name: Departure of René Goulaine de Laudonnière

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1564, French settlers abandoned Charlesfort, their initial settlement attempt in the New World, and with the assistance of a relief force led by René Goulaine de Laudonnière, established Fort Caroline near present-day Jacksonville, Florida. This fort became a significant site for French colonial efforts in North America.

locations.name: Fort Caroline National Memorial, Jacksonville, Florida, United States

events.name: Establishment of Fort Caroline

events.enhanced_description: On July 2, 1564, Mughal Emperor Akbar left Agra under the pretense of hunting elephants, concealing his true intention to punish the rebellious governor of Malwa, Abdullah Khan Uzbeg. This marked a significant moment in Akbar's consolidation of power and his efforts to maintain control over his empire.
events.name: Akbar's Departure from Agra

events.enhanced_description: On July 24, 1564, Min Sekkya ascended to the throne as the new King of Arakan following the death of his half-brother, King Min Saw Hla, who passed away at the age of 31 after a prolonged illness. This transition marked a significant change in leadership for the Arakanese kingdom.
events.name: Min Sekkya Becomes King of Arakan

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1564, Maximilian II succeeded his father, Ferdinand I, as the Holy Roman Emperor. This transition of power was significant in the context of the Habsburg dynasty and the political landscape of Europe during the 16th century.
events.name: Maximilian II Becomes Holy Roman Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1564, Judge Francisco Ceinos was appointed as the new Viceroy of New Spain following the death of Luís de Velasco. This appointment was crucial for the governance of the Spanish colonies in the Americas.
events.name: Francisco Ceinos Becomes Viceroy of New Spain

events.enhanced_description: On August 6, 1564, Akbar, the ruler of the Mughal Empire, achieved a decisive victory over the rebellious governor of Malwa, Abdullah Khan Uzbeg, at Indore. This battle was pivotal in reinforcing Akbar's authority and control over the region.
events.name: Akbar Defeats Abdullah Khan Uzbeg

events.enhanced_description: On August 14, 1564, Swedish forces engaged in a second naval battle at Öland against Denmark, successfully capturing three Danish ships and taking 600 men as prisoners. This victory was part of the ongoing Northern Seven Years' War between Sweden and Denmark.
events.name: Second Naval Battle at Öland

events.enhanced_description: On August 28, 1564, Nils Boije took command of the Swedish Army from King Eric XIV and successfully captured the Danish fortress of Varberg. This event marked a significant achievement in Sweden's military campaign during the Northern Seven Years' War.
events.name: Nils Boije Captures Varberg

events.enhanced_description: On September 4, 1564, the Ronneby Bloodbath occurred in Ronneby, marking a significant and brutal conflict during the Northern Seven Years' War. This event highlighted the intense rivalries and violence between Sweden and Denmark during this period.
events.name: Ronneby Bloodbath

events.enhanced_description: On September 10, 1564, the final battle of Kawanakajima took place between the forces of Takeda Shingen and Uesugi Kenshin, resulting in a stalemate. This battle was one of the most famous conflicts of the Sengoku period in Japan, showcasing the tactical prowess of both commanders.
events.name: Battle of Kawanakajima

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1564, English merchant Anthony Jenkinson returned to London from his second expedition to the Grand Duchy of Moscow, having successfully negotiated an extension of trading rights for the English Muscovy Company. This event marked a significant development in Anglo-Russian trade relations.
events.name: Anthony Jenkinson Returns to London

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1564, Lucrezia Di Siena, recognized as the first well-known female actress in Europe, began her career by signing a contract with the Commedia dell'arte theatre company in Rome. Her contributions significantly impacted the development of theatre and acting in Europe.
events.name: Lucrezia Di Siena Begins Acting Career

events.enhanced_description: On October 23, 1564, King Bayinnaung of Burma led a massive invasion force of 64,000 men, 3,600 horses, and 330 elephants into the Lan Na kingdom, which is now part of Laos. This military campaign aimed to expand the Burmese Empire's influence in Southeast Asia.
events.name: Bayinnaung's Invasion of Lan Na

events.enhanced_description: On October 30, 1564, the Duchy of Savoy signed the Treaty of Lausanne with the Swiss canton of Bern, relinquishing all claims to the canton of Vaud. This treaty was significant in the context of Swiss independence and territorial disputes in the region.
events.name: Treaty of Lausanne

events.enhanced_description: On November 21, 1564, Spanish Conquistador Miguel López de Legazpi set sail from Mexico, embarking on a journey that would lead to the conquest of the Philippine Islands and the founding of Manila. This expedition was pivotal in establishing Spanish colonial rule in the Pacific.
events.name: Miguel López de Legazpi Sails from Mexico

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1564, four divisions of the Burmese Army arrived at Lamphun, just 12.5 miles from Chiang Mai, causing the city's defenses to flee. King Bayinnaung spared the life of King Mekuti of Lan Na and spent the next four months administering the newly annexed territory.
events.name: Burmese Army Arrives at Lamphun

events.enhanced_description: On December 3, 1564, Ivan the Terrible, Tsar of all the Russias, sent a letter of abdication to his government, citing embezzlement and treason by the aristocracy and clergy as his reasons. He subsequently left Moscow for Alexandrovskaya Sloboda, only to be persuaded to return in February 1565.
events.name: Ivan the Terrible's Letter of Abdication

events.enhanced_description: On December 7, 1564, King Charles IX of France agreed to a treaty with the cantons of Switzerland, which included provisions for the French payment of debts owed to the Swiss for loans made to his father, King Henri II. This agreement was significant for Franco-Swiss relations.
events.name: Treaty with Swiss Cantons

events.enhanced_description: In 1565, the pencil was first documented by Conrad Gesner, marking its emergence as a common writing instrument in England. This innovation played a crucial role in the development of writing and drawing tools.
events.name: First documentation of the pencil

events.enhanced_description: In 1565, John Beddoes School was founded in Presteigne, Wales. This institution contributed to the educational landscape of the region and played a role in the development of local education.
events.name: Foundation of John Beddoes School

events.enhanced_description: Herlufsholm School, founded by Herluf Trolle, is one of the oldest schools in Denmark, established to provide a rigorous education based on humanist principles. It has played a significant role in the educational landscape of Denmark since its inception.
events.name: Herlufsholm School is founded at Næstved, Denmark

events.enhanced_description: Bungay Grammar School was established in Bungay, Suffolk, providing education to local children and contributing to the development of education in the region. The school has a long history and has undergone various transformations over the centuries.
events.name: Bungay Grammar School is established in England

events.enhanced_description: On January 3, 1565, Ivan the Terrible instituted the oprichnina, a policy of repression against the boyars (aristocrats) in Russia. This marked a significant shift in his rule, characterized by increased autocracy and violence.
