image.caption: Map showing the territorial phases of the Oprichnina in Muscovy.
image.credit: Kjetil_r , Lokal_Profil — Own work. The background is from Image:Map of Russian, outline.svg
image.date_qualification: Created in 2008; depicts territorial phases from 1565 to 1571.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.5; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.5; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Ivan the Terrible Origins the Oprichnina

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1565, the Battle of Talikota took place, where the Vijayanagara Empire faced a devastating defeat against the Deccan Sultanates. This battle significantly weakened the last Hindu kingdom in South India, leading to the decline of the empire.
events.name: Battle of Talikota

events.enhanced_description: On February 13, 1565, Spanish Conquistador Miguel López de Legazpi landed on the shores of Cebu Island, marking the beginning of Spanish colonization in the Philippines. This event was pivotal in establishing Spanish influence in the region and led to the eventual establishment of Cebu as a significant Spanish settlement.
events.name: Landing of Miguel López de Legazpi in Cebu

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1565, Estácio de Sá founded the city of Rio de Janeiro, originally named São Sebastião do Rio de Janeiro. This event marked the establishment of one of Brazil's most important cities, which would later become a cultural and economic hub.
events.name: Foundation of Rio de Janeiro

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1565, Miguel López de Legazpi made a blood compact (sandugan) with Datu Sikatuna in Bohol, symbolizing friendship and alliance between the Spanish and the local chieftain. This event is significant in Philippine history as it represents the early interactions between Spanish colonizers and indigenous leaders.
events.name: Blood Compact between López de Legazpi and Datu Sikatuna

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1565, Cebu City was established as San Miguel by Miguel López de Legazpi, becoming the first Spanish settlement in the Philippines. This marked a significant step in the Spanish colonization process, laying the groundwork for further expansion in the archipelago.
events.name: Establishment of Cebu City as San Miguel

events.enhanced_description: On May 2, 1565, Huntingdon Grammar School was established in Huntingdon, England. This institution played a crucial role in the education of young men in the region and contributed to the development of educational standards in England.
events.name: Establishment of Huntingdon Grammar School

events.enhanced_description: On May 18, 1565, Ottoman troops landed on the island of Malta, initiating the Great Siege of Malta. This event marked a critical moment in the struggle between the Ottoman Empire and the Knights of St. John, ultimately leading to a significant battle for control of the Mediterranean.
events.name: Beginning of the Great Siege of Malta

events.enhanced_description: On June 4, 1565, the Treaty of Cebu was signed between Miguel López de Legazpi, representing Philip II of Spain, and Rajah Tupas of Cebu. This treaty effectively established Spanish suzerainty over Cebu, solidifying Spanish control in the region.
events.name: Signing of the Treaty of Cebu

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1565, Ashikaga Yoshiteru, the Ashikaga shogun, committed ritual suicide after Matsunaga Hisahide invaded Kyoto. This event marked a significant turning point in the power dynamics of the Ashikaga shogunate and the ongoing conflicts in Japan.
events.name: Ritual Suicide of Ashikaga Yoshiteru

events.enhanced_description: On July 29, 1565, Mary, Queen of Scots, married her half-cousin Henry Stuart, Lord Darnley, at Holyrood Palace in Edinburgh in a Catholic ceremony. This marriage was politically significant and led to further complications in Mary’s reign.
events.name: Marriage of Mary, Queen of Scots and Henry Stuart

events.enhanced_description: On August 6, 1565, Elizabeth I of England granted Sark in the Channel Islands as a fief to Hellier de Carteret, Seigneur of Saint Ouen. This act solidified English control over the islands and established de Carteret's authority.
events.name: Grant of Sark to Hellier de Carteret

events.enhanced_description: On August 26, 1565, the Chaseabout Raid began in Scotland as a rebellion against Mary, Queen of Scots, led by her half-brother, James Stewart, 1st Earl of Moray. This conflict was a significant moment in the power struggle during Mary's reign.
events.name: Beginning of the Chaseabout Raid

events.enhanced_description: On August 28, 1565, the Spanish fleet of Pedro Menéndez de Avilés first sighted land in Florida, marking the beginning of Spanish efforts to establish a foothold in North America. This event led to the founding of St. Augustine, the oldest European settlement in the continental United States.
events.name: Spanish fleet sights land in Florida

events.enhanced_description: On August 31, 1565, the Chaseabout Raid culminated as Moray and at least 1,000 of his rebels arrived in Edinburgh for a confrontation with the Scottish crown. The rebellion was marked by cannon fire from Edinburgh Castle, leading to the retreat of the rebels.
events.name: Arrival of Moray's rebels in Edinburgh

events.enhanced_description: On September 4, 1565, the Spanish fleet of Pedro Menéndez de Avilés landed in Florida to oust the French under Jean Ribault. This military action led to the destruction of the French colony of Fort Caroline, asserting Spanish dominance in the region.
events.name: Spanish fleet lands in Florida

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1565, St. Augustine was established by Pedro Menéndez de Avilés, becoming the oldest surviving European settlement in the modern-day United States. This settlement played a crucial role in the Spanish colonization of North America.
events.name: Establishment of St. Augustine

events.enhanced_description: On September 11, 1565, the Knights of Malta lifted the Great Siege of Malta after four months of intense conflict with the Ottoman Empire. This victory was a significant moment in European history, showcasing the resilience of the Knights and altering the balance of power in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Lifting of the Great Siege of Malta

events.enhanced_description: In October 1565, the first Martello tower, the Tour de Mortella, designed by Giovan Giacomo Paleari Fratino, was completed as part of the Genovese defense system at Mortella Point in Upper Corsica. This architectural design became a significant feature in coastal defense systems.
events.name: Completion of the first Martello tower

events.enhanced_description: On October 11, 1565, Ottavio Gentile Oderico was elected to a two-year term as the Doge of the Republic of Genoa. His leadership came during a period of political complexity and economic challenges for the Republic.
events.name: Election of Ottavio Gentile Oderico as Doge

events.enhanced_description: On October 18, 1565, the Battle of Fukuda Bay occurred, where ships belonging to the Matsura clan of Japan failed to capture a Portuguese trading carrack. This battle marked the first recorded naval engagement between Japan and a European nation.
events.name: Battle of Fukuda Bay

events.enhanced_description: On October 20, 1565, the Battle of Axtorna was fought in Sweden, near Falkenberg, where Daniel Rantzau of the Army of Denmark and Norway led 7,400 troops to defeat over 11,000 Swedish troops commanded by Jacob Henriksson Hästesko. This battle was a significant event in the Northern Seven Years' War.
events.name: Battle of Axtorna

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1565, the army of Burma, under the command of King Bayinnaung, conquered Chiang Mai, the capital of the Siamese Kingdom of Lan Na. This conquest was part of Bayinnaung's campaign to expand Burmese influence in Southeast Asia.
events.name: Conquest of Chiang Mai by Burma

events.enhanced_description: In December 1565, the Mariovo and Prilep rebellion occurred, marking the first recorded uprising by the Macedonian hajduks or voivode against the Ottoman Empire. This rebellion was significant in the context of the Ottoman rule in the Balkans.
events.name: Mariovo and Prilep rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On December 31, 1565, the Burmese Army conquered Vientiane, the main city of the kingdom of Lan Xang (now Laos). This event marked a significant expansion of Burmese territorial control in the region.
events.name: Conquest of Vientiane by Burma

events.enhanced_description: The construction of the first bridge over the Neretva River in Mostar, known as Stari Most (Old Bridge), was completed by the Ottoman Empire. This architectural marvel became a symbol of the city and a significant example of Ottoman engineering.

image.caption: Stari Most during reconstruction in Mostar.
image.date_qualification: Photographed June 2003, according to the supplied image date; this is not a photograph of the bridge’s original 16th-century completion.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 3.0; Copyrighted: True

locations.name: Mostar, Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bosnia and Herzegovina

events.name: Completion of Stari Most in Mostar

events.enhanced_description: On January 7, 1566, Cardinal Michele Ghislieri was elected as Pope Pius V, succeeding Pope Pius IV. His papacy is noted for the implementation of the reforms of the Council of Trent and the establishment of the Roman Catechism.

image.caption: Portrait of Pope Pius V, an enthroned figure making a blessing gesture; oil painting by Bartolomeo Passarotti and workshop.
image.date_qualification: Retrospective portrait, dated circa 1566; contextual image of the pope, not a depiction of the election itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Cardinal Michele Ghislieri is elected as Pope Pius V

events.enhanced_description: On February 24, 1566, Mimura Iechika, a daimyō of Bitchū Province, was assassinated in a significant early instance of gun violence in Japan. The assassination was orchestrated by rival factions, highlighting the intense power struggles of the period.
events.name: Assassination of Mimura Iechika

events.enhanced_description: In March 1566, the Hanseatic city of Lübeck launched the galleon Adler von Lübeck, which was considered one of the largest ships of its time. This event marked a significant achievement in maritime engineering and trade for the Hanseatic League.
events.name: Launch of the galleon Adler von Lübeck

events.enhanced_description: On March 28, 1566, the foundation stone of Valletta was laid by Grand Master Jean Parisot de Valette, marking the beginning of the construction of what would become Malta's capital. The city was built in response to the Great Siege of Malta and reflects the military and cultural aspirations of the Knights of St. John.
events.name: Foundation stone of Valletta is laid

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1566, the Compromise of Nobles was presented to Margaret of Parma, the Governor of the Habsburg Netherlands. This document aimed to address grievances against Spanish rule but ultimately only delayed the onset of the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: Presentation of the Compromise of Nobles

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1566, Charles IX of France returned to Paris after a grand tour of his kingdom that lasted over 27 months, covering approximately 2,500 miles. This journey was significant for strengthening royal authority and understanding the conditions of his realm.
events.name: Charles IX completes his grand tour

events.enhanced_description: On May 13, 1566, Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian II imposed a Reichsexekution against John Frederick II, Duke of Saxony, leading to a siege of Gotha. This action exemplified the tensions within the Holy Roman Empire and the struggle for power among its rulers.
events.name: Maximilian II imposes a Reichsexekution

events.enhanced_description: On May 25, 1566, King Philip II of Spain enacted laws targeting the remaining Spanish Muslims, including restrictions on language and clothing. These measures reflected the broader efforts of the Spanish crown to enforce religious conformity and suppress Islamic practices.
events.name: King Philip II issues laws against Spanish Muslims

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1566, the Augsburg Imperial Coin Edict was issued, establishing the thaler as a new currency in the Holy Roman Empire. This edict standardized coinage and laid the groundwork for modern currency systems in Europe.
events.name: Augsburg Imperial Coin Edict

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1566, Wilhelm von Rosenberg began raising an army in Znojmo, Bohemia, in anticipation of an invasion by the Ottoman Empire. This event underscores the ongoing military tensions in Central Europe during this period.

locations.name: Znojmo, South Moravian Region, Czech Republic

events.name: Wilhelm von Rosenberg raises an army

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1566, Pope Pius V issued an edict to expel most prostitutes from Rome and the Papal States. However, this decree was soon reversed due to the financial implications of losing tax revenue from the regulated brothels.
events.name: Pope Pius V issues edict against prostitution

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1566, Feodor Stefanovich Kolychov was consecrated as the patriarch of the Russian Orthodox Church, with the approval of Tsar Ivan the Terrible. His tenure was marked by conflict with the Tsar, leading to his eventual deposition.
events.name: Feodor Kolychov consecrated as patriarch

events.enhanced_description: On July 28, 1566, John Sigismund Zápolya, the uncrowned claimant to the throne of Hungary, led an invasion of Upper Hungary under the orders of Ottoman Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent. This event illustrates the complex political dynamics of the region during the Ottoman expansion.
events.name: John Sigismund Zápolya leads invasion

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1566, King Philip II of Spain sent a final letter to the administrators and bishops of the Spanish Netherlands, rejecting their request to abolish ordinances treating Protestants as heretics. This decision contributed to rising tensions that would lead to the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: Philip II rejects request to abolish ordinances

events.enhanced_description: On August 6, 1566, the siege of Szigetvár was initiated by Suleiman the Magnificent, marking a significant military campaign of the Ottoman Empire. This siege would become notorious for its fierce battles and the eventual heroic defense by the Hungarian forces.
events.name: Siege of Szigetvár begins

events.enhanced_description: On August 10, 1566, the Beeldenstorm, or 'Iconoclastic Fury,' began as Protestant Calvinists engaged in widespread destruction of religious art across the Low Countries. This movement was a significant expression of the religious tensions of the Reformation.
events.name: The Beeldenstorm begins

events.enhanced_description: On August 16, 1566, the Beeldenstorm reached Ypres, where the St. Martin's Cathedral was plundered, and the library and artifacts of Bishop Martin Rythovius were burned. This event exemplified the violent backlash against Catholic iconography during the Reformation.
events.name: Beeldenstorm arrives at Ypres

events.enhanced_description: On August 25, 1566, the Beeldenstorm reached Leiden, where Calvinist mobs destroyed religious images and artifacts. This act of iconoclasm was part of a broader movement against Catholicism in the region.
events.name: Vandalism of the Beeldenstorm reaches Leiden

events.enhanced_description: On September 7, 1566, Suleiman the Magnificent died in his tent during the siege of Szigetvár, marking the end of an era for the Ottoman Empire. His death occurred just before the siege concluded, leading to the ascension of his son, Selim II.
events.name: Suleiman the Magnificent dies

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1566, the siege of Szigetvár concluded with the annihilation of the Hungarian and Croatian defenders, including their general, Nikola Šubić Zrinski. The fierce battle marked a significant victory for the Ottoman Empire and showcased the valor of the defenders.

image.caption: Johann Peter Krafft’s oil painting depicts Nikola Šubić Zrinski and his defenders charging from the fortress at Szigetvár.
image.credit: Johann Peter Krafft — Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"k/krafft/zrinyi" Web Gallery of Art: http://www.wga.hu/frames-e.html?/html/k/krafft/zrinyi.html Fine Arts in Hungary: http://www.hung-art.hu/frames-e.html?/english/k/krafft/muvek/zrinyi.html
image.date_qualification: Retrospective painting of the 1566 sortie; the artwork is dated 1825, not a contemporary image of the siege.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Siege of Szigetvár ends

events.enhanced_description: On October 2, 1566, Richard Onslow was elected as the Speaker of the English House of Commons by a vote of 82 to 70. His election reflected the political dynamics of the time and the growing importance of the Commons in English governance.
events.name: Richard Onslow elected Speaker of the House of Commons

events.enhanced_description: Catherine of the Austrian Habsburgs, who served as Queen consort of Poland since 1553, departed from Poland to return to her homeland of Austria following the collapse of her marriage to Sigismund II Augustus. Although she never returned to Poland, she retained her title as queen consort until her death in 1572.
events.name: Catherine of the Austrian Habsburgs leaves Poland

events.enhanced_description: Gastón de Peralta, the 3rd Marquess of Falces, was appointed as the Viceroy of New Spain, taking over from Francisco Ceinos. His tenure was cut short when he was dismissed by King Philip II due to allegations of plotting a rebellion against the Spanish crown.
events.name: Gastón de Peralta becomes Viceroy of New Spain

events.enhanced_description: In the city of Kneiphof, located in the Duchy of Prussia, Duke Albert ordered the execution of three councilors—Johann Funck, Matthias Horst, and Hans Schnell—accusing them of inciting political and religious discord. The executions took place publicly in the town's marketplace.
events.name: Beheading of councilors in Kneiphof

events.enhanced_description: In a significant address to the English Parliament, Queen Elizabeth I passionately defended her right to rule and expressed her commitment to England, questioning any reasons to distance herself from her kingdom. This speech was a pivotal moment in asserting national identity during her reign.
events.name: Queen Elizabeth I addresses Parliament

events.enhanced_description: King Philip II of Spain issued a decree to increase the gold content in the Spanish gold escudo from 350 maravedis to 400, thereby enhancing its value and aligning it with 16 silver reales. This change reflected the economic strategies of the Spanish crown during a period of extensive imperial expansion.
events.name: Decree raising gold content in escudo

events.enhanced_description: At Craigmillar Castle, a council of advisers to Mary, Queen of Scots, urged her to divorce her husband, Henry Stuart, Lord Darnley, due to his unpopularity and perceived threat to her reign. When Mary refused, the advisers concluded that Darnley must be eliminated.
events.name: Advisers to Mary, Queen of Scots, recommend divorce

events.enhanced_description: The baptism of Prince James, the son of Mary, Queen of Scots, took place at Stirling Castle, marking a significant event in the royal lineage of Scotland. This ceremony was attended by nobles and clergy, emphasizing the importance of the heir to the Scottish throne.
events.name: Baptism of Prince James

events.enhanced_description: In 1567, King Frederick II of Denmark and Norway established the city of Fredrikstad in Norway. This city was part of his efforts to strengthen Danish control over the region and promote trade.
figures: Frederick II of Denmark and Norway
events.name: Founding of Fredrikstad

events.enhanced_description: The construction of Villa Capra, commonly known as La Rotonda, commenced in 1567, designed by the renowned architect Andrea Palladio. This villa is celebrated for its harmonious proportions and has significantly influenced Western architecture.

image.caption: Photograph of Villa La Rotonda in Vicenza.
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2009-12-09; not a photograph of the 1567 construction.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Construction of Villa Capra "La Rotonda" begins

events.enhanced_description: In 1567, Rugby School was founded, becoming one of the oldest public schools in England. It played a pivotal role in the development of the modern educational system and the sport of rugby.
events.name: Founding of Rugby School

events.enhanced_description: In 1567, the Ming dynasty officially revoked the haijin maritime trade ban, which had restricted foreign trade for decades. This decision marked a significant shift in China's economic policy, allowing for renewed trade with most countries, excluding Japan.
events.name: Ming dynasty revokes haijin maritime trade ban

events.enhanced_description: Captain Juan Pardo led a Spanish expedition that established Fort San Juan in the Native American settlement of Joara, marking the first European settlement in present-day North Carolina. This fort was part of Spain's efforts to expand its influence in the New World.

locations.name: Fort San Juan, North Carolina, United States

events.name: Establishment of Fort San Juan

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Rio de Janeiro, Portuguese forces led by Estácio de Sá successfully expelled French troops from the city, solidifying Portuguese control over the region. This battle was crucial in establishing Portuguese dominance in Brazil.

locations.name: Rio de Janeiro, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

events.name: Battle of Rio de Janeiro

events.enhanced_description: The Jiajing Emperor, Zhu Houcong, passed away in the Forbidden City after a 45-year reign, marking the end of a significant era in the Ming Dynasty. His death led to a succession crisis and changes in imperial policies.
events.name: Death of the Jiajing Emperor

events.enhanced_description: Prince Zhu Zaiji ascended the throne as the Longqing Emperor, succeeding his father, the Jiajing Emperor. His reign would be marked by efforts to stabilize the Ming Dynasty and address internal challenges.
events.name: Ascension of Longqing Emperor

events.enhanced_description: Henry Stuart, Lord Darnley, the husband of Mary, Queen of Scots, was murdered at the Provost's House in Kirk o' Field, Edinburgh. His assassination was a pivotal event that led to a series of political upheavals in Scotland.
events.name: Murder of Lord Darnley

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Oosterweel marked the beginning of the Eighty Years' War, as a Spanish mercenary army ambushed and killed a group of rebels near Antwerp. This conflict would lead to significant changes in the political landscape of the region.
events.name: Battle of Oosterweel

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Thanesar, Mughal Emperor Akbar achieved a decisive victory against over 7,000 warriors of the Sanyasi Hindu sect with a much smaller force of 300 men. This battle showcased Akbar's military strategy and contributed to the consolidation of Mughal power in India.
events.name: Battle of Thanesar

events.enhanced_description: Henrique I Nerika a Mpudi ascended to the throne of the Kingdom of Kongo, succeeding his nephew Bernardo I. His reign would be marked by the challenges of maintaining the kingdom's independence amid European colonial pressures.
events.name: Henrique I becomes ruler of Kongo

events.enhanced_description: The Earl of Bothwell was acquitted of charges related to the murder of Lord Darnley, which had significant implications for his relationship with Mary, Queen of Scots. Following his acquittal, he began to plot to marry Mary, further complicating the political landscape.
events.name: Earl of Bothwell acquitted

events.enhanced_description: The Ainslie Tavern Bond was signed by a group of Scottish clerics and nobles, endorsing the Earl of Bothwell as a suitable husband for Mary, Queen of Scots, and approving his acquittal for the murder of her previous husband. This act further entrenched Bothwell's influence in Scottish politics.
events.name: Ainslie Tavern Bond signed

events.enhanced_description: Earl of Bothwell forcibly took Mary, Queen of Scots, prisoner at his castle in Dunbar, preventing her from traveling to Edinburgh. This act of coercion culminated in a violent assault, significantly impacting Mary's reign and leading to her eventual downfall.
events.name: Bothwell takes Mary prisoner

events.enhanced_description: Under duress, Mary, Queen of Scots, married the Earl of Bothwell, a union that was highly controversial and politically charged. This marriage further alienated her from her subjects and contributed to her eventual abdication.
events.name: Mary marries Bothwell

events.enhanced_description: In a shocking act of violence, King Erik XIV of Sweden and his guards executed five imprisoned nobles at Uppsala Castle, an event that would come to be known as the Sture Murders. This incident highlighted the king's instability and contributed to his eventual downfall.
events.name: Sture Murders

events.enhanced_description: After being defeated by Scottish nobles at the Battle of Carberry Hill, Mary, Queen of Scots, was imprisoned in Lochleven Castle. This imprisonment marked a significant turning point in her tumultuous reign and led to her eventual abdication.
events.name: Mary imprisoned at Lochleven Castle

events.enhanced_description: Mary, Queen of Scots, was forced to abdicate the throne in favor of her one-year-old son, James VI, following a series of political defeats and pressures from Scottish nobles. This event marked the end of her reign and the beginning of a new era in Scottish history.
events.name: Mary abdicates in favor of James VI

events.enhanced_description: Diego de Losada founded the city of Santiago de León de Caracas, which would later become the capital of Venezuela. This establishment was part of the Spanish colonization efforts in South America.
events.name: Founding of Santiago de León de Caracas

events.enhanced_description: James VI was crowned at Stirling, marking the beginning of his reign as king of Scotland. This event was significant as it established the young monarch in a position of power amidst the political turmoil of the time.
events.name: James VI crowned at Stirling

events.enhanced_description: In 1567, the Duke of Alba was dispatched to the Spanish Netherlands with a formidable military force to quell the growing unrest against Spanish rule. His appointment marked a significant escalation in the conflict, leading to the outlawing of William of Orange and the imprisonment of prominent nobles like Lamoral, Count of Egmont.
events.name: The Duke of Alba is sent to the Netherlands

events.enhanced_description: On September 9, 1567, during a dinner in Brussels, the Duke of Alba executed a dramatic arrest of Lamoral, Count of Egmont, and Philip de Montmorency, Count of Horn, on charges of treason. This event underscored the Duke's ruthless approach to suppressing dissent in the Spanish Netherlands.
figures: Philip de Montmorency, Count of Horn
events.name: Duke of Alba arrests Count of Egmont and Count of Horn

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Inabayama Castle culminated on September 27, 1567, when the Oda clan successfully captured Gifu Castle from the Saitō clan after a two-week siege. This victory was pivotal in Oda Nobunaga's campaign to unify Japan during the Sengoku period.
events.name: Siege of Inabayama Castle

events.enhanced_description: The Second War of Religion ignited on September 29, 1567, when Huguenot leaders Louis, Prince of Condé and Gaspard de Coligny attempted to capture King Charles IX and his mother at Meaux. Although they failed, the conflict escalated as Huguenots seized several cities, including Orléans.
events.name: Second War of Religion begins in France

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1567, the first translation of the New Testament into Welsh was published, a significant cultural milestone achieved by William Salesbury. This translation played a crucial role in the spread of Protestantism and literacy in Wales.
events.name: First Welsh New Testament published

events.enhanced_description: On November 21, 1567, the Tōdai-ji Great Buddha Hall in Nara was destroyed after a six-month siege led by Matsunaga Hisahide against the Miyoshi clan. This event marked a significant loss in cultural heritage, with reconstruction not occurring until 1709.
events.name: Destruction of Tōdai-ji Great Buddha Hall

events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1567, Antão de Noronha, the Viceroy of Portuguese India, enforced decrees that prohibited public Hindu rituals and mandated Christian services for all natives aged 15 and older. These measures reflected the colonial policies aimed at converting the local population.
events.name: Antão de Noronha issues decrees in Goa

events.enhanced_description: On December 12, 1567, the Scottish Parliament ratified the Act Anent the demission of the Crown, facilitating the abdication of Mary, Queen of Scots, in favor of her son, James VI. This act confirmed James as the legal ruler, while appointing his half-brother, James Stewart, as regent.
events.name: Scottish Parliament approves Act Anent the demission of the Crown

events.enhanced_description: In 1568, Álvaro I succeeded his stepfather Henrique I as ruler of the Kingdom of Kongo, establishing the Kwilu dynasty that would govern the kingdom without interruption until May 1622. His reign was marked by significant interactions with European powers.
events.name: Álvaro I succeeds as ruler of the Kingdom of Kongo

events.enhanced_description: In 1568, Christopher Watson completed the first English translation of Polybius' The Histories, a significant work that provided insights into the Roman Republic and its military strategies. This translation contributed to the Renaissance's revival of classical knowledge in England.
events.name: Translation of Polybius' The Histories

events.enhanced_description: On June 1, 1568, a mass execution took place at Sablon, Brussels, where 18 signatories of the Compromise of Nobles were beheaded. This brutal act was part of the Spanish repression against the growing dissent in the Netherlands, further escalating tensions that led to the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: Mass execution at Sablon

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1568, Thomas Lancaster was consecrated as the Archbishop of Armagh, becoming the spiritual leader of the Church of Ireland. He succeeded Archbishop Adam Loftus, continuing the Protestant Reformation's influence in Ireland during a period of significant religious conflict.
events.name: Consecration of Thomas Lancaster

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1568, Kılıç Ali Pasha, an Ottoman pirate of Italian origin, was appointed as the Beylerbey of Ottoman Algeria by Sultan Selim II. His leadership marked a significant period of Ottoman naval power and influence in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Appointment of Kılıç Ali Pasha

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Jemmingen, fought on July 21, 1568, saw the Spanish forces under the Duke of Alba decisively defeat the invading army led by Louis of Nassau. This battle was a critical setback for the Dutch rebels in their struggle against Spanish rule.
events.name: Battle of Jemmingen

events.enhanced_description: The Third War of Religion in France began on August 18, 1568, following a failed attempt by Royalist forces to capture Huguenot leaders Condé and Coligny. This conflict was part of the larger series of French Wars of Religion that pitted Catholics against Huguenots.
events.name: Beginning of the Third War of Religion

events.enhanced_description: On September 24, 1568, the Battle of San Juan de Ulúa occurred in the Gulf of Mexico, where a Spanish fleet successfully forced English privateers led by John Hawkins to abandon their campaign. This battle underscored the ongoing tensions between Spain and England during the Anglo-Spanish War.
events.name: Battle of San Juan de Ulúa

events.enhanced_description: On September 29, 1568, King Eric XIV of Sweden was deposed by his half-brothers John and Charles. Following his deposition, John proclaimed himself King John III, marking a significant shift in the Swedish monarchy.
events.name: Deposition of Eric XIV of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1568, William the Silent launched an invasion into the southeastern Netherlands, aiming to rally support against Spanish rule. This action was part of the broader conflict known as the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: William the Silent's invasion

events.enhanced_description: On October 18, 1568, Ashikaga Yoshiaki was installed as Shōgun, marking the beginning of the Azuchi–Momoyama period in Japan. His ascension was significant in the context of the power struggles between feudal lords during this transformative era.
events.name: Installation of Ashikaga Yoshiaki as Shōgun

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Jodoigne, fought on October 20, 1568, resulted in a decisive victory for Spanish forces under the Duke of Alba, who destroyed the rearguard of William the Silent's army. This defeat forced William to abandon his offensive in the Netherlands.
events.name: Battle of Jodoigne

events.enhanced_description: On November 12, 1568, Dutch rebels commanded by William the Silent achieved a significant victory against Spanish Habsburg troops led by Sancho d'Avila at the Battle of Le Quesnoy in northern France. This battle was part of the broader conflict of the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: Battle of Le Quesnoy

events.enhanced_description: On November 22, 1568, the Second Treaty of Roskilde was signed between representatives of Denmark and Sweden, concluding the Northern Seven Years' War. As a result of the treaty, Sweden ceded the Duchy of Estonia to Danish control.
events.name: Second Treaty of Roskilde

events.enhanced_description: On November 27, 1568, during the Burmese–Siamese War, 55,000 troops dispatched by King Bayinnaung arrived at Phitsanulok, Thailand, successfully repelling an attack from the Ayutthaya Kingdom and preparing for an invasion to quell the rebellion led by King Maha Chakkraphat.
events.name: Burmese–Siamese War

events.enhanced_description: On December 24, 1568, the Morisco Revolt against King Philip II of Spain began in Granada, where Aben Humeya was proclaimed as the leader of the Granadan rebels. This uprising was a response to the oppressive policies against the Morisco population in Spain.
events.name: Morisco Revolt

events.enhanced_description: On December 28, 1568, Ludwig III ascended to the title of Duke of Württemberg in German Bavaria following the death of his father, Christoph. His reign would see significant developments in the region during a time of political and religious upheaval.
events.name: Ludwig III becomes Duke of Württemberg

events.enhanced_description: In 1569, Gerardus Mercator introduced the Mercator projection in his world map titled Nova et Aucta Orbis Terrae Descriptio ad Usum Navigantium Emendata. This revolutionary map projection became a standard for navigation, allowing sailors to plot straight-line courses.
events.name: Mercator projection introduced

events.enhanced_description: In 1569, a conspiracy aimed at deposing John III of Sweden and reinstating the imprisoned Eric XIV was uncovered. This political intrigue highlighted the ongoing tensions and power struggles within the Swedish monarchy during the 16th century.
events.name: Conspiracy against John III of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: In 1569, the trade compact of 1536 was renewed, allowing French merchants to operate freely within the Ottoman Empire. This agreement exempted them from Ottoman law and reduced customs duties, reflecting the economic ties between France and the Ottomans.
events.name: Renewal of the trade compact with France

events.enhanced_description: In 1569, Mughal Emperor Akbar founded Fatehpur Sikri to honor the Muslim holy man Shaikh Salim Chisti, who had predicted the birth of Akbar's son, Jahangir. This city would later serve as the Mughal capital and is renowned for its stunning architecture.
events.name: Foundation of Fatehpur Sikri

events.enhanced_description: On January 11, 1569, the first recorded lottery in England began at the west door of St Paul's Cathedral, running for nearly five months. The proceeds were intended for public works, marking a significant moment in the history of gambling and public finance in England.
events.name: First recorded lottery in England

events.enhanced_description: On February 26, 1569, Pope Pius V issued a papal bull expelling all Jews from Italian and French territories, reflecting the intense religious and social tensions of the period. This decree had significant repercussions for Jewish communities in Europe.
events.name: Papal bull expelling Jews

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Jarnac, fought on March 13, 1569, saw Royalist troops under Marshal Gaspard de Tavannes surprise and defeat the Huguenots led by the Prince of Condé, who was captured and subsequently murdered. This battle was a pivotal moment in the ongoing French Wars of Religion.
events.name: Battle of Jarnac

events.enhanced_description: On April 15, 1569, Mahinthrathirat reclaimed the throne of the Ayutthaya Kingdom in what is now Thailand, following the death of King Maha Chakkraphat. His ascension was part of the larger context of the Burmese–Siamese War.

locations.name: Ayutthaya, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya, Thailand

events.name: Reclamation of the Ayutthaya throne

events.enhanced_description: On May 6, 1569, the lottery held at St Paul's Cathedral concluded with the selection of a winner, marking the end of the first recorded lottery in England. This event highlighted the growing popularity of lotteries as a means of public fundraising.
events.name: End of St. Paul Cathedral lottery

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1569, King Bayinnaung of Burma successfully quelled a revolt by Setthathirath of Lan Xang (now Laos), effectively ending Lan Xang's attempt to assist the Ayutthaya Kingdom in resisting Burmese conquest. This victory solidified Bayinnaung's power in the region.

locations.name: Ayutthaya, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya, Thailand

events.name: King Bayinnaung's victory

events.enhanced_description: In May 1569, Kasim Pasha of the Ottoman Empire initiated a military campaign to conquer Astrakhan, deploying tens of thousands of troops. The campaign included an ambitious plan to construct a canal linking the Black Sea to the Caspian Sea, aimed at facilitating naval operations, but ultimately proved unfeasible.
events.name: Ottoman attempt to conquer Astrakhan

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1569, German Protestant troops arrived to reinforce the Huguenot leader Gaspard II de Coligny near Limoges, France. This military support was part of the ongoing conflicts during the French Wars of Religion, highlighting the international dimensions of the struggle.
events.name: German Protestant troops reinforce Coligny

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1569, the Union of Lublin was enacted, uniting the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania into a single state known as the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. This significant political union was ratified following votes in the Assemblies of several Lithuanian provinces, marking a pivotal moment in Eastern European history.
events.name: Union of Lublin

events.enhanced_description: Beginning on July 24, 1569, Huguenot forces led by Gaspard II de Coligny and the young Prince Henry of Navarre laid siege to Poitiers, a stronghold of Catholic resistance. The siege ultimately failed, and the Huguenots retreated on September 7, marking a significant setback in their campaign during the French Wars of Religion.
events.name: Siege of Poitiers

events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1569, Burmese forces invaded Siam and captured the city of Ayutthaya, leading to Siam becoming a vassal state of Burma. This event marked a significant shift in power dynamics in Southeast Asia during the 16th century.
events.name: Burma invades Siam

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Orthez took place on August 24, 1569, where Huguenot forces under Gabriel, comte de Montgomery, defeated the Royalist troops led by General Terride. The battle ended with a massacre of Catholic soldiers, reflecting the brutal nature of the French Wars of Religion.
events.name: Battle of Orthez

events.enhanced_description: On September 7, 1569, a Royalist army led by the Duc d'Anjou and Marshal Tavannes forced Gaspard II de Coligny to abandon the siege of Poitiers. This event marked a critical turning point in the ongoing conflicts between Huguenots and Catholics in France.
events.name: Siege of Poitiers abandoned

events.enhanced_description: On September 17, 1569, Pope Pius V issued the papal bull Consueverunt Romani Pontifices, which established specific elements for the devotion of the Rosary. This document played a significant role in the Catholic Church's promotion of the Rosary as a form of prayer.
events.name: Papal bull Consueverunt Romani Pontifices

events.enhanced_description: On September 26, 1569, Kasim Pasha concluded his military campaign against Astrakhan after realizing his troops were running low on supplies. This decision marked the end of a significant but ultimately unsuccessful Ottoman attempt to expand their influence in the region.
events.name: Kasim Pasha ends attempt to conquer Astrakhan

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1569, the first complete printed Bible in Spanish, known as La Biblia, was published in Basel by Casiodoro de Reina. This landmark publication played a crucial role in the spread of Protestantism in the Spanish-speaking world.
events.name: First complete printed Bible in Spanish

events.enhanced_description: On September 29, 1569, Maha Thammarachathirat was installed by the Burmese Army as the vassal king of Ayutthaya. This event solidified Burmese influence over the region during a period of significant political upheaval.
events.name: Maha Thammarachathirat installed as vassal king

events.enhanced_description: On October 3, 1569, the Battle of Moncontour occurred, where Royalist forces under Gaspard de Saulx Tavannes and the Duc d'Anjou decisively defeated the Huguenots led by Gaspard II de Coligny. The battle resulted in heavy casualties for the Huguenots, with 8,000 killed and 3,000 taken prisoner.
events.name: Battle of Moncontour

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1569, the Rising of the North commenced as Catholic nobles, the Earl of Westmorland and the Earl of Northumberland, gathered 700 men at Brancepeth Castle in County Durham. Their aim was to overthrow Queen Elizabeth I and place the Catholic Mary, Queen of Scots, on the English throne, marking a significant moment in the struggle between Protestant and Catholic factions in England.
events.name: Rising of the North begins

events.enhanced_description: On November 11, 1569, Danish General Daniel Rantzau arrived at the Swedish-held Varberg Castle and ordered artillery bombardment. The siege was short-lived, ending on November 14, after Rantzau was killed by cannon fire, illustrating the brutal realities of 16th-century warfare.
events.name: Siege of Varberg Castle

events.enhanced_description: The siege of Varberg Castle by Danish forces concluded on November 14, 1569, after three days of intense bombardment. The Swedish defenders managed to withstand the siege, marking a notable event in the ongoing conflicts between Denmark and Sweden.
events.name: Siege of Varberg Castle ends

events.enhanced_description: On November 26, 1569, Francisco Álvarez de Toledo was appointed as the new Spanish Viceroy of Peru, succeeding Lope García de Castro. His tenure would be marked by significant administrative reforms and efforts to consolidate Spanish control over the vast territories of South America.
events.name: Francisco Álvarez de Toledo becomes Viceroy of Peru

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1569, Kanbara Castle, held by the Hōjō clan, fell after a siege by Takeda Katsuyori of the Takeda clan. The defeat led to the suicide of Hōjō Ujinobu, marking a significant moment in the power struggles of feudal Japan.
events.name: Fall of Kanbara Castle

events.enhanced_description: On December 13, 1569, an English counterattack against the Northern rebels commenced as Thomas Radclyffe, 3rd Earl of Sussex, marched from York with 10,000 men. The rebels, numbering 6,000, dispersed and fled northward, effectively ending the Rising of the North.
events.name: Counterattack against Northern rebels

events.enhanced_description: The siege of Nicosia by the Ottoman Empire began in 1570 and lasted for seven weeks, culminating in the city's fall. This siege was a critical event in the Ottoman conquest of Cyprus.
events.name: Siege of Nicosia Begins

events.enhanced_description: In 1570, Spanish conquistador Juan de Salcedo, serving under Miguel López de Legazpi, began the conquest of the Kingdom of Maynila. This marked the start of Spanish colonization in the Philippines, significantly altering the region's political landscape.
events.name: Conquest of the Kingdom of Maynila

events.enhanced_description: In 1570, the construction of the original Catedral Nuestra Señora de La Asunción began, marking the establishment of the oldest church in Venezuela. This architectural endeavor played a significant role in the religious and cultural development of the region.
events.name: Construction of Catedral Nuestra Señora de La Asunción

events.enhanced_description: By 1570, the Whitechapel Bell Foundry was known to be in existence in London, establishing itself as a significant manufacturer of bells. It would later become the oldest manufacturing company in Great Britain before closing in 2017.
events.name: Whitechapel Bell Foundry

events.enhanced_description: In 1570, Andrea Palladio published 'I quattro libri dell'architettura' (The Four Books of Architecture), which laid the foundation for modern Western architecture. This seminal work emphasized classical principles and had a profound influence on architecture in Europe and America.
events.name: Andrea Palladio publishes I quattro libri dell'architettura in Venice

events.enhanced_description: In 1570, a significant volcanic eruption began in the Santorini caldera, part of the Aegean volcanic arc. This eruption contributed to the geological transformation of the island and had lasting effects on the local environment and settlements.
events.name: Volcanic eruption in the Santorini caldera begins

events.enhanced_description: By 1570, the Andean population of the Viceroyalty of Peru had reached approximately 1.3 million, reflecting the demographic changes following Spanish colonization. This population growth was influenced by the introduction of new agricultural practices and the integration of indigenous peoples into colonial society.
events.name: The Andean population of the Viceroyalty of Peru reaches 1.3 million

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1570, a devastating earthquake with an estimated magnitude of 8.3 struck Concepción, Chile. This catastrophic event caused significant destruction and loss of life, marking one of the most powerful earthquakes recorded in the region's history.
events.name: Earthquake in Concepción

events.enhanced_description: On March 28, 1570, the ambassador of Ottoman Sultan Selim II presented a demand to the governing Council of the Venetian Republic, requesting the surrender of Cyprus. The Council's rejection of this demand set the stage for the subsequent conflict between Venice and the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Ottoman Demand for Cyprus

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1570, Colin Campbell of Glenorchy received permission from the Regent, the Earl of Morton, to execute Gregor Roy MacGregor, the chief of Clan Gregor and his son-in-law. The execution took place publicly at Balloch, highlighting the brutal power struggles of the time.
events.name: Execution of Gregor Roy MacGregor

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1570, Pope Pius V issued the papal bull Regnans in Excelsis, excommunicating Queen Elizabeth I of England and all who supported her. This act intensified the religious and political tensions between Catholic and Protestant factions in England.
events.name: Excommunication of Queen Elizabeth I

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1570, Abraham Ortelius published Theatrum Orbis Terrarum, the first modern atlas. This groundbreaking work compiled maps from various sources, significantly influencing cartography and the understanding of geography in the Renaissance.
events.name: Publication of Theatrum Orbis Terrarum

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1570, the Kingdom of Livonia was established, marking a significant political development in the Baltic region. This kingdom emerged from the complex interplay of local and foreign powers during the Northern Wars.
events.name: Establishment of the Kingdom of Livonia

events.enhanced_description: On July 3, 1570, the Ottoman conquest of Cyprus commenced as over 60,000 troops landed near Larnaca. This marked the beginning of a protracted military campaign that would lead to significant changes in the island's governance.
events.name: Ottoman Conquest of Cyprus Begins

events.enhanced_description: On July 14, 1570, Pope Pius V issued Quo primum, which promulgated the 1570 edition of the Roman Missal. This document standardized the liturgical practices of the Catholic Church, influencing worship for centuries.
events.name: Pope Pius V Issues Quo primum

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1570, Thomson Snell & Passmore was founded, becoming the oldest law firm in continuous operation in the United Kingdom. This establishment has played a significant role in the legal landscape of England.
events.name: Founding of Thomson Snell & Passmore

events.enhanced_description: On July 30, 1570, the allied forces of Oda Nobunaga and Tokugawa Ieyasu achieved a decisive victory against the Azai and Asakura clans at the Battle of Anegawa. This battle was a crucial moment in the unification of Japan during the Sengoku period.

image.caption: Anegawa Historic Battlefield in Shiga Prefecture, Japan.
image.date_qualification: The image date is 2011-10-03, not the 1570 battle date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Battle of Anegawa

events.enhanced_description: On August 8, 1570, the Peace of Saint-Germain was signed, effectively ending the Third War of Religion in France. This treaty granted the Huguenots religious freedom and political autonomy, marking a significant step towards religious tolerance.
events.name: Peace of Saint-Germain

events.enhanced_description: On August 16, 1570, the Treaty of Speyer was signed between John Sigismund Zápolya, Prince of Transylvania, and Maximilian II, King of Hungary. This treaty aimed to stabilize relations between the two leaders amidst ongoing conflicts in Central Europe.
events.name: Treaty of Speyer

events.enhanced_description: On September 9, 1570, Nicosia fell to the Ottoman forces commanded by General Lala Mustafa Pasha. The siege resulted in the massacre of Venetian defenders and the enslavement of women and children, marking a dark chapter in the history of Cyprus.
events.name: Fall of Nicosia

events.enhanced_description: On September 10, 1570, a group of ten Spanish Jesuit missionaries landed on the Virginia Peninsula to establish the Ajacán Mission. This mission aimed to convert the local Indigenous population to Christianity but would ultimately face tragic consequences.
events.name: Ajacán Mission Established

events.enhanced_description: On September 25, 1570, the Ishiyama Hongan-ji War began as Oda Nobunaga launched simultaneous attacks on the fortresses of Ishiyama Hongan-ji and Nagashima, marking the start of a protracted conflict against the Ikkō-ikki faction.
events.name: Ishiyama Hongan-ji War Begins

events.enhanced_description: On October 3, 1570, Princess Anna of Austria arrived in Spain to become the Queen Consort of her uncle, King Philip II. Her arrival followed a proxy marriage, and she sought to influence the King regarding the fate of political prisoners.
events.name: Arrival of Princess Anna of Austria

events.enhanced_description: On November 17, 1570, a major earthquake struck Ferrara, Italy, at 3:00 AM, destroying 40% of the city's buildings and resulting in 171 deaths. The aftershocks continued for four years, further impacting the region.
events.name: Earthquake in Ferrara

events.enhanced_description: On December 13, 1570, the Treaty of Stettin was signed, officially ending the Northern Seven Years' War. This treaty marked a significant resolution to the conflicts in the Baltic region.
events.name: Treaty of Stettin

events.enhanced_description: The introduction of mercury in the silver extraction process at the Potosí mine significantly increased output, initiating a massive flow of silver that connected the New and Old Worlds. This innovation had profound economic implications for global trade.
events.name: Mercury use in silver extraction at Potosí

events.enhanced_description: The Swedish Church Ordinance of 1571 established the first complete order for the Protestant Swedish church, emphasizing the importance of education by mandating elementary schooling for all children in cities. This ordinance played a crucial role in shaping the religious and educational landscape of Sweden.
events.name: Swedish Church Ordinance 1571

events.enhanced_description: Taipalsaari was founded in 1571, contributing to the development of settlements in the region. This establishment reflects the broader patterns of settlement and community formation in Finland during this period.
events.name: Foundation of Taipalsaari

events.enhanced_description: On January 11, 1571, the Austrian nobility were granted freedom of religion, a significant step towards religious tolerance in the Habsburg territories. This decree allowed nobles to practice their faith without interference, reflecting the changing attitudes towards Protestantism and Catholicism in the region.
events.name: The Austrian nobility are granted freedom of religion

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1571, the Royal Exchange opened in London, serving as a hub for merchants and traders. This establishment marked a significant development in the commercial landscape of England, facilitating trade and commerce in the growing city.
events.name: The Royal Exchange opens in London, England

events.enhanced_description: On February 4, 1571, Spanish Jesuit missionaries at the Ajacán Mission on the Virginia Peninsula were massacred by local Native Americans. This tragic event highlighted the tensions between European colonizers and indigenous populations during the early stages of colonization in North America.
events.name: Massacre of Spanish Jesuit missionaries at Ajacán Mission

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1571, the Order of the Knights of Saint John officially transferred the capital of Malta from Birgu to Valletta. This move was part of a broader strategy to fortify the island and enhance its defenses against Ottoman threats.
events.name: The Order of the Knights of Saint John transfers the capital of Malta

events.enhanced_description: On April 2, 1571, the 3rd Parliament of Elizabeth I convened in Westminster with 438 members. This assembly was significant for addressing various political and religious issues of the time, reflecting the complexities of governance in Elizabethan England.
events.name: The 3rd Parliament of Elizabeth I assembles

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1571, the Ridolfi plot, a conspiracy to assassinate Queen Elizabeth I and place Mary, Queen of Scots on the English throne, was foiled by the capture of Ridolfi's messenger. This event underscored the political tensions and threats faced by Elizabeth's reign.
events.name: The Ridolfi plot to assassinate Queen Elizabeth I is foiled

events.enhanced_description: On April 17, 1571, Pope John XIV of Alexandria began his 15-year reign as the leader of the Coptic Christian Church. His leadership was marked by efforts to strengthen the Coptic community amidst challenges from both Islamic and Catholic authorities.

locations.name: Monastery of St. Macarius, Wadi El Natrun

events.name: Pope John XIV of Alexandria begins reign

events.enhanced_description: On April 21, 1571, General Altan Khan was granted authority to rule the western provinces of China by the Ming dynasty Emperor Longqing in exchange for tribute. This arrangement highlighted the complex relationships between the Ming dynasty and Mongol leaders during this period.
events.name: General Altan Khan granted authority in China

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1571, Moscow was set ablaze by the Crimean army under the command of Devlet I Giray. This devastating event was part of the ongoing conflicts between the Crimean Khanate and the Russian state, leading to significant destruction and loss.
events.name: Moscow is burnt by the Crimean army

events.enhanced_description: On May 25, 1571, the Holy League was established as an alliance among several states, including the Papal States and the Republic of Venice, for mutual defense against the Ottoman Empire. This coalition aimed to protect Christian maritime interests in the Mediterranean.
events.name: The Holy League is established

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1571, Queen Elizabeth I granted royal assent to several laws passed by the 3rd Parliament, including the Bulls from Rome Act 1571. This act aimed to prevent the publication of papal bulls in England, reflecting the ongoing religious tensions of the time.
events.name: Queen Elizabeth I gives royal assent to laws

events.enhanced_description: On June 3, 1571, following the Battle of Bangkusay Channel, Spanish Conquistador Miguel López de Legazpi completed the conquest of the Kingdom of Maynila, establishing Manila as the capital of the Philippines. This marked a significant moment in the Spanish colonization of Southeast Asia.

image.caption: Portrait of Miguel López de Legazpi, published in the Spanish magazine La Hormiga de Oro.
image.credit: Celestí Sadurní i Deop — ( 16 April 1887 ). " Miguel López de Legaspi ". La Hormiga de Oro (16): 252. ISSN 2171-7591 .
image.date_qualification: Portrait published in 1887, centuries after the 1571 conquest; it is not a contemporary event image.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Conquest of the Kingdom of Maynila is complete

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1571, Miguel López de Legazpi established a Spanish fortress at Manila Bay after negotiating a peace pact with Rajah Sulayman, the Crown Prince of Luzon. This event solidified Spanish control over the region and marked Manila as the administrative capital of the Spanish East Indies.
events.name: Establishment of a Spanish fortress at Manila Bay

events.enhanced_description: On June 25, 1571, Queen Elizabeth's Grammar School was founded in Horncastle, Lincolnshire. This institution represented the growing emphasis on education during the Elizabethan era, providing a foundation for future generations.
events.name: Queen Elizabeth's Grammar School, Horncastle, is founded

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1571, Jesus College was established in Oxford by Welsh cleric and lawyer Hugh Price. This college became part of the University of Oxford, contributing to the academic and cultural landscape of England.
events.name: Jesus College is established in Oxford

events.enhanced_description: On July 14, 1571, the Siege of Chaliyam began in what is now Kerala, India, as the Zamorin of Kozhikode, Mana Vikrama, sent troops to starve out the Portuguese-held Chale fortress. The siege culminated in the surrender of the fort later that year, marking a significant conflict in the region.
events.name: Siege of Chaliyam begins

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1571, St Olave's Grammar School was founded in Tooley Street, London. This establishment contributed to the educational landscape of the city during the Elizabethan period.
events.name: St Olave's Grammar School is founded

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1571, the Ottoman conquest of Cyprus was concluded with the surrender of Famagusta. This event marked the establishment of Cyprus as an eyalet of the Ottoman Empire, significantly altering the political landscape of the Eastern Mediterranean.

locations.name: Famagusta, Famagusta District, Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus

events.name: The Ottoman conquest of Cyprus is concluded

events.enhanced_description: Liliw, a municipality in Laguna, Philippines, was founded by Gat Tayaw and his followers. This establishment marked the beginning of organized local governance in the region, contributing to the cultural and political landscape of the area.
events.name: Foundation of Liliw

events.enhanced_description: John Erskine, Earl of Mar, was appointed as the Regent of Scotland to govern on behalf of the young King James VI following the assassination of Matthew Stewart, 4th Earl of Lennox. This event was pivotal in the power struggles of the Scottish nobility during the turbulent period of the Reformation.
events.name: John Erskine becomes Regent of Scotland

events.enhanced_description: The House of Commons of England introduced its first pro forma bill, a significant step in asserting its authority over legislative matters. This event symbolized the growing power of the Commons in the English political system.
events.name: Introduction of the first pro forma bill in the House of Commons

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Mount Hiei, led by Oda Nobunaga, resulted in the overwhelming defeat of the warrior monks of the Sōhei. This brutal campaign exemplified Nobunaga's military prowess and his ruthless approach to consolidating power in Japan.
events.name: Siege of Mount Hiei

events.enhanced_description: In the naval Battle of Lepanto, a coalition of Spanish, Venetian, and Papal forces, commanded by Don John of Austria, achieved a decisive victory over the Ottoman fleet led by Müezzinzade Ali Pasha. This battle marked a significant turning point in the struggle for naval supremacy in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Battle of Lepanto

events.enhanced_description: The Mexican Inquisition commenced with the first session of the Tribunal of the Holy Office of the Inquisition in New Spain, aimed at investigating and punishing heresy against the Roman Catholic Church. This marked the beginning of a significant religious and cultural enforcement in the New World.

image.caption: Facade of the Palace of the Inquisition, now the Museum of Mexican Medicine, facing Santo Domingo Plaza in Mexico City.
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2009-05-23; not a photograph of the Inquisition’s 1571 commencement.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Beginning of the Mexican Inquisition

events.enhanced_description: Pope Pius V appointed Michele Bonelli as legate a latere to work directly with King Charles IX of France, following Bonelli's previous role as legate to Spain and Portugal. This move underscored the Vatican's interest in influencing French politics during a time of religious conflict.
events.name: Michele Bonelli sent as legate to France

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Craibstone, Clan Gordon defeated Clan Forbes in a fierce conflict near Aberdeen. The battle resulted in significant casualties for Clan Forbes, highlighting the ongoing clan rivalries in Scotland during this period.
events.name: Battle of Craibstone

events.enhanced_description: Henry XI, Duke of Liegnitz, faced a severe debt crisis, escalating from 80,000 to 700,000 thalers over 11 years. In a desperate attempt to refinance, he pressured representatives of the Congress of Estates to pledge their goods as collateral, leading to their imprisonment when they refused.
events.name: Henry XI's debt crisis in Liegnitz

events.enhanced_description: In 1572, Tupac Amaru and several Inca nobles were executed in Cuzco on the orders of the Spanish colonial Viceroy, Francisco de Toledo. This brutal act marked a significant moment in the Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire and the destruction of its cultural heritage.
events.name: Execution of Tupac Amaru and Inca nobles

events.enhanced_description: In 1572, the Ottoman Empire began deporting 10 percent of families from various provinces in Anatolia to the newly-conquered island of Cyprus. This policy aimed to populate the island and strengthen Ottoman control, offering tax exemptions to the relocated families.
events.name: Ottoman deportation to Cyprus

events.enhanced_description: In 1572, Supernova SN 1572 was first observed in the constellation Cassiopeia by Cornelius Gemma. Tycho Brahe noted it shortly thereafter, using this event to challenge the prevailing belief that stars were immutable and unchanging.
events.name: Supernova SN 1572 observed

events.enhanced_description: In 1572, the Neo-Inca State, the last independent remnant of the Inca Empire, was conquered by Spanish forces. This marked the end of significant Inca resistance against Spanish colonization in Peru.
events.name: Conquest of the Neo-Inca State

events.enhanced_description: In 1572, Girolamo Mercuriale from Forlì published 'De morbis cutaneis', the first scientific tract on dermatology. This work laid the foundation for future studies in skin diseases and treatments.
events.name: Publication of De morbis cutaneis

events.enhanced_description: In 1572, mathematician Rafael Bombelli defined imaginary numbers, a significant advancement in the field of mathematics that would later influence complex number theory.

image.caption: Title page of Rafael Bombelli’s Algebra, a printed book.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Book printed by editor Giovanni Rossi
image.date_qualification: Book cover printed in Bologna in 1579; it is a later publication associated with Bombelli’s work, not a depiction of the definition of imaginary numbers in 1572.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Definition of imaginary numbers

events.enhanced_description: In 1572, the national epic of Portugal, 'Os Lusíadas' by Luís de Camões, was first published. This work celebrated the Portuguese Age of Discovery and remains a cornerstone of Portuguese literature.
events.name: Publication of Os Lusíadas

events.enhanced_description: In 1572, Georg Braun began the publication of his urban atlas 'Civitates orbis terrarum' in Cologne. This work became one of the most important collections of city views and maps of the time.
events.name: Publication of Civitates orbis terrarum

events.enhanced_description: Thomas Howard, 4th Duke of Norfolk, was tried for treason due to his involvement in the Ridolfi plot aimed at restoring Catholicism in England. His execution on June 2 marked a significant moment in the ongoing religious conflicts of the time.
events.name: Trial of Thomas Howard, 4th Duke of Norfolk

events.enhanced_description: Queen Elizabeth I issued a proclamation revoking all commissions due to the frauds they had fostered, reflecting her efforts to maintain control and integrity within her administration. This action was part of her broader strategy to consolidate power.
events.name: Elizabeth I revokes commissions

events.enhanced_description: Harrow School was founded with a royal charter from Queen Elizabeth I, establishing it as one of the leading educational institutions in England. This foundation contributed to the development of education and culture in the country.
events.name: Foundation of Harrow School

events.enhanced_description: Maharana Pratap was crowned as the new Rana of Mewar in Udaipur following the death of his father, Udai Singh II. His reign would be marked by resistance against Mughal expansion and a strong sense of Rajput pride.
events.name: Maharana Pratap crowned as Rana of Mewar

events.enhanced_description: Mem de Sá, the Portuguese Governor-General of Brazil, died after 14 years in office, leaving a significant legacy in the administration of the colony. He was succeeded by Lourenço da Veiga, who continued the efforts to consolidate Portuguese control in the region.

locations.name: Rio de Janeiro, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

events.name: Death of Mem de Sá

events.enhanced_description: Pope Pius V issued the papal bull Supremi omnipotentis Dei, which granted indulgences to Roman Catholics who recited the penitential psalms, reflecting the Catholic Church's efforts to provide spiritual relief and reinforce religious practices during the Counter-Reformation.
events.name: Papal bull Supremi omnipotentis Dei

events.enhanced_description: Queen Elizabeth I summoned a new Parliament, which convened on May 4, 1572. This assembly was crucial for addressing various political and economic issues facing England at the time.
events.name: Summoning of a new Parliament by Elizabeth I

events.enhanced_description: The Sea Beggars, a group of Netherlandish Calvinist rebels, captured the port city of Brielle, igniting a wave of uprisings against Spanish Habsburg rule in Holland and Zeeland. This event marked a significant escalation in the Dutch Revolt.
events.name: Capture of Brielle

events.enhanced_description: Pope Gregory XIII succeeded Pope Pius V as the 226th pope, taking office during a critical period of the Counter-Reformation. His papacy would be marked by efforts to reform the Church and address the challenges posed by Protestantism.
events.name: Succession of Pope Gregory XIII

events.enhanced_description: At the Battle of Kizaki, Shimazu Yoshihiro led a small force of 300 men to a stunning victory against the 3,000-strong Ito clan. This battle exemplified the strategic brilliance of Yoshihiro and the intense clan rivalries of the period.
events.name: Battle of Kizaki

events.enhanced_description: The Sea Beggars captured the city of Gorkum, leading to the imprisonment of several Roman Catholic priests. This event further escalated tensions during the Dutch Revolt against Spanish rule.
events.name: Capture of Gorkum

events.enhanced_description: The city council of Haarlem voted to join the Dutch Revolt against King Philip II of Spain, a significant act of defiance that prompted a military response from the Spanish crown. This decision was pivotal in the broader context of the struggle for independence in the Netherlands.
events.name: Haarlem joins the Dutch Revolt

events.enhanced_description: The Sea Beggars executed 19 previously imprisoned Roman Catholic priests at Brielle, an event that became known as the Martyrs of Gorkum. This act highlighted the religious tensions and violence during the Dutch Revolt against Spanish rule.
events.name: Martyrs of Gorkum executed

events.enhanced_description: In July 1572, Sir Humphrey Gilbert led an expedition of 1,500 volunteers from England to assist the Sea Beggars, a group of Dutch rebels fighting against Spanish rule. This expedition was part of the larger context of the Eighty Years' War, which sought to establish Dutch independence from Spanish control.
events.name: Humphrey Gilbert leads 1,500 volunteers from England, on an expedition to assist the Sea Beggars

events.enhanced_description: On July 19, 1572, the Wanli Emperor ascended the throne of the Ming Dynasty at the tender age of nine. His reign would last for 48 years, during which he would oversee significant cultural and political changes in China, although his later years were marked by decline and corruption.

image.caption: Portrait of the Wanli Emperor (Ming Shenzong).
image.date_qualification: Image date is supplied as “Ming Dynasty (1368-1644)”; no more precise depicted date is established.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Wanli Emperor of China ascends the throne at the age of nine

events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1572, the Battle of Molodi took place, where the forces of Tsar Ivan IV of Russia decisively defeated a large army of Crimean Tatars and Ottomans. This victory was crucial in preventing the Ottoman Empire from expanding further into Russian territory.
events.name: Battle of Molodi

events.enhanced_description: On August 18, 1572, Huguenot King Henry III of Navarre married Margaret of Valois in a politically motivated union aimed at reconciling Protestants and Catholics in France. This marriage, however, failed to bring peace and was soon overshadowed by the violence of the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre.
events.name: Marriage of Henry III of Navarre and Margaret of Valois

events.enhanced_description: The St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre began on August 24, 1572, when thousands of Huguenots were killed in Paris at the behest of King Charles IX, with the complicity of his mother, Catherine de' Medici. This brutal event marked a significant escalation in the French Wars of Religion, leading to further conflict and bloodshed.
events.name: St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre

events.enhanced_description: On September 25, 1572, Rudolf II was crowned King of Hungary at St. Martin's Cathedral in Pozsony, now Bratislava. His reign would be marked by a focus on the arts and sciences, as well as the challenges of managing a diverse empire.
events.name: Coronation of Rudolf as King of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: On October 2, 1572, the Spanish Army entered Mechelen, where the mostly Catholic population surrendered without resistance. However, the Duke of Alba authorized his troops to conduct three days of violence, resulting in widespread slaughter and pillaging.
events.name: Spanish Fury at Mechelen

events.enhanced_description: On October 20, 1572, soldiers of the Spanish Tercios waded across the estuary of the Scheldt to relieve the siege of Goes, a significant event during the Eighty Years' War. This maneuver showcased the military prowess of the Spanish forces in the ongoing conflict.
events.name: Relief of Goes

events.enhanced_description: Beginning on November 9, 1572, the Siege of Sancerre saw Catholic forces lay siege to the Huguenot stronghold of Sancerre. The city held out for nearly eight months, demonstrating remarkable resilience in the face of siege warfare.
events.name: Siege of Sancerre

events.enhanced_description: On November 14, 1572, the Spanish Army massacred the residents of Zutphen, a tragic event during the Eighty Years' War. This act of violence exemplified the brutal tactics employed by the Spanish forces against Dutch rebels.
events.name: Massacre in Zutphen

events.enhanced_description: On November 22, 1572, the Spanish Army massacred nearly all of the 3,000 residents of Naarden, leaving only 60 survivors. This brutal event was part of the Spanish campaign during the Eighty Years' War and highlighted the extreme violence of the conflict.
events.name: Massacre in Naarden

events.enhanced_description: On December 10, 1572, the Kingdom of Portugal divided its colony in Brazil into two separate colonies, appointing one Governor-General in Rio de Janeiro and another in Bahia. This administrative change aimed to improve governance and control over the vast territory.

locations.name: Rio de Janeiro, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

events.name: Division of Portuguese Brazil

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Haarlem commenced on December 11, 1572, as the Duke of Alba's Spanish forces aimed to capture the city from the Dutch rebels. This siege would last until July 13, 1573, becoming one of the pivotal events in the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: Siege of Haarlem begins

events.enhanced_description: In 1573, Sarsa Dengel, the emperor of Ethiopia, achieved a significant victory over the Oromo in a battle near Lake Zway. This conflict was part of the larger struggle for control and dominance in the region during the late 16th century.
events.name: Battle near Lake Zway

events.enhanced_description: In 1573, the first Spanish galleon, laden with silver intended for trade with the Ming Dynasty of China, landed in Manila. This event marked the beginning of a lucrative trade route that would significantly impact global commerce and the economies of both Spain and China.
events.name: First Spanish Galleon to Manila

events.enhanced_description: In 1573, the production of Luzhou Laojiao liquor began in Luzhou, Sichuan, China. This liquor is known for its unique flavor and has become an important part of Chinese culture and cuisine.
events.name: Luzhou Laojiao liquor production

events.enhanced_description: In 1573, Queen Elizabeth's Grammar School for Boys was established in Barnet, England. This institution has played a significant role in the education of young men in the area and reflects the educational reforms of the period.
events.name: Formation of Queen Elizabeth's Grammar School

events.enhanced_description: On January 25, 1573, at the Battle of Mikatagahara, Takeda Shingen's forces defeated Tokugawa Ieyasu in a significant engagement during Japan's Sengoku period. This battle showcased the military strategies and prowess of the Takeda clan.
events.name: Battle of Mikatagahara

events.enhanced_description: The Articles of the Warsaw Confederation were signed on January 28, 1573, establishing religious freedom in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. This landmark agreement was crucial in promoting tolerance among various religious groups, particularly Protestants and Catholics, during a time of significant religious conflict in Europe.
events.name: Articles of the Warsaw Confederation are signed, sanctioning religious freedom in Poland

events.enhanced_description: The Wanli Era commenced on February 2, 1573, marking the beginning of the reign of the nine-year-old Emperor Zhu Yijun in the Ming dynasty. This era is noted for its cultural achievements and challenges, including internal strife and external threats that would shape the future of China.
events.name: The Wanli Era begins in Ming dynasty China

events.enhanced_description: On February 6, 1573, the Battle of Kerestinec took place, where General Gašpar Alapić led Croatian forces to victory against the rebel troops commanded by Matija Gubec. This battle was part of the Croatian-Slovene Peasant Revolt, which sought to challenge the oppressive nobility.
events.name: Battle of Kerestinec

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Stubica occurred on February 9, 1573, where Croatian troops under General Alapić defeated the peasant rebellion led by Matija Gubec.
