Following their victory, the Croatian forces initiated a brutal campaign against the rebels, leading to the capture and trial of Gubec and his associates.
events.name: Battle of Stubica

events.enhanced_description: Beginning on February 11, 1573, the Siege of Sommières was part of the Fourth War of Religion in France, where Marshal Henri de Montmorency laid siege to the Huguenot-held town. The siege lasted nearly two months, highlighting the intense religious conflicts of the period.
events.name: Siege of Sommières

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1573, Matija Gubec, the leader of the peasant revolt, was executed in a gruesome public display ordered by the Croatian Viceroy Juraj Drašković. This brutal punishment was intended to deter further rebellion against the nobility and showcased the harsh realities of peasant life in Croatia.
events.name: Execution of Matija Gubec

events.enhanced_description: The siege of Noda Castle began on February 16, 1573, following the assassination of Takeda Shingen, the leader of the Takeda clan. The siege marked a significant conflict between the Takeda and Tokugawa clans, culminating in the surrender of the castle just a few weeks later.

locations.name: Noda Castle, Shinshiro, Aichi Prefecture, Japan

events.name: Siege of Noda Castle

events.enhanced_description: On February 23, 1573, the First Desmond Rebellion in Ireland came to an end at Kilmallock, where James FitzMaurice FitzGerald surrendered to John Perrot. This rebellion was part of the larger conflict between the English crown and Irish lords, highlighting the tensions of the period.
events.name: End of the First Desmond Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: The Ottoman–Venetian War concluded on March 7, 1573, with a peace treaty that formalized the transfer of Cyprus from Venice to the Ottoman Empire. This treaty marked a significant shift in power in the Eastern Mediterranean and solidified Ottoman control over the region.

image.caption: Near-contemporary painting depicting the Battle of Lepanto, a naval engagement between Christian forces and the Ottoman fleet.
image.date_qualification: Painting dated broadly to the late 16th century; it depicts the 1571 Battle of Lepanto, not the 1573 peace settlement.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: End of the Ottoman–Venetian War

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1573, Francis Drake and his crew captured a wagon train of silver near Nombre de Dios, Panama, marking one of the most lucrative moments of his expedition to the New World. This event underscored the wealth of the Spanish colonies and the growing competition among European powers for control of these resources.
events.name: Francis Drake's capture at Nombre de Dios

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1573, Polish and Lithuanian nobles convened in Warsaw to elect a successor to the deceased King Sigismund II Augustus. This election was notable for its competitive nature, with candidates from France, the Holy Roman Empire, Sweden, and Russia vying for the throne.
events.name: 1573 Polish–Lithuanian royal election

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Sommières concluded on April 9, 1573, with the surrender of the Huguenot defenders. Despite the loss of 2,500 royal troops, General Montmorency spared the defenders from retaliation, reflecting the complexities of the ongoing religious wars in France.
events.name: Siege of Sommières ends

events.enhanced_description: On April 22, 1573, the Battle of Borsele was fought during the Eighty Years' War, where Dutch Calvinist rebels, known as the Geuzen, intercepted a fleet of Spanish ships. This battle exemplified the ongoing struggle for independence from Spanish rule in the Netherlands.
events.name: Battle of Borsele

events.enhanced_description: On May 16, 1573, Henry, Duke of Anjou, was elected as the King of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth by the Polish nobility. His election marked a significant moment in the political landscape of Eastern Europe, as he was the first French king to ascend the Polish throne.
events.name: Election of Henry, Duke of Anjou

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Haarlemmermeer took place on May 26, 1573, where Geuzen ships attempted to break the siege of Haarlem but were defeated by a combined Spanish and Amsterdam fleet. This battle was part of the larger conflict during the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: Battle of Haarlemmermeer

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1573, Henry, Duke of Anjou, negotiated an end to the long-standing Siege of La Rochelle, which had been ongoing for nearly nine months against the Huguenots. This agreement was significant in the context of the French Wars of Religion, as it aimed to stabilize the region.
events.name: Negotiation to end the Siege of La Rochelle

events.enhanced_description: Córdoba was founded on July 6, 1573, by Jerónimo Luis de Cabrera in the Viceroyalty of Peru. This city would later become one of the most important cultural and educational centers in Argentina.
events.name: Foundation of Córdoba

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1573, the Edict of Boulogne was signed by Charles IX of France, granting limited rights to Huguenots and effectively ending the Fourth War of Religion. This edict was a crucial step towards religious tolerance in France during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Edict of Boulogne

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Haarlem concluded on July 12, 1573, when Spanish forces under the Duke of Alva captured the city after a grueling seven-month siege. This event marked a significant victory for the Spanish during the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: Siege of Haarlem ends

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 1573, the Duke of Alva initiated the siege of Alkmaar in North Holland. This siege would last for seven weeks before the Spanish forces ultimately retreated, marking a turning point in the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: Siege of Alkmaar begins

events.enhanced_description: On August 27, 1573, Oda Nobunaga expelled the 15th Ashikaga shōgun, Ashikaga Yoshiaki, from Kyoto, effectively dismantling the Ashikaga shogunate. This event marked the end of the Muromachi and Sengoku periods, ushering in the Azuchi–Momoyama period of Japanese history.
events.name: Oda Nobunaga drives Ashikaga Yoshiaki out of Kyoto

events.enhanced_description: On September 16, 1573, Oda Nobunaga completed the elimination of the Asakura clan following the sieges of Hikida Castle and Ichijōdani Castle. This decisive action solidified Nobunaga's power in the region and contributed to his campaign of unification in Japan.
events.name: Elimination of the Asakura clan

events.enhanced_description: The siege of Odani Castle concluded on September 26, 1573, with the elimination of the Azai clan by Oda Nobunaga. This victory was part of Nobunaga's broader strategy to consolidate power and eliminate rival clans during the tumultuous Sengoku period.

locations.name: Odani Castle Ruins, Takashima, Shiga Prefecture, Japan

events.name: Siege of Odani Castle

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Alkmaar was a pivotal event during the Eighty Years' War, where the Spanish forces abandoned their siege, marking a significant victory for the Dutch rebels known as the Geuzen. This event symbolized the resilience of the Dutch resistance against Spanish rule and contributed to the eventual independence of the Netherlands.
events.name: Siege of Alkmaar

events.enhanced_description: On October 11, 1573, Spanish forces under the command of John of Austria captured Tunis with minimal resistance, reasserting Spanish influence in North Africa. This event was part of the broader struggle for control over the Mediterranean region during the 16th century.
events.name: Capture of Tunis

events.enhanced_description: On November 29, 1573, the Duke of Alva resigned as the Governor-General of the Netherlands, paving the way for Luis de Requesens, who sought to implement a more conciliatory approach towards the Dutch rebels. This change in leadership was significant in the context of the ongoing Eighty Years' War.
events.name: Duke of Alva Resignation

events.enhanced_description: On December 3, 1573, the French Duke of Anjou, who had been elected King Henry of Poland, departed from Metz with a large entourage, arriving in Kraków on February 18. His election and subsequent journey marked a significant moment in the political landscape of both France and Poland.
events.name: Departure of Henry of Anjou

events.enhanced_description: On December 11, 1573, the Governor of Portuguese India issued an edict that stripped Hindu followers of many rights, including the right to receive Jonoa, a share of village community income. This action reflected the tensions between colonial authorities and local populations in the region.
events.name: Edict in Portuguese India

events.enhanced_description: On December 17, 1573, Portuguese colonists were expelled from the Maldives by Mohamed Bodu Takurufanu al-Azam, marking a significant shift in control over the islands. This event was part of the broader resistance against colonial powers in the Indian Ocean region.
events.name: Expulsion from the Maldives

events.enhanced_description: On December 23, 1573, the Council of Ten in the Republic of Venice voted to grant safe conduct to Spanish and Portuguese Jews. This decision was significant in the context of the Jewish diaspora and the treatment of Jews in Europe during the Renaissance.
events.name: Safe Conduct for Jews in Venice

events.enhanced_description: In February 1574, the Fifth War of Religion against the Huguenots began in France, escalating the ongoing conflict between Catholics and Protestants. This war was marked by significant violence and political intrigue, further complicating the religious landscape of France.

image.caption: Portrait of Catherine de' Medici, widow of Henry II of France.
image.date_qualification: Circa 1560 (image date; predates the event date supplied as 1574-01-01).
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Fifth War of Religion begins

events.enhanced_description: In April 1574, the fort of Narnala in the Deccan region fell to the Ahmadnagar Sultanate, leading to the annexation of the Berar Sultanate. This event was part of the ongoing power struggles in India during the Mughal era.

locations.name: Narnala Fort, Amravati District, Maharashtra, India

events.name: Fall of Narnala Fort

events.enhanced_description: In 1574, Manila was officially granted cityhood, marking a significant milestone in its development as a key center of trade and administration in the Philippines. This status contributed to Manila's growth and importance in the Spanish colonial empire.
events.name: Manila gains cityhood

events.enhanced_description: In 1574, Prince El-Mirza of Kakheti was defeated in his bid for the throne by his half-brother, Alexander II. This conflict was part of the ongoing power struggles within the Georgian nobility.
events.name: Defeat of Prince El-Mirza of Kakheti

events.enhanced_description: In 1574, the Liturgical Battle royal between the Reformation and Counter-Reformation began in Sweden, continuing until the Uppsala Synod of 1593. This conflict represented the broader religious tensions in Europe during the Reformation.
events.name: Liturgical Battle in Sweden

events.enhanced_description: In 1574, La Alameda in Seville was laid out as Europe's first public garden. This development marked a significant cultural shift towards public spaces and urban greenery in European cities.
events.name: La Alameda, Seville

events.enhanced_description: On January 22, 1574, Abu Abdallah Mohammed II ascended to the throne as the Sultan of Morocco following the death of his father, Abdallah al-Ghalib. His reign marked a period of political transition and challenges within the Moroccan empire.
events.name: Abu Abdallah Mohammed II becomes Sultan of Morocco

events.enhanced_description: On January 27, 1574, Bhagwant Das was appointed as the new Maharaja of the Kingdom of Amber in Agra, India, following the death of his grandfather, Raja Bharmal. His leadership played a crucial role in the political dynamics of the region during the Mughal era.
events.name: Bhagwant Das becomes Maharaja

events.enhanced_description: On January 29, 1574, the Battle of the Scheldt was fought off the coast of the Netherlands between the Spanish fleet and a combined Dutch and English fleet. The Spanish suffered significant losses, with 15 ships sunk and over 1,200 men killed or captured, marking a critical moment in the naval conflict of the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: Battle of the Scheldt

events.enhanced_description: On March 2, 1574, Swedish troops launched an attack on Wesenberg Castle in Estonia but suffered heavy losses, with at least 1,000 men killed in the attempt to capture it from the Russian Army. This battle exemplified the intense military conflicts in the region during the Northern Wars.
events.name: Swedish attack on Wesenberg Castle

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1574, a violent confrontation occurred within the Swedish Army between Scottish and German mercenaries, resulting in several hundred Scots dead compared to only 30 Germans. This internal conflict highlighted the complexities of mercenary warfare during the period.
events.name: Scottish-German Mercenaries Fight

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1574, the Battle of Mookerheyde took place, where Spanish forces under Sancho de Avila defeated the rebel forces led by Louis of Nassau, who was killed in the battle. This defeat was a significant setback for the Dutch resistance during the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: Battle of Mookerheyde

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1574, King Charles IX of France died at the Château de Vincennes from tuberculosis. His death led to his brother, Henry of Anjou, ascending the throne as Henry III of France, with their mother, Catherine de' Medici, acting as regent until his arrival.

locations.name: Château de Vincennes, Vincennes, Île-de-France, France

events.name: Death of King Charles IX of France

events.enhanced_description: Construction of The White Tower began on June 10, 1574, in what is now the Czech Republic. This architectural project reflects the artistic and cultural developments of the period.
events.name: Construction of The White Tower

events.enhanced_description: On July 12, 1574, Selim II, the Sultan of the Ottoman Empire, launched a military campaign to reclaim Tunis from the control of the Holy Roman Empire, deploying over 250 warships and 100,000 troops. This ambitious attempt aimed to restore North Africa to Muslim control and reassert Ottoman dominance in the region.
events.name: Selim II's Attempt to Reclaim Tunis

events.enhanced_description: On July 13, 1574, John George, Elector of Brandenburg, ordered the establishment of the Evangelisches Gymnasium zum Grauen Kloster in Berlin. This institution has since evolved into one of Germany's most prestigious preparatory schools, reflecting the elector's commitment to education and the Protestant Reformation.
events.name: Founding of the Evangelisches Gymnasium zum Grauen Kloster

events.enhanced_description: On July 26, 1574, Kılıç Ali Pasha initiated the construction of an Ottoman fortress along the Moroccan coastline, strategically positioned across from Andalusia, Spain. This fortification was part of the Ottoman Empire's broader efforts to expand its influence in the Mediterranean region.
events.name: Construction of Ottoman Fortress in Morocco

events.enhanced_description: On August 24, 1574, the Tunisian port of La Goulette fell to Ottoman forces after a six-week siege. This event marked a significant moment in the Ottoman expansion into North Africa, consolidating their control over key maritime routes.
events.name: Fall of La Goulette to Ottoman Troops

events.enhanced_description: On August 30, 1574, Guru Ram Das was appointed as the fourth Guru of the Sikh faith. His leadership was pivotal in establishing the foundations of Sikhism, including the founding of the city of Amritsar, which became a central religious site for Sikhs.

image.caption: Miniature painting of Guru Ram Das seated beside an attendant holding a fly-whisk.
image.credit: Family workshop (or atelier) of Nainsukh of Guler — Gurdeep Kour. A Search for the ‘Darshan’ of Sikh Gurus among Pahari Rulers. Discovery, 2019, 55(282), 220-234
image.date_qualification: Retrospective painting from circa 1800, not a contemporary depiction of his appointment as Guru.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Guru Ram Das becomes the Fourth Sikh Guru

events.enhanced_description: In September 1574, a conspiracy to assassinate John III of Sweden was uncovered, led by Charles de Mornay and involving several prominent figures, including members of the Swedish nobility. This plot highlighted the political tensions and rivalries within the Swedish court during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Assassination Plot Against John III of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1574, the last defenders of the Holy Roman Empire surrendered the city of Tunis to Ottoman General Cığalazade Yusuf Sinan Pasha. This event marked the end of significant resistance against Ottoman control in North Africa.
events.name: Surrender of Tunis to Ottoman General

events.enhanced_description: On October 3, 1574, the city of Leiden, which had been under siege by Spanish forces, was relieved by a fleet of Sea Beggars led by Louis Boisot. This victory was a turning point in the Dutch struggle for independence from Spanish rule.
events.name: Relief of Leiden

events.enhanced_description: On November 22, 1574, Spanish sailor Juan Fernández discovered the Juan Fernández Islands in the South Pacific Ocean. This discovery contributed to the European understanding of the Pacific and the geography of the region.

image.caption: Rough map of some Chilean islands in the Pacific Ocean, including the Juan Fernández Islands.
image.date_qualification: Map dated 2007-09-09; it is not contemporary with the discovery.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

locations.name: Juan Fernández Islands, Valparaíso Region, Chile

events.name: Discovery of the Juan Fernández Islands

events.enhanced_description: On December 15, 1574, Selim II, the 50-year-old Sultan of the Ottoman Empire, died after a drunken fall in the Topkapi Palace, resulting in a fractured skull. His death marked a significant transition in the Ottoman leadership.
events.name: Death of Selim II

events.enhanced_description: On December 22, 1574, Prince Murad bin-Selim of the Ottoman Empire completed the murders of his four younger brothers, Suleyman, Abdullah, Osman, and Cihangir, by strangulation. This brutal act was part of the violent power struggles within the Ottoman dynasty.
events.name: Murders of Ottoman Princes

events.enhanced_description: On December 27, 1574, Murad III, the eldest son of Selim II, was formally enthroned as the Sultan of the Ottoman Empire after eliminating his brothers as rivals. His reign would see significant developments in the empire's administration and military.
events.name: Enthronement of Murad III

events.enhanced_description: On January 21, 1575, Queen Elizabeth I of England granted a monopoly on the production of printed sheet music to composers Thomas Tallis and William Byrd. This significant patronage helped to elevate English music during the Renaissance.
events.name: Monopoly on Printed Sheet Music

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1575, William I of Orange founded Leiden University, which became a center of learning and a symbol of Dutch resistance against Spanish rule. The university played a crucial role in the intellectual and cultural development of the Netherlands.
events.name: Founding of Leiden University

events.enhanced_description: On February 11, 1575, Portuguese explorer Paulo Dias de Novais arrived in southeastern Africa to begin the colonization of what is now Angola. His expedition marked the beginning of significant Portuguese influence in the region.
events.name: Colonization of Angola

events.enhanced_description: On February 13, 1575, the formal coronation of Henry III as King of France took place at Reims Cathedral. This ceremony followed his ascension to the throne after the death of his brother, Charles IX, and marked the continuation of the Valois dynasty.
events.name: Coronation of Henry III of France

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1575, the Mughal Empire decisively defeated the Karrani dynasty of Bengal at the Battle of Tukaroi, located near present-day Balasore District in Odisha. This victory solidified Mughal control over Bengal and expanded their influence in the region.

image.caption: Manohar’s retrospective illustration of the Battle of Tukaroi.
image.date_qualification: The image is dated 1590, fifteen years after the battle; the depicted event took place on 3 March 1575.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Tukaroi

events.enhanced_description: On April 2, 1575, English privateer Gilbert Horseley and his crew conducted three days of raids on Spanish settlements and ships in the Bay of Honduras. This event exemplified the ongoing conflicts between English privateers and Spanish colonial interests in the Americas.
events.name: Raids by Gilbert Horseley

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1575, Antoine I de Gramont, Lord Sovereign of the Principality of Bidache, promulgated a legal code for his people. This code was significant in establishing governance and legal order in the principality.
events.name: Legal Code Promulgated by Antoine I de Gramont

events.enhanced_description: On April 18, 1575, Bayinnaung, the King of Burma, returned to his capital at Pegu from Vientiane after installing Voravongsa I as the Burmese-appointed monarch of the Kingdom of Lan Xang, now known as Laos. This event underscored the expansion of Burmese influence in Southeast Asia.
events.name: Bayinnaung Returns to Pegu

events.enhanced_description: On May 12, 1575, King Henry III of France was stripped of his Polish and Lithuanian titles after failing to return to Kraków by the deadline set by the Polish nobility. This incident reflected the complexities of his dual monarchy and the expectations of the Polish nobility.
events.name: Stripping of Henry III's Titles

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1575, Lutheran missionaries met with Jeremias II Tranos, the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople, to present a Greek translation of the Augsburg Confession. This meeting aimed to discuss potential reforms in the Eastern Orthodox Church, but ultimately faced strong objections from the Patriarch.

image.caption: Portrait of Jeremias II Tranos, depicted as a Greek bishop.
image.date_qualification: A portrait of the event's central figure, not a depiction of the 1575 meeting. The saved image date is described as 16th century.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Lutheran Missionaries Meet with Patriarch Jeremias II

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1575, William I of Orange, a key figure in the Dutch struggle for independence from Spanish rule, married Charlotte of Bourbon, a union that strengthened his political alliances and support. This marriage was significant in the context of the Eighty Years' War, as it helped consolidate William's position against Spanish dominance.
events.name: William I of Orange marries Charlotte of Bourbon

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Nagashino, fought on June 28, 1575, marked a pivotal moment in Japanese warfare, as Oda Nobunaga's forces utilized firearms effectively against the cavalry of Takeda Katsuyori. This battle is often regarded as Japan's first modern battle, showcasing the transition from traditional samurai combat to more strategic military tactics.
events.name: Battle of Nagashino

events.enhanced_description: On July 7, 1575, the Raid of the Redeswire occurred, marking the last significant battle between England and Scotland. Sir John Carmichael led the Scottish forces to victory against Sir John Forster's English troops, highlighting the ongoing tensions and conflicts along the Anglo-Scottish border during this period.
events.name: Raid of the Redeswire

events.enhanced_description: On July 26, 1575, Edmund Grindal was appointed as the Archbishop of Canterbury, succeeding Matthew Parker. Grindal's tenure was marked by his efforts to promote the Elizabethan Religious Settlement and his struggles against the Puritan movement within the Church of England.

image.caption: Oil portrait of Edmund Grindal, Archbishop of Canterbury.
image.credit: Attributed to Dirk Vos / Follower of Dirk Vos — http://www.archbishopofcanterbury.org/1733?mediaid=777&sectionid=1739
image.date_qualification: Portrait dated 1580, five years after his appointment; it is a portrait, not a depiction of the appointment event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Edmund Grindal succeeds Matthew Parker as Archbishop of Canterbury

events.enhanced_description: On August 5, 1575, Henry Sidney was appointed as the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, a position that placed him in charge of English governance in Ireland during a time of significant unrest and rebellion. His leadership was crucial in managing the complex political landscape of Ireland under English rule.
events.name: Henry Sidney is appointed Lord Lieutenant of Ireland

events.enhanced_description: In September 1575, the Spanish government declared bankruptcy as a direct consequence of the financial strains caused by the Eighty Years' War against the Dutch. This financial crisis led to significant implications for Spain's military and political strategies in Europe.

image.caption: Oil painting of a Spanish flagship exploding during the Battle of Gibraltar.
image.credit: Cornelis Claesz van Wieringen / Formerly attributed to Hendrick Cornelisz Vroom — Rijksmuseum - https://www.rijksmuseum.nl/en/collection/SK-A-2163
image.date_qualification: Retrospective depiction of the Battle of Gibraltar on 25 April 1607; the painting is dated 1621, later than the 1575 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Spanish government in bankruptcy due to the Eighty Years' War

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1575, Paulo Dias de Novais was appointed as the first Portuguese Governor of Angola, marking the beginning of formal Portuguese colonial administration in the region. His governance laid the groundwork for the establishment of Portuguese influence in West Africa.
events.name: Paulo Dias de Novais becomes the first Portuguese Governor of Angola

events.enhanced_description: On September 25, 1575, Rudolf II of Habsburg was crowned King of Bohemia at St. Vitus Cathedral in Prague, a significant event that underscored the Habsburgs' influence in Central Europe. The coronation was presided over by Archbishop Antonín Brus of Mohelnice, reflecting the intertwining of politics and religion during this period.
events.name: Rudolf of Habsburg crowned King of Bohemia

events.enhanced_description: On September 26, 1575, the future Spanish author Miguel de Cervantes was captured by the Ottoman Albanian pirate Arnaut Mami during an attack on the Spanish galley Sol off the Catalan coast. Cervantes would spend the next five years as a slave in Algeria before being ransomed, an experience that would profoundly influence his later writings.
events.name: Miguel de Cervantes taken hostage

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1575, the Battle of Dormans took place, where Catholic forces under Henry I, Duke of Guise, defeated Protestant troops, capturing notable figures including Philippe de Mornay. This battle was part of the ongoing French Wars of Religion, highlighting the intense sectarian conflicts of the era.
events.name: Battle of Dormans

events.enhanced_description: On October 22, 1575, the city of Villa de la Asunción, now known as Aguascalientes, was founded in New Spain by permission from Philip II of Spain. This establishment was part of the broader Spanish colonial efforts to expand their territories and influence in the Americas.
events.name: Foundation of Villa de la Asunción

events.enhanced_description: On November 8, 1575, the Sejm of Poland convened in Warsaw to elect a new King following the absence of King Henryk from France. The assembly considered 11 candidates, reflecting the political complexities and power struggles within the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth during this period.
events.name: Sejm of Poland meets to elect a new King

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1575, Ferhad Pasha Sokolović triumphantly returned to Constantinople with the decapitated head of General Auersperg following his victory at the Battle of Budačka. This event underscored the Ottoman Empire's military prowess and dominance in the region during the late 16th century.
events.name: Ferhad Pasha returns to Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: On November 22, 1575, Portuguese navigator Manuel de Mesquita Perestrelo embarked from Mozambique on a mission to map the coastline of the region. His work contributed to the European understanding of African geography and maritime routes during the Age of Discovery.
events.name: Portuguese navigator Manuel de Mesquita Perestrelo departs from Mozambique

events.enhanced_description: On December 12, 1575, under pressure from Papal nuncio Vincenzo Lauro, the Primate of Poland, Jakub Uchański, declared Maximilian II as the new King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania. This decision came amidst a contentious election process, reflecting the intricate political dynamics of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
events.name: Election of Maximilian II as King of Poland

events.enhanced_description: On December 16, 1575, an earthquake struck Valdivia, Chile, causing significant destruction in the region. This event was part of a series of seismic activities that would later be known for their impact on the development of the area.
events.name: Earthquake hits Valdivia

events.enhanced_description: In December 1576, James Burbage opened The Theatre in London, marking the establishment of the first permanent public playhouse in Britain and a significant milestone in the history of English theatre.
events.name: Opening of The Theatre

events.enhanced_description: In 1576, the Cocoliztli epidemic swept through the territory of New Spain, causing millions of deaths and significantly impacting the indigenous population and colonial society.
events.name: Cocoliztli epidemic in New Spain

events.enhanced_description: In 1576, Thomas Whythorne wrote one of the earliest examples of autobiography in English, contributing to the development of personal narrative in literature.
events.name: Early English autobiography

events.enhanced_description: In 1576, the Loci Communes of Peter Martyr Vermigli, edited by Robert le Maçon, were published in London, reflecting the theological debates of the time.
events.name: Publication of Loci Communes

events.enhanced_description: In 1576, Dartford Grammar School was founded in Dartford, Kent, by William d'Aeth, Edward Gwyn, and William Vaughn, contributing to the educational landscape of England.
events.name: Founding of Dartford Grammar School

events.enhanced_description: In 1576, Sutton Valence School was founded by William Lambe in Sutton Valence, Kent, further enriching the educational institutions of England.
events.name: Founding of Sutton Valence School

events.enhanced_description: In 1576, Konstanty Wasyl Ostrogski founded Ostroh Academy in Ostroh, Rivne Oblast, which became the first university-level school in Eastern Europe.

image.caption: Portrait of Konstanty Wasyl Ostrogski, a painted work by Teofil Kopystynsky.
image.credit: Teofil Kopystynsky — Львівський історичний музей. Вялікае княства Літоўскае: Энцыклапедыя. У 3 т. / рэд. Г. Пашкоў і інш. Т. 1: Абаленскі — Кадэнцыя. — Менск: Беларуская Энцыклапедыя, 2005. — 684 с.: іл. ISBN 985-11-0314-4 .
image.date_qualification: Portrait of the academy's founder, not a depiction of the academy's founding. The supplied image date lists both a 16th-century date and a 19th-century date; no single supported display date is available.
image.image_date: 16 th century date QS:P,+1550-00-00T00:00:00Z/7 19 th century date QS:P,+1850-00-00T00:00:00Z/7
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Founding of Ostroh Academy

events.enhanced_description: On January 25, 1576, Portuguese explorer Paulo Dias de Novais established the settlement of São Paulo da Assunção de Loanda, which would later become the capital of Angola, Luanda. This settlement marked a significant step in the Portuguese colonization of Africa.
events.name: Foundation of São Paulo da Assunção de Loanda

events.enhanced_description: On February 5, 1576, King Henry of Navarre, who had been held captive in France since 1572, escaped to Tours. His escape was significant as he formally reverted to Protestantism, highlighting the religious tensions of the time.
events.name: Escape of King Henry of Navarre

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1576, Peter Wentworth, a Puritan Member of Parliament, was arrested while delivering a speech criticizing the suppression of free speech. His bold statement that 'the devil was the first author of them' led to his immediate imprisonment in the Tower of London.
events.name: Arrest of Peter Wentworth

events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1576, Ottoman forces led by Abd al-Malik captured the city of Fez, part of the Saadi Sultanate, in an effort to overthrow Sultan Muhammed al-Mutawakkil. This event marked a significant moment in the struggle for control in North Africa.
events.name: Capture of Fez by Ottoman Forces

events.enhanced_description: The Third Battle of Ishiyama began on April 14, 1576, as Oda Nobunaga sent 10,000 soldiers against the Ashikaga shogunate to capture the Honganji Temple in Osaka. This battle was part of Nobunaga's campaign to consolidate power in Japan.
events.name: Third Battle of Ishiyama

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, 1576, Dutch leader Willem van Oranje signed documents for the Union of Delft, creating a federation of Holland and Zeeland. This union was crucial in the struggle for independence from Spanish rule during the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: Union of Delft

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1580, Stephen Báthory was formally crowned as the Grand Duke of Lithuania at the Vilnius Cathedral. His reign marked a significant period in the history of the Grand Duchy, as he worked to strengthen its ties with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
events.name: Crowning of Stephen Báthory

events.enhanced_description: On May 6, 1576, the Edict of Beaulieu was negotiated by François, Duke of Anjou, ending the Fifth War of Religion in France. This edict granted freedom of worship to Protestant Huguenots, marking a temporary resolution to the religious conflicts.
events.name: Edict of Beaulieu

events.enhanced_description: On May 14, 1576, Tahmasp I, the Shah of Safavid Iran, died after being accidentally poisoned by his physician, Abu Naser Gilani. His death led to a power struggle that destabilized Iran for years.
events.name: Death of Tahmasp I

events.enhanced_description: On May 15, 1576, Haydar Mirza Safavi declared himself the new Shah of Safavid Iran following the death of his father, Tahmasp I. However, he was assassinated later that day by palace guards loyal to his brother, Ismail Mirza.
events.name: Ascension of Haydar Mirza Safavi

events.enhanced_description: On May 27, 1576, a Dutch attempt to lift the Siege of Zierikzee failed after Spanish forces were tipped off about a surprise attack. The Dutch Admiral Lodewijk van Boisot was killed during the battle, marking a setback for the Dutch Republic.

image.caption: Map of Zierikzee depicting the siege by Spanish troops.
image.credit: Bor, Pieter — Contributer's property, scanned donderdag 12 juli 2007, 12:53:22
image.date_qualification: The supplied image date is “between 1575 and 2007”; this is not a precise date for the map or a depicted moment.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Failed Dutch Attempt to End Siege of Zierikzee

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1576, Dutch forces withdrew from their attempt to free Zierikzee, leaving the city to defend itself. The defenders began negotiations with the Spanish attackers, led by General Cristóbal de Mondragón.
events.name: Withdrawal from Siege of Zierikzee

events.enhanced_description: On June 18, 1576, the Mughal Imperial forces, led by Man Singh I of Amer, decisively defeated the Mewar Kingdom under Maharana Pratap in the Battle of Haldighati. This battle was a significant conflict in the Mughal expansion in India.
events.name: Battle of Haldighati

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1576, Alonso de Solís, appointed by Spain as Governor of La Florida, was killed in the colonial capital of San Agustín, now St. Augustine, Florida. His death highlighted the challenges of Spanish colonial governance in the region.

locations.name: Castillo de San Marcos National Monument, St. Augustine, Florida, United States

events.name: Assassination of Alonso de Solís

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1576, English navigator Martin Frobisher sighted Greenland during his quest for the Northwest Passage. This discovery was part of the broader European exploration of the Arctic regions.
events.name: Martin Frobisher sights Greenland

events.enhanced_description: On July 12, 1576, the Mughal Empire annexed Bengal after defeating the Bengal Sultanate at the Battle of Rajmahal. This victory expanded Mughal control in the Indian subcontinent.
events.name: Mughal Empire annexes Bengal

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1576, rebellious Spanish troops plundered the Flemish city of Aalst, using it as a base for further attacks on other cities. This event underscored the instability caused by mutinous troops in the region.
events.name: Plunder of Aalst by Spanish Troops

events.enhanced_description: On July 29, 1576, the Siege of Zierikzee ended with the surrender of the defenders to the Spanish Army. This marked a significant victory for Spain in the ongoing conflict with the Dutch.
events.name: Surrender of Zierikzee

events.enhanced_description: On August 11, 1576, English navigator Martin Frobisher entered the bay that would later be named after him during his search for the Northwest Passage. This exploration was part of the broader European interest in finding new trade routes.
events.name: Frobisher enters Frobisher Bay

events.enhanced_description: On August 23, 1576, Takahara Castle of the Itō clan was captured by 30,000 men led by warlord Shimazu Yoshihisa after a four-day siege. This event was part of the ongoing conflicts during Japan's Sengoku period.
events.name: Capture of Takahara Castle

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1576, Ismail Mirza, who had proclaimed himself Shah of Safavid Iran, marched into Qazvin and ascended the throne as Shah Ismail II. His ascension marked the beginning of a tumultuous reign.

image.caption: Retrospective manuscript illustration of Shah Esmaeil II enthroned.
image.date_qualification: 17th century; not a contemporary depiction of the 1576 accession.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Ascension of Ismail II

events.enhanced_description: On September 2, 1576, Simeon Bekbulatovich stepped down as Grand Prince of All Russia as Ivan IV, known as Ivan the Terrible, returned to Moscow after a leave of absence. Ivan rewarded Bekbulatovich with the title of Grand Prince of Tver.
events.name: Return of Ivan IV to Moscow

events.enhanced_description: On September 4, 1576, rebels led by Jacques de Glymes of Brabant arrested members of the Council of State in Brussels. This event was part of the larger context of rebellion against Spanish rule in the Netherlands.
events.name: Arrest of Council of State in Brussels

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1576, the States General of the Netherlands was convened by leaders from Brabant and Hainaut to address the issue of mutinous Spanish troops. This gathering was crucial in the ongoing struggle for independence from Spanish rule.
events.name: Convocation of the States General of the Netherlands

events.enhanced_description: On September 10, 1576, after a year-long siege, the Spanish Army abandoned its siege of the Dutch city of Woerden. This marked a significant moment in the ongoing conflict between the Spanish and the Dutch.
events.name: Abandonment of the Siege of Woerden

events.enhanced_description: On September 16, 1576, the States of Flanders convened a significant meeting near Ghent, where the Roman Catholic clergy, led by Martinus Rythovius, advocated for measures to protect the Catholic faith amidst the rising Protestant influence in the Low Countries.
events.name: Meeting of the States of Flanders

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1576, Maximilian II, the Holy Roman Emperor, died unexpectedly in Regensburg while preparing for an invasion of Poland. His death led to his son Rudolf II ascending to the Imperial Throne shortly thereafter.
events.name: Death of Maximilian II

events.enhanced_description: On October 20, 1576, Spanish rebels launched a violent assault on the city of Maastricht, resulting in widespread plunder and the deaths of many civilians in an event that would later be referred to as the 'Spaanse Furie' or Fury of Spain.
events.name: Spaanse Furie

events.enhanced_description: On October 26, 1576, Ludwig of Simmern was appointed as the new Elector Palatine of the Rhine, taking office in Heidelberg just ten days after the death of his father, Frederick III.
events.name: Ludwig VI becomes Elector Palatine

events.enhanced_description: On November 1, 1576, Rudolf II was crowned as the Holy Roman Emperor, marking the beginning of his reign over the vast territories of the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Crowning of Rudolf II

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1576, during the Eighty Years' War, mutinous Spanish soldiers sacked the city of Antwerp, leading to widespread destruction over three days and significantly impacting the city's economy and populace.
events.name: Sack of Antwerp

events.enhanced_description: On November 8, 1576, the States General of the Netherlands convened in Ghent to unite against the pillaging Spanish mutineers, leading to a significant political alliance among the provinces.
events.name: Pacification of Ghent

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1576, Shah Ismail II of Iran initiated a brutal campaign against perceived threats to his rule, executing his half-brothers Suleiman Mirza and Mustafa Mirza, among others, over the following months.

image.caption: Photograph of Qahqaheh Castle.
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2015-05-01; a later photograph of a site associated with Ismail II, not a contemporary image of the executions.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Executions by Shah Ismail II

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1576, representatives of France's three estates convened at the Estates General in Blois, where a narrow majority from the Third Estate voted to outlaw Protestantism, reflecting the deepening religious tensions in France.
events.name: Estates General of 1576

events.enhanced_description: On December 19, 1576, representatives of the Second Estate voted in favor of outlawing Protestantism in France, a decision that intensified the ongoing religious conflicts within the kingdom.
events.name: Outlawing Protestantism in France

events.enhanced_description: On December 22, 1576, the clergy of the First Estate joined the Second Estate in voting to outlaw Protestantism in France, further solidifying the anti-Protestant stance of the French government.
events.name: Clergy join vote against Protestantism

events.enhanced_description: Francis Drake led an English expedition that circumnavigated the Earth, returning to England with treasure and spices. The voyage included covert raids on Spanish ports and shipping.

image.caption: Hand-coloured engraved world map tracing Francis Drake’s circumnavigation route.
image.date_qualification: A retrospective map of the voyage, not a contemporary record of the event itself. Its date is given as circa 1590.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Francis Drake’s circumnavigation

events.enhanced_description: On January 9, 1577, the Second Union of Brussels was formed, initially excluding the Protestant counties of Holland and Zeeland, which later led to open rebellion across the Netherlands.
events.name: Second Union of Brussels

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1577, the 'Perpetual Edict' was signed in Marche-en-Famenne by Spanish Governor-General Don Juan de Austria and representatives of the Dutch rebellion, aiming to remove Spanish troops from the Netherlands.
events.name: Signing of the Perpetual Edict

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1577, the Cathay Company was formed in England to sponsor Martin Frobisher's expedition back to the New World in search of gold, reflecting the era's exploration ambitions.
events.name: Formation of the Cathay Company

events.enhanced_description: On April 17, 1577, General Jan Zborowski led the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth army to a decisive victory at the Battle of Lubieszów, defeating a rebel force from Danzig and capturing thousands of prisoners.
events.name: Battle of Lubieszów

events.enhanced_description: On May 27, 1577, English explorer Martin Frobisher set sail from Blackwall in his flagship, HMS Ayde, along with two other ships, embarking on an expedition to North America in search of gold.
events.name: Martin Frobisher's Expedition

events.enhanced_description: The Bergen Book, also known as the Solid Declaration of the Formula of Concord, was published in Wittenberg, serving as a crucial Lutheran confessional document. It aimed to unify various Lutheran factions by clarifying doctrinal positions, building upon earlier works like the Torgau Book.
events.name: The Bergen Book published

events.enhanced_description: Sebastiano Venier was elected as the new Doge of the Republic of Venice on June 11, 1577, following the death of Alvise Mocenigo. His leadership would be marked by significant events, including the ongoing conflicts with the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Sebastiano Venier becomes Doge of Venice

events.enhanced_description: On June 12, 1577, the French city of Issoire surrendered, leading to the massacre of approximately 3,000 Protestant Huguenots by royal troops under Francis, Duke of Anjou, on orders from King Henry III. This brutal event was part of the larger French Wars of Religion.
events.name: Massacre of Huguenots in Issoire

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1577, Mirza Salman Jaberi was appointed as the Grand Vizier of Persia by Shah Ismail II, taking over from Mirza Shokrollah Isfahani. This appointment was significant in the context of the Safavid dynasty's governance.
events.name: Mirza Salman Jaberi appointed Grand Vizier of Persia

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1577, Mehmed II Giray ascended to the position of Khan of Crimea following the death of his father, Devlet I Giray, due to a plague. His rule would be marked by the complexities of Ottoman vassalage and regional politics.
events.name: Mehmed II Giray becomes Khan of Crimea

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1577, Ludvig Munk was appointed as the Governor-General of Norway, a position that would place him in charge of the administration of the region during a time of political tension in Scandinavia.
events.name: Ludvig Munk appointed Governor-General of Norway

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1577, Göran Boije was appointed as the new Duke of Estonia, ruling over a territory that was part of the Swedish Empire during a period of significant political change in Northern Europe.
events.name: Göran Boije becomes Duke of Estonia

events.enhanced_description: On August 23, 1577, Martin Frobisher concluded his expedition to Canada, returning to England aboard the ships Ayde, Gabriel, and Michael. His voyages were significant in the context of early English exploration of North America.
events.name: Martin Frobisher ends expedition to Canada

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1577, King Min Phalaung of Arakan entered his newly constructed palace in Mrauk U during dedication ceremonies. This event marked a significant moment in the cultural and political history of the region.
events.name: Min Phalaung enters new palace in Arakan

events.enhanced_description: On September 17, 1577, the Treaty of Bergerac was signed between King Henry III of France and the Huguenots, aiming to bring peace during the ongoing French Wars of Religion. This treaty was a crucial step in the complex negotiations between the crown and Protestant factions.
events.name: Treaty of Bergerac signed

events.enhanced_description: On September 23, 1577, Martin Frobisher returned to Bristol, England, bringing with him the first Inuit people to see Europe: Kalicho, Arnaq, and Arnaq's son, Nutaaq. Unfortunately, none of them survived long after their arrival.
events.name: First Inuit people brought to Europe

events.enhanced_description: On October 19, 1577, Giovanni Battista Gentile Pignolo was elected as the new Doge of the Republic of Genoa, succeeding Prospero Centurione Fattinanti. His term would be marked by the challenges of governance in a city-state during a turbulent period.

image.caption: Portrait of Giovanni Battista Gentile Pignolo, Doge of Genoa.
image.date_qualification: The portrait’s date is not provided; the image description gives his tenure as 1577–1579.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Giovanni Battista Gentile Pignolo elected Doge of Genoa

events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1577, two Protestant members of the Ghent city council, Jan van Hembyze and François van Ryhove, proclaimed the Calvinist Republic of Ghent. This declaration marked a significant moment in the struggle for Protestant rights in the region.
events.name: Proclamation of the Calvinist Republic of Ghent

events.enhanced_description: On November 6, 1577, Aztec astronomers in Mexico made the first recorded observation of the Great Comet of 1577. This event was followed by observations in Italy and Japan, and the comet was later tracked by astronomer Tycho Brahe.
events.name: First recorded observation of the Great Comet of 1577

events.enhanced_description: On November 13, 1577, the Battle of Tedorigawa took place, where Uesugi Kenshin's forces decisively defeated those of Oda Nobunaga. This battle marked Kenshin's last significant victory before his death in the following year.
events.name: Battle of Tedorigawa

events.enhanced_description: On November 19, 1577, as defeat loomed during the siege of Shigisan, Matsunaga Hisahide chose to commit suicide. His death marked a significant turning point in the power struggles of feudal Japan.
events.name: Matsunaga Hisahide commits suicide

events.enhanced_description: On December 13, 1577, Francis Drake set sail from Plymouth, England, aboard the Pelican, leading an expedition against the Spanish along the Pacific coast of the Americas. This journey would ultimately lead to his circumnavigation of the globe.
events.name: Francis Drake's expedition begins

events.enhanced_description: In early 1578, the city of Bruges, which was under Spanish control, fell to Dutch rebels. This event was part of the broader Dutch Revolt against Spanish rule, contributing to the shifting power dynamics in the region.
events.name: Fall of Bruges to Dutch rebels

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of the Spoiling Dyke took place on the Isle of Skye, where the Clan MacLeod emerged victorious over the MacDonalds of Uist in a fierce feud. This conflict was part of the broader clan rivalries that characterized Scottish history during this period.
events.name: Battle of the Spoiling Dyke

events.enhanced_description: In 1578, the Ottoman Empire successfully conquered Abkhazia, a region on the Black Sea coast, marking a significant expansion of Ottoman influence in the Caucasus. This conquest was part of the broader Ottoman campaigns in the region during the late 16th century.
events.name: Ottoman conquest of Abkhazia

events.enhanced_description: In a decisive battle, Sarsa Dengel, the Emperor of Ethiopia, defeated Bahr negus Yeshaq and his Ottoman allies, effectively ending a significant rebellion. This victory solidified Sarsa Dengel's power and marked a pivotal moment in Ethiopian history.
events.name: Sarsa Dengel defeats Yeshaq

events.enhanced_description: In 1578, Sonam Gyrso received the title of Talaï from Prince Atlan Khan, marking his ascension as the third Dalai Lama of Tibet. This event was significant in the establishment of the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism and the political-religious structure of Tibet.
events.name: Sonam Gyrso becomes the third Dalai Lama

events.enhanced_description: The last outbreak of sweating sickness occurred in England in 1578, a mysterious and deadly illness that had plagued the country intermittently since the 15th century. This final outbreak marked the end of a significant chapter in English medical history.
events.name: Last outbreak of sweating sickness in England

events.enhanced_description: In 1578, the Portuguese provided crucial military assistance to Lord Ōmura Sumitada, the first Christian daimyo in Japan, in repelling an attack on Nagasaki by the Ryūzōji clan. This event highlights the growing influence of European powers in Japan during the Sengoku period.
events.name: Portuguese assistance to Lord Ōmura Sumitada

events.enhanced_description: The fur trade began in Newfoundland in 1578, marking the start of a lucrative industry that would significantly impact the economy and indigenous populations of North America. This trade would lay the groundwork for future colonial expansion by European powers.
events.name: Fur trade begins in Newfoundland

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1578, Mohammad Khodabanda ascended to the throne of Persia after deposing his sister, Pari Khan Khanum, who had been ruling in the absence of a king. His reign was marked by political turmoil and his first act was the execution of his sister, solidifying his power but also setting a violent tone for his rule.
events.name: Mohammad Khodabanda begins his reign as Shah of Persia

events.enhanced_description: On February 13, 1578, following the Battle of Gembloux, Spanish forces captured the city of Leuven, forcing Willem, Prince of Orange, to flee Brussels and relocate to Antwerp. This event was part of the larger conflict of the Dutch Revolt against Spanish rule.
events.name: Capture of Leuven by Spanish troops

events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1578, Nicolò da Ponte was elected as the new Doge of the Republic of Venice after a lengthy election process that included 44 ballots. His election followed the death of Sebastiano Venier, marking a significant transition in Venetian leadership.
events.name: Election of Nicolò da Ponte as Doge of Venice

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1578, James Douglas, 4th Earl of Morton, resigned as the last regent for King James VI of Scotland, a position he had held since November 24, 1572. His resignation marked a pivotal moment in the political landscape of Scotland during a time of significant turmoil.
events.name: Resignation of James Douglas, 4th Earl of Morton

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1578, the Siege of Otate commenced in Japan following the death of the warlord Uesugi Kenshin. This conflict marked a significant power struggle in the Echigo Province as various factions vied for control.
events.name: Siege of Otate begins

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1578, the Duel of the Mignons resulted in the deaths of two favorites of King Henry III of France and two favorites of Henry I, Duke of Guise. This incident highlighted the intense rivalries and factionalism within the French court during the Wars of Religion.
events.name: Duel of the Mignons

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1578, the Alteratie took place in Amsterdam, resulting in the expulsion of 24 Catholic members from the city government. This event marked a significant shift in the political landscape of Amsterdam, establishing a Calvinist Protestant majority in the council.
events.name: Alteratie in Amsterdam

events.enhanced_description: On May 31, 1578, Martin Frobisher set sail from Harwich, England, with 15 ships on his third expedition to North America. This voyage aimed to explore the northern territories and establish English claims in the New World.
events.name: Martin Frobisher's third expedition to North America

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1578, Humphrey Gilbert received letters patent from the English crown to establish a colony in North America. This grant marked a significant step in the English colonization efforts in the New World.
events.name: Humphrey Gilbert granted letters patent

events.enhanced_description: On June 20, 1578, the Frobisher expedition reached Greenland as part of their journey to North America. This expedition was significant for its exploration of the Arctic regions and the search for a Northwest Passage.
events.name: Frobisher expedition reaches Greenland

events.enhanced_description: On June 30, 1578, Francis Drake put Thomas Doughty on trial for treason and attempted mutiny while docked in what is now Argentina. Doughty was convicted and executed, highlighting the tensions within Drake's expedition during their circumnavigation of the globe.
events.name: Trial and execution of Thomas Doughty

events.enhanced_description: On July 2, 1578, the Frobisher expedition reached Canada and entered what is now known as Frobisher Bay. This journey was marked by challenges, including the wrecking of one of their ships on an iceberg.
events.name: Frobisher expedition reaches Canada

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1578, the Battle of Rijmenam took place near Antwerp, where a combined Dutch and English force led by the Count of Boussu and John Norreys defeated Spanish troops commanded by Don Juan de Austria. This battle was a significant victory for the Dutch in their struggle for independence from Spanish rule.
events.name: Battle of Rijmenam

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1578, King Sebastian of Portugal was killed in the Battle of Alcácer Quibir while fighting against Moorish forces in North Africa. His death led to a succession crisis in Portugal, as his uncle, Cardinal Henry, was named heir to the throne.

image.caption: Detail of a 1629 illustration depicting the Portuguese army at the Battle of Alcácer Quibir.
image.date_qualification: The depicted battle occurred on 4 August 1578; the image is a detail of an illustration published in 1629, photographed on 2006-09-24.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.5; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.5; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Death of King Sebastian of Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1578, after renaming his flagship from Pelican to Golden Hind, Francis Drake and his fleet began their passage through the Strait of Magellan. This crucial navigation marked a significant moment in Drake's circumnavigation of the globe.

image.caption: Portrait of Sir Francis Drake, painted by Henry Bone.
image.date_qualification: April 1829; retrospective portrait, 251 years after the event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Francis Drake's fleet begins passage through the Strait of Magellan

events.enhanced_description: On August 31, 1578, the Frobisher expedition departed North America, concluding their exploration efforts in the region. This marked the end of a significant journey aimed at establishing English presence in the New World.
events.name: Frobisher expedition departs North America

events.enhanced_description: On September 6, 1578, Francis Drake's fleet completed its traverse of the Strait of Magellan, entering the Pacific Ocean. This journey was fraught with challenges, including violent storms that led to the loss of the supply ship Marigold and its crew.
events.name: Completion of Drake's traverse of the Strait of Magellan

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1578, Alessandro Farnese succeeded his uncle, Don John, as Governor of the Spanish Netherlands. His leadership would play a crucial role in the ongoing conflicts between the Spanish crown and the Dutch rebels.
events.name: Alessandro Farnese becomes Governor of the Spanish Netherlands

events.enhanced_description: On October 21, 1578, the Battle of Wenden occurred, where Russian forces were defeated by the Swedes, who subsequently took control of Polotsk. This battle was part of the broader conflicts in the region during the Livonian War.
events.name: Battle of Wenden

events.enhanced_description: On November 19, 1578, Humphrey Gilbert and Walter Ralegh set out from Plymouth, England, leading an expedition to establish a colony in North America. However, the expedition faced numerous challenges and was forced to turn back six months later.
events.name: Gilbert and Ralegh expedition to North America

events.enhanced_description: On December 9, 1578, after more than five years of combat, the Protestant Huguenot citadel of Ménerbes negotiated a surrender to French Catholic forces. This event marked a significant moment in the ongoing Wars of Religion in France.
events.name: Surrender of Ménerbes

events.enhanced_description: In 1579, Akbar the Great, the Mughal Emperor of India, abolished the jizya tax, which was imposed on non-Muslim residents. This decision was part of Akbar's broader policy of religious tolerance and aimed to foster unity among his diverse subjects.
events.name: Abolition of the jizya tax by Akbar

events.enhanced_description: In 1579, Akbar the Great issued a mazhar, a formal declaration signed by leading ulamas, which positioned him as the highest religious authority in the Mughal Empire. This allowed him to interpret the Quran and was a significant step in his efforts to integrate different faiths within his realm.
events.name: Akbar issues a mazhar

events.enhanced_description: In 1579, the municipality of Boac was founded in Marinduque, Philippines. This establishment marked the beginning of organized governance in the region, which would play a significant role in the local culture and community development.
events.name: Foundation of Boac municipality

events.enhanced_description: In 1579, the Bible of Kralice began publication, marking the first complete translation of the Bible into the Czech language. Prepared by the Unity of the Brethren, this translation was significant for the Czech Protestant community and contributed to the spread of Reformation ideas.

locations.name: Kralice nad Oslavou, Vysočina, Czech Republic

events.name: Publication of the Bible of Kralice

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1579, the Union of Arras was established, uniting the southern Netherlands under the governance of the Duke of Parma in the name of King Philip II of Spain. This political maneuver was a response to the ongoing Dutch Revolt against Spanish rule.
events.name: Union of Arras

events.enhanced_description: The Union of Utrecht, established on January 23, 1579, united the northern provinces of the Netherlands in a confederation known as the United Provinces. This alliance was crucial in the fight against Spanish rule and marked a significant step towards Dutch independence.
events.name: Union of Utrecht

events.enhanced_description: On February 4, 1579, the Ghent Republic joined the Union of Utrecht, strengthening the coalition of northern provinces against Spanish rule. This union was pivotal in the ongoing struggle for independence in the Low Countries.
events.name: Ghent Republic joins the Union of Utrecht

events.enhanced_description: On February 28, 1579, Willem IV van den Bergh's seizure of Boxmeer Castle was condemned by other members of the Union of Utrecht, highlighting the internal conflicts within the coalition against Spanish authority. This incident underscored the complexities of political alliances during the Dutch Revolt.
events.name: Seizure of Boxmeer Castle

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1579, the English galleon Golden Hind, captained by Francis Drake, captured the Spanish freighter Nuestra Señora de la Concepción off the coast of Ecuador. This event was a significant act of piracy that contributed to Drake's reputation and the ongoing conflict between England and Spain.
events.name: Capture of Nuestra Señora de la Concepción

events.enhanced_description: On March 2, 1579, the Battle of Borgerhout took place in Flanders, where Spanish troops under the command of the Duke of Parma overwhelmed rebels fighting for the Union of Utrecht. This battle was part of the larger conflict of the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: Battle of Borgerhout

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Maastricht began on March 12, 1579, as Spanish troops under the command of Alexander Farnese, Duke of Parma, targeted this key stronghold of Dutch resistance. The siege would last nearly four months, culminating in the city's capture.
events.name: Siege of Maastricht begins

events.enhanced_description: On April 10, 1579, in the village of Cuers near Toulon, rebel peasants killed approximately 600 nobles and upper-class gentlemen of the Catholic League. This massacre was part of the broader conflicts during the French Wars of Religion.
events.name: Massacre in Cuers

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1579, the Treaty of Arras was concluded between Spain and members of the Union of Arras, establishing a separate peace for certain provinces while the Union of Utrecht continued its resistance. This treaty was a significant moment in the ongoing conflict in the Low Countries.
events.name: Treaty of Arras concluded

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Mimaomote occurred on May 21, 1579, where Doi Kiyonaga defeated the forces of Kumu Yorinobu. This battle was part of the ongoing power struggles during Japan's Sengoku period.
events.name: Battle of Mimaomote

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1579, Francis Drake landed in what is now California during his circumnavigation of the globe, claiming the territory for Queen Elizabeth I. This claim laid the groundwork for future English colonial endeavors on the North American continent.
events.name: Francis Drake claims California

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1579, Maastricht surrendered to Spanish troops after a prolonged siege led by the Duke of Parma. This surrender marked a significant victory for the Spanish during the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: Maastricht surrenders

events.enhanced_description: On July 13, 1579, the city of Karlovac was founded in Croatia. This city would later become an important military and cultural center in the region.
events.name: Founding of Karlovac

events.enhanced_description: On July 17, 1579, James FitzMaurice FitzGerald landed at Smerwick with a small force, initiating the Second Desmond Rebellion against English rule in Ireland. This rebellion was part of the larger conflict between Irish lords and English authorities.

image.caption: Monument commemorating the Smerwick Harbour massacre at the Field of the Heads.
image.date_qualification: Photograph of a monument dating from 1980, commemorating the 1580 Smerwick Harbour massacre; photographed 2007-05-26. It is a later site memorial, not an image of the rebellion’s July 1579 beginning.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Second Desmond Rebellion begins

events.enhanced_description: On August 6, 1579, representatives of the Union of Utrecht declared that they would no longer recognize the authority of King Philip II of Spain. This declaration was a pivotal moment in the struggle for Dutch independence.
events.name: Union of Utrecht declares independence

events.enhanced_description: On August 17, 1579, Yasuke, a man of African origin, arrived in Japan and began serving Oda Nobunaga. His presence as a foreign samurai became a notable aspect of Japanese history and culture during the Sengoku period.
events.name: Yasuke arrives in Japan

events.enhanced_description: On August 30, 1579, during the Livonian War, the city of Polotsk fell to the forces of Stephen Báthory, Grand Duke of Lithuania and King of Poland. This event marked a significant territorial gain for the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
events.name: Fall of Polotsk

events.enhanced_description: On September 10, 1579, King Min Phalaung of the Kingdom of Mrauk U acquired his first white elephant, a symbol of royal power and prosperity. This event was significant in the cultural and political context of Southeast Asia.
events.name: King Min Phalaung acquires white elephant

events.enhanced_description: On September 12, 1579, amendments were made to the Treaty of Arras, which involved further concessions to Spain by the Union of Arras. This treaty was significant in the context of the Eighty Years' War, as it aimed to solidify Spanish control over the southern provinces of the Netherlands.
events.name: Amendments to the Treaty of Arras

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1579, a mutual assistance pact was signed in Lucerne, Switzerland, between representatives of Roman Catholic cantons. This agreement was facilitated by Jakob Christoph Blarer von Wartensee, the Catholic Bishop of Basel, and aimed to strengthen the political and military alliances among the Catholic cantons during a time of religious conflict.
events.name: Mutual Assistance Pact in Switzerland

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1579, Alauddin Mansur Syah ascended to the throne as the new Sultan of Aceh following the death of Sultan Zainul Abidin. His reign marked a significant period in the history of Aceh, known for its expansion and consolidation of power in the region.
events.name: Alauddin Mansur Syah becomes Sultan of Aceh

events.enhanced_description: On October 11, 1579, Sokollu Mehmed Pasha, the Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire for over 14 years, was assassinated in Istanbul. His death marked a turning point in Ottoman politics, leading to a period of instability and power struggles within the empire.
events.name: Assassination of Sokollu Mehmed Pasha

events.enhanced_description: On October 13, 1579, Semiz Ahmed Pasha was appointed as the new Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire by Sultan Murad III. His appointment came in the wake of the assassination of Sokollu Mehmed Pasha, and he faced significant challenges in maintaining stability within the empire.
events.name: Appointment of Semiz Ahmed Pasha

events.enhanced_description: On October 19, 1579, King James VI of Scotland made his ceremonial entry into Edinburgh at the age of 13, marking his assumption of the throne after being declared to have reached the age of majority. This event symbolized the end of regency rule that had governed Scotland since 1567.
events.name: James VI's Ceremonial Entry into Edinburgh

events.enhanced_description: On October 20, 1579, Nicolò Doria was elected to a two-year term as the new Doge of the Republic of Genoa. His leadership came during a period of political and economic challenges for the republic, which was a significant maritime power in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Election of Nicolò Doria as Doge of Genoa

events.enhanced_description: On November 3, 1579, John Stubbs, an English puritan known for his pamphlets against the doctrines of the Church of England, was convicted of sedition. As punishment, his right hand was amputated, a brutal act that highlighted the tensions between religious dissenters and the established church.
events.name: Conviction of John Stubbs

events.enhanced_description: On November 13, 1579, during the Second Desmond Rebellion, rebel troops led by Gerald FitzGerald, 14th Earl of Desmond, carried out the Sack of Youghal. They massacred the English Army garrison and pillaged local homes, reflecting the intense conflict between Irish rebels and English rule.
events.name: Sack of Youghal during the Second Desmond Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On November 21, 1579, Iancu Sasul was appointed as the new Prince of Moldavia after Peter the Lame stepped down for the second time. This change in leadership was part of the ongoing political instability in the region during the late 16th century.
events.name: Iancu Sasul becomes Prince of Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: On November 23, 1579, Jeremias II Tranos was removed from his position as Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople and replaced by his rival Metrophanes III. This event was significant in the context of the Eastern Orthodox Church and its internal power struggles.
events.name: Removal of Jeremias II Tranos as Ecumenical Patriarch

events.enhanced_description: On December 16, 1579, after Willem van Pamele, the Spanish Governor of Flanders, was forced to flee during the Dutch Revolt, the Duke of Parma ordered the Catholic members of the Council of Flanders to convene in Douai. This meeting was crucial for maintaining Spanish control over the region amidst the ongoing rebellion.
events.name: Council of Flanders convenes in Douai

events.enhanced_description: On December 24, 1579, German astronomer Michael Maestlin made the first cataloging of the Pleiades star cluster, recording 11 separate stars visible to the naked eye. His detailed illustrations and measurements contributed significantly to the field of astronomy.
events.name: Michael Maestlin catalogs the Pleiades

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1579, Protestant French troops under Matthieu Merle launched a surprise attack on the Roman Catholic cathedral in Mende during Mass, resulting in the deaths of approximately 400 civilians. This event exemplified the violent religious conflicts of the time.
events.name: Attack on the Cathedral in Mende

events.enhanced_description: In 1580, the Billy Mitchell volcano on Bougainville Island experienced a catastrophic eruption, classified as a Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) 6 event. This eruption had significant geological and environmental impacts on the region.
events.name: Catastrophic Eruption of Billy Mitchell Volcano

events.enhanced_description: In 1580, the first session of the Jewish Vaad (Council of Four Lands) was held in Lublin, Poland. This assembly brought together 70 delegates from local Jewish communities to address taxation and other pressing issues.
events.name: First Session of the Jewish Vaad

events.enhanced_description: In 1580, Jan Zamoyski established the Old City of Zamość in Poland, which would later become a significant cultural and economic center. The city is known for its Renaissance architecture and is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
events.name: Establishment of the Old City of Zamość

events.enhanced_description: In 1580, an influenza pandemic swept across the globe, originating in Asia and rapidly spreading through Africa, Europe, and the Americas. The outbreak resulted in significant mortality, including over 10% of the population of Rome.
events.name: Influenza Pandemic

events.enhanced_description: In 1580, Ibrahim Adil Shah II ascended to the throne as the Sultan of Bijapur following the death of his father, Ali Adil Shah I. His reign would be marked by cultural advancements and military challenges within the Deccan region.
events.name: Ibrahim Adil Shah II Becomes Sultan of Bijapur

events.enhanced_description: On January 31, 1580, the death of Henry, King of Portugal, without direct heirs, led to a succession crisis. This conflict involved potential successors, including King Philip II of Spain and Infanta Catherine, Duchess of Braganza, ultimately resulting in the Iberian Union.
events.name: Portuguese Succession Crisis of 1580

events.enhanced_description: On February 16, 1580, during the annual Carnaval de Romans, a massacre occurred where 20 artists were killed. This tragic event highlighted the ongoing tensions and violence associated with the religious conflicts in France during this period.
events.name: Massacre at Carnaval de Romans

events.enhanced_description: On February 28, 1580, three Jesuit priests from Portuguese Goa, including Rodolfo Acquaviva, arrived in Agra as guests of Mughal Emperor Akbar the Great. This visit marked the beginning of significant interactions between Christianity and Islam in the Mughal Empire.
events.name: Arrival of Jesuit priests in Agra

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1580, Michel de Montaigne signed the preface to his most significant work, 'Essays', which would be published later that year. This work is considered a foundational text in modern skepticism and the essay genre.
events.name: Publication of Montaigne's Essays

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1580, George de Lalaing, Count of Rennenberg, defected from the Union of Utrecht and the Dutch Republic, surrendering the province of Groningen to King Philip II of Spain. This act was a significant setback for the Dutch Revolt against Spanish rule.
figures: George de Lalaing, Count of Rennenberg
events.name: Defection of George de Lalaing

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1580, King Philip II of Spain became King of Portugal under the name Philip I, following the death of King Henry of Portugal without heirs. This event marked the beginning of the Iberian Union, a personal union of the crowns that lasted until 1640.
events.name: Iberian Union

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1580, the Dover Straits earthquake occurred, causing significant tremors felt across southern England and northern France. This earthquake is one of the most notable seismic events in British history.
events.name: Dover Straits earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On April 9, 1580, English and Scottish mercenaries, allied with the Dutch Republic, launched a brutal assault on the city of Mechelen in the Spanish Netherlands. The attack resulted in the deaths of 60 civilians and extensive looting of homes and churches, reflecting the intense conflict during the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: English Fury at Mechelen
