events.enhanced_description: In May 1580, Charles II, Archduke of Austria, established the Lipizzan stud, which would become famous for breeding the Lipizzaner horse. This breed is renowned for its performance in classical dressage and has a rich history tied to the Spanish Riding School in Vienna.
events.name: Establishment of the Lipizzan Stud

events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1580, Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah was proclaimed Sultan of Golconda at the young age of 15, following the death of his father, Ibrahim Quli Qutb Shah Wali. His reign would later see the establishment of Hyderabad as a major cultural and economic center.
events.name: Proclamation of Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1580, rebels from the Dutch Union of Utrecht, supported by French soldiers, executed a surprise attack on the city of Diest in the Duchy of Brabant. The swift assault overwhelmed the Spanish garrison, marking a significant victory in the ongoing struggle for independence from Spanish rule.
figures: Rebels of the Dutch Union of Utrecht
events.name: Attack on Diest

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1580, England signed a commercial treaty with the Ottoman Empire, facilitating trade between the two nations. Sultan Murad III's correspondence with Queen Elizabeth I emphasized mutual benefits, allowing English merchants to trade in Ottoman territories.
events.name: Treaty with the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: On June 25, 1580, the Book of Concord was published, compiling key Lutheran confessional documents. This publication played a vital role in unifying Lutheran beliefs and practices during the Reformation.
events.name: Publication of the Book of Concord

events.enhanced_description: On July 12, 1580, the Ostrog Bible was printed in Ostroh, becoming the first complete Bible translation into a Slavic language (Old Church Slavonic). This monumental work by Ivan Fyodorov significantly contributed to the cultural and religious landscape of Eastern Europe.
events.name: Printing of the Ostrog Bible

events.enhanced_description: On July 24, 1580, António, Prior of Crato, was proclaimed King of Portugal by his supporters in Santarém amid the Portuguese succession crisis. His claim was contested, leading to a brief but intense struggle for the Portuguese throne.
events.name: Proclamation of António, Prior of Crato

events.enhanced_description: On August 25, 1580, the Battle of Alcântara took place, where Spanish forces led by Fernando Álvarez de Toledo defeated the armies of António, Prior of Crato. This decisive battle solidified Philip II of Spain's claim to the Portuguese throne.
events.name: Battle of Alcântara

events.enhanced_description: On September 26, 1580, Francis Drake returned to Plymouth, England, completing his historic circumnavigation of the globe aboard the Golden Hind. This voyage marked him as the first Englishman to achieve this feat, significantly enhancing England's maritime reputation.
events.name: Francis Drake's Return

events.enhanced_description: On September 29, 1580, five provinces of the Dutch Republic signed the Treaty of Plessis-les-Tours, recognizing Francis, Duke of Anjou, as their sovereign. This treaty was part of the ongoing struggle for independence from Spanish rule.
events.name: Treaty of Plessis-les-Tours

events.enhanced_description: On October 4, 1580, Lorenzo Suárez de Mendoza arrived in Mexico City to assume his role as the Viceroy of New Spain. His administration would oversee significant developments in Mexico and Central America during the Spanish colonial period.
events.name: Arrival of Lorenzo Suárez de Mendoza

events.enhanced_description: On October 15, 1580, King Bayinnaung of Burma dispatched a naval force to invade the Kingdom of Mrauk U. The invasion ultimately failed after a year, leading to the withdrawal of Burmese troops following Bayinnaung's death.
events.name: Failed Invasion of Mrauk U

events.enhanced_description: On February 23, 1581, the Spanish Army was forced to abandon the siege of Steenwijk after more than four months of attempts. This event highlighted the challenges faced by Spanish forces during the Eighty Years' War against the Dutch Republic.
events.name: Siege of Steenwijk

events.enhanced_description: On October 24, 1580, the War of the Portuguese Succession concluded as Spanish forces defeated the last Portuguese resistance in Porto. This victory led to Portugal being ruled by the Spanish crown for the next 60 years.
events.name: End of the War of the Portuguese Succession

events.enhanced_description: On November 10, 1580, the Siege of Smerwick concluded after three days when the commander of the besieged forces surrendered to the English. Following the surrender, approximately 400 soldiers were executed under orders from the English Lord Deputy of Ireland, Baron Grey de Wilton.
events.name: Siege of Smerwick

events.enhanced_description: On December 31, 1580, James Douglas, 4th Earl of Morton, was arrested during a Privy Council meeting in Holyrood on accusations related to the murder of Lord Darnley. He was later convicted of conspiracy and executed on June 2, 1581.
events.name: Arrest of James Douglas, 4th Earl of Morton

events.enhanced_description: In 1581, Chancellor Zhang Juzheng of the Ming Dynasty implemented the Single Whip Reform, a significant tax reform that streamlined tax collection by assessing taxes on properties recorded in the land census and requiring payment in silver. This reform aimed to improve the efficiency of tax collection and reduce corruption, impacting the economic structure of the Ming Dynasty.
events.name: Single Whip Reform imposed by Zhang Juzheng

events.enhanced_description: The Trier witch trials began in 1581, marking one of the largest witch hunts in the Holy Roman Empire. This series of trials reflected the widespread fear of witchcraft during the Reformation and resulted in the execution of numerous individuals accused of witchcraft, showcasing the intersection of religion, superstition, and law in early modern Europe.
events.name: Trier witch trials begin

events.enhanced_description: In 1581, John Dee, an influential mathematician and occultist, attempted to practice angel magic with Barnabas Saul, although they met with no success. Dee's work during this period contributed to the development of his Enochian language and reflected the era's fascination with the mystical and the scientific.
events.name: John Dee practices angel magic

events.enhanced_description: In 1581, Guru Arjan Dev succeeded his father, Guru Ram Das, as the fifth Guru of the Sikhs. His leadership marked a significant period in Sikh history, during which he compiled the Adi Granth, the holy scripture of Sikhism, and promoted the principles of equality and community service.
events.name: Guru Arjan Dev becomes the fifth Guru of Sikhs

events.enhanced_description: In 1581, John IX of Haugwitz, the last Bishop of Meissen, resigned his office in response to the pressures of the Reformation. His resignation symbolized the decline of the Catholic Church's influence in the region and the shift towards Protestantism in Saxony.
events.name: John IX of Haugwitz resigns as Bishop of Meissen

events.enhanced_description: On January 11, 1581, Chandrasen Rathore, the ruler of the Kingdom of Marwar, died at the age of 39. His death created a power vacuum that allowed the Mughal Empire to expand its influence over the region.

image.caption: Painting depicting Chandrasen, ruler of Marwar.
image.date_qualification: A 19th-century painting depicting a 16th-century ruler; it is a portrait, not a contemporary image of his death.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Death of Chandrasen Rathore

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Drohiczyn was concluded on January 14, 1581, marking the end of the Livonian War. This treaty resulted in the incorporation of the city of Riga into the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, significantly altering the balance of power in the region.
events.name: The Treaty of Drohiczyn

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1581, the Treaty of Plessis-les-Tours was ratified in Bordeaux, granting François, Duke of Anjou, executive authority over the Dutch Republic. This treaty was a significant step in the ongoing struggle for control and influence in the Netherlands during the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: The Treaty of Plessis-les-Tours

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1581, Prince Shin Thissa was appointed as the Governor of Nyaungyan by his father, King Bayinnaung. This marked the beginning of Shin Thissa's political career, which would eventually lead him to become King of Burma in 1599.
events.name: Appointment of Prince Shin Thissa

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1581, the Parliament of England enacted the Act against Reconciliation to Rome, imposing heavy fines on those practicing Roman Catholicism. This legislation was part of the broader context of religious conflict during the English Reformation.
events.name: Act against Reconciliation to Rome

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1581, Philip II of Spain was crowned Philip I of Portugal, marking the formal establishment of the Iberian Union. This union significantly impacted the political landscape of Europe and the colonial empires of both nations.
events.name: Crowning of Philip I of Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1581, following his successful circumnavigation of the globe, Francis Drake was knighted by Queen Elizabeth I of England. This honor recognized his contributions to English naval power and exploration.
events.name: Francis Drake is knighted

events.enhanced_description: On May 15, 1581, Zsigmond Báthory, the 8-year-old son of Kristóf Báthory, was elected as the new voivode of Transylvania. This election occurred shortly before Kristóf's death, leading to a significant shift in leadership in the region.
events.name: Election of Zsigmond Báthory

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1581, Thiri Thudhamma Yaza was appointed as the new Viceroy of Martaban following the death of Minye Nandameit. This appointment was significant in the context of the political landscape of Burma during the reign of King Bayinnaung.
events.name: Appointment of Thiri Thudhamma Yaza

events.enhanced_description: On June 2, 1581, James Douglas, 4th Earl of Morton, was executed in Edinburgh after being convicted of conspiracy in the murder of Henry Stuart, Lord Darnley. His execution marked a significant moment in the turbulent politics of Scotland during the reign of King James VI.
events.name: Execution of James Douglas, 4th Earl of Morton

events.enhanced_description: On June 14, 1581, the representatives of the States General of the Netherlands voted to declare the throne of the Union of Utrecht vacant due to the erratic behavior of King Philip II of Spain. This decision was a pivotal moment in the struggle for Dutch independence.

image.caption: The first page of the Act of Abjuration, a printed declaration issued by the States General of the Netherlands.
image.date_qualification: The 1581 document is relevant as the declaration itself, but it is not a depiction of the earlier vote declaring the throne vacant.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Declaration of the throne vacancy

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1581, the Knights Hospitaller deposed Jean de la Cassière as Grandmaster and appointed Mathurin Romegas in his place. This change in leadership reflected the internal conflicts within the Order during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Deposition of Jean de la Cassière

events.enhanced_description: On July 14, 1581, the English Jesuit Edmund Campion was arrested in London. His arrest was part of the broader persecution of Catholics in England during the reign of Elizabeth I.
events.name: Arrest of Edmund Campion

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1581, at a meeting of the States General of the Union of Utrecht in Antwerp, representatives voted to proclaim their independence from Spain in the Act of Abjuration. This act marked a significant step in the Dutch struggle for independence.
events.name: Act of Abjuration

events.enhanced_description: On July 26, 1581, the Act of Abjuration was signed at The Hague by representatives of eight Dutch provinces, declaring independence from Spanish rule. This act was a culmination of the growing discontent with Philip II's rule.
events.name: Signing of the Act of Abjuration

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1581, Spanish troops under Claude de Berlaymont captured the city of Breda after a surprise attack. This event was marked by the brutal massacre of 584 citizens, known as the 'Haultepenne Fury'.
events.name: Capture of Breda

events.enhanced_description: On September 6, 1581, a mercenary army from Sweden, led by Pontus De la Gardie, captured Narva from Russian forces. This event was part of the larger conflict during the Livonian War.
events.name: Capture of Narva

events.enhanced_description: On September 23, 1581, Martín Enríquez de Almanza arrived in Lima to assume the role of Viceroy of Peru, succeeding Francisco de Toledo. His appointment came during a critical period of colonial administration in South America.
events.name: Arrival of Martín Enríquez de Almanza

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1581, warlord Oda Nobunaga launched an invasion of Iga Province, commanding 42,000 troops against 10,000 defenders. This swift campaign demonstrated Nobunaga's military prowess and solidified his control over central Japan.
events.name: Oda Nobunaga invades Iga Province

events.enhanced_description: On October 8, 1581, the Tenshō Iga War concluded with the surrender of Kashiwara Castle to Oda Nobunaga. This victory marked a significant consolidation of Nobunaga's power in Japan.
events.name: End of the Tenshō Iga War

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1581, King Bayinnaung of Burma, known for creating the largest empire in mainland Southeast Asia, died at the age of 65. His death marked the end of an era and led to significant changes in the region's political landscape.
events.name: Death of King Bayinnaung

events.enhanced_description: On October 15, 1581, the Ballet Comique de la Reine premiered at the court of Catherine de' Medici in the Louvre Palace, marking the first narrative ballet. This performance was part of the wedding celebrations for Marguerite of Lorraine and showcased the artistic trends of the French Renaissance.
events.name: Ballet Comique de la Reine

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1581, Jean de la Cassière was restored as the Grandmaster of the Knights Hospitaller by Pope Gregory XIII, reaffirming his leadership during a tumultuous period for the Order. This restoration was significant as it came during a time of political and religious strife in Europe, particularly with the Protestant Reformation affecting Catholic orders.

image.caption: Coat of arms associated with Jean de la Cassière.
image.date_qualification: The image is a coat of arms, not a depiction of the 1581 restoration event. No image date is supplied.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Jean de la Cassière is restored as Grandmaster of the Knights Hospitaller

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1581, Jesuit priest Edmund Campion was executed for treason in London, a martyrdom that highlighted the intense religious conflict in England during the Reformation. His execution was part of a broader crackdown on Catholic dissenters by the Protestant government, marking a significant moment in the history of religious persecution in England.
events.name: Execution of Edmund Campion

events.enhanced_description: In March 1582, the New Testament of the Douai Bible, translated into English by Father Gregory Martin from Latin, was published for use in the Roman Catholic Church. This translation was significant as it provided English-speaking Catholics with access to the scriptures in their own language during a time of religious upheaval.
events.name: Publication of the Douai Bible New Testament

events.enhanced_description: In 1582, the Kumbum Monastery was founded in Tibet, becoming a significant site for Tibetan Buddhism. The monastery is known for its unique architecture and as a center for the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism.
events.name: Foundation of Kumbum Monastery

events.enhanced_description: In 1582, Jesuit missionary Matteo Ricci was granted entry into Ming dynasty China, marking a significant moment in cultural exchange between Europe and Asia. His work laid the foundation for future Jesuit missions and the introduction of Western science and philosophy to China.
events.name: Matteo Ricci enters Ming dynasty China

events.enhanced_description: In 1582, the Sultanate of Morocco began its southward expansion in pursuit of greater control over the trans-Saharan trade routes. This movement was part of Morocco's broader strategy to enhance its economic power and influence in the region.
events.name: Moroccan Sultanate's Expansion

events.enhanced_description: In 1582, the Cagayan battles took place in the Philippines, marking the only recorded clashes between European regular soldiers and samurai warriors. These encounters highlighted the cultural and military exchanges occurring during the period of European exploration.
events.name: Cagayan Battles

events.enhanced_description: On January 2, 1582, the University of Würzburg was refounded, continuing its legacy as a center of learning in Bavaria. This refounding was part of a broader movement in Europe to establish universities that would promote education and scholarship during the Renaissance.
events.name: University of Würzburg is refounded

events.enhanced_description: On January 15, 1582, Russia ceded its conquered territories in Livonia, which included parts of modern-day Latvia and Estonia, to the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. This transfer marked a significant shift in power dynamics in the Baltic region during the ongoing conflicts of the Livonian War.
events.name: Russia cedes conquered areas in Livonia

events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1582, François, Duke of Anjou, arrived in the Netherlands, where he was welcomed by William the Silent. This visit was part of the ongoing struggle for control in the region during the Eighty Years' War, as Anjou sought to gain influence and support among the Dutch rebels against Spanish rule.
events.name: François, Duke of Anjou, arrives in the Netherlands

events.enhanced_description: On February 24, 1582, Pope Gregory XIII proclaimed the Gregorian Calendar, which was designed to correct the inaccuracies of the Julian calendar. This reform, which included advancing the date by 10 days, significantly impacted how time was measured and observed in the Western world.
events.name: Pope Gregory XIII proclaims the Gregorian Calendar

events.enhanced_description: On March 9, 1582, scryer Edward Kelley arrived at John Dee's house in London, where they began practicing angelic magic together. This collaboration led to the development of the Enochian language, which Dee claimed was revealed to him through his magical practices.
events.name: Edward Kelley arrives at John Dee's house

events.enhanced_description: On April 2, 1582, the Ancuancu earthquake struck the village of Ancuancu in modern-day La Paz Department, Bolivia, reportedly burying all its inhabitants except for one chief. This catastrophic event led to the formation of the Jacha Kalla (Achocalla) valley, marking a significant geological change in the region.
events.name: Ancuancu earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On April 3, 1582, during the Battle of Temmokuzan, Takeda Katsuyori and his household committed suicide as they faced the collapse of the Takeda clan. This event marked a significant turning point in the Sengoku period of Japan, leading to the decline of one of the most powerful clans of the time.
events.name: Battle of Temmokuzan

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1582, King James VI of Scotland signed a charter creating Tounis College, which would later evolve into the University of Edinburgh. This establishment was a significant development in Scottish education, contributing to the intellectual landscape of the time.
events.name: Creation of Tounis College

events.enhanced_description: On April 16, 1582, Spanish conquistador Hernando de Lerma founded the settlement of Salta in modern-day Argentina. This establishment was part of the Spanish colonial expansion in South America and played a crucial role in the region's development.
events.name: Founding of Salta, Argentina

events.enhanced_description: On April 17, 1582, Toyotomi Hideyoshi departed from Himeji Castle with 20,000 soldiers, beginning his march toward the Bitchū Province to lay siege to Takamatsu Castle. This military campaign was a pivotal moment in Hideyoshi's rise to power during the Sengoku period.

image.caption: Utagawa Kuniyoshi nishiki-e depicting Takamatsu Castle surrounded by floodwater.
image.credit: Utagawa Kuniyoshi — ブレイズマン ( talk ) 06:44, 1 October 2010 (UTC)
image.date_qualification: Published in 1860, 278 years after the 1582 siege.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

locations.name: Himeji Castle, Himeji City, Hyōgo Prefecture, Japan

events.name: Siege of Takamatsu begins

events.enhanced_description: On June 8, 1582, heavy rains and the dikes constructed by Hideyoshi's forces transformed the area around Takamatsu Castle into a lake, significantly impacting the siege's dynamics. This engineering feat was part of Hideyoshi's strategy to weaken the castle's defenses.

locations.name: Takamatsu Castle, Takamatsu City, Kagawa Prefecture, Japan

events.name: Siege of Takamatsu: Heavy rains create a lake

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1582, the Honnō-ji Incident occurred in Kyoto, where the powerful warlord Oda Nobunaga was assassinated by Akechi Mitsuhide, a former ally. This betrayal marked a critical turning point in the unification of Japan, leading to a power struggle that would shape the country's future.
events.name: Honnō-ji Incident

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1582, following the assassination of Oda Nobunaga, Shimizu Muneharu surrendered Takamatsu Castle to Toyotomi Hideyoshi. In a final act of loyalty, Muneharu committed seppuku, ensuring the safety of the castle's defenders, which underscored the intense loyalty and honor prevalent in samurai culture.

locations.name: Takamatsu Castle, Takamatsu City, Kagawa Prefecture, Japan

events.name: Surrender of Takamatsu Castle

events.enhanced_description: On July 2, 1582, Toyotomi Hideyoshi's forces decisively defeated Akechi Mitsuhide's smaller army at the Battle of Yamazaki. This victory not only avenged Nobunaga's assassination but also solidified Hideyoshi's power, paving the way for his eventual unification of Japan.
events.name: Battle of Yamazaki

events.enhanced_description: On July 26, 1582, during the War of the Portuguese Succession, Spanish admiral Santa Cruz achieved a decisive victory over a larger mercenary fleet at the Battle of Ponta Delgada. This battle marked a significant naval engagement in the conflict, showcasing the strategic importance of the Azores in European maritime power struggles.
events.name: Battle of Ponta Delgada

events.enhanced_description: On August 23, 1582, the Raid of Ruthven occurred when Presbyterian nobles led by William Ruthven kidnapped King James VI of Scotland while he was hunting in Perthshire. This coup aimed to reform the Scottish government and highlighted the tensions between the monarchy and Protestant factions during this period.
events.name: Raid of Ruthven

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1582, John Maxwell, 8th Lord Maxwell, was installed as the regent of Scotland by Ruthven and his co-conspirators. This political maneuver followed the execution of James Douglas, 4th Earl of Morton, who had been implicated in the murder of Henry Stuart, Lord Darnley, and was significant in the power struggles of the Scottish nobility.
events.name: Installation of John Maxwell as Regent of Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On October 4, 1582, the Julian calendar was officially discarded in Italy, Poland, Portugal, and Spain as Pope Gregory XIII implemented the Gregorian calendar. This reform corrected the drift of the calendar with respect to the equinoxes, leading to a significant change in how time was measured in the Western world.
events.name: Implementation of the Gregorian Calendar

events.enhanced_description: On October 26, 1582, General Yermak Timofeyevich completed the Russian conquest of Siberia at the Battle of Chuvash Cape, forcing Kuchum Khan to abandon Qashliq, the capital of the Khanate of Sibir. This victory marked a significant expansion of Russian territory into Siberia.
events.name: Battle of Chuvash Cape

events.enhanced_description: On November 29, 1582, the renowned playwright William Shakespeare married Anne Hathaway, who was pregnant at the time. This union would later influence Shakespeare's works and personal life, as he became one of the most significant figures in English literature.
events.name: Marriage of William Shakespeare and Anne Hathaway

events.enhanced_description: On December 9, 1582, France officially adopted the Gregorian calendar, discarding the Julian calendar. This transition was part of a broader movement across Europe to standardize the measurement of time.
events.name: Adoption of the Gregorian Calendar in France

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1583, the Duchy of Savoy adopted the Gregorian calendar, aligning itself with the reforms initiated by Pope Gregory XIII. This decision was part of a wider acceptance of the new calendar system across Europe.
events.name: Duchy of Savoy adopts Gregorian Calendar

events.enhanced_description: After a protracted siege lasting 75 days, Dutch Republic commander Hendrik van Bonnivet surrendered the city of Eindhoven to the Spanish Netherlands in 1583. This event was part of the larger conflict known as the Eighty Years' War, which sought to establish Dutch independence from Spanish rule.
events.name: Surrender of Eindhoven

events.enhanced_description: On January 18, 1583, François, Duke of Anjou, launched an attack on Antwerp, a key city in the ongoing conflicts of the Eighty Years' War. This military action was part of the broader struggle for control in the Low Countries.
events.name: François, Duke of Anjou attacks Antwerp

events.enhanced_description: On February 4, 1583, Gebhard Truchsess von Waldburg, newly converted to Calvinism, married Agnes von Mansfeld-Eisleben while retaining his position as Archbishop-Elector of Cologne. This controversial marriage sparked tensions within the Catholic Church and led to significant political conflict.
events.name: Marriage of Gebhard Truchsess von Waldburg

events.enhanced_description: On February 7, 1583, the Siege of Eindhoven commenced as the Spanish Army laid siege to the walled city during the Eighty Years' War. This military action was part of the broader conflict between Spanish forces and the Dutch rebels.
events.name: Siege of Eindhoven begins

events.enhanced_description: On March 10, 1583, Queen Elizabeth I established the Queen Elizabeth's Men troupe of actors, directed by Edmund Tilney, the royal Master of the Revels. This troupe played a significant role in the development of English theatre during the Elizabethan era.
events.name: Foundation of Queen Elizabeth's Men

events.enhanced_description: On April 9, 1583, a Burmese Army force of 16,000 men, commanded by Thado Dhamma Yaza II and Nawrahta Minsaw, returned to the royal capital of Pegu after a successful punitive expedition against the Shan States in modern-day Yunnan, China. Their return was celebrated as a significant military achievement.
events.name: Burmese Army welcomed in Pegu

events.enhanced_description: In 1583, the Kingdom of England established its first diplomatic relations with the Ottoman Empire, marking a significant step in international diplomacy. This relationship would pave the way for future trade and political alliances between England and the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Establishment of diplomatic relations with the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, 1583, a significant clash occurred between a 50,000-man force of the Persian Empire and the Ottoman Empire in the Caucasus region, resulting in a decisive defeat for the Ottomans. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts for control over the region.
events.name: Battle between Persian and Ottoman forces

events.enhanced_description: On May 11, 1583, the three-day Battle of Torches concluded on the Caspian Sea, where Ottoman troops defeated forces of the Persian Empire. This battle was part of the larger conflict between the two empires for dominance in the region.
events.name: Battle of Torches

events.enhanced_description: On May 21, 1583, the Battle of Shizugatake took place in Japan, where Toyotomi Hideyoshi defeated Shibata Katsuie. This victory was pivotal in Hideyoshi's rise to power and led to the construction of Osaka Castle.
events.name: Battle of Shizugatake

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1583, Ernest of Bavaria was elected as the Roman Catholic Archbishop of Cologne, opposing Gebhard Truchsess von Waldburg. This election led to the Cologne War, a significant conflict within the Electorate of Cologne.
events.name: Election of Ernest of Bavaria as Archbishop of Cologne

events.enhanced_description: On May 28, 1583, the first installment of the translation of the Bible into the Slovene language by Jurij Dalmatin was published in Wittenberg. This translation was a significant milestone in the development of the Slovene language and literature.
events.name: Publication of the Slovene Bible

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1583, Spanish troops under the command of Alexander Farnese, Duke of Parma, overwhelmed a combined army of Dutch, French, and English soldiers at the Battle of Steenbergen. This battle resulted in significant casualties and showcased the military prowess of the Spanish forces during the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: Battle of Steenbergen

events.enhanced_description: In 1583, the Royal Exchange in London issued the first known life insurance policy to William Gibbons, promising a payout to his beneficiaries upon his death. This landmark event marked the beginning of life insurance as a formal financial practice, although the Royal Exchange initially refused to pay after Gibbons' death, leading to a court case that established important legal precedents.
events.name: First known life insurance policy issued

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1583, King James VI of Scotland successfully escaped from Falkland Prison after being held hostage for ten months following the Raid of Ruthven. His escape was a significant turning point in his reign, allowing him to regain control and eventually lead Scotland towards greater stability.
events.name: King James VI escapes from Falkland Prison

events.enhanced_description: The Cuncolim Revolt, occurring on July 25, 1583, is recognized as the first documented battle in India's struggle for independence against European colonial powers, specifically the Portuguese. The Desais of Cuncolim led this uprising, marking a significant moment in the history of resistance against colonial rule in India.
events.name: Cuncolim Revolt

events.enhanced_description: On August 5, 1583, Sir Humphrey Gilbert claimed the island of Newfoundland for England, establishing a foothold that marked the beginning of the British Empire in North America. This act of colonization was pivotal in the expansion of English influence across the Atlantic.

locations.name: St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada

events.name: Claiming of Newfoundland

events.enhanced_description: On August 19, 1583, Petru Cercel entered Bucharest and was proclaimed Prince of Wallachia. His reign was marked by efforts to modernize the principality and strengthen its ties with Western Europe.
events.name: Petru Cercel becomes Prince of Wallachia

events.enhanced_description: On August 29, 1583, the English ship Delight, part of Sir Humphrey Gilbert's expedition, became the first of over 350 vessels to run aground on Sable Island. This incident highlighted the treacherous nature of the waters around the island and the challenges faced by early explorers.
events.name: Shipwreck of Delight

events.enhanced_description: On September 4, 1583, King James VI of Scotland awarded Colonel William Stewart a gift in recognition of his role in rescuing the King from captivity. This gesture underscored the importance of loyalty and service during a tumultuous period in Scottish history.
events.name: Gift to Colonel William Stewart

events.enhanced_description: On September 9, 1583, the Squirrel, Sir Humphrey Gilbert's flagship, sank in a storm while returning from North America, resulting in the loss of all hands except one. This tragedy marked a significant loss for the English colonial efforts in the New World.
events.name: Sinking of the Squirrel

events.enhanced_description: On October 14, 1583, the University of Edinburgh, originally known as Tounis College, held its first classes with over 80 students. This event marked the establishment of one of the leading universities in the world, contributing significantly to education and scholarship in Scotland.
events.name: University of Edinburgh holds first classes

events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1583, King Philip II of Spain ordered the transfer of Abada, a rhinoceros, from the Casa de Campo public park in Madrid to the menagerie at his residence in El Escorial. This event reflects the fascination with exotic animals during the Renaissance and the king's interest in natural history.

image.caption: Philippe Galle’s 1584 engraving of Abada the rhinoceros.
image.credit: Philip Galle — Unknown source Unknown source
image.date_qualification: Engraving dated 1584; the transfer occurred on 16 October 1583.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

locations.name: San Lorenzo de El Escorial, Community of Madrid, Spain

events.name: Transfer of Abada the rhinoceros

events.enhanced_description: On October 17, 1583, Peter the Lame ascended to the throne of Moldavia for the third and final time, ruling until 1591. His reign was marked by political instability and external pressures from neighboring powers.
events.name: Peter the Lame becomes Prince of Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: The Third Council of Lima concluded on October 18, 1583, after two months of deliberation aimed at establishing a consistent doctrine for the Roman Catholic Church in the Viceroyalty of Peru. The council's decisions included the treatment of native populations and the use of local languages in evangelism.
events.name: Third Council of Lima concludes

events.enhanced_description: On October 24, 1583, Jan van Hembyze was appointed as the last leader of the Calvinist Republic of Ghent following a coup against the ruling Count of Flanders. His leadership was short-lived, as it soon led to a siege by Spanish forces under General Alexander Farnese.
events.name: Jan van Hembyze becomes leader of the Calvinist Republic of Ghent

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1583, Francis Throckmorton was arrested for instigating a plot to overthrow Queen Elizabeth I of England. His subsequent conviction for treason and execution in 1584 underscored the intense political tensions of the period.
events.name: Arrest of Francis Throckmorton

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1583, Willem IV van den Bergh, the Stadtholder of Guelders, was arrested along with his family on charges of treason. His imprisonment was a reflection of the political instability in the Dutch Republic during the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: Arrest of Willem IV van den Bergh

events.enhanced_description: On November 13, 1583, Akbar, the Emperor of the Mughal Empire, founded the city of Allahabad (modern-day Prayagraj) as a strategic fortress. This city would later become an important cultural and political center in India.
events.name: Foundation of Allahabad

events.enhanced_description: On November 24, 1583, Philippe Hurault de Cheverny was appointed as the new Chief Minister of France by King Henri III, following the death of René de Birague. Hurault's tenure would last until 1589, during a period marked by political strife and religious conflict.
events.name: Appointment of Philippe Hurault de Cheverny

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Godesberg concluded on December 17, 1583, when Catholic forces under Prince-elector-archbishop Ernest of Bavaria captured the strategic position from the Calvinist defenders led by Gebhard Truchsess von Waldburg. This event was part of the larger Cologne War, which reflected the religious and political conflicts of the time.

locations.name: Bonn Minster, Bonn, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany

events.name: Siege of Godesberg

events.enhanced_description: In 1584, Italian heretic Jacopo Brocardo proclaimed this year as the beginning of a significant new apocalyptic cycle, reflecting the tumultuous religious and cultural climate of the time. His views were part of a broader discourse on prophecy and eschatology prevalent in late 16th-century Europe.
events.name: Apocalyptic Inauguration According to Jacopo Brocardo

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1584, Ratu Hijau ascended to the throne as queen regnant of the Malay Patani Kingdom, marking a significant moment in the region's history.
events.name: Ratu Hijau becomes queen regnant

events.enhanced_description: In 1584, Belgian cartographer Abraham Ortelius included illustrations of Ming dynasty-era Chinese carriages with masts and sails in his atlas, Theatrum Orbis Terrarum, highlighting the cultural exchanges between East and West.
events.name: Abraham Ortelius features Chinese carriages

events.enhanced_description: On January 11, 1584, Sir Walter Mildmay received a royal license from Queen Elizabeth I to establish Emmanuel College in Cambridge. This institution became a significant center for education and scholarship in England.
events.name: Sir Walter Mildmay is given a royal licence to found Emmanuel College

events.enhanced_description: On January 16, 1584, George Haydock, a Roman Catholic priest imprisoned in the Tower of London, declared Queen Elizabeth I a heretic during his interrogation. Convicted of treason, he was executed on February 12, 1584.
events.name: George Haydock's interrogation and execution

events.enhanced_description: On February 2, 1584, Prince Naresuan of the Ayutthaya Kingdom led an army to suppress a rebellion by Thado Minsaw, the Viceroy of the Ava Kingdom, under orders from King Nanda Bayin of Burma. This event marked the beginning of Naresuan's own rebellion against Burmese rule.
events.name: Prince Naresuan's military campaign

events.enhanced_description: On February 22, 1584, Jeremias II Tranos, the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople, was deposed and exiled to Rhodes after being falsely accused of various charges. He was succeeded by Pachomius II Patestos.
events.name: Deposition of Jeremias II Tranos

events.enhanced_description: On March 5, 1584, the town of Karlstad in Sweden was granted city status, marking an important development in its administrative history.
events.name: Karlstad gains city status

events.enhanced_description: On March 28, 1584, Ivan the Terrible, the first Tsar of Russia, died in Moscow. He was succeeded by his son, Feodor I, marking a significant transition in Russian leadership.
events.name: Death of Ivan the Terrible

events.enhanced_description: On April 24, 1584, Prince Naresuan of the Ayutthaya Kingdom successfully suppressed the rebellion led by Thado Minsaw of the Ava Kingdom, solidifying his power in the region.
events.name: Prince Naresuan suppresses rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On April 28, 1584, the Battle of Komaki began between Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu. This conflict marked a significant moment in the power struggle during Japan's Sengoku period.
events.name: Battle of Komaki begins

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1584, the conflict between Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu culminated in the Battle of Nagakute, a pivotal engagement in the ongoing struggle for power in Japan.
events.name: Battle of Nagakute

events.enhanced_description: On June 1, 1584, following the death of the Duc d'Anjou, Henry of Navarre, a Huguenot leader, became the heir-presumptive to the French throne, significantly impacting the religious and political landscape of France.
events.name: Henry of Navarre becomes heir-presumptive

events.enhanced_description: On June 4, 1584, Walter Raleigh dispatched Philip Amadas and Arthur Barlowe to explore the Outer Banks of Virginia, where they discovered Roanoke Island, laying the groundwork for future English colonization efforts.

image.caption: Map of the Roanoke area by John White.
image.date_qualification: Map dated 1585–1593, later than the 1584 exploration; it is contextual geography, not a depiction of the expedition.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Exploration of the Outer Banks

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1584, the towns of Valka and Valga, located in modern-day Latvia and Estonia, respectively, received city rights from Polish King Stefan Bathory, enhancing their political status.
events.name: City rights granted to Walk

events.enhanced_description: On July 3, 1584, the Siege of Antwerp commenced, initiated by the Spanish Army. This siege would last for 13 months, culminating in the city's surrender on August 17, 1585.
events.name: Siege of Antwerp begins

events.enhanced_description: On July 5, 1584, the Maronite College was established in Rome, serving as an important institution for the education of Maronite clergy and fostering relations between the Maronite Church and the Catholic Church.

image.caption: Church of Saint Maron in Rome’s Ludovisi district.
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2008-08-16; this is a later site image, not an image from 1584.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Establishment of the Maronite College

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1584, Willem van Oranje, the leader of the Dutch Republic, was assassinated in Delft by Balthasar Gérard. This marked a significant moment in the Dutch struggle for independence from Spanish rule.
events.name: Assassination of Willem van Oranje

events.enhanced_description: On August 6, 1584, Russian General Yermak Timofeyevich was killed in an ambush while leading an expedition against the Khanate of Sibir. This event marked a significant setback in the Russian conquest of Siberia.
events.name: Yermak Timofeyevich's death in Siberia

events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1584, Italian printer Antonio Ricardo received permission to establish the first printing press in South America in Lima, Peru. He printed the first publication, a four-page outline of the Gregorian calendar.
events.name: First printing press in South America

events.enhanced_description: On August 11, 1584, the Tenshō embassy, Japan's first diplomatic mission to Europe, arrived in Lisbon, Portugal, with four Japanese teenagers who had converted to Christianity, marking a significant cultural exchange.
events.name: Tenshō embassy arrives in Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On September 17, 1584, the Calvinist Republic of Ghent fell after a 13-month siege, with Jan van Hembyze surrendering the city to Alexander Farnese, Governor of the Spanish Netherlands, ending a significant chapter in the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: Fall of the Calvinist Republic of Ghent

events.enhanced_description: On October 26, 1584, the Battle of Slunj took place, where Croatian forces, aided by Habsburg troops, successfully repelled an Ottoman invasion led by Ferhad Pasha Sokolović, demonstrating the resilience of the Croatian military.
events.name: Battle of Slunj

events.enhanced_description: On November 23, 1584, in response to the Throckmorton plot, Queen Elizabeth I convened a new session of the English House of Commons, appointing John Puckering as Speaker and passing significant legislation to ensure her safety.

locations.name: House of Commons, Palace of Westminster

events.name: Queen Elizabeth convenes House of Commons

events.enhanced_description: On November 24, 1584, Albert Fontenay sent an enciphered letter to Mary, Queen of Scots, which would later serve as crucial evidence in her trial for treason during the Babington Plot, leading to her conviction.
events.name: Albert Fontenay's letter to Mary, Queen of Scots

events.enhanced_description: On December 31, 1584, the Treaty of Joinville was secretly signed between the French Catholic League and Spain, solidifying their alliance against Protestant forces in France.
events.name: Treaty of Joinville signed

events.enhanced_description: The Kingdom of Luba was founded by Kongolo Mwamba in 1585, establishing a significant political entity in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo. This kingdom played a crucial role in the region's history, influencing trade and cultural exchanges.

locations.name: Mbuji-Mayi, Kasai-Oriental, Democratic Republic of the Congo

events.name: Foundation of the Kingdom of Luba

events.enhanced_description: In 1585, the first recorded commercial importation of chocolate to Europe occurred, bringing cacao from Veracruz, Mexico, to Seville, Spain. This event marked the beginning of chocolate's journey to becoming a popular delicacy in Europe.
events.name: First Commercial Importation of Chocolate to Europe

events.enhanced_description: On January 21, 1585, Queen Elizabeth I ordered the banishment of Robert Nutter, Thomas Worthington, and 18 other Roman Catholic priests from England. They were placed aboard the ship Mary Martin of Colchester and transported to France, reflecting the intense religious conflicts of the period.
events.name: Banishing of Catholic Priests from England

events.enhanced_description: On February 16, 1585, Pachomius II was deposed from his position as Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople by fellow bishops, marking a significant shift in the leadership of the Eastern Orthodox Church. He was replaced by Theoleptus II, indicating ongoing power struggles within the church.
events.name: Deposition of Pachomius II

events.enhanced_description: On February 21, 1585, King Johan III of Sweden married Gunilla Bielke in a ceremony at Västerås, which was notably boycotted by his siblings. This marriage was significant as it aimed to shift the Catholic government's stance towards Protestants in Sweden.
events.name: Marriage of King Johan III of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: Pope Gregory XIII, known for instituting the Gregorian calendar, died on April 10, 1585, after a nearly 13-year papacy. His death prompted a papal conclave to elect a successor, reflecting the ongoing influence of the papacy in European politics.
events.name: Death of Pope Gregory XIII

events.enhanced_description: The papal conclave commenced on April 21, 1585, at the Vatican in Rome, coinciding with Easter Sunday. With only 42 of the 60 cardinals present, early voting indicated a divided preference among the cardinals, highlighting the complexities of papal elections.
events.name: Papal Conclave Begins

events.enhanced_description: On April 24, 1585, Cardinal Felice Piergentile was elected as Pope Sixtus V during the conclave held at the Vatican. His election marked a significant moment in the Catholic Church, as he would later implement various reforms.
events.name: Election of Pope Sixtus V

events.enhanced_description: The coronation of Pope Sixtus V took place on May 1, 1585, in Vatican City. This event symbolized the beginning of his papacy and the potential for significant changes within the Catholic Church.
events.name: Coronation of Pope Sixtus V

events.enhanced_description: On May 19, 1585, Spain seized English ships in its ports, an act that escalated tensions and precipitated the Anglo-Spanish War (1585–1604). This conflict would have lasting implications for both nations and their colonial ambitions.
events.name: Seizure of English Ships by Spain

events.enhanced_description: In June 1585, Toyotomi Hideyoshi launched an invasion of the Japanese island of Shikoku with an army of 113,000 men. This military campaign was a significant step in Hideyoshi's efforts to unify Japan under his rule.
events.name: Invasion of Shikoku by Toyotomi Hideyoshi

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1585, a massive 9.2 magnitude earthquake struck the Aleutian Islands, unleashing a devastating tsunami that affected coastal regions as far away as Hawaii and Japan. This natural disaster highlighted the geological volatility of the Pacific region.
events.name: Aleutian Islands Earthquake and Tsunami

events.enhanced_description: On July 7, 1585, the Treaty of Nemours was signed, compelling King Henry III of France to concede to the demands of the Catholic League. This treaty marked the beginning of the Eighth War of Religion, also known as the War of the Three Henrys.
events.name: Treaty of Nemours

events.enhanced_description: On July 12, 1585, the final battle of the invasion of Shikoku commenced with the siege of Ichinomiya Castle. This siege was a critical moment in Toyotomi Hideyoshi's campaign to consolidate power in Japan.
events.name: Siege of Ichinomiya Castle

events.enhanced_description: On July 29, 1585, Ralph Lane, leader of the Roanoke expedition, negotiated an agreement with Granganimeo, a representative of the Secotan people. This agreement allowed the English to settle on Roanoke Island, although the Secotans refused to provide assistance due to prior conflicts.

locations.name: Roanoke Island, Dare County, North Carolina, United States

events.name: Negotiation with the Secotan People

events.enhanced_description: On August 6, 1585, Chōsokabe Motochika surrendered the island of Shikoku to Toyotomi Hideyoshi after a 26-day siege of Ichinomiya Castle. This surrender marked a significant victory for Hideyoshi in his campaign to unify Japan.
events.name: Surrender of Shikoku

events.enhanced_description: On August 8, 1585, English explorer John Davis entered Cumberland Sound in Baffin Island during his quest for the Northwest Passage. His explorations contributed to the understanding of the Arctic regions and the search for new trade routes.

locations.name: Cumberland Sound, Baffin Island, Nunavut, Canada

events.name: John Davis Enters Cumberland Sound

events.enhanced_description: On August 14, 1585, Queen Elizabeth I of England agreed to establish a protectorate over the Netherlands, signaling England's commitment to support the Dutch Revolt against Spanish rule. This decision was pivotal in the context of the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: Queen Elizabeth I Establishes Protectorate over the Netherlands

events.enhanced_description: On August 17, 1585, Spanish forces commanded by the Duke of Parma captured Antwerp, leading to the expulsion of Protestants and a mass exodus of its inhabitants. This event significantly diminished Antwerp's status as a major trade center in Europe.
events.name: Capture of Antwerp by Spanish Forces

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1585, the Treaty of Nonsuch was signed, committing England to support the Dutch Revolt against Spanish rule. This treaty marked England's formal entry into the Eighty Years' War, altering the dynamics of the conflict.
events.name: Signing of the Treaty of Nonsuch

events.enhanced_description: On September 11, 1585, the rebellion of An-Nasir al-Hasan bin Ali in Yemen was quashed when he was betrayed and handed over to the Ottoman governor. His capture marked the end of a significant challenge to Ottoman authority in the region.
events.name: End of An-Nasir al-Hasan's Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On September 15, 1585, English Catholic priest John Adams was banished from England along with 72 other priests, and transported to Boulogne in France. This mass banishment reflected the ongoing religious persecution in England during this period.
events.name: Banishing of John Adams and Other Priests

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1585, King Henry IV of Navarre was excommunicated by Pope Sixtus V, effectively declaring that French Catholics were not obliged to recognize his claim to the throne. This act intensified the religious and political conflicts in France.
events.name: Excommunication of King Henry IV of Navarre

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of IJsseloord concluded on October 15, 1585, after nine days of intense fighting, resulting in the successful recapture of Arnhem by English and Dutch forces from Spanish control. This event was part of the larger context of the Eighty Years' War, which saw the Dutch struggle for independence from Spanish rule.
events.name: Siege of IJsseloord

events.enhanced_description: On November 18, 1585, Álvaro Manrique de Zúñiga was appointed Viceroy of New Spain by King Philip II of Spain. His tenure marked a significant period in the colonial administration of Mexico, overseeing various administrative and economic policies.
events.name: Appointment of Álvarez Manrique de Zúñiga as Viceroy

events.enhanced_description: On November 28, 1585, during the Anglo-Spanish War, English privateer Francis Drake captured the island of Santiago in Cape Verde. This strategic victory was part of Drake's broader campaign against Spanish maritime interests.
events.name: Capture of Santiago

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1585, Hadim Mesih Pasha was appointed as the new Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire by Sultan Murad III. His appointment marked a significant moment in the administrative history of the empire during a period of both internal and external challenges.
events.name: Appointment of Hadim Mesih Pasha

events.enhanced_description: On December 20, 1585, Mughal Emperor Akbar ordered an invasion of Kashmir with a force of 5,000 men, following an incident of disrespect from Yousuf Shah Chak. This military action was part of Akbar's broader strategy to consolidate Mughal control over the region.
events.name: Akbar's Invasion of Kashmir

events.enhanced_description: In 1587, a severe famine broke out in Ming dynasty China, exacerbating social unrest and contributing to the eventual decline of the dynasty. This famine highlighted the vulnerabilities of agrarian societies to climatic and economic fluctuations.
events.name: Severe famine in Ming dynasty China

events.enhanced_description: In 1587, The Rose Theatre was founded in London by Philip Henslowe, becoming one of the first permanent theatres in England. This venue played a crucial role in the development of English drama and the theatrical arts during the Elizabethan era.
events.name: Foundation of The Rose Theatre

events.enhanced_description: In 1587, the chapbook Historia von D. Johann Fausten was printed by Johann Spies in Frankfurt, marking the first published version of the Faust story. This work would have a lasting impact on literature and popular culture, influencing countless adaptations.
events.name: Publication of Historia von D. Johann Fausten

events.enhanced_description: In 1587, Everard Digby's De Arte Natandi was published, becoming the first treatise on swimming in England. This work contributed to the understanding of swimming techniques and safety, reflecting the growing interest in physical education.
events.name: Publication of De Arte Natandi

events.enhanced_description: In 1587, St. Dominic's Church was established in Macau, becoming one of the oldest churches in the region. This church played a significant role in the spread of Christianity in Asia and remains a symbol of the cultural exchange between East and West.
events.name: Establishment of St. Dominic's Church

events.enhanced_description: In 1587, Hailuoto, an island in the Bothnian Bay, was separated from the grand parish of Saloinen to become an independent parish. This change reflected the growing administrative needs of the region and the importance of local governance.
events.name: Separation of Hailuoto from Saloinen

events.enhanced_description: On January 7, 1587, Sir Walter Raleigh appointed John White as the Governor of the Roanoke Colony, which was to be established later that year on Roanoke Island, North Carolina. This appointment was part of Raleigh's efforts to establish a permanent English settlement in the New World.

locations.name: Roanoke Island, Dare County, North Carolina, United States

events.name: Appointment of John White as Governor of Roanoke Colony

events.enhanced_description: On January 14, 1587, Toyotomi Hideyoshi ended Portuguese control of the port of Nagasaki after six years, reclaiming it for Japan. This action was part of Hideyoshi's broader efforts to consolidate power and limit foreign influence in Japan.
events.name: End of Portuguese Control of Nagasaki

events.enhanced_description: On February 5, 1587, King Nanda of Burma appointed his eldest son, Minye Kyawswa II, as Viceroy of Ava, with the capital at Inwa. This appointment was significant in the context of the Burmese monarchy and its administrative structure.
events.name: Appointment of Minye Kyawswa II as Viceroy of Ava

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1587, Mary, Queen of Scots, was executed at Fotheringhay Castle, following her conviction for treason. This event marked a significant moment in the power struggles of the time, as Mary was a legitimate heir to the English throne, and her death had profound political implications.
events.name: Execution of Mary, Queen of Scots

events.enhanced_description: A period of exceptionally severe cold began in western Europe on February 12, 1587, lasting until February 24. This harsh winter had significant impacts on agriculture and daily life across the region.
events.name: Severe Cold in Western Europe

events.enhanced_description: On February 27, 1587, Sir Anthony Cope was imprisoned in the Tower of London after presenting a Puritan revision of the Anglican Book of Common Prayer to the Speaker of the House of Commons, Sir John Puckering. This incident highlighted the tensions between different religious factions in England.
events.name: Imprisonment of Sir Anthony Cope

events.enhanced_description: On March 6, 1587, Álvaro II Nimi a Nkanga ascended to the throne of the Kingdom of Kongo, following the death of his father, Álvaro I. His reign was marked by efforts to maintain the kingdom's influence amidst European colonial pressures.
figures: Álvaro I Nimi a Lukeni lua Mvemba
events.name: Álvaro II Nimi a Nkanga becomes ruler of the Kingdom of Kongo

events.enhanced_description: On March 15, 1587, an English privateer accepted a commission from the Kingdom of England to disrupt Spanish freighters trading with Italy. This action was part of the ongoing conflict between England and Spain during the Anglo-Spanish War.
events.name: Commission of English Privateer

events.enhanced_description: On April 20, 1587, the Burmese siege of Ayutthaya, the capital of the Ayutthaya Kingdom, failed after six months, leading to the withdrawal of King Nanda Bayin's troops. This event was a significant setback for Burma in the ongoing Burmese–Siamese War.

locations.name: Ayutthaya, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya, Thailand

events.name: Failure of the Siege of Ayutthaya

events.enhanced_description: On April 29, 1587, English privateer Sir Francis Drake led a raid in the Bay of Cádiz, sinking at least 23 ships of the Spanish fleet in an operation known as 'Singeing the King of Spain's Beard.' This raid was part of Drake's broader campaign against Spanish maritime power.
events.name: Singeing the King of Spain's Beard

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1587, the second expedition to establish an English colony at Roanoke Island departed from England, carrying two ships, supplies, and 121 settlers under the command of John White. This expedition aimed to re-establish the previously abandoned colony.

locations.name: Roanoke Island, Dare County, North Carolina, United States

events.name: Second Expedition to Roanoke Island

events.enhanced_description: On May 19, 1587, explorer John Davis set out from Dartmouth, Devon, for his third attempt to find the Northwest Passage. His expeditions were significant in the age of exploration, contributing to the European understanding of the Arctic regions.
events.name: John Davis's Attempt to Find the Northwest Passage

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1587, most of Kyushu surrendered to Toyotomi Hideyoshi, following a siege that began on May 3. This event was part of Hideyoshi's campaign to unify Japan under his rule.
events.name: Surrender of Kyushu to Toyotomi Hideyoshi

events.enhanced_description: On June 20, 1587, Gabriel VIII was enthroned as the new Pontiff of the Coptic Christian Church in Egypt, filling a vacancy that had existed for nine months. His papacy would last until his death in 1603.
events.name: Election of Pope Gabriel VIII

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1587, a group of English settlers arrived on Roanoke Island to re-establish the deserted colony. This marked a significant moment in early American colonial history, although the fate of these settlers remains a mystery.

locations.name: Roanoke Island, Dare County, North Carolina, United States

events.name: Arrival of English Settlers at Roanoke Island

events.enhanced_description: On August 18, 1587, according to legend, Saul Wahl was named king of Poland, only to be deposed the following day. This brief and unusual episode reflects the complexities of Polish succession during this period.
events.name: Saul Wahl Named King of Poland

events.enhanced_description: On August 19, 1587, Polish and Lithuanian nobles elected Sigismund III Vasa, King of Sweden, as the ruler of Poland following the death of Stephen Báthory. This election marked the beginning of a significant reign that would see the unification of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
events.name: Election of Sigismund III Vasa

events.enhanced_description: On August 22, 1587, a faction of Polish nobles opposed to Sigismund Vasa proclaimed Maximilian III, Archduke of Austria, as the ruler of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. This act of defiance initiated the War of the Polish Succession, a conflict that would shape the political landscape of Eastern Europe.
events.name: Proclamation of Maximilian III as King

events.enhanced_description: On August 27, 1587, Governor John White departed from the Roanoke Colony, located on Roanoke Island, North Carolina, to return to England for supplies. His absence would lead to the mysterious disappearance of the colony, which remains one of America's oldest unsolved mysteries.

image.caption: Map of the Roanoke area by John White.
image.date_qualification: The source gives the map date as between 1585 and 1593; this is not the event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

locations.name: Roanoke Island, Dare County, North Carolina, United States

events.name: John White leaves Roanoke Colony

events.enhanced_description: On September 9, 1587, the faculty at the University of Leuven condemned 34 propositions by Jesuit scholar Michel Baius, igniting a campaign against the Jesuits by traditional Belgian Catholics. This event highlighted the tensions within the Catholic Church during the Counter-Reformation.
events.name: Condemnation of Baius' Propositions

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1587, Vincenzo Gonzaga was crowned Duke of Mantua in a ceremony that solidified his rule over the Duchy. His reign would be marked by cultural patronage and political maneuvering in the complex landscape of Italian city-states.
events.name: Coronation of Vincenzo Gonzaga

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1587, King Alexander II of Kakheti signed an oath of allegiance to Feodor I, the Tsar of Russia, at Gremi. This act was significant in the context of the shifting power dynamics in the Caucasus region during the late 16th century.
events.name: Oath of Allegiance by King Alexander II

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1587, ‘Abbas I, known as ‘Abbas the Great,’ succeeded to the throne as Shahanshah of Iran. His reign would be characterized by significant cultural and military achievements, marking a high point in the Safavid Empire.
events.name: Shah ‘Abbas I succeeds as Shahanshah

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1587, Sigismund Vasa, accompanied by a fleet of Swedish ships, landed in Poland to confront the invasion led by Maximilian III and the Austrian army. This marked a critical moment in the War of the Polish Succession.
events.name: Sigismund Vasa lands in Poland

events.enhanced_description: On October 14, 1587, during the War of the Polish Succession, Archduke Maximilian of Austria initiated the siege of Kraków, while Jan Zamoyski, the Polish Army's hetman, prepared to defend the city. This conflict would be pivotal in determining the future of the Polish crown.
events.name: Siege of Kraków begins

events.enhanced_description: On October 18, 1587, the first Filipinos landed in North America at Morro Bay, California. This event marks an important moment in the history of Filipino migration and cultural exchange in the Americas.
events.name: Landing of the first Filipinos in North America

events.enhanced_description: On October 20, 1587, the Battle of Coutras took place, where Huguenot forces led by Henry of Navarre defeated the Royalist troops commanded by Anne de Joyeuse, who was killed in the battle. This victory was significant in the ongoing French Wars of Religion.
events.name: Battle of Coutras

events.enhanced_description: On October 31, 1587, Leiden University Library opened its doors to the public, becoming one of the oldest libraries in the Netherlands. This institution has played a crucial role in the preservation and dissemination of knowledge in the region.
events.name: Opening of Leiden University Library

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1587, during his circumnavigation of the globe, English explorer Thomas Cavendish captured the Spanish galleon Santa Ana, seizing a treasure worth 2.1 million pesos. This event underscored the fierce competition between European powers for wealth and dominance in the New World.
events.name: Capture of the Spanish galleon Santa Ana

events.enhanced_description: On November 14, 1587, Davide Vacca was elected to a two-year term as the new Doge of the Republic of Genoa. His leadership would influence the political and economic landscape of this important maritime republic.
events.name: Election of Davide Vacca as Doge

events.enhanced_description: On November 22, 1587, Archduke Maximilian III launched a final assault on Kraków, which was repelled by the Polish defenders. This event marked a significant moment in the War of the Polish Succession, showcasing the resilience of Polish forces.
events.name: Final Austrian attack on Kraków

events.enhanced_description: On November 29, 1587, Maximilian III withdrew his forces, effectively ending the siege of Kraków. This withdrawal marked a turning point in the War of the Polish Succession, allowing Polish forces to regain control.
events.name: End of the Siege of Kraków

events.enhanced_description: On December 27, 1587, Sigismund III Vasa was formally crowned as King Zygmunt Waza of Poland and Duke of Lithuania in a grand ceremony in Kraków. His reign would significantly impact the political landscape of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
events.name: Coronation of Sigismund III Vasa

events.enhanced_description: William Morgan's translation of the Bible into Welsh was a significant cultural milestone, making the scriptures accessible to Welsh speakers and fostering a sense of national identity. This translation played a crucial role in the preservation of the Welsh language and culture during a time of increasing English dominance.
events.name: William Morgan's Welsh translation of the Bible is published

events.enhanced_description: The Armada Portrait of Elizabeth I was commissioned to commemorate the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588, symbolizing England's naval supremacy and Elizabeth's strength as a monarch. The painting serves as a powerful political statement and a reflection of the Elizabethan era's cultural achievements.

image.caption: The Armada Portrait of Elizabeth I, an allegorical painting depicting the queen against a backdrop representing the Spanish Armada’s defeat.
image.date_qualification: The supplied image metadata dates this portrait to 1588; that is the depicted work’s date, not an upload date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The Armada Portrait of Elizabeth I of England is created

events.enhanced_description: On January 22, 1588, Pope Sixtus V issued the papal bull Immensa aeterni Dei, reorganizing the Roman Curia and establishing 15 congregations of cardinals. This significant reform aimed to enhance the efficiency and authority of the Catholic Church during the Counter-Reformation.
events.name: Papal Bull Immensa aeterni Dei

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1588, the Battle of Pitschen occurred, where Polish and Lithuanian troops commanded by Jan Zamoyski faced an invading Austrian force led by Maximilian III. The battle ended with Maximilian's surrender, marking a decisive victory for the Polish forces in the War of the Polish Succession.
events.name: Battle of Pitschen

events.enhanced_description: On February 9, 1588, the sudden death of Álvaro de Bazán, 1st Marquis of Santa Cruz, occurred amidst preparations for the Spanish Armada. His passing forced King Philip II of Spain to reallocate command of the fleet, impacting Spain's naval strategy during a critical period.
events.name: Death of Álvaro de Bazán

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Colombo, which took place in 1588, ended when Portuguese Admiral Pedro Teixeira arrived with a fleet of 80 ships, liberating the capital of Portuguese Ceylon from the forces of King Rajasinha I of Sitawaka. Following the defeat, Rajasinha and his troops retreated to their stronghold at Seethawakapura.
events.name: Siege of Colombo

events.enhanced_description: Shah Abbas I was officially declared Emperor of the Safavid Empire on the first day of the New Year according to the Zoroastrian calendar in 1588. His reign marked a significant period of cultural and political revival in Persia, following his initial rise to power in 1587.
events.name: Ascension of Shah Abbas I

events.enhanced_description: In March 1588, the English Army began recruiting volunteers in anticipation of a Spanish invasion. This effort was formalized with the enactment of the first military pension act on April 10, 1593, which aimed to support soldiers who had been injured or disabled in service.
events.name: Recruitment of Volunteers by the English Army

events.enhanced_description: Christian IV ascended to the throne of Denmark–Norway on April 4, 1588, following the death of his father, Frederick II. His reign would be marked by ambitious projects and military conflicts that aimed to expand Danish influence.

image.caption: Retrospective illustration of the unveiling of the Christian IV statue at Stortorvet, Oslo.
image.credit: Severin Worm-Petersen — Oslo Museum: image no. OB.F01133 (Byhistorisk samling), via oslobilder.no.
image.date_qualification: Depicted event: 28 September 1880, nearly three centuries after the accession on 4 April 1588.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Christian IV becomes King of Denmark–Norway

events.enhanced_description: On May 12, 1588, the Day of the Barricades occurred in Paris when Henry I, Duke of Guise, seized control of the city, forcing King Henry III to flee. This event was a pivotal moment in the French Wars of Religion, highlighting the intense power struggles between the Catholic League and the monarchy.
events.name: Day of the Barricades

events.enhanced_description: On May 28, 1588, the Spanish Armada, consisting of 130 ships and 30,000 men, began its journey from the Tagus estuary under the command of the Duke of Medina Sidonia. This fleet was intended to invade England, marking a significant moment in the Anglo-Spanish conflict.
events.name: Departure of the Spanish Armada

events.enhanced_description: On June 18, 1588, English captain Thomas Cavendish and his fleet, while sailing back to England, stumbled upon the Portuguese-controlled island of Saint Helena. This marked the first recorded sighting of the island by English explorers, which had been under Portuguese control for decades.

locations.country: Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha
locations.name: Saint Helena

events.name: Discovery of Saint Helena

events.enhanced_description: On June 19, 1588, a storm scattered parts of the Spanish Armada, leading to a significant setback for the fleet. The Duke of Medina Sidonia returned to Coruña for repairs and urged King Philip II to reconsider the invasion plans, but the king insisted on continuing.
events.name: Storm scatters the Spanish Armada

events.enhanced_description: On July 15, 1588, King Henry III of France signed the Edict of Union in Rouen, conceding to the demands of the Catholic League and the Duke of Guise. This agreement prohibited French Protestants from participating in government, allowing Henry III to regain control of Paris.
events.name: Edict of Union

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1588, the first naval engagement between the English and Spanish fleets occurred off the coast of Plymouth, resulting in a decisive victory for the English forces commanded by Lord Howard of Effingham and Sir Francis Drake. This battle marked the beginning of a series of confrontations during the Anglo-Spanish War.
events.name: First Engagement of English and Spanish Fleets

events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1588, the English fleet achieved another victory against the Spanish fleet off the coast of the Isle of Portland. This engagement further weakened the Spanish Armada's position as it attempted to invade England.

locations.name: Isle of Portland, Dorset, England, United Kingdom

events.name: English Fleet Defeats Spanish Fleet

events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1588, the English fleet secured another victory against the Spanish fleet off the coast of Flanders. This battle was part of the ongoing conflict between England and Spain during the Spanish Armada campaign.
events.name: English Fleet Defeats Spanish Fleet off Flanders

events.enhanced_description: On August 9, 1588, after two days of attempting to reach the coast of Flanders, the Duke of Medina Sidonia decided to return the Spanish Armada to Spain. This decision came after facing significant losses and challenges during the campaign.
events.name: Return of the Spanish Armada

events.enhanced_description: On August 12, 1588, much of the Spanish Armada was destroyed by storms while attempting to navigate around Scotland and Ireland. The English fleet, having avoided the storm, called off their pursuit, leading to significant losses for the Spanish.
events.name: Destruction of the Spanish Armada by Storms

events.enhanced_description: On August 19, 1588, Queen Elizabeth I delivered a rousing speech to her troops at Tilbury, rallying them against the impending threat of the Spanish Armada. Her words inspired confidence and determination among the soldiers, reinforcing their resolve to defend England.

image.caption: Old engraving depicting Elizabeth I at Tilbury.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — old engraving
image.date_qualification: Retrospective engraving dated broadly to the 18th–19th century; it is an illustration of the Tilbury event, not a contemporary photograph. The exact depicted date is not established.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

locations.name: Tilbury, Thurrock, Essex, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Speech to the Troops at Tilbury

events.enhanced_description: On August 29, 1588, Toyotomi Hideyoshi, the Chancellor of the Realm in Japan, issued the katanagari edict, which mandated the confiscation of swords from individuals suspected of opposing his rule. This move was part of Hideyoshi's broader efforts to consolidate power and control over the samurai class.
events.name: Katanagari Edict by Toyotomi Hideyoshi

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1588, Ottoman general Serdar Ferhad Pasha captured the Ganja Fortress in present-day Azerbaijan. This event was part of the broader Ottoman expansion into the region during the late 16th century.

image.caption: Ganja Fortress, with surviving walls in Ganja, Azerbaijan.
image.date_qualification: A photograph of the fortress site, not a depiction of its 1588 capture. The saved image date is 2012-01-02.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Capture of Ganja Fortress

events.enhanced_description: In October 1588, Bernardino Baldi completed the first biography of Nicolaus Copernicus, the renowned astronomer known for his heliocentric model of the universe. This biography contributed to the understanding and appreciation of Copernicus's groundbreaking work in astronomy.
events.name: Completion of the First Biography of Nicolaus Copernicus

events.enhanced_description: On November 13, 1588, Dutch Republic and English forces captured the fortress of Bergen op Zoom after a 41-day siege. This victory was significant in the context of the Eighty Years' War, as it strengthened the position of the Dutch against Spanish rule.

locations.name: Bergen op Zoom, North Brabant, Netherlands

events.name: Capture of Bergen op Zoom

events.enhanced_description: On November 15, 1588, the English Navy ship Great Spaniard, previously a Spanish Armada ship named San Salvador, sank off the coast of the Isle of Purbeck. The incident resulted in the loss of 23 crew members, while the survivors were rescued by an English man-o-war boat.
events.name: Sinking of the Great Spaniard

events.enhanced_description: On December 5, 1588, the Order of Augustinian Recollects was formally recognized as a separate province from the Order of Saint Augustine, an event known as the Día de la Recolección or Day of Recollection. This recognition marked an important development in the history of religious orders within the Catholic Church.
events.name: Recognition of the Order of Augustinian Recollects

events.enhanced_description: On December 23, 1588, King Henry III of France ordered the assassination of the Duke of Guise and his brother, Cardinal of Guise, in a decisive move against his ultra-Catholic enemies. This act led to widespread unrest and forced Henry III to ally with Henry of Navarre.
