events.enhanced_description: On January 12, 1609, the Basque witch trials began in Spain when the Inquisition court in Logroño ordered the arrest of four women, including María de Jureteguía and María Chipía de Barrenetxea. This marked the start of a series of trials that would lead to widespread persecution.
events.name: Start of the Basque Witch Trials

events.enhanced_description: On January 15, 1609, Avisa Relation oder Zeitung began publication in Wolfenbüttel, marking one of the world's first newspapers. This publication played a significant role in the dissemination of news and information in early modern Europe.
events.name: Publication of Avisa Relation oder Zeitung

events.enhanced_description: On January 31, 1609, the Bank of Amsterdam was established, becoming a cornerstone of modern banking and finance. It played a crucial role in the economic development of the Dutch Republic and influenced banking practices worldwide.
events.name: Establishment of the Bank of Amsterdam

events.enhanced_description: On February 4, 1609, the last day of Keichō 13 according to the Japanese lunar calendar marked a significant temporal milestone in Japan's historical timeline. This date is often referenced in the context of the cultural and political developments of the period.
events.name: Last Day of Keichō 13

events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1609, General Jacob De la Gardie led the Swedish Army from Vyborg to defend the Russian Empire against the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth during the Polish-Muscovite War. This military action was part of the broader conflict affecting Eastern Europe.
events.name: Swedish Army Marches to Defend Russia

events.enhanced_description: On March 19, 1609, the Dutch warship Mauritius sank off the coast of Cape Lopes Gonçalves in modern-day Gabon. The wreckage of the ship remained undiscovered until 1985, highlighting the challenges of maritime navigation during this period.
events.name: Sinking of the Dutch Warship Mauritius

events.enhanced_description: On March 24, 1609, the Lithuanian Navy, commanded by Grand Hetman Jan Karol Chodkiewicz, successfully broke the blockade of Riga by sinking two Swedish warships off the coast of Salacgrīva. This victory was significant in the context of the ongoing Polish-Muscovite War.
events.name: Lithuanian Navy Breaks Blockade of Riga

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1609, Johann Wilhelm, the Roman Catholic Duke of the United Duchies of Jülich-Cleves-Berg, died in Düsseldorf without heirs. His death triggered the War of the Jülich Succession, as various factions vied for control of the duchies.
events.name: Death of Johann Wilhelm, Duke of Jülich-Cleves-Berg

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1609, King Philip III of Spain signed an edict expelling the Moriscos, descendants of Muslims who converted to Christianity, from Spain. This decision was part of the broader efforts to enforce religious uniformity in the kingdom.

image.caption: Painting by Vicent Mestre depicting Moriscos disembarking at the port of Oran.
image.date_qualification: Painting dated 1613; not a contemporary photograph of the edict’s signing.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Edict for the Expulsion of Moriscos

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1609, soldiers of the Shimazu clan invaded Ryukyu Island, capturing the castle and beginning the process of making the Ryukyu Kingdom a vassal of Satsuma Han. Despite this, Ryukyu retained its status as a tribute state to the Ming and Qing dynasties.
events.name: Invasion of Ryukyu by Shimazu Clan

events.enhanced_description: On April 9, 1609, the Treaty of Antwerp was signed, establishing the Twelve Years' Truce in the Eighty Years' War between the Netherlands and Spain. This agreement allowed the Dutch East India Company to trade within the Spanish Empire, significantly impacting European trade dynamics.
events.name: Treaty of Antwerp and the Twelve Years' Truce

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1609, London publisher Thomas Thorpe issued Shakespeare's Sonnets, accompanied by a dedication to 'Mr. W.H.' This publication has sparked much debate regarding its authenticity and the identity of its dedicatee.

image.caption: Title page of Shakespeare’s Sonnets, a quarto published by Thomas Thorpe.
image.date_qualification: The title page is from the 1609 quarto associated with the publication; the saved image date is 1609.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Publication of Shakespeare's Sonnets

events.enhanced_description: On May 23, 1609, the Second Virginia Charter was officially ratified, replacing the council with a governor who held absolute control over the colony. This change marked a significant shift in governance for the Jamestown settlement.
events.name: Ratification of the Second Virginia Charter

events.enhanced_description: On June 2, 1609, a fleet of nine English ships, led by the Sea Venture, departed from England to deliver supplies to Jamestown, Virginia. The fleet encountered a storm, leading to the wreck of the Sea Venture in Bermuda on July 24.

image.caption: Memorial plaque at Gates Bay, Bermuda, commemorating the Sea Venture survivors’ landing.
image.date_qualification: The image depicts a later memorial, not the 1609 fleet departure or wreck. The supplied original image date is 2014-10-27 09:50:07.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Departure of the Sea Venture Fleet

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1609, the War of the Jülich Succession commenced after the Margraviate of Brandenburg and the Duchy of Palatinate-Neuburg signed a treaty in Dortmund. This conflict arose over the succession of the Roman Catholic United Duchies of Jülich-Cleves-Berg.
events.name: Beginning of the War of the Jülich Succession

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Tashiskari was a significant conflict where General Giorgi Saakadze led the forces of the Kingdom of Kartli against the invading Ottoman troops. This battle was crucial in preventing the Ottomans from capturing Tbilisi, thereby maintaining Georgian sovereignty during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Battle of Tashiskari

events.enhanced_description: In a notable naval engagement, a fleet from the Kingdom of Spain, supported by a French warship, confronted a larger Tunisian fleet in the Mediterranean Sea. The Spanish and French forces achieved a decisive victory, sinking 21 of the 23 Tunisian ships, showcasing the naval power of European states during this era.
events.name: Battle in the Mediterranean Sea

events.enhanced_description: French explorer Samuel de Champlain, accompanied by 60 men in 24 canoes, became the first European to explore Lake Champlain. This exploration was pivotal in establishing French claims in North America and set the stage for future interactions with Indigenous peoples.
events.name: Samuel de Champlain enters Lake Champlain

events.enhanced_description: The 'Letter of Majesty' granted by Rudolf II allowed for religious freedom in Bohemia, a significant step towards tolerance in a region marked by religious conflict. This decree was part of the broader tensions leading up to the Thirty Years' War.
events.name: Bohemia granted freedom of religion

events.enhanced_description: The German Catholic League was formed in Munich by Maximilian I to counter the Protestant Union, marking a significant moment in the religious conflicts of the Holy Roman Empire. This alliance aimed to protect Catholic interests and maintain peace within the empire.
events.name: Formation of the German Catholic League

events.enhanced_description: A devastating hurricane struck the Caribbean Sea, scattering nine ships of the London Company that were en route to Jamestown. This natural disaster resulted in significant loss, with only a fraction of the settlers reaching Virginia, exacerbating the challenges faced by the colony.
events.name: Hurricane separates ships en route to Jamestown

events.enhanced_description: The Sea Venture, flagship of the London Company's fleet, was deliberately wrecked by Admiral George Somers during a storm in Bermuda. This act saved the ship from sinking and led to the establishment of the first English settlement on the island by the survivors.
events.name: Wrecking of the Sea Venture

events.enhanced_description: Samuel de Champlain engaged in a battle between the Huron and Iroquois at Crown Point, New York, where he killed two Iroquois chiefs. This confrontation significantly influenced French-Iroquois relations for the next century, marking Champlain's role in North American geopolitics.

locations.name: Crown Point, New York, United States

events.name: Champlain participates in battle with Iroquois

events.enhanced_description: The Spanish galleon San Francisco sank in a storm off the coast of Japan, resulting in the loss of 56 crew members. Survivors managed to reach Yubanda, marking a tragic event in the maritime history of Spanish trade in Asia.
events.name: Sinking of the San Francisco

events.enhanced_description: Four ships arrived at Jamestown, Virginia, bringing nearly 300 men, women, and children to supply the struggling English colonists. Unfortunately, most supplies were spoiled, and many passengers were afflicted with illness, highlighting the ongoing hardships faced by the colony.
events.name: Supplies arrive at Jamestown

events.enhanced_description: English astronomer Thomas Harriot made history by creating the first detailed drawing of the Moon based on his observations through a telescope. This groundbreaking work contributed to the field of astronomy and paved the way for future celestial studies.
events.name: Thomas Harriot's drawing of the Moon

events.enhanced_description: Galileo Galilei showcased his first telescope to officials in Venice, marking a pivotal moment in the history of science. His demonstration not only impressed his contemporaries but also revolutionized the study of astronomy.
events.name: Galileo demonstrates his telescope

events.enhanced_description: Henry Hudson became the first European to observe Delaware Bay during his exploration in 1609. This discovery was part of his broader journey that contributed to European knowledge of the North American coastline.
events.name: Henry Hudson sees Delaware Bay

events.enhanced_description: Henry Hudson entered New York Bay aboard the Halve Maen, marking a significant moment in the exploration of North America. This entry laid the groundwork for future Dutch claims and settlements in the region.
events.name: Henry Hudson enters New York Bay

events.enhanced_description: In a significant leadership change at Jamestown, Captain George Percy took over as president of the Council, replacing Captain John Smith, who returned to England. This transition marked a critical moment in the governance of the struggling colony.
events.name: George Percy replaces John Smith in Jamestown

events.enhanced_description: The expulsion of the Moriscos from Valencia was executed in accordance with the edict signed by Philip III, reflecting the intense religious persecution of the time. This event led to the displacement of thousands and had lasting impacts on Spanish society.
events.name: Expulsion of the Moriscos from Valencia

events.enhanced_description: A version of the nursery rhyme 'Three Blind Mice' was published in London, attributed to the teenage editor Thomas Ravenscroft. This publication contributed to the cultural landscape of early 17th-century England.
events.name: Publication of Three Blind Mice

events.enhanced_description: Archduke Matthias of Austria was formally crowned as Mátyás II, King of Hungary, in a ceremony held in Budapest. This event solidified his rule and marked a significant moment in the Habsburg dynasty's influence over Hungary.
events.name: Matthias II crowned King of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: A treaty was signed between Spanish nobleman Rodrigo de Vivero and Tokugawa Ieyasu, the former shogun of Japan, establishing a Spanish factory in eastern Japan. This agreement marked an important step in the expansion of Spanish influence in Asia.
events.name: Treaty signed in Japan

events.enhanced_description: The Biblioteca Ambrosiana, one of the first public libraries in the world, was opened in Milan by Cardinal Federico Borromeo. This library was notable for its innovative design, housing books on shelves rather than chaining them to tables, thus promoting greater access to literature and knowledge.

image.caption: The Biblioteca Ambrosiana in Milan, Italy.
image.date_qualification: A photograph of the library site, not a depiction of its 1609 opening. Image date: 2022-08-27.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Opening of the Biblioteca Ambrosiana

events.enhanced_description: In 1610, Dr. Bonham's Case was decided by Chief Justice Edward Coke, establishing the principle that common law could limit the powers of Parliament and the monarchy, a landmark decision in English legal history.
events.name: Dr. Bonham's Case

events.enhanced_description: In 1610, Nurhaci, the Manchu tribal leader, severed relations with the Ming dynasty, setting the stage for the rise of the Qing dynasty and the eventual fall of the Ming.
events.name: Nurhaci breaks relations with the Ming dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In 1610, the Douay–Rheims Bible was published, translating the Bible from the Latin Vulgate into English, a significant work for the Catholic Church and English-speaking Catholics.
events.name: Publication of the Douay–Rheims Bible

events.enhanced_description: In 1610, Jakob Böhme experienced a profound inner vision, leading him to believe he had gained a deeper understanding of the cosmos and a special vocation from God, influencing later mystical and philosophical thought.
events.name: Jakob Böhme's inner vision

events.enhanced_description: In 1610, work commenced on the Wignacourt Aqueduct in Malta, a significant engineering project aimed at improving the water supply to Valletta, showcasing the ingenuity of the time.
events.name: Start of the Wignacourt Aqueduct

events.enhanced_description: The Nossa Senhora da Graça, a Portuguese carrack, sank near Nagasaki after a fierce four-night battle against Japanese samurai. This incident underscores the tensions between European powers and Japan during the early 17th century.
events.name: Nossa Senhora da Graça incident

events.enhanced_description: On January 7, 1610, Galileo Galilei first observed the four largest moons of Jupiter—Ganymede, Callisto, Europa, and Io—using his telescope. This discovery was pivotal in supporting the heliocentric model of the solar system.
events.name: Galileo observes Galilean moons

events.enhanced_description: English courtier Thomas Roe embarked on an expedition to The Guianas and the Amazon River, aiming to explore and establish trade relations in the region. This journey was part of England's broader efforts to expand its influence in South America.
events.name: Thomas Roe's expedition to The Guianas

events.enhanced_description: Galileo Galilei published 'Sidereus Nuncius', the first printed scientific record of observations made through a telescope. This groundbreaking work detailed his discoveries of celestial bodies and significantly advanced the field of astronomy.
events.name: Publication of Sidereus Nuncius

events.enhanced_description: On March 22, 1610, Mikhail Skopin-Shuisky liberated Moscow from rebel forces, a pivotal moment during the Time of Troubles in Russia. His actions helped restore order and stability in the capital, which had been plagued by conflict.
events.name: Liberation of Moscow from rebels

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Brussol was signed between Charles Emmanuel I, Duke of Savoy, and a representative of King Henry IV of France in Bruzolo. The treaty aimed to coordinate efforts to expel Spanish forces from Italy, but it was ultimately rendered ineffective due to Henry IV's assassination shortly thereafter.
events.name: Signing of the Treaty of Brussol

events.enhanced_description: William Shakespeare's play 'The Tragedie of Macbeth' was performed for the first time at the Globe Theatre in London. This iconic tragedy would go on to become one of Shakespeare's most famous works, exploring themes of ambition, guilt, and fate.
events.name: First performance of Macbeth

events.enhanced_description: Marie de' Medici was formally crowned as Queen Consort of France in a grand ceremony. This event was significant as it solidified her role in the French court, especially as her husband, King Henry IV, prepared for military engagements abroad.
events.name: Coronation of Marie de' Medici

events.enhanced_description: King Henry IV of France was assassinated in Paris by François Ravaillac, a Catholic extremist opposed to Henry's policies. This shocking event led to a power vacuum and the ascension of Henry's young son, Louis XIII, under the regency of Marie de' Medici.
events.name: Assassination of Henry IV of France

events.enhanced_description: Thomas Gates, acting as temporary Governor, arrived in Jamestown with survivors from the wrecked Sea Venture. They found the settlement in dire straits after the 'starving time', with many structures destroyed and a desperate situation among the remaining colonists.

image.caption: Map of Jamestown Island terrain, marking the discovered and traditionally supposed locations of 1607 James Fort.
image.credit: National Park Service : base map * Maps_template-fr.svg : Eric Gaba ( Sting - fr:Sting ) *derivative work: bamse ( talk )* User:Morgan Riley : coloration, clean-up, legend, and arrangement — Page X of Archeology Evidence at Jamestown" by the National Park Service, available at the Internet Archive * File:Maps template-en.svg (compass rose)
image.date_qualification: The image description dates the depicted terrain to the middle of the 20th century; the map file metadata gives 2014-03-01 as the image date. Neither date is the arrival date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Arrival of Thomas Gates in Jamestown

events.enhanced_description: Temporary Governor Thomas Gates issued The Divine, Moral, and Martial Laws in Jamestown, establishing a strict legal framework aimed at restoring order and discipline among the colonists. These laws reflected the challenges of governance in the early years of the Virginia colony.
events.name: Issuance of The Divine, Moral, and Martial Laws

events.enhanced_description: François Ravaillac, the assassin of King Henry IV of France, was executed in a brutal manner by being pulled apart by horses in the Place de Grève, Paris. His execution was a public spectacle, reflecting the intense political tensions of the time following the king's assassination.

image.caption: Engraved bust portrait of François Ravaillac by Crispin de Passe.
image.credit: Crispin de Passe (1564 ?-1637), graveur. — This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID btv1b8401565f/f1
image.date_qualification: Portrait, not a depiction of the execution. Dated circa 1610 in the saved image metadata.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Execution of François Ravaillac

events.enhanced_description: The masque Tethys' Festival was performed at Whitehall Palace to celebrate the investiture of Henry Frederick, Prince of Wales. This elaborate performance showcased the artistic and cultural richness of the Jacobean court.
events.name: Tethys' Festival performance

events.enhanced_description: Temporary Governor Gates made the controversial decision to abandon Jamestown due to the dire conditions faced by the settlers. This decision highlighted the struggles of early colonial life in America and the challenges of sustaining the settlement.
events.name: Governor Gates decides to abandon Jamestown

events.enhanced_description: Governor Gates' convoy met the ships of Governor Thomas West, 3rd Baron De La Warr, at Mulberry Island. This meeting was crucial for the future of the Jamestown settlement, as it brought much-needed supplies and leadership.
figures: Thomas West, 3rd Baron De La Warr
events.name: Gates' convoy meets Governor De La Warr's ships

events.enhanced_description: The convoy led by Temporary Governor Gates, along with the ships of Governor Lord De La Warr, successfully landed at Jamestown. This event marked a turning point in the colony's fortunes, as it brought new leadership and resources.
figures: Thomas West, 3rd Baron De La Warr
events.name: Gates' convoy lands at Jamestown

events.enhanced_description: Henri Membertou, Grand Chief of the Mi'kmaq nation, became the first North American aboriginal person to accept baptism into the Christian faith. He signed the Concordat of 1610, which recognized the Mi'kmaq as an independent nation in the eyes of the Roman Catholic Church.
events.name: Henri Membertou's baptism

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Klushino, the outnumbered forces of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth achieved a remarkable victory against the combined Russian and Swedish armies. This battle was pivotal, leading to the occupation of Moscow by Polish troops.
events.name: Battle of Klushino

events.enhanced_description: John Guy set sail from Bristol with 39 other colonists for Newfoundland, marking an important moment in the early English colonization of North America. This expedition aimed to establish a permanent settlement in the New World.
events.name: John Guy sails for Newfoundland

events.enhanced_description: Lady Arbella Stuart, a claimant to the English throne, was imprisoned for secretly marrying William Seymour, 2nd Duke of Somerset, without royal permission. This act of defiance against the monarchy underscored the political intrigues of the time.
events.name: Lady Arbella Stuart imprisoned

events.enhanced_description: Vasili Ivanovich Shuisky, who had proclaimed himself Tsar of Russia, was deposed by the Seven Boyars, a group of noblemen seeking stability in the nation. This event marked a significant shift in Russian leadership during a tumultuous period.

image.caption: Reproduction by Władysław Bartynowski of Tomasz Makowski’s engraving after a painting by Tomasz Dolabella, depicting Vasili IV before King Sigismund III.
image.credit: Tomasz Makowski — National Library of Poland
image.date_qualification: The supplied image date is 1613; the event is dated 27 July 1610, so this is a later depiction, not an image made at the event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Vasili Ivanovich Shuisky deposed

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Jülich commenced as a combined force from the Dutch Republic, the Kingdom of France, and the Margraviate of Brandenburg laid siege to the walled city. This conflict was part of the larger War of the Jülich Succession.

image.caption: Retrospective illustration of the siege and capture of Jülich by Maurice of Orange.
image.date_qualification: The image is dated 1649, 39 years after the 1610 siege; it is not a contemporary event photograph.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Siege of Jülich begins

events.enhanced_description: Henry Hudson sailed into what is now known as Hudson Bay, mistakenly believing he had found a passage to the Pacific Ocean. This exploration was significant in the search for the Northwest Passage and contributed to European knowledge of North America.
events.name: Henry Hudson enters Hudson Bay

events.enhanced_description: During the Anglo-Powhatan Wars, the English launched a major attack on the Paspahegh village, resulting in the capture and execution of the native queen and her children. This violent confrontation marked a significant escalation in hostilities between the settlers and the indigenous peoples.
events.name: Attack on Paspahegh village

events.enhanced_description: Claudio Monteverdi's musical work, Vespro della Beata Vergine (Vespers for the Blessed Virgin), was first published in Venice and dedicated to Pope Paul V. This work is considered a landmark in the development of Baroque music.
events.name: Publication of Monteverdi's Vespers

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Jülich concluded with the surrender of the Holy Roman Imperial city to Maurice of Nassau, commander of the Dutch Republic troops. This event marked a significant victory in the War of the Jülich Succession.
events.name: Siege of Jülich ends

events.enhanced_description: King Anaukpetlun of Burma successfully retook the Kingdom of Toungoo as rebel leader Natshinnaung surrendered the city of Taungoo. This event was part of the larger struggle for control in Burma during the early 17th century.
events.name: Retaking of the Kingdom of Toungoo

events.enhanced_description: The Seven Boyars voted to have King Wladyslaw IV of Poland recognized as Tsar Vladislav of Russia, inviting the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth to take control of the city. This decision reflected the political instability in Russia during this period.
events.name: Vote for King Wladyslaw IV of Poland as Tsar

events.enhanced_description: Frederick V, at the young age of 14, became the new Prince-Elector of the Rhineland Palatinate following the death of his father, Frederick IV. His ascension marked a significant moment in the political landscape of the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Frederick V becomes Prince-Elector

events.enhanced_description: Forces of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth captured Moscow, beginning their occupation of the Kremlin for the next two years. This event was a critical moment in the Polish-Russian War, significantly impacting the region's power dynamics.
events.name: Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth captures Moscow

events.enhanced_description: Under the command of Hetman Stanisław Żółkiewski, Polish forces took control of the Kremlin during the Polish-Russian War. This occupation marked a significant shift in power and influence in Eastern Europe.
events.name: Poland takes control of the Kremlin

events.enhanced_description: The coronation of Louis XIII of France took place, marking the formal beginning of his reign. This event was significant in the context of French monarchy and the political landscape of Europe.
events.name: Coronation of Louis XIII of France

events.enhanced_description: The War of the Jülich Succession concluded as the Protestant Union and the Catholic League agreed to withdraw their forces from Germany and disband them by the year's end. This resolution marked a significant moment in the religious and political conflicts of the time.
events.name: End of the War of the Jülich Succession

events.enhanced_description: After the Parliament of England provided King James I with only £100,000 of the agreed £600,000 in debt relief, the King demanded the remaining funds. This led to outrage in Parliament and the abandonment of the Great Contract.
events.name: King James demands debt relief funds

events.enhanced_description: The Basque witch trials came to an end after nearly two years, with only six individuals condemned to execution out of approximately 7,000 accused. This event highlighted the intense fear and hysteria surrounding witchcraft in early 17th-century Spain.
events.name: End of the Basque witch trials

events.enhanced_description: The cession of Larache, a port city in Morocco, took place as Sultan Mohammed esh Sheikh el Mamun transferred control of the city to Spain in exchange for military support against his brother. This agreement marked a significant moment in Spanish-Moroccan relations.
events.name: Cession of Larache to Spain

events.enhanced_description: On November 26, 1610, French astronomers Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc and Joseph Gaultier made the first detailed observations of the Orion Nebula, significantly advancing the field of astronomy and enhancing the understanding of celestial phenomena.
events.name: First detailed observations of the Orion Nebula

events.enhanced_description: On December 8, 1610 (Old Style), English astronomer Thomas Harriot became the first person to observe sunspots through a telescope, marking a pivotal moment in the study of solar phenomena.
events.name: First observation of sunspots through a telescope

events.enhanced_description: On December 19, 1610, Pieter Both was appointed as the first Governor-General of the Dutch East Indies, overseeing Dutch colonial interests in the region and establishing a foundation for future governance.
events.name: Pieter Both becomes first Governor-General of the Dutch East Indies

events.enhanced_description: On December 20, 1610, John Roberts, a Benedictine monk, was executed for high treason in Wales, a victim of the anti-Catholic sentiments of the time. He would later be canonized as a saint in 1970.

image.caption: A portrait depicting Saint John Roberts O.S.B.
image.date_qualification: Portrait of Saint John Roberts O.S.B., not a depiction of his execution. The portrait creation date is not established by the saved evidence.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Execution of John Roberts

events.enhanced_description: On December 21, 1610, the second False Dmitry was assassinated by Peter Urusov, a Tatar prince, in Moscow. This event marked a significant moment in the Time of Troubles, a period of political instability in Russia.
events.name: Assassination of the second False Dmitry

events.enhanced_description: The Aix-en-Provence possessions in 1611 were a series of alleged cases of demonic possession that sparked significant public interest and fear in the region. These events reflect the intersection of religion, superstition, and societal response in early modern France.
events.name: Aix-en-Provence possessions

events.enhanced_description: John Rolfe made a significant agricultural contribution to Jamestown by importing tobacco seeds from Trinidad. This introduction of Nicotiana tabacum would later transform the economy of the Virginia colony.
events.name: John Rolfe imports tobacco

events.enhanced_description: Thomas Dale founded the city of Henricus on the James River, establishing a new settlement with the assistance of 350 men. This settlement was part of the broader efforts to strengthen the English presence in Virginia.
events.name: Founding of Henricus

events.enhanced_description: In 1789, Ethiopia experienced a severe famine that affected large portions of the population. This famine was a result of various factors, including drought and political instability, leading to widespread suffering and hardship.
events.name: Famine in Ethiopia

events.enhanced_description: Construction began on Naqsh-e Jahan Square in Isfahan, Persia, which would become one of the largest public squares in the world and a masterpiece of Persian architecture. This project was part of the Safavid dynasty's efforts to enhance the city's grandeur.
events.name: Construction of Naqsh-e Jahan Square

events.enhanced_description: Itoh Gofuku was founded in Nagoya, Japan, marking the beginning of a significant retail establishment that would evolve into the well-known Matsuzakaya department store. This store specialized in silk, reflecting the region's rich textile heritage.

image.caption: Exterior of the South Building of Matsuzakaya Nagoya store.
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2015-10-24; this is a later site image, not a depiction of the 1611 foundation.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Foundation of Itoh Gofuku

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1611, Maximilien de Béthune, Duke of Sully, was forced to resign as chief minister of France by Queen regent Marie de' Medici's Regency Council, marking a significant shift in French politics.
events.name: Resignation of Maximilien de Béthune

events.enhanced_description: On February 27, 1611, Frisian astronomers Johannes and David Fabricius observed sunspots through a telescope, contributing to the early understanding of solar activity, although their findings were initially overlooked.
events.name: Sunspots observed by Johannes and David Fabricius

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1611, George Abbot was enthroned as the Archbishop of Canterbury, a pivotal role in the Church of England during a time of religious transformation.
events.name: George Abbot enthroned as Archbishop of Canterbury

events.enhanced_description: On March 9, 1611, the Battle of Segaba took place in Begemder, where Yemana Kristos, brother of Emperor Susenyos I, successfully quelled a rebellion led by Melka Sedeq, solidifying the emperor's power.
events.name: Battle of Segaba

events.enhanced_description: On March 19, 1611, the Moscow Uprising erupted against the Polish-Lithuanian occupation, resulting in a devastating fire and the deaths of thousands of Muscovites, highlighting the city's resistance to foreign rule.
events.name: Moscow Uprising

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1611, Denmark-Norway declared war on Sweden, leading to the capture of Kalmar, a strategic city, and escalating tensions in the region during the Northern Wars.

image.caption: A map of Kalmar by P.O. Hallman.
image.date_qualification: Map of Kalmar dated 1906, centuries after the 1611 declaration of war; it provides geographic context, not a depiction of the event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Denmark-Norway declares war on Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1611, False Dmitry III, claiming to be the son of Ivan the Terrible, arrived in Ivangorod and proclaimed himself Tsar Dmitry Ivanovich I, further complicating the political landscape of Russia during the Time of Troubles.
events.name: False Dmitry III proclaims himself Tsar

events.enhanced_description: On April 28, 1611, the Colegio de Nuestra Señora del Santísimo Rosario was established in Manila, which would later become the University of Santo Tomas, a significant institution in Philippine education.
events.name: Establishment of Colegio de Nuestra Señora del Santísimo Rosario

events.enhanced_description: On April 30, 1611, a priest implicated in the Aix-en-Provence possessions was executed, highlighting the tensions surrounding religious beliefs and practices in France during this period.
events.name: Execution of priest involved in Aix-en-Provence possessions

events.enhanced_description: On May 2, 1611, the Authorized King James Version of the Bible was published for the first time by Robert Barker in London, becoming one of the most significant translations in the English language.
events.name: Publication of the King James Version of the Bible

events.enhanced_description: On May 9, 1611, at the age of 16, Emperor Go-Mizunoo succeeded his father, Emperor Go-Yōzei, as the Emperor of Japan, marking a new chapter in the imperial lineage.
events.name: Emperor Go-Mizunoo succeeds his father

events.enhanced_description: On May 11, 1611, the first known performance of William Shakespeare's play The Winter's Tale took place at the Globe Theatre in London, contributing to the rich tapestry of English literature and theatre.
events.name: First performance of The Winter's Tale

events.enhanced_description: Between May and December 1611, entrepreneur Thomas Sutton founded Charterhouse School on the site of an old Carthusian monastery in Charterhouse Square, London, establishing a prestigious educational institution.
events.name: Foundation of Charterhouse School

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1611, the Siege of Smolensk concluded successfully for the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth after nearly two years of conflict, marking a significant victory in the struggle for control over Russia.
events.name: Siege of Smolensk

events.enhanced_description: In a dramatic turn of events, English explorer Henry Hudson, along with his son John and seven crewmen, were set adrift in Hudson Bay following a mutiny aboard the ship Discovery. This incident marked the end of Hudson's exploration efforts, and he and his crew were never seen again.
events.name: Henry Hudson set adrift

events.enhanced_description: The Perpetual Edict was proclaimed by Archduke Albert VII and his wife Isabella, marking a significant step in the governance of the Southern Netherlands, which was under Austrian control. This edict aimed to stabilize the region amidst ongoing conflicts.
events.name: Proclamation of the Perpetual Edict

events.enhanced_description: The Swedish Empire's army, led by Jacob De la Gardie, successfully captured the city of Novgorod after a nine-day battle, marking a pivotal moment in the struggle for control over the region. Novgorod would remain under Swedish control for the next eight years.
events.name: Capture of Novgorod

events.enhanced_description: Sir Thomas Gates returned to Jamestown, Virginia, with 280 settlers, provisions, and cattle, taking charge of the colony's governance. He emphasized the need to strengthen the fortifications to ensure the safety and survival of the settlement.
events.name: Sir Thomas Gates returns to Virginia

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of Kuyucu Murad Pasha, Nasuh Pasha was appointed as the new Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire, taking on a crucial leadership role during a period of significant political challenges.
events.name: Nasuh Pasha becomes Grand Vizier

events.enhanced_description: Greek Orthodox bishop Dionysios Skylosophos led a surprise attack on the city of Yanya, aiming to liberate it from Ottoman rule. Despite initial success, the Ottoman forces, commanded by Aslan Pasha, ultimately defeated the rebels, leading to Skylosophos's capture and execution.
events.name: Attack on Yanya

events.enhanced_description: At just 16 years old, Gustav II Adolf ascended to the throne as King of Sweden, following the death of his father, Charles IX. His reign would later be marked by significant military and political developments in Europe.
events.name: Gustav II Adolf becomes King of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: William Shakespeare's last solo play, The Tempest, was performed for the first time at Whitehall Palace in London. This play is often regarded as one of his most significant works, exploring themes of magic, betrayal, and redemption.
events.name: First performance of The Tempest

events.enhanced_description: The week-long Conquest of Bakla culminated in the fall of the Chandradwip kingdom, leading to the Mughal annexation of Barisal into the Bengal Subah. This event marked a significant expansion of Mughal influence in the region.
events.name: Conquest of Bakla

events.enhanced_description: The Sanriku earthquake, measuring 8.1 on the Richter scale, struck off the coast of Japan, triggering a devastating tsunami that resulted in the deaths of nearly 5,000 people in northern Honshu. This disaster highlighted the region's vulnerability to seismic activity.
events.name: Sanriku earthquake

events.enhanced_description: During a celebratory banquet hosted by Mubariz Khan, commander of the Mughal Empire Army, news arrives that Pashtun rebel leader Khwaja Usman and his men have evacuated Bokainagar. This event underscores the ongoing tensions and conflicts within the Mughal Empire.
events.name: Mubariz Khan's banquet

events.enhanced_description: In 1612, Nagoya Castle was completed in Japan, serving as a symbol of power for the Tokugawa shogunate. The castle's architecture and design reflect the era's military and cultural significance.
events.name: Completion of Nagoya Castle

events.enhanced_description: The Okamoto Daihachi incident occurred in 1612 in Japan, involving a significant event in the context of Japanese history. Details about the incident are limited, but it reflects the complexities of the period.
events.name: Okamoto Daihachi incident

events.enhanced_description: In 1612, Thomas Shelton published the first English translation of the first half of Miguel de Cervantes' 'Don Quixote', making it the first translation of this seminal Spanish novel into any language. This translation played a crucial role in introducing Spanish literature to the English-speaking world.
events.name: Translation of Don Quixote

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1612, Edward Wightman, a radical Anabaptist, was executed by burning at the stake in Lichfield, marking the last known execution for heresy in England. His execution reflected the intense religious conflicts of the time, particularly against dissenting Protestant sects.
events.name: Edward Wightman burned at the stake

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1612, Prince Khurram, the son of Mughal Emperor Jahangir, married Arjumand Banu Begum in a grand ceremony in Delhi. This union would later lead to Khurram ascending the throne as Shah Jahan, who commissioned the Taj Mahal in memory of his beloved wife.
events.name: Marriage of Prince Khurram and Arjumand Banu Begum

events.enhanced_description: On May 25, 1612, a Sicilian-Spanish galley fleet achieved a significant victory against Tunisian forces at La Goulette. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts in the Mediterranean, showcasing the naval power of the Spanish Empire.
events.name: Battle of La Goulette

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1612, Archduke Matthias of Austria was formally elected as the Holy Roman Emperor. His reign marked a significant period in the Habsburg dynasty, influencing the political landscape of Europe.
events.name: Election of Archduke Matthias as Holy Roman Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On June 26, 1612, Matthias was crowned Holy Roman Emperor in a ceremony held at the Frankfurt Cathedral. This event solidified his authority and marked the continuation of Habsburg influence in European politics.
events.name: Coronation of Matthias as Holy Roman Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1612, Min Khamaung ascended to the throne as the new King of Arakan following the death of his father, King Min Razagyi. His reign would be marked by the challenges of maintaining sovereignty in a region influenced by larger empires.
events.name: Min Khamaung becomes King of Arakan

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1612, four women and one man were hanged in Northamptonshire following the infamous witch trials. This event was part of the broader witch hunt phenomenon that swept through Europe during this period.
events.name: Northamptonshire witch trials

events.enhanced_description: On July 24, 1612, Marcantonio Memmo was elected as the Doge of the Republic of Venice, winning 38 out of 41 votes in the Venetian council. His election followed the death of the previous Doge, Leonardo Donato.
events.name: Election of Marcantonio Memmo as Doge of Venice

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1612, ten individuals known as the Pendle witches were hanged after being found guilty of practicing witchcraft in Lancashire. This event is one of the most famous witch trials in English history.
events.name: Pendle witch trials

events.enhanced_description: On August 26, 1612, the Battle of Kringen took place, resulting in the destruction of a Scottish mercenary force in Norway. This battle highlighted the conflicts involving mercenaries during the early 17th century.
events.name: Battle of Kringen

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1612, the Battle of Moscow occurred, where a relief force from the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, led by General Jan Karol Chodkiewicz, attempted to break the Russian siege of the Kremlin. The battle ended in heavy casualties for both sides, with the Russians ultimately prevailing.
events.name: Battle of Moscow (1612)

events.enhanced_description: On September 2, 1612, the Lutheran Duchy of Prussia became the first Protestant government to adopt the Gregorian calendar, aligning itself with Roman Catholic nations. This decision marked a significant shift in the region's approach to timekeeping.
events.name: Adoption of the Gregorian calendar by Prussia

events.enhanced_description: On September 5, 1612, the East India Company established the 'Honourable East India Company's Marine' to protect its freighters, marking the beginning of naval operations that would evolve into the Royal Indian Navy. This development was crucial for the company's maritime trade.
events.name: Establishment of the Honourable East India Company's Marine

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1612, retreating Polish and Lithuanian troops burned the city of Vologda in retaliation for their defeat at the Battle of Moscow. This act of destruction was part of the larger conflict between the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and Russia.
events.name: Burning of Vologda

events.enhanced_description: On October 27, 1612, the forces of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth surrendered unconditionally to Russian militia after being besieged in Moscow for over two years. This marked a pivotal moment in the struggle for control of the Russian capital.
events.name: Surrender of Polish-Lithuanian forces in Moscow

events.enhanced_description: On November 20, 1612, the Treaty of Nasuh Pasha was signed between the Ottoman Empire and the Safavid Empire, resulting in the Ottomans ceding territories captured after 1555 in exchange for a payment of silk. This treaty was significant in the ongoing territorial disputes between the two empires.
events.name: Treaty of Nasuh Pasha

events.enhanced_description: On November 30, 1612, the Battle of Swally took place off the coast of India, where forces of the British East India Company engaged Portuguese naval forces, resulting in a decisive English victory. This battle marked a significant step in establishing British dominance in Indian waters.
events.name: Battle of Swally

events.enhanced_description: On December 15, 1612, Simon Marius became the first person to observe the Andromeda Galaxy through a telescope, marking a significant milestone in astronomical studies. His observations contributed to the understanding of the universe beyond the Milky Way.
events.name: First observation of the Andromeda Galaxy

events.enhanced_description: On December 28, 1612, Galileo Galilei observed the planet Neptune during its conjunction with Jupiter, mistakenly cataloging it as a fixed star due to its slow motion. This observation, while not recognized as a planet until later, was a crucial step in the history of astronomy.
events.name: Galileo observes Neptune

events.enhanced_description: The ruler of the principality of Martaban, Binnya Dala, surrendered to the armies of King Anaukpetlun of Burma, marking a significant consolidation of power for the Burmese king during his campaign against Portuguese and local rivals.
events.name: Surrender of Binnya Dala

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1613, the Date Maru, a Japanese ship carrying a diplomatic mission led by Hasekura Tsunenaga, sighted Cape Mendocino on the California coast. This event marked one of the earliest known contacts between Japan and North America, highlighting the expanding global interactions of the early 17th century.
events.name: Date Maru reaches North America

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1613, the Earl of Somerset married Frances Howard, following the annulment of her previous marriage to Robert Devereux, 3rd Earl of Essex. This marriage was notable not only for its political implications but also inspired John Donne's Eclogue, reflecting the intertwining of personal and public life in the early 17th century.
events.name: Earl of Somerset marries Frances Howard

events.enhanced_description: In 1613, a devastating locust swarm struck La Camarque in France, causing widespread destruction to crops and impacting the local economy. This event was part of a series of natural disasters that plagued Europe during this period, highlighting the vulnerability of agrarian societies to environmental changes.
events.name: Locust swarm destroys La Camarque, France

events.enhanced_description: In 1613, Kuwait City was founded, marking the beginning of what would become a significant urban center in the Arabian Peninsula. Its strategic location along trade routes contributed to its growth and development in the centuries that followed.
events.name: Kuwait City is founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1613, Sultan Agung ascended to the throne of the Kingdom of Mataram in Java, Indonesia. His reign is noted for significant military campaigns and efforts to consolidate power, which would shape the political landscape of Java for decades.

locations.name: Yogyakarta, Special Region of Yogyakarta, Indonesia

events.name: Sultan Agung of Mataram takes the throne

events.enhanced_description: In 1613, Sir Thomas Dale initiated the settlement of Bermuda City near Jamestown, Virginia, which would later evolve into part of Hopewell. This settlement was part of the broader colonial expansion efforts in North America during the early 17th century.
events.name: Bermuda City settlement near Jamestown

events.enhanced_description: On January 11, 1613, workers in a sandpit in the Dauphiné region of France discovered a skeleton alleged to belong to a 30-foot tall man, thought to be the remains of the legendary Gallic king Teutobochus. This discovery sparked interest and speculation about prehistoric giants.
events.name: Discovery of giant skeleton in France

events.enhanced_description: On January 20, 1613, King James I of England successfully mediated the Treaty of Knäred between Denmark and Sweden, helping to resolve conflicts between the two nations. This treaty was significant in the context of Northern European politics.
events.name: Treaty of Knäred

events.enhanced_description: On February 14, 1613, Elizabeth, the daughter of King James I of England, married Frederick V, Elector Palatine, in a politically significant union that aimed to strengthen Protestant alliances in Europe. This marriage would have lasting implications for the Thirty Years' War.
events.name: Marriage of Elizabeth Stuart and Frederick V

events.enhanced_description: In a strategic military maneuver, King Anaukpetlun of Burma blockaded the Portuguese port of Syriam with a formidable fleet of 80 warships and 3,000 men. His efforts aimed to undermine Portuguese colonial power in the region, showcasing the growing strength of the Burmese kingdom.
events.name: King Anaukpetlun of Burma blockades the Portuguese port at Syriam

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1613, an assembly of the Russian Empire elected Mikhail Romanov as Tsar, marking the end of the tumultuous Time of Troubles. His ascension initiated the Romanov dynasty, which would rule Russia for over 300 years.
events.name: Election of Mikhail Romanov as Tsar of Russia

events.enhanced_description: The first English child born in Canada, to Nicholas Guy, marked a significant moment in the early colonial history of Newfoundland. This event symbolized the establishment of English presence in North America.

locations.name: Cuper's Cove, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada

events.name: Birth of the first English child in Canada

events.enhanced_description: Explorer Samuel de Champlain was appointed as the first unofficial Governor of New France, a pivotal role that would shape the future of French colonization in North America. His leadership and explorations laid the groundwork for the expansion of French influence in the region.
events.name: Samuel de Champlain becomes Governor of New France

events.enhanced_description: Burmese soldiers successfully breached the walls of the Portuguese colonial fortress at Syriam, leading to the sacking of the city. The Portuguese Governor Filipe de Brito e Nicote and rebel Burmese General Natshinnaung were captured and executed, marking a significant victory for the Burmese forces.
events.name: Burmese soldiers sack Syriam

events.enhanced_description: In a controversial act, Englishman Samuel Argall captured the Algonquian princess Pocahontas in Passapatanzy, Virginia, intending to ransom her for English prisoners held by her father, Chief Powhatan. This event would have lasting implications for relations between Native Americans and English settlers.
events.name: Capture of Pocahontas

events.enhanced_description: Following his election as Tsar, Mikhail Romanov arrived in Moscow on May 12, 1613, to officially begin his reign. His leadership would stabilize Russia after years of turmoil and set the stage for the Romanov dynasty's long rule.
events.name: Mikhail Romanov arrives in Moscow

events.enhanced_description: King Anaukpetlun restored Hanthawaddy as the capital of Burma, relocating the government from Ava. This move was part of his broader efforts to consolidate power and strengthen the Burmese kingdom.
events.name: Hanthawaddy restored as capital of Burma

events.enhanced_description: During the War of the Montferrat Succession, the defenders of Nizza Monferrato successfully repelled a nine-day siege by the troops of Charles Emmanuel I, Duke of Savoy. This victory was significant in maintaining the independence of the city amidst regional conflicts.
events.name: Siege of Nizza Monferrato

events.enhanced_description: After receiving official recognition as the French Governor of New France, Samuel de Champlain embarked on an exploration westward from Quebec along the Ottawa River. This journey was crucial for establishing French claims and understanding the geography of North America.
events.name: Samuel de Champlain's exploration along the Ottawa River

events.enhanced_description: On June 28, 1613, John Rolfe made the first shipment of Virginia-grown tobacco to England aboard the ship The Elizabeth. This marked the beginning of tobacco's significance as a cash crop in the American colonies and its impact on transatlantic trade.
events.name: First shipment of Virginia tobacco to England

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1613, a fire broke out during a performance of Shakespeare's Henry VIII, leading to the destruction of London's famed Globe Theatre. This incident marked a significant moment in the history of English theatre.

image.caption: Preliminary sketch of the second Globe Theatre by Wenceslaus Hollar.
image.date_qualification: Depicts the second Globe Theatre in 1647, after the 1613 fire; not contemporary documentation of the event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Fire destroys the Globe Theatre

events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1613, the first American-grown tobacco, produced in the British colony of Virginia, arrived in England. This shipment further established tobacco as a lucrative export and a key component of colonial economy.
events.name: First American-grown tobacco arrives in England

events.enhanced_description: Diego Marín de Negron, the Spanish Governor of Rio de la Plata y Paraguay, was assassinated by poisoning at his palace in Buenos Aires on July 26, 1613. His death highlighted the political instability and power struggles within the Spanish colonial administration.
events.name: Assassination of Diego Marín de Negron

events.enhanced_description: On July 28, 1613, Gregor Richter, the chief pastor of Görlitz, publicly denounced Jacob Boehme as a heretic during his Sunday sermon. This event underscored the tensions between emerging philosophical ideas and established religious doctrines of the time.
events.name: Gregor Richter denounces Jacob Boehme

events.enhanced_description: On August 29, 1613, Sicilian forces under de Aragon defeated the trade fleet of the Ottoman Empire, concluding the Battle of Cape Corvo. This victory was significant in asserting Sicilian naval power against Ottoman expansion in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Battle of Cape Corvo

events.enhanced_description: On September 29, 1613, the New River was officially opened, providing London with a new source of drinking water from Hertfordshire. This engineering feat was crucial for improving public health and sanitation in the growing city.
events.name: Opening of the New River

events.enhanced_description: On October 21, 1613, Gabriel Bathory was removed from office by a vote of the nobles meeting at Gyulafehérvár (now Alba Iulia). His refusal to vacate the palace led to his murder shortly thereafter, highlighting the volatile political landscape of Transylvania.
events.name: Removal of Gabriel Bathory from office

events.enhanced_description: On October 23, 1613, Gabriel Bethlen was elected as the new Prince of Transylvania, following the tumultuous removal of Gabriel Bathory. His election marked a new chapter in the region's governance and political alliances.

image.caption: Portrait painting of Gábor Iktári Bethlen, prince of Transylvania.
image.credit: Unidentified painter — originally uploaded to pl.wikipedia by Tompot ( talk · contribs ) on 26 November 2005, 16:59 under the file name Gabor Bethlen-Hungary National Musem.jpg . ( +/− )
image.date_qualification: A portrait of Bethlen, not a depiction of his 1613 election. The supplied image date identifies the painting as 17th century, with a stated date of 1650; supported display date is unavailable.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Election of Gabriel Bethlen as Prince of Transylvania

events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1613, Hasekura Tsunenaga departed Japan in the Date Maru, leading a diplomatic mission to the Holy See. This journey aimed to establish trade relations between Japan and the East India Company, reflecting the era's global maritime ambitions.

image.caption: A historic letter from the Japanese embassy to Spain, sent by Date Masamune and kept in Seville Town Hall.
image.credit: See below — Photo by E Asterion u talking to me? 00:24, 28 August 2006 (UTC). Transferred from en.wikipedia to Commons by Clpo13 using MTC! .
image.date_qualification: A document associated with the Keichō Embassy, not a depiction of its departure from Japan. The original image date is described as early 17th century; no supported display date is available.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 2.5; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 2.5; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Keichō embassy departs Japan

events.enhanced_description: On November 3, 1613, Robert Carr was created the 1st Earl of Somerset, reflecting his close relationship with King James I. This title marked a significant elevation in his status within the English court.
events.name: Creation of Robert Carr as 1st Earl of Somerset

events.enhanced_description: On November 30, 1613, King Anaukpetlun of Burma dispatched an army of 4,000 troops to expel Siamese occupiers from the Tenasserim coast. This military action was part of his broader campaign to reclaim and consolidate Burmese territories.
events.name: King Anaukpetlun sends troops to Tenasserim

events.enhanced_description: On December 26, 1613, the Burmese Army achieved a significant victory over the Siamese Army at Tavoy, a strategic location in present-day Myanmar. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts between the Kingdom of Burma and the Kingdom of Siam, which shaped the regional power dynamics in Southeast Asia.
events.name: Burmese Army defeats the Siamese Army at Tavoy

events.enhanced_description: On December 27, 1613, Mateo Leal de Ayala was appointed as the new Governor of Rio de la Plata y Paraguay, succeeding Diego Marín de Negron, who had been poisoned earlier that year. This appointment marked a significant moment in the colonial administration of the region, which would later evolve into modern-day Argentina, Paraguay, and parts of Chile.

locations.historical_name: Rio de la Plata y Paraguay
locations.name: Buenos Aires, Argentina

events.name: Mateo Leal de Ayala becomes Governor of Rio de la Plata y Paraguay

events.enhanced_description: In 1614, Pocahontas, the daughter of Chief Wahunsenacawh of the Powhatan tribe, was forced into marriage with English colonist John Rolfe in Jamestown, Virginia. This marriage symbolized the complex interactions between Native Americans and English settlers during the colonial period.
events.name: Pocahontas marries John Rolfe

events.enhanced_description: In 1614, the Addled Parliament was convened in England as the second parliament of King James I, marking the first parliamentary session in over nine years. The assembly lasted only two months and failed to pass any laws, reflecting the political discontent of the time.
events.name: The Addled Parliament is assembled

events.enhanced_description: In 1614, the Republic of the Netherlands and the Kingdom of Sweden entered into a treaty in The Hague, marking a significant diplomatic relationship between the two nations during the Thirty Years' War. This treaty laid the groundwork for future cooperation and trade.
events.name: Treaty between the Republic of the Netherlands and the Kingdom of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: In 1614, Scottish mathematician John Napier published 'Mirifici Logarithmorum Canonis Descriptio', which outlined his groundbreaking discovery of logarithms and introduced the decimal mark. This work significantly influenced mathematics and astronomy, paving the way for future developments.
events.name: Publication of Mirifici Logarithmorum Canonis Descriptio

events.enhanced_description: In 1614, Tisquantum, a member of the Wampanoag Nation, was kidnapped by English sea captain Thomas Hunt. After being enslaved and later freed, Tisquantum returned to Plymouth, Massachusetts, where he would play a crucial role in assisting the Pilgrims with agriculture and trade.
events.name: Kidnapping of Tisquantum

events.enhanced_description: The 'Fama Fraternitatis', the first of three allegorical Rosicrucian manifestoes, was published in 1614 within the Holy Roman Empire. This publication sparked interest in Rosicrucianism and influenced various philosophical and esoteric movements.
events.name: Publication of the Fama Fraternitatis

events.enhanced_description: In 1614, the play 'The Duchess of Malfi' by John Webster was performed at the Globe Theatre in London. This tragic play has since become a classic of English literature, known for its exploration of themes such as power, corruption, and the human condition.
events.name: Performance of The Duchess of Malfi

events.enhanced_description: On January 22, 1614, Hasekura Tsunenaga led a Japanese trade expedition that arrived on the Mexican coast, marking a significant moment in Japan's early international relations. The expedition aimed to establish trade ties with New Spain and included a diverse group of samurai, merchants, and interpreters.
events.name: Hasekura Tsunenaga's trade expedition arrives in New Spain

events.enhanced_description: On January 27, 1614, the Noordsche Compagnie was established in the Netherlands at Vlieland as a cartel in the whaling market. This organization played a crucial role in the Dutch whaling industry, which was vital for the economy during the early 17th century.
events.name: Noordsche Compagnie founded

events.enhanced_description: On February 1, 1614, Japan issued an edict banning the practice of Christianity and ordering the expulsion of foreign missionaries. This marked a significant turning point in Japan's relationship with Christianity and foreign influence, leading to a period of isolation.
events.name: Christianity banned in Japan

events.enhanced_description: On February 2, 1614, Abbas the Great, the Safavid Emperor of Iran, executed his oldest son, Crown Prince Mohammad Baqer Mirza, amid suspicions of a conspiracy against him. This act exemplified the brutal power struggles within the Safavid dynasty and the lengths to which rulers would go to secure their thrones.
events.name: Abbas the Great executes Crown Prince Mohammad Baqer Mirza

events.enhanced_description: On February 14, 1614, King James I of England issued a proclamation aimed at curbing the practice of dueling, which had become a significant social issue. This proclamation reflected the king's efforts to maintain order and civility in a society marked by honor-based violence.
events.name: King James I issues proclamation Against Private Challenges

events.enhanced_description: On February 20, 1614, Matthias I, Holy Roman Emperor, directed the restoration of Roman Catholic rule in Aachen, allowing the Army of Flanders to lay siege to the town. This event was part of the larger context of religious and political conflicts in Europe during the Thirty Years' War.
events.name: Matthias I restores Catholic rule to Aachen

events.enhanced_description: On March 15, 1614, construction began on Takada Castle in Japan, which would serve as a significant military and administrative center in the region. The castle's architecture and strategic location reflected the feudal power dynamics of the time.
events.name: Construction begins on Takada Castle

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1614, the States General of the Republic of the Seven United Netherlands authorized the New Netherland Company to monopolize trade in the New World. This decision was pivotal in establishing Dutch colonial interests in North America.

image.caption: Adriaen Block’s map of his expedition to North America, showing Long Island and the term New Netherland.
image.credit: Adriaen Block — digitalized by the Dutch National Archive ( perm link )
image.date_qualification: Map from 1614, associated with Block’s expedition; it is contextual evidence for the company’s exploration and region, not a depiction of the States General’s authorization.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: States General authorizes New Netherland Company

events.enhanced_description: On May 14, 1614, an earthquake struck the Azores islands, leveling the village of Vila Franca do Campo. This natural disaster had a profound impact on the local population and economy, illustrating the geological volatility of the region.

locations.name: Vila Franca do Campo, Azores, Portugal

events.name: Earthquake strikes the Azores

events.enhanced_description: On May 15, 1614, Marie de' Medici, the Queen Regent of France, convened the Estates General to address a rebellion led by Henri II, Prince of Condé. This assembly was a crucial moment in the political landscape of France, reflecting the tensions between the monarchy and nobility.
events.name: Marie de' Medici convenes Estates General

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1614, the Battle of Rohatyn took place, where mutinous Polish troops known as the 'konfederacja' were defeated by the loyal Polish Army led by General Stanisław Koniecpolski. This battle was significant in maintaining the integrity of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth during a period of internal strife.
events.name: Battle of Rohatyn

events.enhanced_description: On June 7, 1614, King James I dissolved the Addled Parliament, which had failed to pass any legislation during its brief session. This event underscored the political tensions and challenges faced by the monarchy in governing England.
events.name: The Addled Parliament is dissolved

events.enhanced_description: On July 6, 1614, Ottoman forces launched a final raid on the island of Malta, specifically targeting the town of Żejtun. The Knights Hospitaller, under the leadership of Grand Master Alof de Wignacourt, successfully repelled the attack, preserving Maltese sovereignty.
events.name: Raid of Żejtun

events.enhanced_description: On July 16, 1614, Tsar Michael I ordered the public execution of Ivan Dmitriyevich, the three-year-old son of the False Dmitry, as a reprisal for the latter's claim to the Russian throne. This brutal act underscored the political tensions and power struggles of the Time of Troubles in Russia.
events.name: Execution of Ivan Dmitriyevich

events.enhanced_description: The University of Groningen was established on August 23, 1614, becoming one of the oldest universities in the Netherlands. It played a crucial role in the development of higher education and scholarship in the region.

image.caption: Coat of arms of Rijksuniversiteit Groningen.
image.credit: rode raaf — Hoge Raad van Adel
image.date_qualification: The image is dated 2018; it depicts the university’s coat of arms, not the 1614 founding event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False; Restrictions: insignia

events.name: Establishment of the University of Groningen

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Aachen began on August 24, 1614, when the Spanish Army of Flanders, commanded by Ambrogio Spinola, attacked the city with a force of 15,000 troops. The defense, consisting of only 600 men from Brandenburg, surrendered shortly after the siege commenced.

image.caption: Retrospective oil painting depicting the Siege of Aachen by Spinola’s Spanish Army of Flanders.
image.date_qualification: Depicted event: 1614; artwork date recorded as after 1614.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Siege of Aachen

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1614, Sir Julius Caesar was appointed as the Master of the Rolls in England, a significant position within the judicial system. His tenure contributed to the development of legal practices in early 17th-century England.
events.name: Sir Julius Caesar becomes Master of the Rolls

events.enhanced_description: On October 2, 1614, Louis XIII officially assumed full power as King of France at the age of 23, ending the regency of his mother, Marie de' Medici. Despite this transition, Marie retained significant influence over the French government.
events.name: Louis XIII assumes full power as King of France

events.enhanced_description: On October 11, 1614, explorer Adriaen Block and a group of Amsterdam merchants petitioned the States General of the Northern Netherlands for exclusive trading rights in the region he had explored and named 'New Netherland'. This petition marked a significant step in the Dutch colonization efforts in North America.
events.name: Adriaen Block petitions for trading rights in New Netherland

events.enhanced_description: The second War of the Jülich Succession, which had reignited earlier in the year, came to an end on October 13, 1614. This conflict involved various European powers and was pivotal in the territorial disputes of the time.

image.caption: Map of the Duchies of Jülich-Cleve-Berg.
image.credit: Ziegelbrenner — Own work /based on (1) & (2) /Source of Information: Putzger – Historischer Weltatlas, 89. Auflage, 1965; Westermanns Großer Atlas zur Weltgeschichte, 1969; Haacks geographischer Atlas. VEB Hermann Haack Geographisch-Kartographische Anstalt, Gotha/Leipzig, 1. Auflage, 1979; dtv-Atlas zur Weltgeschichte 1. Von den Anfängen bis zur Französischen Revolution; 23. Aufl. 1989, ISBN 3-423-03001-1 .
image.date_qualification: The map depicts the duchies during 1614–1672; it is not a contemporary photograph of the war’s end. The supplied image date is 2011-03-17.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: End of the second War of the Jülich Succession

events.enhanced_description: On October 17, 1614, Grand Vizier Nasuh Pasha was assassinated on the orders of Sultan Ahmed I, highlighting the volatile political landscape of the Ottoman Empire during this period. His death marked a significant shift in the power dynamics within the empire.
events.name: Assassination of Grand Vizier Nasuh Pasha

events.enhanced_description: The last session of the French Estates General began on October 27, 1614, with 464 deputies representing various social classes. This session would close on February 23, 1615, marking the end of a significant institution in French governance until the French Revolution.
events.name: Last session of the French Estates General

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Xanten was signed on November 12, 1614, effectively ending the War of the Jülich Succession. This treaty was crucial in stabilizing the region and resolving territorial disputes among the involved powers.
events.name: Treaty of Xanten

events.enhanced_description: On November 19, 1614, hostilities erupted as Toyotomi Hideyori attempted to restore Osaka Castle, prompting Tokugawa Ieyasu to mobilize his forces. This conflict marked a significant moment in the struggle for power in Japan during the early Edo period.
events.name: Hostilities over Osaka Castle

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Osaka began on December 4, 1614, as Tokugawa Ieyasu sought to eliminate the threat posed by Toyotomi Hideyori and his supporters. This siege was a pivotal moment in the consolidation of power by the Tokugawa shogunate.
events.name: Siege of Osaka

events.enhanced_description: In 1615, the New Netherland Company was granted a three-year monopoly on trade in North America, specifically between the 40th and 45th parallels. This monopoly was a significant step in the Dutch colonial expansion in the New World.
events.name: New Netherland Company granted monopoly

events.enhanced_description: During Easter in 1615, Persian Safavid forces led by Shah Abbas the Great attacked the David Gareja monastery complex in Georgia, killing all the monks and destroying invaluable manuscripts and artworks. This event exemplified the religious and cultural conflicts of the era.
events.name: Massacre at David Gareja

events.enhanced_description: In 1615, Mary Talbot, Countess of Shrewsbury, was released from the Tower of London in recognition of her role in uncovering the murder of Sir Thomas Overbury. Her release marked a significant moment in the political intrigues of the time.
events.name: Release of Mary Talbot from the Tower of London

events.enhanced_description: The Somers Isles Company was established to oversee the administration and development of Bermuda, which had been discovered by English explorer Sir George Somers. This company played a crucial role in the early colonial governance of Bermuda, facilitating settlement and economic activities.
events.name: The Somers Isles Company is founded to administer Bermuda

events.enhanced_description: In 1615, John Browne was appointed as the first King's Gunfounder in England, a position that underscored the importance of gun manufacturing in the context of national defense and military readiness during the early 17th century.
events.name: John Browne is created the first King's Gunfounder in England

events.enhanced_description: In 1615, Austrian merchants were granted significant economic privileges within the Ottoman Empire, marking a pivotal moment in the trade relations between the two powers. This agreement facilitated increased commerce and diplomatic ties, enhancing the economic landscape of the region.
events.name: Austrian merchants receive economic privileges in the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: The Perse School was founded in 1615 by Dr. Stephen Perse, establishing a legacy of academic excellence in Cambridge. The school has since become one of the leading independent schools in the UK, emphasizing a strong educational foundation.
events.name: The Perse School in Cambridge, England, is founded by Dr Stephen Perse

events.enhanced_description: Wilson's School was established in 1615 by Royal Charter, providing a structured educational environment in Wallington. The school has a rich history and continues to serve as a prominent educational institution in the area.

image.caption: Front entrance of Wilson’s School.
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2012-10-02; depicts the school site, not the 1615 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Wilson's School in Wallington, near London, is founded by Royal Charter

events.enhanced_description: The Grolsch Brewery was founded in 1615 in Groenlo, Netherlands, marking the beginning of a brewing tradition that would grow to become internationally recognized. Grolsch is known for its distinctive swing-top bottles and premium lagers.
events.name: The Grolsch Brewery is founded in Groenlo, Netherlands

events.enhanced_description: In 1615, Konoike Shinroku established an office in Osaka, initiating the shipment of tax-rice from western Japan. This move significantly impacted the rice trade and economic structure of the region, enhancing Osaka's role as a commercial hub.
events.name: Konoike Shinroku opens an office in Osaka, and begins shipping tax-rice from western Japan to Osaka

events.enhanced_description: In 1615, Johannes Kepler published 'Dissertatio cum Nuncio Sidereo', a significant work that responded to Galileo Galilei's discovery of Jupiter's moons. This publication contributed to the ongoing debate about heliocentrism and the nature of celestial bodies.
events.name: Johannes Kepler publishes Dissertatio cum Nuncio Sidereo, in response to Galileo's discovery of Jupiter's moons

events.enhanced_description: In 1615, Portuguese Jesuit missionary Manuel Dias introduced the telescope to China through his work 'Tian Wen Lü', marking a significant moment in the exchange of scientific knowledge between Europe and Asia.
events.name: Manuel Dias introduces the telescope for the first time in China

events.enhanced_description: In 1615, the second volume of Miguel de Cervantes's 'Don Quixote' was published, achieving similar acclaim as the first volume. This work solidified Cervantes's reputation as one of the greatest writers in the Spanish language and literature.

image.caption: Gustave Doré’s engraved illustration for Chapter I of Don Quixote, depicting a scene from the novel.
image.credit: Héliodore Pisan / After Gustave Doré — The History of Don Quixote , by Cervantes. The Text edited by J. W. Clark, M.A. (Sometime Fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge) and a Biographical Notice of Cervantes by T. Teignmouth Shore, M.A. Illustrated by Gustave Doré. In Two Parts. Part I. Cassell & Company, Limited, London, Paris, New York & Melbourne. All Rights Reserved. MCMVI
image.date_qualification: Retrospective illustration for the novel, originally published in 1863; the edition represented is from 1906. It is not an image of the 1615 publication event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The second volume of Miguel de Cervantes's Don Quixote is published

events.enhanced_description: On January 30, 1615, Japan's diplomatic mission, led by Hasekura Tsunenaga, met with King Philip III of Spain in Madrid. This meeting aimed to establish diplomatic relations and explore potential trade agreements between Japan and Spain.
events.name: Japan's diplomatic mission to Spain
